rule: Every paper first published in the listed journals during the window, newest first. Fields, tasks and named datasets are assigned from keyword patterns. Abstracts are shown for open-access or Creative Commons papers.

papers.title: GOntact: using chromatin contacts to infer target genes and Gene Ontology enrichments for cis-regulatory elements.
papers.authors: Laverré A, Tannier E, Veber P, Necsulea A.
papers.abstract: Cis -regulatory elements (CREs) can be efficiently predicted genome-wide, but identifying their target genes remains challenging. Regulatory interactions between genes and CREs can take place over long genomic distances, often bypassing genes. Inferring CRE targets based on genomic proximity, as traditionally done in genomic studies, can thus be misleading. Thanks to chromosome conformation capture techniques, chromatin contacts between CREs and gene promoters can be assayed at the genome-wide scale, thus permitting more accurate predictions of CRE target genes. Here, we present a standalone computational tool and webserver named GOntact, which infers CRE target genes using chromosome conformation capture data. GOntact can be used to derive Gene Ontology (GO) enrichments for CRE sets, thus providing a basis for functional interpretation. We apply GOntact on enhancers active in several embryonic tissues, using Promoter Capture Hi-C data to infer chromatin contacts between genes and CREs. We show that GOntact predicts functional annotations that are coherent with enhancer activity. Compared to genomic proximity, GOntact predicts consistent but more specific functional annotations. With the increasing availability of high-resolution chromatin contact data, we believe that GOntact can provide better-informed target genes and functional predictions for CREs. GOntact is available at https://gontact.univ-lyon1.fr (webserver) and https://gitlab.in2p3.fr/anamaria.necsulea/GOntact (standalone command-line tool).

papers.title: CLIPittyClip: a single-command framework for CLIP sequencing data analysis.
papers.authors: Yi S, Luna JM.
papers.abstract: Crosslinking immunoprecipitation (CLIP) sequencing is the standard method for mapping RNA-binding protein (RBP) binding sites transcriptome wide, yet most analysis pipelines are either modular toolkits requiring manual assembly or large-scale workflows built for consortium infrastructure. Here, we present CLIPittyClip, a single-command pipeline that processes CLIP data from raw FASTQ files to a peak matrix and crosslink site outputs, supports five major CLIP read architectures and runs entirely locally on standard laptop hardware. The pipeline introduces CLink, a Python reimplementation of CLIP Tool Kit crosslink-induced truncation and mutation site analyses that is up to 27-fold faster while recovering equivalent binding motifs and crosslink site resolution. Using CLIP data for a prototypical RBP, we performed systematic parameter sweeps for two peak callers to establish empirically calibrated defaults for the pipeline. We validated CLIPittyClip against published ELAVL1, HNRNPC, and RBFOX2 datasets spanning BrdU-CLIP, iCLIP, eCLIP, and PAR-CLIP architectures, and confirmed compatibility with downstream analyses for differential binding and motif analysis. CLIPittyClip provides a fast, local, and practical processing layer for CLIP data analysis in a single-lab setting and is freely available at https://github.com/LunaRNALab/CLIPittyClip.

papers.title: Genome-wide analysis of TMD-associated local ribosome accumulation reveals stress- and eS7-associated remodeling in Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
papers.authors: Li M.
papers.abstract: Local ribosome accumulation near transmembrane domains (TMDs) may report cotranslational events in membrane-protein biogenesis, but its spatial organization and stress responsiveness remain unclear. Saccharomyces cerevisiae ribosome-profiling data were reanalyzed using a replicate-aware, TMD-centered workflow. Two untreated wild-type baseline samples showed maximal accumulation approximately 75 nucleotides downstream of annotated TMD starts. At this position, 2896 TMDs met strict eight-sample coverage criteria; 2892 were testable using quasi-likelihood negative-binomial models of target-window counts relative to gene-wide non-TMD coding background. Forty-one TMDs showed an ER-stress effect in wild-type cells, six in eS7-4KR cells, and 22 showed a genotype-by-stress interaction at false discovery rate (FDR) < 0.05. Interaction-effect directions were concordant across models, but only eight of the 22 primary interactions met FDR < 0.05 in both target/background models; 16 remained significant after global correction across 11 positions. Baseline signals were heterogeneous. Aromatic-residue fraction remained associated with local accumulation in a prespecified joint model. Mean-based upper-tail topology associations weakened with one-TMD-per-protein resampling; continuous protein-level comparisons were nonsignificant. Functional enrichment was sensitive to the number of tested TMDs per gene and was treated as exploratory. These results identify spatially resolved, stress- and eS7-associated ribosome-occupancy differences without equating footprint enrichment with proven translational pausing.

papers.title: scMINA: an interpretable workflow for paired scRNA-scATAC multiome integration and regulatory prioritization.
papers.authors: Zhang S, Hu H, Wang X, Xiong C, Kanekiyo T, Asmann YW, Ren Y.
papers.abstract: Single-cell multiomic technologies that jointly profile transcriptomic and epigenomic states provide unprecedented opportunities to investigate cellular heterogeneity and gene regulatory mechanisms in complex diseases. However, analysis of paired single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) and chromatin accessibility (scATAC-seq) data remains computationally challenging due to modality-specific technical variation, integration complexity, and limited interpretability of downstream regulatory inference. Here, we present scMINA (single-cell Multimodal Integration and Network Attribution), a modular and interpretable analytical workflow for the analysis of paired single-cell multiome datasets. scMINA comprises coordinated modules for multimodal integration, technical covariate correction, and regulatory feature prioritization, enabling systematic characterization of cellular states across transcriptomic and epigenomic modalities. In addition, scMINA incorporates explainable artificial intelligence-based attribution strategies to prioritize candidate genes and transcription factors associated with cell-state heterogeneity and disease-related regulatory alterations. We applied scMINA to the single-cell multiome data from the Seattle Alzheimer's Disease Brain Cell Atlas, where the workflow robustly resolved major glial cell populations and identified regulatory features associated with Alzheimer's disease pathology. By coupling multimodal integration with interpretable regulatory prioritization, scMINA provides a practical workflow for systematic analysis and biological interpretation of paired scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq datasets.

papers.title: Early terminated transcripts and missing proteins reflect artifacts in bacterial proteomes.
papers.authors: Insana G, Martin MJ, Pearson WR.
papers.abstract: The high redundancy of many bacterial proteomes can be used to evaluate proteome quality and identify sequence errors. We have used MMseqs2 clustering with subsequent filtering to identify clusters that contain sequences from at least 50% of the clustered proteomes to build sets of core proteins that include proteins from 95% of the clustered bacteria. These clusters typically capture >80% of proteins in the bacteria. Because these clusters have highly uniform length (the median cluster has >99% of its proteins at the mode length), short ( 133%) proteins are likely artifacts. Most "outlier" proteins are found in fewer than 10% of clusters, and "high-outlier" clusters are over-represented in a small fraction of proteomes, which often have poor proteome BUSCO fragment scores. Short-outlier proteins are artifacts; at least 80% of short-outlier genomes contain mode-length copies of the protein, which were missed because of frameshifts, termination codons, or initiation codon choice. MMseqs2 clustering with 50% participation provides robust sets of core bacterial proteins and can be used to identify lower-quality proteomes and proteins.

papers.title: Ontologizer 3: a cross-platform desktop application for frequentist and Bayesian GO enrichment analysis.
papers.authors: Ramlow L, Scholtes J, Danis D, Robinson PN.
papers.abstract: We present Ontologizer 3, an easy-to-use cross-platform desktop application for Gene Ontology (GO) overrepresentation analysis. Ontologizer 3 offers two complementary methods. The first is a frequentist approach that evaluates GO terms individually using a one-sided Fisher's exact test, yielding term-level significance values. The second is a Bayesian approach that jointly evaluates terms using model-based gene set analysis (MGSA), yielding term-level posterior probabilities. Due to substantial overlap among annotated gene sets resulting from the GO's hierarchical structure, the two methods produce different results. The frequentist approach tends to report a lengthy list of terms with strong annotation overlap, whereas, MGSA yields a parsimonious set of terms that explain the observed gene activity. Using simulated data with a known ground truth, we demonstrate that both methods reliably identify the causal term, but MGSA achieves substantially higher precision. Ontologizer 3 is implemented as a Tauri application with a Rust backend and an Angular frontend, presenting enriched terms in tabular and graphical form. The software is freely available under the MIT licence at https://github.com/P2GX/ontologizer-gui. Installation packages for Macintosh, Windows, and Debian-based Linux are available on the GitHub Releases page.

papers.title: Rp-Bp and the Ribotools box for translatome profiling.
papers.authors: Boileau E, Bencun M, Tuorto F, Vries ISN, Fahjen P, Mertins P, Dieterich C.
papers.abstract: We present the Ribotools "box" for the analysis of matched ribosome profiling (Ribo-seq) and RNA sequencing data. Ribotools can be used in standalone mode or in combination with Rp-Bp for Ribo-seq quality control, open reading frames discovery, translation efficiency, and differential expression analyses. In this work, we use Ribotools to profile the differentiation of human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) into cardiomyocytes to reveal a remarkably coherent transition from plastic, signaling-driven to stable, structurally committed cardiac cells, staged through multiple layers of translational control. Together with complementary proteomics, the resulting dataset provides a rich multi-omics resource for investigating the hiPSC model of cardiac lineage commitment. Additionally, we present a reproducible and extensible pipeline for benchmarking translation efficiency analysis tools. Ribotools and Rp-Bp are available on Bioconda and help to make research accessible and reproducible. Detailed documentation, test datasets, and tutorials are available at https://ribotools.readthedocs.io and https://rp-bp.readthedocs.io.

papers.title: DirectClean: artifact-aware preprocessing and read rescue for Oxford Nanopore direct-cDNA transcriptome sequencing.
papers.authors: Guo Q, Li Y, Yang R.
papers.abstract: Oxford Nanopore direct-cDNA sequencing enables full-length transcriptome profiling without PCR amplification, but recurrent chimeric artifacts introduced during reverse transcription and library preparation can compromise isoform reconstruction and gene-fusion analysis. These include foldback inversions, aberrant primer configurations, internal adapter concatemers, and homopolymer-mediated template-switching events. Existing preprocessing strategies primarily address primer-based orientation and adapter detection, leaving several direct-cDNA-specific artifact classes unresolved and often discarding reads that still contain usable transcript sequence. We developed DirectClean, an artifact-aware preprocessing and read-rescue framework integrating strand orientation, artifact removal, and junction-level splitting of recoverable chimeric reads. Benchmarking across four direct-cDNA datasets showed consistently higher read and base retention with DirectClean than with Pychopper. In VCaP, DirectClean retained 65.2% of reads compared with 57.6% for Pychopper, supported additional transcripts, and reduced the chimeric read rate from 30.9% in raw data to 16.9%. Semi-synthetic validation demonstrated accurate rescue of adapter-associated and A/T-rich chimeric reads, and matched real-data analyses showed no enrichment of novel transcript models in split-derived reads relative to matched untouched reads. DirectClean provides a reproducible, openly available framework for artifact-aware preprocessing of direct-cDNA transcriptomes and improves the reliability of downstream isoform and fusion analyses.

papers.title: WasteFams: a database of protein families from global wastewater microbiomes.
papers.authors: Galaras A, Chasapi IN, Aplakidou E, Chasapi MN, Lamari E, Diplari S, Georgakopoulos-Soares I, Karatzas E, Baltoumas FA, Kyrpides NC, Pavlopoulos GA.
papers.abstract: Wastewater surveillance has emerged as a critical tool for global epidemiology, yet the functional diversity of wastewater microbiomes remains poorly characterized at the protein level. Here, we present WasteFams, the first comprehensive database dedicated to the systematic exploration of protein families in wastewater metagenomic and metatranscriptomic studies worldwide. Integrating data from 580 metagenomes, 132 metatranscriptomes, and 1709 reference genomes (504 metagenomes, 129 metatranscriptomes, and 1151 reference genomes after filtering), WasteFams catalogs 3887 non-redundant protein families (containing ⪰100 members) derived from over 105 million predicted proteins. Each protein family is enriched with multi-layered annotations, including AlphaFold3 structural predictions, taxonomic classifications, and biome-specific metadata. To further expand their functional annotation, we integrated deep genomic context analysis to link protein families to mobile genetic elements, biosynthetic gene clusters, antibiotic resistance genes, and CRISPR elements. Accessible through the EnvoFams portal, WasteFams provides a user-friendly interface featuring advanced search capabilities, sequence and structural similarity tools, and interactive visualization modules. As global initiatives increasingly leverage wastewater for public health and environmental insights, WasteFams can serve as a critical resource for discovering novel microbial functions, monitoring resistance mechanisms, and exploring the biotechnological potential of secondary metabolites within wastewater-engineered ecosystems.

papers.title: MAJIQ V3: Scalable and accurate RNA splicing analysis with splicegraph algebra and improved intron retention modeling.
papers.authors: Aicher JK, Slaff B, Jewell S, Gazzara MR, Bhoj EJK, Barash Y.
papers.abstract: RNA splicing plays important roles in cell-type-specific expression of gene isoforms and is causally linked to numerous diseases. Previously, our group developed Modeling Alternative Junction Inclusion Quantification (MAJIQ) V1 and V2 for RNA splicing detection, quantification, and visualization from RNA sequencing. Here we report an update, MAJIQ V3, that offers critical new functionality together with faster and more accurate quantification algorithms. MAJIQ V3 enables users to combine splicegraphs, quantify splicing from an RNA-seq experiment with respect to a splicegraph, and compare one splicegraph to another, enabling new patterns of performant RNA splicing analyses from RNA-seq. MAJIQ V3 utilizes a new probabilistic model for detecting intron retention, correcting a bias that resulted from previous heuristics. MAJIQ V3 benefits from a full re-implementation utilizing more performant I/O patterns, data structures, and algorithms. We demonstrate the benefits of MAJIQ V3 using GTEx and LRGASP data for different analysis scenarios involving different dataset sizes.

papers.title: ModCRElib: a standalone package to model cis-regulatory elements.
papers.authors: Gohl P, Fornes O, Bota PM, Meseguer A, Bonet J, Molina-Fernández R, Planas-Iglesias J, Hernández AC, Gallego O, Fernandez-Fuentes N, Oliva B.
papers.abstract: The ModCRElib package provides various tools for the analysis and modelling of transcription factor (TF)-DNA and regulatory complex inter-protein interactions. It takes structural information on these interactions to predict TF-binding motifs, generate binding profiles along DNA sequences that score the binding affinity, predict TF-binding sites, and model the structure of higher order regulatory complexes. It is capable of working with a variety of input data formats and sources. The user may follow the analysis pipeline as outlined in the documentation or the user can make use of any of the multiple functionalities in an isolated manner. The package takes the service offered by the ModCRE server and enables users to apply its tools in an unrestricted and customizable manner. In this paper we provide five example uses of ModCRElib. This includes (i) TF-binding affinity prediction, (ii) TF ensemble pattern of bindings (aggregation of motifs), (iii) characterization of specificity in TF-binding sites along target DNA sequences, (iv) modelling TF bound to predicted binding sites, and (v) the generation of statistical potential derived scoring profiles of TF interacting with DNA.

papers.title: Cell DiffErential Expression by Pooling (CellDEEP) highlights issues in differential gene expression in scRNA-seq.
papers.authors: Cheng Y, Kettlewell T, Laidlaw RF, Hardy OM, McCluskey A, Otto TD, Somma D.
papers.abstract: Accurate identification of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in single-cell RNA sequencing data remains challenging. Single-cell-specific statistical models often report large numbers of candidate genes but can exhibit inflated false positive rates, whereas pseudobulk approaches improve false discovery control at the cost of reduced sensitivity. To overcome the noise and bias that other tools have, and allow the user to have more control of the DEG process, we present CellDEEP, which uses a cell aggregation (metacell) approach. This tool provides a framework for flexible selection of pooling strategies and parameterization for differential expression analysis. Benchmarking on simulated and real datasets, including COVID-19 and rheumatoid arthritis, shows that CellDEEP often outperforms other methods, consistently reduces false positives compared to single-cell methods and recovers more true positives than pseudobulk methods. Our work shifts the focus from selecting a single 'best' method to an approach that reduces cell-level noise while preserving biological signal, together with transparent validation framework, advancing more reliable differential-expression analysis in single-cell transcriptomics.

papers.title: CAMELLIA: an alignment-free pipeline integrating k-mer feature selection and supervised classification for genomic sequence subtyping.
papers.authors: Saita TM, Pimenta-Zanon MH, de Queiroz ATL, Bressan GM, Lopes FM.
papers.abstract: Scalable analysis of biological sequences is essential for functional characterization, biomarker discovery, and therapeutic and vaccine development. Alignment-based pipelines often fail to capture intraspecific variation and become computationally limited on large datasets, while alignment-free methods treat each class as homogeneous, ignoring sample heterogeneity. We present CAMELLIA (Combining AlignMent-free fEature seLection cLassIficAtion), an alignment-free framework that combines feature selection with explainable machine learning for genomic sequence analysis and classification. CAMELLIA identifies subgroups within classes and ensures underrepresented subgroups are captured by the selected features, yielding a more accurate and scalable data-driven representation. Sequences are represented as graphs, from which structural patterns are extracted as features for supervised classifiers, enabling accurate class discrimination. In an HIV-1 case study, CAMELLIA accurately classified sequences into eight subtypes, reduced processing time versus MEGA (MUSCLE) and FAMSA, matched CASTOR-KRFE under identical splits, and outperformed COMET and REGA in accuracy. Beyond predictive performance, CAMELLIA recovered structural patterns beyond class labels, improving feature selection and interpretability. We further examined feature-count sensitivity, showing how selected feature numbers relate to underfitting or noise-driven overfitting. By balancing scalability, accuracy, and interpretability, CAMELLIA offers a new lens for genomic sequence classification and sets a new standard for data-driven, heterogeneity-aware analysis.

papers.title: DNA augmentations for semi-supervised learning in genomic sequence classification.
papers.authors: Yoo H, Rosen GL.
papers.abstract: Semi-supervised learning (SSL) is a natural fit for genomics, where unlabeled sequences are abundant but high-quality labels are scarce due to costly curation. However, most SSL pipelines rely on generic perturbations that are not tailored to biological constraints, and it remains unclear which augmentation designs yield reliable gains for DNA sequence classification. In this application note, we present an empirical study of genome-aware weak-strong augmentation recipes for pseudo-label-based SSL, focusing on FixMatch and FlexMatch with a GROVER DNA language model backbone. Across two classification benchmarks-antimicrobial resistance (AMR) drug-class prediction from AMR gene sequences and multi-class oncovirus family classification from simulated 150 bp tumor-like reads-we systematically evaluate 25 weak/strong augmentation pairs constructed from biologically motivated operators, including reverse-complement, codon-level back-translation, mild masking/substitution (NN), high-rate substitution, and length-preserving insertion-deletion (indel). We find consistent trends: (i) moderate, sequence-preserving perturbations yield the best accuracy-stability trade-off, (ii) excessive masking or aggressive mutation increases variance and degrades performance, and (iii) short-segment masking (NN) for weak augmentation followed by an indel rate (around 5%) for strong augmentation emerge as a robust strategy to learn from unlabeled genomic data. We release implementations and recommended defaults to facilitate reproducible SSL for genomic sequence modeling under limited-label regimes.

papers.title: UniProt data pruning and the growing invisibility of the dark proteome.
papers.authors: Al-Fatlawi A, Schroeder M.
papers.abstract: The protein resource UniProtKB has undergone a major, multi-stage reorganization of its protein space, implemented from release 2025_04 through release 2026_02. Analysis of UniProtKB and UniParc records accessed on 20 January 2026 showed that 125.9 million entries were last present in UniProtKB in 2025 and are now represented in UniParc, while ~200.0 million entries remained in UniProtKB at the access date. Of these, 58.9 million were designated for removal in release 2026_02, whereas 141.2 million were classified as retained. The reorganization retains all reviewed UniProtKB/Swiss-Prot entries (the expert-curated subset of UniProtKB), along with proteins from selected reference proteomes and unreviewed entries with additional biologically important data, including experimentally determined three-dimensional structures. The expected benefits include reduced redundancy, easier navigation, and a protein set that is more tractable for annotation and routine searches. However, the reorganization may reduce the visibility of protein sequences from uncultured microorganisms and metagenomic surveys, phylogenetically underrepresented lineages, particularly many archaeal groups, proteins belonging to the so-called "dark proteome," and strain-level variants of well-studied species such as Escherichia coli . We argue that the main consequence is not the loss of the sequences themselves, because affected proteins remain recoverable through UniParc and related resources, but a reduction in their discoverability, annotation context, and accessibility within routine workflows. These effects are likely to be most important for biodiversity-oriented analyses, retrospective reuse of older datasets, studies of specialized protein families, and downstream pipelines that rely on UniProtKB as an annotation hub. As UniProt shifts toward a more explicitly reference-proteome-centered model, a critical question arises: What are the implications of UniProtKB contraction for the representation of evolutionary diversity across the tree of life, particularly in under-sampled and uncultured lineages?

papers.title: Representation and detection of inversions in pangenome graphs.
papers.authors: Romain S, Dubois S, Legeai F, Lemaitre C.
papers.abstract: Pangenome graphs are increasingly used in genetic diversity analyses because they reduce reference bias in read mapping and enhance variant discovery and genotyping from SNPs to structural variants. In pangenome graphs, variants appear as bubbles, which can be detected by dedicated bubble calling tools. Although these tools report essential information on the variant bubbles, such as their position and allele walks in the graph, they do not annotate the type of the detected variants. While simple SNPs, insertions, and deletions are easily distinguishable by allele size, large balanced variants like inversions are harder to differentiate among the large number of unannotated bubbles and remain underexplored in pangenome graph benchmarks and analyses. In this work, we focused on inversions, which have been drawing renewed attention in evolutionary genomics studies in the past years, and aimed to assess how this type of variant is handled by state of the art pangenome graph pipelines. We identified two distinct topological motifs for inversion bubbles: one path-explicit and one alignment-rescued, and developed a tool to annotate them from bubble-caller outputs. We constructed pangenome graphs with both simulated data and real data using four state of the art pipelines, and assessed the impact of inversion size, genome divergence, and variant density on inversion representation and accuracy. Our results reveal substantial differences between pipelines in simulated graphs, with some inversions either misrepresented or lost. In addition, recovery rates are strikingly low in real human datasets, highlighting major challenges in analyzing inversions through pangenomic approaches.

papers.title: Pan-cancer multi-omics analysis reveals upregulation of the POLE2 subunit of DNA polymerase epsilon and its associations with patient survival and cellular pathways beyond DNA replication.
papers.authors: Krasilia A, Chaudhry D, Fijalkowska IJ, Dmowski M.
papers.abstract: DNA polymerase epsilon (Polε) is essential for high-fidelity leading-strand synthesis. It comprises a catalytic subunit, POLE, and three accessory subunits, including POLE2. In contrast to POLE, the biological functions and clinical significance of POLE2 remain unexplored. POLE2 is vital for the assembly of Polε and for interactions with the CMG helicase. Yeast studies show that dysfunction of its ortholog, Dpb2, causes genomic instability and impaired cell cycle progression. To investigate the significance of POLE2, this study provides a comprehensive multi-omics analysis across tumor types. We show that POLE2 upregulation is associated with decreased overall survival in a cancer-type-specific manner. Its expression levels, rather than copy number variation (CNV), emerge as a more reliable prognostic marker. POLE2 expression regulatory mechanisms include promoter methylation, isoform usage, and epigenetic regulators. Elevated POLE2 messenger RNA levels rarely translate into increased protein levels, possibly because of abundant non-coding isoforms. Co-expression and pathway enrichment analyses reveal an association between POLE2 and transcriptional regulation involving E2F, EZH2, and RB. Our findings highlight POLE2 as a contributor to genome stability, a candidate cancer biomarker, and a possible therapeutic target.

papers.title: Data-Driven Virus Discovery with Virushunter and Virusgatherer.
papers.authors: Chuprikova L, Chong LC, Ruff S, Seitz S, Lauber C.
papers.abstract: We present Virushunter and Virusgatherer, a bipartite computational workflow for discovering viral genomes from unprocessed next-generation sequencing data. Virushunter conducts a profile Hidden Markov Model-based sequence homology search for viral hallmark protein-coding sequence reads to construct microcontigs, which are used as seeds for targeted viral genome assembly by Virusgatherer. We showcase the application of Virushunter and Virusgatherer through an RNA virus-wide screen in 3348 bat transcriptome sequencing experiments from the Sequence Read Archive. Many of the discovered viruses are likely prototypes of new putative virus species, including a novel alphacoronavirus identified in a South American velvety free-tailed bat and a novel rhabdovirus in a European barbastelle bat. The tools are implemented as a reproducible Snakemake pipeline, which is available at https://github.com/lauberlab/VirusHunterGatherer.

papers.title: Controlling for DNA dosage with whole-genome sequencing improves ATAC-seq peak calling.
papers.authors: Vroland C, Salma M, Zhigulev A, Sahlen P, Soler E, Bréhélin L, Lecellier CH.
papers.abstract: ATAC-seq is a powerful method for mapping chromatin accessibility and identifying cis -regulatory elements (CREs) across cell types. We reveal that ATAC-seq peak calling is compromised by local biases in DNA dosage, arising from copy number variations but also from DNA replication timing. As part of the FANTOM consortium's efforts, we propose enhancing the model-based analysis of ChIP-seq pipeline by integrating whole-genome sequencing (WGS) data, analogous to input controls in ChIP-seq analyses. This adjustment increases both the number and width of ATAC peaks, with improved proximity to transcription start sites. These ATAC peaks exhibit canonical CRE epigenetic marks and are enriched for trait- and disease-associated genetic variants. Furthermore, the number of peaks called with WGS enhances the correlation with gene expression levels compared to peaks called without WGS control. Collectively, these results demonstrate that integrating WGS as a control significantly enhances the accuracy of ATAC-seq peak calling. Critically, even low-depth WGS data suffice to improve peak calling, making this approach cost effective and scalable. We implemented this method as an open-source Nextflow pipeline for accessibility and reproducibility. By challenging the assumption of uniform genomic visibility, our approach also holds broad implications for other DNA sequencing-based technologies.

papers.title: Detect de novo expressed ORFs in transcriptomes with DESwoMAN.
papers.authors: Grandchamp A, Lebherz M, Dohmen E.
papers.abstract: De novo gene emergence refers to the process by which new genes arise from mutations in previously non-coding genomic regions. Investigating early stages of de novo gene emergence is essential for understanding the mechanisms that enable gene formation from scratch. Several workflows have been developed to detect and study the early stage of de novo gene emergence in specific species. However, no software currently exists that can automatically identify and characterize novel, unannotated open reading frames from a transcriptome, and analyse their mutations and fixation patterns within or across species. We introduce DESwoMAN ( D e novo E mergence S tudy W ith O utgroup M ut A tio N s), a software tool designed to (i) detect newly expressed non-canonical ORFs (neORFs) in transcriptomes, (ii) filter neORFs with no homology to outgroup genes, and (iii) search for syntenic sequences homologous to neORFs in outgroup genomes (and optionally transcriptomes) and analyse mutations in coding features between these sequences. We applied DESwoMAN with two different strategies to three setups. Our results highlight the tool's capabilities and demonstrate its potential for elucidating the early stages of de novo gene emergence. DESwoMAN is available at https://github.com/AnnaGrBio/DESWOMAN. It is implemented in Python3 and comes with a docker image on DockerHub for easy installation and execution including all dependencies.

papers.title: Integrating network medicine and foundation models reveals cell-type-specific regulatory alterations in Alzheimer's disease.
papers.authors: Álvarez-Pérez A, Rodríguez-González A, Baumbach J, Prieto-Santamaría L, Oubounyt M.
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease is a complex neurodegenerative disorder characterized by progressive cognitive decline and neuroinflammation. Although its molecular hallmarks are well documented, cell-type-specific mechanisms driving gene dysregulation remain elusive. While single-cell RNA sequencing resolves cellular states, most studies focus on individual genes rather than coordinated programs. Moreover, a gap persists between interpretable network-based models and artificial intelligence foundation models, which capture complex interactions but lack mechanistic transparency. Whether these approaches converge or provide complementary views remains unclear. We present an integrated study combining SCANet, for reconstructing co-expression and gene regulatory networks, with scGPT foundation model. Applied to over 1.3 million cells across 18 cell types, this approach revealed that Alzheimer-associated transcriptional changes concentrate within coherent co-expression modules, for extracellular matrix organization, immune signaling, and neuronal communication. Genes prioritized by scGPT were largely embedded within SCANet modules, indicating convergence at the gene level; however, higher-order architecture agreement was limited and cell-type-specific. Thus, scGPT highlights influential genes, whereas SCANet resolves their modular organization, providing complementary information. By integrating both methods, we recovered known Alzheimer-related pathways and identified novel regulatory candidates, including the CEBPB-CENPQ axis in vulnerable SST-GABA interneurons. This demonstrates that combining network biology with foundation models enables gene prioritization and mechanistic interpretation.

papers.title: Nanopore sequencing combined with adaptive sampling and NanoExpansion enables accurate characterization of repeat expansion disorders.
papers.authors: Morandi L, Casadei F, De Fanti S, Bonan L, Ravaioli F, Palombo F, Fiorentino A, de Pasqua S, Vacchiano V, Avoni P, Rizzo G, Capellari S, Ruggeri E, Donadio V, Castellani G, Bacalini MG, Lodi R, Liguori R, Carelli V, Tonon C.
papers.abstract: Expansion repeat disorders are caused by abnormal expansions of short tandem repeats (STRs). We evaluated targeted long-read nanopore sequencing for comprehensive characterization of STR expansions in 132 participants, including patients with myotonic dystrophy type 1 (DM1, n = 51) and DM2 ( n = 3) already characterized by Southern blot, C9orf72 -associated amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS n = 11) evaluated by repeat primed polymerase chain reaction (RP-PCR; validation group), suspected spinocerebellar ataxia (SCA, n = 46), cerebellar ataxia with neuropathy and vestibular areflexia syndrome (CANVAS; n = 13), Huntington's disease (1), Kennedy disease (1), Friedreich ataxia (FRDA, 2), and 4 healthy controls (test group). Native DNA was sequenced using adaptive sampling (AS) on Oxford Nanopore GridION or PromethION-2Solo platforms. Long-PCR sequencing was performed for comparison. We also developed NanoExpansion, a Python-based tool for sizing expanded alleles and detecting sequence interruptions. We correctly characterized all DM1, DM2, ALS, FRDA, Huntington's disease, and Kennedy disease cases, and identified eight SCA27B, two SCA37, three SCA31, one SCA3, and nine CANVAS cases. Compared with the AS approach, long-PCR underestimated alleles exceeding 800 repeats. Repeat interruptions were detected in 27/51 (52.9%) DM1 cases and 1/10 (10%) ALS, but not in CANVAS, FRDA, Huntington's disease, Kennedy disease, or SCA cases. This integrated sequencing analysis pipeline provides accurate, comprehensive characterization of repeat expansion disorders and has the potential to improve routine genetic diagnosis.

papers.title: Characterization of immunoglobulin loci in Pongo abelii and Pongo pygmaeus: Insights from multi-genome annotation and IMGT-based curation.
papers.authors: Batool S, Zeitoun G, Debbagh C, Dhioui B, Folch G, Jabado-Michaloud J, Giudicelli V, Kossida S.
papers.abstract: Antibodies, or immunoglobulins (IGs), are central to the vertebrate adaptive immune system, yet the genomic architecture of IG loci remains poorly characterized in many nonhuman primates. In this study, we present the first comprehensive genomic analysis of the IG loci (IGH, IGL, and IGK) in two critically endangered orangutan species; Pongo abelii (Sumatran orangutan) and Pongo pygmaeus (Bornean orangutan) across seven genome assemblies. Using IMGT-standardized biocuration framework combined with read-level structural validation, we identified previously undocumented haplotype-specific variation, including multigene duplications and deletions, and expansions of variable gene families within the analyzed assemblies. Recombination signal sequence and switch region analyses revealed conserved regulatory motifs with potential implications for V(D)J recombination and class-switch recombination. These findings underscore the complexity and evolutionary adaptability of IG loci in great apes and highlight the value of orangutans as key references for understanding immune system evolution in the Hominidae lineage.

papers.title: Automated GenePy gene-burden computation via a reproducible Nextflow workflow integrated with the Genomics England (GEL) Lifebit platform.
papers.authors: Nazari I, Cheng G, Ashton J, Ennis S.
papers.abstract: Interpretation of rare-disease genomes remains constrained by variant-centric analytical frameworks that insufficiently capture the cumulative impact of multiple variants within a gene. GenePy provides an individual-level, gene-based burden metric that integrates variant consequence, allele frequency, and zygosity into a unified quantitative score, enabling a transition from discrete variant annotation to aggregated gene-level interpretation. In the context of Genomics England (GEL), this formulation supports a panel-agnostic, genotype-to-phenotype diagnostic strategy for unresolved monogenic disorders by prioritizing genes with elevated mutational burden per individual. Here, we present a fully automated, containerized GenePy workflow deployed through Nextflow and integrated within the GEL Research Environment via the Lifebit CloudOS platform. This implementation provides scalable, secure, and governance-compliant computation of gene-level burden scores across population-scale cohorts. The workflow harmonizes variant annotation, quality control, and chunked data aggregation within modular, reproducible processes designed for high-throughput execution on cloud-native infrastructure. By enabling robust, portable, and auditable gene-level scoring across large rare-disease sequencing datasets, this framework enhances analytical resolution and supports downstream statistical prioritization, integrative phenotype matching, and hypothesis generation within genotype-to-phenotype diagnostic workflows.

papers.title: BioLM-Score: Language-Prior Conditioned Probabilistic Geometric Potentials for Protein-Ligand Scoring.
papers.authors: Yang Z, Chen B, Xu D, Wang J, Bai R, Zhu Z, Ji J.
papers.abstract: Motivation Protein-ligand scoring must address affinity prediction, pose selection, and virtual screening, but these objectives are not necessarily optimized together. Geometric likelihood models may generalize poorly when training-set structural coverage is limited. We test whether pretrained biomolecular representations improve scoring under a controlled geometric baseline. Results BioLM-Score integrates frozen protein and molecular language-model embeddings into a residue-atom distance-likelihood framework via gated graph convolutions. We evaluate geometry-only, jointly trained, and two-stage fine-tuned variants, using the jointly trained variant for the primary controlled comparisons. All three DEKOIS 2.0 screening endpoints improve over the matched geometric baseline with target-level paired support, but affinity scoring and ranking do not improve uniformly. Under a time-split protocol, scoring is significantly lower and ranking is also lower than the geometric baseline, while screening gains persist. On BDB2020+, the difference in affinity correlation between BioLM-Score and GenScore narrows after LP-PDBBind-compatible retraining. Shuffling protein embeddings at inference reduces the screening advantage. However, retrained shuffle controls recover much of the performance, so correct alignment is not established as necessary. BioLM-Score strengthens geometric scoring on screening tasks without retraining the language models. Availability and implementation Code, dataset-split identifiers, preprocessing and evaluation scripts, and language-model embedding-generation utilities are available at https://github.com/SZU-ADDG/BioLM-Score. An archival code snapshot and pretrained model weights are available at doi:10.5281/zenodo.21878818. Supplementary information Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

papers.title: An RNA-targeting ADP-ribosyltransferase toxin uncouples mRNA stability from productive translation.
papers.authors: Lv F, Weng G, Whitney JC.
papers.abstract: Messenger RNA (mRNA) modifications regulate transcript stability and translation efficiency across diverse biological systems, but the consequences of toxin-mediated mRNA modification in bacteria remain poorly understood. RhsP2 was recently identified as an RNA-targeting interbacterial ADP-ribosyltransferase toxin, but whether mRNAs are physiological substrates remained unknown. Here, we show that RhsP2 targets mRNA coding sequences and in doing so prevents their efficient translation. eCLIP-seq reveals preferential association of RhsP2 with UAAG-enriched motifs, and biochemical analyses showed that these sequences are preferred substrates for ribose 2'-OH ADP-ribosylation. Unexpectedly, modified mRNAs were broadly stabilized despite impaired protein synthesis, demonstrating that RhsP2 uncouples transcript stability from productive translation. Monosome- and disome-seq analyses show that RhsP2-modified mRNAs induce ribosome stalling and collision, and in vitro translation reactions demonstrate that ADP-ribosylation of mRNAs is sufficient to block translation elongation. Together, these findings establish mRNA ADP-ribosylation as a mechanism of toxin-mediated translational sabotage in which chemically modified transcripts accumulate while disrupting protein synthesis.

papers.title: Structure of a dopamine-binding RNA aptamer reveals metal-mediated ligand recognition.
papers.authors: Siwik SH, Stelzig D, Hall SD, Batey RT.
papers.abstract: The selection of small-molecule-binding RNA aptamers enables the creation of ligand-responsive RNA tools, yet most aptamers fail to operate reliably across diverse environments. Scaffolded selection addresses this limitation by preserving the tertiary architecture of a riboswitch scaffold while driving the evolution of a new ligand-binding pocket. Using the purine riboswitch aptamer, we previously generated dopamine-binding aptamers. Here, we report the crystal structures of two representative variants in their apo and dopamine-bound states to define how they recognize ligand while maintaining scaffold integrity. The structures demonstrate that scaffolded selection enforces global fold conservation and retains the defining tertiary interactions of the parental riboswitch. Local remodeling, triggered by deletions acquired during selection, rewires the three-way junction to build extensive interaction networks that host the dopamine-binding pocket. A deeply buried potassium ion anchors ligand recognition, while the RNA engages the catechol ring through stacking and hydrogen bonding interactions. Structure probing shows minimal conformational changes upon ligand binding, indicating that the aptamers adopt a largely preorganized fold. The balance between structural stability and local plasticity expands the capacity of a single RNA fold to recognize chemically distinct ligands and positions scaffolded selection as a powerful platform for engineering robust RNA-based sensing and regulatory devices.

papers.title: QPD: a comprehensive database integrating global quarantine regulations with biological, molecular, and spatial resources.
papers.authors: Zhao C, Xiao Y, Li Z, Zou M, Wang Z, Zhu Y, Jin J, Wang Q, Wang S, Liu Y, He K, Li F.
papers.abstract: Quarantine pests pose major threats to global biosafety, agriculture, and biodiversity. However, information of their regulatory status, biology, distribution, and molecular resources remains fragmented across multiple sources, which hinders the in-depth analysis of quarantine pests. Here, we present the Quarantine Pest Database (QPD, https://qpests.insect-genome.com), an open-access resource that integrates global regulations with biological knowledge, multi-omics sequences, and distribution of quarantine pests. QPD integrates official quarantine pest lists, complementary phytosanitary notifications, and distribution records of 231 countries and regions, covering 9849 regulated pest taxa, 7666 host plants, 2057 genome assemblies, 4877 transcriptomes, and 1 311 846 DNA barcode sequences. We also provide 21 747 habitat suitability maps for 4350 quarantine pests under historical and future climate conditions. Each pest entry contains the comprehensive information of standardized taxonomy and jurisdiction-specific quarantine status with host associations, distribution records, morphological descriptions, images, literature references, and available omics resources. Moreover, QPD provides interactive browsing and retrieval, DNA barcode finding, global distribution visualization, and model-based habitat suitability maps. To the best of our knowledge, QPD is the first database to integrate global quarantine regulations with biological, molecular, and spatial information of quarantine pests, providing a centralized resource for the community of pest risk assessment and biosecurity research.

papers.title: GPCRdb in 2027: new structure and ligand data and analysis tools, and updated data mapper and snakeplot visualizations.
papers.authors: Xiao B, Simonyan AA, Rodríguez-Espigares I, Caroli J, Andreassen SN, Flynn AJ, Kermani AA, Bhat V, Longden J, Ausekar A, Kooistra AJ, Keserű GM, Pándy-Szekeres G, Gloriam DE.
papers.abstract: G protein-coupled receptors database (GPCRdb) enables research on GPCRs through tailored resources for reference data, analysis, visualization, experiment design, and dissemination. Our 7th major update to GPCRdb brings extensive updates to the structural and ligand resources, along with several improvements that facilitate easier use. The Structure coverage page has been overhauled to better overview all experimental structures and to break these down into a GPCR class, receptor family, or an individual receptor. We have expanded the annotation on the Structures page by combining AI with manual curation. We add structure models of drug- and peptide-GPCR complexes generated by Boltz-2 and AlphaFold2-Multimer, respectively, and score their confidence. For ligands, we have enhanced the data in the GPCR-ligand interactions resource, implemented variants distinguishing stereoisomers, salts, and labeled versions, assigned persistent identifiers enabling lookup and database cross-linking, and visualized peptide sequences in 2D. Finally, the Data mapper page now has a simplified data input directly in the web interface enabling swift mapping of users' own data for receptors visualized as a GPCRome wheel, tree, clusters, list, or heatmap. Together, these new features aid a multitude of use cases spanning from basic research on GPCR structure-function to drug design. GPCRdb is available at https://gpcrdb.org.

papers.title: PVDive: the plant virus diversity database.
papers.authors: Osojnik A, Reimer LC, Menzel W, Margaria P, Krenz B, Koblitz J.
papers.abstract: Plant viruses are a diverse class of infectious agents affecting agricultural crop production, plant health, and international movement of plant material. While availability and accessibility of scientific data related to plant viruses is essential for plant protection activities, scientific research, diagnostics, plant breeding, and beyond, publicly available data on plant viruses are at present not easily accessible; they are non-standardized, scattered across different resources, poorly interlinked, and not easily searchable by scientists or digital agents. We present PVDive (Plant Virus Diversity Database; https://pvdive.dsmz.de), a freely accessible resource providing high-quality, standardized, and integrated data associated with plant viruses. PVDive primarily offers information at the level of individual plant virus isolates and samples originating from the plant virus collection of the Leibniz Institute DSMZ (Germany). The data are integrated with information on plant virus species and host plants available in existing public resources and their access is centralized in a single platform. Through an intuitive, user-friendly interface with a number of search functionalities and a RESTful application programming interface, PVDive improves findability, accessibility, retrievability, and interoperability of plant virus data. To support data exploration, the platform also includes tools such as advanced search, sequence viewer, host gallery, and interactive data views.

papers.title: proMGE2-a planetary-scale resource of mobile genetic elements in microbial (meta)genomes.
papers.authors: Grekova A, Schudoma C, Letunic I, Kim CY, Podlesny D, Fullam A, Schmidt TSB, Orakov A, Mende D, Schiller J, Erbstein KOE, Bartmanski B, Zimmermann-Kogadeeva M, Zimmermann M, Kuhn M, Bork P, Khedkar S.
papers.abstract: proMGE is a resource of prokaryotic mobile genetic elements (MGEs) that systematically catalogues MGEs from prokaryotes, their intercellular spread, antimicrobial resistance gene carriage, and MGE nesting interactions. We present proMGE2 featuring a 6X expansion, a total of >16.4 million MGEs from 670k high-quality isolate genomes, and 180k metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs), spanning diverse MGE categories: transposons and insertion sequences, phages, phage-like elements, conjugative elements, mobility islands, and integrons. proMGE2 includes MGEs from MAGs derived from environmental microbiomes, encompassing ~50k samples across several major habitat types. proMGE2 provides a standardized MGE reference collection of >5 million non-redundant MGE sequences drawn from our curated database, and enables identification of MGEs in user-provided genomes. proMGE2 captures MGE diversity and their functional potential at unprecedented scale to support future research of mobile genetic elements and transfer of genetic material in microbes. The database is available at http://promge.embl.de/.

papers.title: PDBe in 2027: integrating literature annotations, molecular dynamics data, and AI-ready access.
papers.authors: Afonso MQL, Vollmar M, Bellaiche A, Choudhary P, Nair SS, Todor M, Midlik A, Pidruchna I, Lawal DK, Cordery C, Harrus D, Kunnakkattu IR, Appasamy SD, Ellaway JIJ, Escobar CA, Díaz Leines G, Balasubramaniyan B, Paramval UP, Austin J, Abbara R, Anadón DB, Berka K, Bertoni D, Biggin PC, Bueno WM, Evans GL, Gaborova R, Ganguly S, Goldtzvik Y, Hospital A, Tsenkov MI, Lynch CI, Orozco M, Pechlivanis N, Phan LX, Raček T, Sehnal D, da Silva Neto AM, Špačková A, Stansfeld PJ, Svobodová R, Tanweer A, Ehiguese FO, Fleming JR, Velankar S.
papers.abstract: The Protein Data Bank in Europe (PDBe; pdbe.org) provides open access to experimentally determined biomacromolecular structures and enriches these data with biological and functional context. Here, we describe recent developments that expand the information connected to PDB structures and introduce new ways for researchers and computational tools to access it. Literature integration has been extended to additional open-access publications, substantially increasing the availability of residue-level annotations mined from the scientific literature. Cross-links to molecular dynamics simulations in MDposit have been established, and simulation-derived residue-level annotations, including relative solvent accessibility and membrane-related properties, have been integrated into PDBe-KB (pdbekb.org). PDBe entry pages now expose additional experimental and sequence information, links to related resources, and extended PDB identifiers. Protein channel, tunnel, and pore analyses generated using MOLE have also been incorporated into our weekly release pipeline and made available for download. Improved API documentation facilitates the discovery of data fields and search parameters, while three Model Context Protocol servers facilitate agentic access to the PDBe APIs, Search, and the PDBe-KB knowledge graph. Together, these developments make structural data and its wider biological context easier to discover, interpret, and reuse through both conventional and agentic workflows.

papers.title: CROST 2.0: an expanded repository of spatial transcriptomics.
papers.authors: Wang G, Zhao W, Qian Q, Peng H, Liu H, Fang X, Bao Y, Xiao J, Qu H.
papers.abstract: CROST (https://ngdc.cncb.ac.cn/crost) is a public spatial transcriptomics resource that offers curated datasets, standardized analytical results, structured spatial knowledge, and interactive exploration tools. In version 2.0, our collection has expanded to 544 projects and 3538 samples, nearly a three-fold increase from version 1.0 (182 projects and 1033 samples). We have also substantially expanded the derived resources for spatial colocalization and spatially variable cancer genes. To facilitate spatial microenvironment analysis, CROST 2.0 introduces an analytical framework comprising niche-associated differential expression, spatially resolved gene-set activity analysis, spatial interaction hotspot and topic analyses, and molecular and cell-type niche analysis. CROST 2.0 also provides the Spatial Compare function to compare spatial gene expression, cell-type distributions, and niche composition across samples. It introduces the Cancer NicheDE module to systematically characterize cancer niche-associated differential expression and integrates an online cell-type annotation tool, SCType, enabling the use of single-cell reference information in spatial transcriptomic analysis. These updates extend CROST into an integrated spatial transcriptomics resource for characterizing spatial microenvironments, investigating cancer-associated spatial features, and comparing spatial patterns across samples.

papers.title: Peptide-binding motifs define the functional architecture of human leukocyte antigens.
papers.authors: Crivello P, Hetzel M, Racle J, Gfeller D, Arrieta-Bolaños E, Fleischhauer K.
keywords: Hla Class I And Class Ii
papers.abstract: Background Peptide presentation by polymorphic human leukocyte antigens (HLA) is central to adaptive and innate immunity. HLA polymorphism gives rise to allele-specific peptide-binding motifs (PBM) that shape the immunopeptidomes presented across individuals. However, the global functional architecture imposed by this diversity remains poorly understood. Methods Here, we leveraged large-scale immunopeptidomics datasets to perform a comprehensive analysis of PBM across HLA class I (HLA-A, -B, -C) and class II (HLA-DR, -DQ, -DP) molecules. PBM were derived from public resources and de novo motif deconvolution of 334,089 class II peptides, followed by hierarchical clustering to define functional groups. We systematically evaluated the association of these groups with immunopeptidome overlap and their relation to established models of HLA functional diversity. Results We identified 40 discrete PBM-defined functional groups across 155 class I and 93 class II allotypes. Molecules within the same PBM group showed significantly higher immunopeptidome similarity compared to those across groups. In class II, PBM grouping was further shaped by HLA-DRB3/4/5 paralogues and by α-chain polymorphism in HLA-DQ and -DP, which modulated group assignment of specific β-chains. PBM classification showed only partial concordance with serological antigen groups and evolutionary divergence metrics, but captured differences in peptide repertoires with higher resolution than existing sequence- or epitope-based models. Overall, PBM-based grouping provided a more direct representation of immunopeptidome diversity. Conclusions This pan-HLA PBM framework comprehensively maps the functional architecture of antigen presentation and provides a unified platform to functionally classify HLA diversity. By capturing immunopeptidome divergence, PBM groups offer a foundation for improving the interpretation of HLA variation in immunogenetics, transplantation, and immune-mediated diseases.

papers.title: G-quadruplex profiling using single-cell CUT&Tag offers insight into the epigenetic landscape of the developing mouse brain.
papers.authors: Lyu J, Hetey S, Öztürk MA, Castelo-Branco G, Bartosovic M, Elsässer SJ.
papers.abstract: Background G-quadruplexes (G4s) are non-canonical DNA structures that have gained increasing attention for their potential roles in gene regulation and role in neurodegenerative diseases and cancer. Despite their biological significance, G4 structures have not been studied systematically across tissues and cell types. Results In this study, we employ G4 single-cell CUT&Tag (G4 scCUT&Tag) to characterize G4 landscapes in postnatal mouse brain cells, leveraging single-cell analytical approaches commonly used in scRNA-Seq and scATAC-Seq datasets. Using conventional single-cell omics workflows to process and explore our data, we distinguish distinct cell lineages based on G4 heterogeneity and establish that a subset of lineage-specific genes show unique promoter G4s. Multi-omics integration with scRNA-Seq gene expression profiles, using both a covariance-based technique (canonical correlation analysis) and a transfer learning-based approach, enables more accurate cell-type annotation. These integrations not only reveal correlations between G4 signal and gene expression, but demonstrate that G4 scCUT&Tag enables detailed examination of G4 heterogeneity in complex tissues and supports integrative analysis of G4 profiles with other omics layers, offering new insights into the epigenomic landscapes of the developing brain. Conclusions Our findings establish G4 scCUT&Tag as a framework for investigating the cellular heterogeneity of G4 landscapes in complex tissues and provide a basis for exploring their relationships with gene regulation and other layers of chromatin organization.

papers.title: Benchmarking precision matrix estimation methods for differential co-expression network analysis.
papers.authors: Overmann M, Grabert G, Kacprowski T.
papers.abstract: Background Gene expression profiling is widely used to investigate disease mechanisms, but classical approaches such as differential expression or pairwise correlation analyses provide limited interpretability. Network-based differential co-expression methods that model conditional dependencies through partial correlations offer richer insights, yet their application in high-dimensional settings requires estimation of precision matrices. Numerous precision matrix estimation methods (PMEMs) have been proposed, but these are typically validated in a narrow range of simulation settings and benchmarked against only a small number of competing methods, so their relative performance under diverse conditions remains unclear. Results Simulated gene expression datasets with known ground truth correlation structures were used to benchmark a broad set of PMEMs for their suitability in differential co-expression network analysis of transcriptomic data. Performance was strongly affected by data characteristics, including covariance structure, matrix density, covariance values, sample size-to-dimension ratio, and sampling distribution. Among the evaluated methods, GLassoElnetFast generally achieved high accuracy in recovering differential edges across the simulated scenarios, although high signal-to-noise ratios and sufficient sample sizes remain essential for reliable inference. Applying a subset of these methods to a real transcriptomic dataset reproduced this estimator-dependent variability, with limited overlap between the differential edges recovered by different methods. Conclusions Evaluation across diverse simulation conditions demonstrated that no single metric or condition was sufficient to assess PMEM performance. Therefore, less extensive evaluations may only capture part of this variability and limit the generalizability of their conclusions. Our simulation and benchmarking framework supports future method development and ensures reproducible evaluation of newly developed approaches.

papers.title: Network-guided prioritization of plasma protein signatures across 23 diseases.
papers.authors: Kong X, Yang H, Li M, Zhang T, Bueno Álvez M, Liao X, Song X, Meng L, Altay Ö, Sener LT, Zhang C, Uhlén M, Mardinoglu A.
papers.abstract: Population-scale plasma proteomics has begun to map the circulating proteome across human diseases, yet reducing these large datasets to interpretable compact protein panels that remain accurate across independent cohorts is a major challenge. Here, we developed a network-guided framework that links the Human Disease Blood Atlas (HDBA) to the UK Biobank Pharma Proteomics Project (UKB-PPP) through 1154 proteins quantified in both cohorts and evaluates protein signatures across 23 human diseases. For each disease, we considered two classification tasks: disease versus healthy and disease versus diseases. Compact protein panels achieved a mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.741 and 0.736 for the two tasks, compared with 0.827 and 0.797 for a baseline model comprising all shared proteins, and outperformed this baseline in 7 of 23 diseases per task. Integrating panel membership with differential protein levels and disease-associated co-expression modules reveals disease-enriched candidates from disease-shared proteins associated with multiple conditions. This framework provides a structured, systems-level basis for prioritizing plasma protein signatures across diverse diseases.

papers.title: Intrinsic neural dynamics reveal a body-part-specific topography in mouse secondary motor cortex.
papers.authors: Xu W, Yagielski AJ, Thibodeaux DN, Carmona LM, Ugorji K, Shahsavarani S, Kim SH, Lodgher F, Zhao HT, Malan EA, Xu L, Freeman C, Bisht A, Swayze K, Cambareri M, Li W, Hillman EMC.
papers.abstract: The mammalian sensory cortex (S1) has a well-characterized body part-specific topography. However, most motor cortex atlases to date are only coarsely defined. Here, we demonstrate that optical mapping of neuronal activity in awake mice reveals a distinct, body-part specific organization of mouse secondary motor cortex (M2). This M2 topography was identified by recognizing that intrinsic neuronal fluctuations are selectively synchronized between homologous sub-regions of S1 and M2. These fluctuations were strongest during rest and quenched during movement, and were not prominent in corticospinal neurons (CSNs), indicating that they do not represent motor output. Functional characterization of M2 sub-regions during spontaneous movements confirms body-part specificity, and stronger engagement during multi-effector coordinated actions. Structural connectivity atlas tracings from S1 regions confirm projections to homologous M2 sub-regions. These results reveal an important underlying topography within M2, and demonstrate intrinsic neuronal dynamics as a window into the functional architecture of the motor cortex.

papers.title: Multi-omics-constrained kinetic models quantify pathway rewiring and predict metabolic vulnerabilities in BRCA1-deficient ovarian cancer.
papers.authors: Toumpe I, Masid M, Hatzimanikatis V, Miskovic L.
papers.abstract: Time-resolved, network-wide consequences of cancer metabolic reprogramming remain poorly understood. We built multi-omics-constrained, near-genome-scale kinetic ensembles for isogenic BRCA1 wild-type and BRCA1-mutant ovarian cancer cells. Covering over 2,100 reactions, the ensembles enabled uncertainty-quantified simulations of nutrient, metabolite, and enzyme perturbations. Metabolic control analysis identified 28 enzyme-mediated vulnerabilities; 24 are linked to experimental or approved DrugBank compounds, whereas four lack documented drug associations. Independent DepMap data supported a subset of these candidates. All 28 emerged directly from the mechanistic model structure and multi-omics constraints, with no calibration to known drug targets or cancer-dependency data. Simulations of thymidylate synthase, hexokinase, and triokinase inhibition predicted target- and physiology-specific changes in pathway use, energy metabolism, and a shared ceramide-linked stress response. Mapping predicted enzyme-activity shifts to BRCA1-associated transcription factors suggested regulatory routes underlying differences between the two states. These ensembles provide a reusable framework for time-resolved, mechanistic hypothesis generation across cancers and other diseases. A record of this paper's transparent peer review process is included in the supplemental information.

papers.title: RNA sequencing reveals molecular subtypes across adenocarcinoma, squamous, and small cell lung cancer.
papers.authors: Arora S, Suresh L, Thirimanne NH, Glatzer G, Jensen M, Fatherree JP, Konnick EQ, Levine KM, Brooks AN, Houghton MA, Pritchard CC, MacPherson D, Berger AH, Holland EC.
papers.abstract: This study combines RNA sequencing data from 1,824 tumors across major lung cancer types to examine how tumor gene expression patterns relate to histologic diagnoses. The resulting reference landscape identifies nine transcriptional clusters, including a neuroendocrine-like adenocarcinoma group and regions with mixed histology. The clusters also show associations with clinical features, genetic alterations, immune characteristics, and survival. An interactive Oncoscape resource allows researchers to explore the integrated data and compare patient tumors with patient-derived xenograft models.

papers.title: Distinct extraembryonic transcription factors converge on a shared DNA methylation-Polycomb state.
papers.authors: Haggerty C, Mackowiak SD, Cui M, Pohl G, Mattei AL, Wagner W, Smith ZD, Meissner A.
papers.abstract: Extraembryonic tissues and many cancers share unusual DNA methylation landscapes, but how these states arise remains unclear. Here, we use GATA6- and CDX2-driven reprogramming of mouse embryonic stem cells to track genome-wide epigenetic remodeling during acquisition of extraembryonic cell fates. Despite activating distinct transcriptional programs from non-overlapping genomic targets, both transcription factors trigger rapid and genomically synchronized convergence to cancer-like DNA methylation patterns, including simultaneous global DNA methylation loss and de novo methylation of Polycomb-regulated CpG islands. We find that this wave of DNA methylation reprogramming co-occurs with global H3K27me3 redistribution alongside promoter H3K4 methylation loss. Experimental models of cellular senescence, as well as human aging and cancer cohorts, reveal related but progressively more extensive disruption of these same chromatin boundaries. Together, these data define a tractable system for studying coordinated genome-wide transitions between canonical and non-canonical epigenomic states.

papers.title: Handshake: Partner-specific protein-protein binding site prediction at scale using ProstT5 and cross-chain attention.
papers.authors: Haspel N.
papers.abstract: Partner-specific protein-protein binding site prediction, identifying which residues of a protein form the interface when bound to a specific partner, remains a challenging task with significant implications for drug discovery and understanding of protein structure and function. Existing computational methods are limited by small training datasets, inconsistent redundancy filtering, and reliance on three-dimensional structural information at test time. Here we present a sequence-only, partner-specific protein-protein interface predictor called HandShake. It combines ProstT5, a protein language model pre-trained on structural data, with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), a cross-chain attention mechanism and a contact supervision head. Our method can detect both binding interfaces and pairwise contact matrices. We trained our model on very large datasets of non-redundant protein-protein pairs derived from the PPInterface dataset, the most comprehensive structural protein-protein database to date, and evaluated it on systematically filtered benchmarks at four redundancy thresholds (30%-90% sequence identity). We demonstrate that sequence redundancy inflates reported AUROC by up to 0.079 and MCC by up to 0.145 on identical models, representing a substantial methodological confound in the field. Even at 30% redundancy threshold, our results (AUROC = 0.811, MCC = 0.367, F1 = 0.45) exceed the best published sequence-only result on this convention. Our method also achieves comparable performance to existing partner-specific methods that use explicit structural information. The comprehensive training and evaluation dataset, in addition to the systematic redundancy inflation, can help gain insight into protein-protein interactions and the abilities and limitations of current detection methods.

papers.title: Entangled stoichiometric objectives shape microbial catabolism.
papers.authors: Remeijer M, Bruggeman FJ.
papers.abstract: The understanding of fundamental relationships between energetic and biosynthetic parameters of catabolism and anabolism is a central challenge in microbiology. The large diversity of microbial metabolisms can be compared on the basis of our current definitions of catabolism and anabolism. Catabolism has two functions: synthesising charged energy carriers and carbon precursors. Energy carriers, however, are also involved in precursor synthesis, complicating the analysis. We introduce an unbiased method to quantify stoichiometric relationships between catabolism and anabolism in genome-scale metabolic models. We compare catabolic strategies across diverse (heterotrophic) microbial species and growth conditions, focusing on states of maximal biomass yield per unit of energy source. Catabolic networks turn out to vary greatly, due to variation in the energy and carbon source for growth and the requirement to make suitable precursors for anabolism. We find that the ATP requirement for 1 gram biomass ranges between 72.8 and 148.0 mmol, precursor sets range between 4 and 14 in size, and acetyl-CoA is the only universal precursor across species. An important varying factor is the amount of ATP that is produced or consumed during precursor synthesis. This causes the remaining ATP demand, which is produced in catabolism, to vary. We conclude that the diversity of heterotrophic catabolism results from entanglement between charging of energy carriers and precursor synthesis. The state of maximal energetic efficiency is reached by maximizing the yield of charged energy carriers during precursor synthesis and simultaneously minimizing the demand for charged energy carriers in the conversion of precursors into macromolecules. Our formal analysis of catabolic diversity using a rigorous definition of catabolism's two functions shows that microbial metabolism cannot be simplified in this manner; it rather shows that these two functions are intertwined due to the precise biochemistry.

papers.title: Modeling distinct pathogenesis of early- and late-onset preeclampsia via hierarchical representation learning of interactome.
papers.authors: Sufriyana H, Wu YW, Chiu HS, Sumazin P, Su EC.
papers.abstract: Objectives We developed and validated the pathogenesis models by hierarchical representation learning of interactomes connecting endometrial maturation, placentation, chorioamnionitis, and hemolysis, elevated liver enzyme, and low platelet (HELLP) syndrome. Methods We utilized 19 gene sets from our previous work to infer interactomes to develop (n = 177) and validate (n = 352) explainable artificial intelligence models for each preeclampsia subtype using deep-insight visible neural network, gradient-weighted class activation mapping, and large language model. Results The hierarchically learned representations identified novel genes for late-onset preeclampsia (LOPE), similar to chorioamnionitis (ANKRD13A, SLA), and HELLP syndrome (PDE5A). We also identified novel genes for early-onset preeclampsia (EOPE), similar to HELLP syndrome (SWAP70, GREM2, GPR146, PIP5K1B, EZR). Conclusions Our pathogenesis models connected HELLP syndrome with both LOPE and EOPE. However, chorioamnionitis was only connected with LOPE.

papers.title: Interaction-finder: automated literature-based discovery of biological entity associations with quote-level provenance.
papers.authors: Chapman T, Lassmann T.
papers.abstract: Identifying interactions between biological entities is a cornerstone of molecular research, but assembling such lists from the literature is slow and tedious. For many research questions, no curated database exists, leaving researchers to survey the relevant literature themselves. We present interaction-finder, a tool that automates this process: given a topic string and user-defined entity types, it discovers relevant literature through LLM-guided iterative search, extracts candidate associations from full-text articles, and produces a ranked list where every association is backed by quoted passages verified against the source text. A self-contained interactive HTML report enables rapid triage of the results. Evaluated across 60 topics in three domains (celltype-cellmarker, disease-gene, and ligand-receptor), interaction-finder recovers up to 4.3× as many known associations as the best of single-shot prompting and an off-the-shelf deep-research framework, with all extracted quotes verified against source text. To assess candidates unrecognised from the gold-standard databases, we scored each candidate using an independent LLM judge blind to the tool's reasoning. Across the three domains, unverified candidates score similarly to gold-standard associations. We find the gold-standard associations are enriched at the top of our ranked candidates, with an overall recall@20 of 0.61. Interaction-finder is freely available at https://github.com/tecosaur/interaction_finder under an MIT licence.

papers.title: ASAOT: an accentuated structure-differentiated asymmetric optimal transport model for cell type and single-cell spatial mapping.
papers.authors: Sun Z, Shi Z, Zhang Y, Nan M, Gao J.
papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics (STs) characterizes spatiotemporal gene expression and facilitates analysis of cellular architecture and cell-cell crosstalk within tissue microenvironments. However, existing spatial deconvolution methods employ globally fixed smoothing without local sharpening, which blurs cellular boundaries and impedes reconstruction of layered, heterogeneous cellular patterns in brain tissue. Here, we present Accentuated Structure-differentiated Asymmetric Optimal Transport (ASAOT), a deconvolution framework built on structure-enhanced asymmetric optimal transport. Coupled with spatial neighborhood constraints, ASAOT introduces a differentiated accentuated sharpening term to maintain global spatial continuity, enhance boundary detection, and preserve spot-level expression heterogeneity. Using asymmetric optimal transport, the framework jointly estimates spot-wise cell-type proportions and performs spatial assignment of reference single-cell coordinates. Benchmarks on diverse simulated datasets demonstrate that ASAOT achieves competitive overall accuracy and robustness across moderate spatial resolutions, with the best average comprehensive rank among tested methods. Applications to mouse olfactory bulb and cerebral cortex datasets demonstrate that ASAOT reduces signal diffusion and boundary distortion, effectively recovering layered brain anatomy and stratified cell distributions to build interpretable spatial maps of reference single-cell profiles. Collectively, ASAOT addresses critical drawbacks of conventional methods via a sharpening regularization term, serving as a reliable tool for STs analysis and mechanism exploration of tissue spatial organization.
