papers.title: RecA protein activates the E. coli topoisomerase III catenation function: essential role of the RecA ATPase.
papers.authors: Phan KL, Dunbar EL, Cox MM.
papers.abstract: RecA protein loaded into lesion-containing post-replication gaps must engage in strand exchange utilizing DNA substrates with no free ends, a process that is topologically constrained. The process can be mimicked by examining RecA-mediated DNA strand exchange between a circular ssDNA and a partially homologous circular supercoiled DNA. RecA protein can pair these substrates but cannot promote a net strand exchange. On its own, topoisomerase III promotes little reaction with the same two substrates. However, the two proteins together promote a robust reaction that rapidly, within 1-2 min, converts the substrates quantitatively to catenanes and hemicatenanes. The results reveal an important new functional interaction for bacterial topoisomerase III. The reaction is tightly coupled to RecA-mediated ATP hydrolysis. The rate of RecA-promoted ATP hydrolysis controls not just the extent but also the rate of the catenation/hemicatenation reaction. The ssDNA substrate is also required. Post-replication gaps are created in essentially every replication cycle and can be lethal if left unresolved. Given the need for rapid gap amelioration prior to the arrival of a new replication fork, the strong enzymatic and topological collaboration between RecA and topoisomerase III may have been a major evolutionary driver for the RecA ATPase activity.

papers.title: Hypernova: a faster and brighter light-producing deoxyribozyme.
papers.authors: Svehlova K, Kurfürst J, Jakubec M, Curtis EA.
papers.abstract: As a functional nucleic acid motif is optimized, better variants become less abundant in sequence space and significantly more difficult to identify. Here, we used two types of libraries to discover an improved variant of a previously optimized light-producing deoxyribozyme called Supernova. One library was designed in such a way that most mutations were consistent with the sequence requirements and secondary structure of this catalytic motif. The second contained short stretches of random sequence in place of AAAA spacers previously introduced in minimization experiments. Catalytically active sequences were isolated from each library using single and multiple round selections. Mutations from the best deoxyribozymes were then combined to yield an improved variant containing 12 mutations, which we named Hypernova. The rate of Hypernova at subsaturating substrate concentrations was up to 97-fold higher than that of Supernova, and its initial rate of light production was up to 30-fold faster. In addition, sensors constructed using Hypernova outperformed those made from Supernova in three different assays. These results indicate that Hypernova can enhance the performance of light-producing deoxyribozyme sensors for applications such as diagnostics and high-throughput screening.

papers.title: DIANA-miRGen v5: TSS characterization and transcriptional regulation of miRNAs in human and mouse.
papers.authors: Giannoukakos S, Miliotis M, Bouloutsos A, Xiropotamos P, Guigó R, Georgakilas GK, Hatzigeorgiou AG.
papers.abstract: Characterizing microRNA transcriptional regulation is challenging because primary microRNA transcripts undergo rapid nuclear processing, leaving full-length molecules poorly represented in conventional transcriptomic data. DIANA-miRGen v5 addresses this annotation gap by combining Capture Long-read Sequencing (CLS) data, generated within GENCODE to improve non-coding RNA annotation, with GENCODE reference gene and transcript annotations to resolve miRNA host contexts. For human, the database provides experimentally informed, transcript-anchored host and promoter annotations for 1560/1918 pre-miRNA loci (81.3%), represented by 1302 distinct reference transcripts. CLS-derived human transcription start sites (TSSs) are accompanied by overlap information from FANTOM5 CAGE, ENCODE PRO-cap, and RAMPAGE. Transcription factor (TF)-filtered ChIP-Atlas data annotate candidate TF occupancy within windows extending 10 kb upstream and 2 kb downstream of selected host TSSs, yielding 4 901 330 human gene-level host-window overlap records. For mouse, annotations cover 994/1227 loci (81.0%), comprising 785 distinct reference transcripts. Mouse TSSs obtained from CLS include FANTOM5 CAGE overlap information, while ChIP-Atlas analysis yielded 2 378 918 gene-level host-window overlap records. The redesigned interface supports linked gene- and transcript-level exploration, interactive genome visualization, contextual tracks, bulk downloads, and open access through a REST API. DIANA-miRGen v5 is freely available without registration at http://microrna.gr/mirgenv5/.

papers.title: Evo2VED: a database of DNA large language model-derived scores for variant interpretation.
papers.authors: Zhu R, Zhou X, Liang I, Mendes M, Engchuan W, Safarian N, Zhou H, Cheng H, Trost B, Breetvelt E, Vorstman J, Tang H, O'Brien SJ, Scherer SW, Ohno-Machado L.
papers.abstract: The Evo2 Variant Effect Database (Evo2VED; https://dnallmved.org/) is a publicly accessible resource cataloging precomputed Evo2-derived variant effect scores, defined as allelic score differences, for 6.48 million human variants common in the gnomAD non-Finnish European population. Evo2VED includes scores from the 7B and 40B models under three scoring schemes, alongside annotations of variant function, evolutionary constraint, allele age, and disease associations. It integrates genome-wide association study (GWAS) data from UK Biobank, FinnGen, and the Million Veteran Program. Three complementary modules support variant-level interpretation, regional and region-set exploration, and trait-level analysis through flexible queries, interactive visualizations, and downloadable results. Evo2VED also catalogs associations between Evo2 annotations and per-SNP heritability across thousands of traits from these biobanks. A guided workflow connects GWAS with associated regions and individual variant evidence. Case studies of hypertension and depression illustrate how regional comparisons of Evo2 scores and GWAS signals can guide candidate variant prioritization. Evaluations using massively parallel reporter assays, molecular QTLs, fine-mapping probabilities, and clinical annotations assess associations with Evo2 scores alone and their added value beyond conservation and regulatory annotations. By providing accessible scores, contextual annotations, and comparative analyses, Evo2VED facilitates exploration and application of genomic language model predictions in human genetics research.

papers.title: TransCirc 2.0: a multi-species resource for translatable circular RNAs and cognate translation products.
papers.authors: Xie D, Ling Y, Li D, Zhou H, Fan X, Cao R, Zhang G, Wang Z.
papers.abstract: TransCirc is an evidence-integrated database for evaluating the translation potential of circular RNAs (circRNAs) and their putative products. Here, we present TransCirc 2.0, a major update that expands this resource from a primarily human-focused database to 10 vertebrate species, comprising more than 2.8 million circRNAs and increasing coverage by approximately 10-fold through the integration of standardized full-length circRNA sequences. Within the original multi-evidence framework, we incorporate additional evidence, including translation initiation sites, internal ribosome entry sites, N6-methyladenosine, ribosome/polysome association, and mass spectrometry (MS), together with circRNA-specific open reading frame and sequence-composition annotations. In light of recent advances in AI-based RNA modeling, we further incorporate multiple regulatory features predicted by TranslationAI and LAMAR. The circRNA-encoded proteins are further annotated for degron-associated stability and degradation properties, while MS-supported peptides are evaluated for potential MHC-I presentation. Collectively, these updates establish a cross-species framework linking full-length circRNA sequences with multi-level translation evidence and downstream product annotations, supporting systematic evaluation of circRNA translation potential and putative translation products. TransCirc 2.0 is freely available at https://www.biosino.org/transcirc/.

papers.title: ADMETatlas: an online database of peptide ADMET evidence toward peptide therapeutic development.
papers.authors: Yi J, Tian Y, Deng Y, Gu X, Fu X, Jiang D, Lyu A, Cao D.
papers.abstract: Peptide therapeutics are expanding rapidly, yet poor permeability and limited in vivo stability still decide whether a candidate reaches the clinic. Judging these properties is difficult, because one sequence can be studied as different molecular forms or products, and reported values carry different experimental contexts. Despite the continuous accumulation of measurements of peptide absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity (ADMET), few open-access resources keep each value attached to the material tested and its assay context. Herein, we present ADMETatlas, a curated peptide ADMET, safety, and developability database. Currently, ADMETatlas contains 39 641 measurements at 17 measured end points across 37 467 canonical peptide identities, 110 drug products, and 10 computed descriptors. Each measurement retains its value, unit, formal end point, assay context, and primary reference. Peptide identities, molecular forms, and products are cross-linked at the resolution each source supports. In addition to browsing and retrieval, a developability module profiles single candidates and compares several side by side. Applications to GLP-1 receptor agonists and polymyxin B show how route and formulation change the reading of peptide pharmacokinetics. We hope that ADMETatlas will prove useful in evidence-based peptide optimization and condition-aware modeling. ADMETatlas is freely available, without registration, at https://admetatlas.scbdd.com/.

papers.title: M2iOR: a quantitative, context-resolved atlas of insect odorant receptor-odorant interactions.
papers.authors: Geslin D, Pitakbut T, Lanrezac A, de Fouchier A, Bouchouireb Z, Thorhallsson AT, Gilardot D, Meslin C, Montagné N, Jacquin-Joly E, Fiorucci S, Groot AT, Topin J.
papers.abstract: Olfactory detection in insects relies on interactions between odorant molecules and odorant receptors (ORs) expressed in olfactory sensory neurons. Although numerous studies have characterized insect OR-ligand interactions, these data remain scattered across the literature and heterogeneous in terms of species, experimental systems, and reporting standards, limiting their systematic analysis. Here, we present the Molecule to Insect Odorant Receptor database (M2iOR, https://m2ior.chemsensim.fr/), a curated, publicly accessible resource designed to centralize and standardize odorant-receptor interaction data. In its current release, M2iOR compiles 35 891 bioassay experiments describing 30 348 distinct insect OR-molecule pairs, extracted from 41 peer-reviewed publications and public databases. The resource integrates ligand structures, receptor sequences, species names, mixture information, and detailed experimental metadata. M2iOR provides flexible query tools allowing users to retrieve activity profiles for individual molecules or compound sets, and identify agonists and nonagonists for specific insect ORs, enabling comparative analyses across receptors, species, or bioassay systems. Advanced filtering based on curated metadata and batch search functionality support high-throughput analyses. For each query, users can visualize and download a curated aggregation of experimental results, including a binarized combinatorial representation of olfactory coding suitable for downstream computational studies. M2iOR provides a comprehensive framework for data-driven research in insect olfaction and comparative chemosensory biology.

papers.title: The Biodiversity Cell Atlas database: a curated resource for comparative single-cell genomics across the eukaryotic tree of life.
papers.authors: Saraiva-Agostinho N, Becerra A, Pashkovskaia T, van Waardenburg B, Elek A, Borges Perdomo C, Hermoso Pulido T, Zolotarov G, Grau-Bové X, Sumanaweera D, Ponomarenko J, Papatheodorou I, Lawniczak M, Sebé-Pedrós A.
papers.abstract: Single-cell genomics has transformed the study of cellular diversity, but the resulting atlases are scattered across publications, formats, and annotation standards. Efforts to make these data findable and interoperable have focused largely on aggregating and harmonizing existing model organism datasets. The Biodiversity Cell Atlas database is an open resource that addresses this gap by uniformly (re)processing, curating, and comparing whole-organism single-cell atlases sampled across the eukaryotic tree of life. Starting from raw sequencing data, each dataset is processed through a consistent workflow and enriched with standardized quality-control metrics, metacell-level aggregation, gene co-expression modules, and phylogeny-based orthology and functional annotation, enabling both gene- and cell type-centric exploration within species as well as principled comparisons between them. The portal currently hosts 39 datasets across 33 species spanning 13 eukaryotic phyla, and offers multiple levels of access, from raw and filtered count matrices to normalized, aggregated, and analysis-ready data layers. These are accessible through an interactive web interface (https://portal.biodiversitycellatlas.org) and a documented REST API (https://portal.biodiversitycellatlas.org/api/v1/). All data, code, and infrastructure are continuously released and maintained under open licenses, providing a curated and reusable foundation for comparative single-cell genomics.

papers.title: HGMetaADR: a multimodal heterogeneous graph meta-learning framework for generalized adverse drug reaction prediction.
papers.authors: Fu Y, Wang M, Li R, Gao J, Liu K, Lu J, He S, Bo X.
keywords: Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions
papers.abstract: Early identification of adverse drug reactions (ADRs), which refer to harmful or unintended responses to medications taken at normal doses, is crucial for reducing clinical trial failures and associated economic costs. However, existing ADR datasets often exhibit a long-tailed label distribution and lack sufficient training examples for rare side effects, making it difficult for vanilla supervised learning models to generalize to underrepresented classes. To address these issues, we propose HGMetaADR, a novel heterogeneous graph-based meta-learning framework for ADR prediction. Built upon a multimodal biomedical knowledge graph, this approach integrates complementary drug-related data, including molecular structures, protein sequences, side effects, and therapeutic indications. It employs a hierarchical attention mechanism to capture semantic dependencies across heterogeneous entities and adopts a model-agnostic meta-learning strategy to enhance adaptation to small-sample classes. We evaluate HGMetaADR under three scenarios-few-shot, zero-shot, and majority-to simulate real-world conditions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that HGMetaADR consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. Furthermore, ablation studies and pathway enrichment analyses reveal the underlying biological mechanisms linking protein targets, therapeutic indications, and side effects, thereby validating the effectiveness of incorporating heterogeneous biomedical knowledge into ADR modeling.

papers.title: Surrogate-guided self-play Monte Carlo tree search for antimicrobial peptide sequence optimization and in vitro antibacterial assessment.
papers.authors: Lu JJ, Chung CR, Chang CH, Wu LC, Hsu JB, Tsai CY, Lee TY, Horng JT.
papers.abstract: The rapid emergence of multidrug-resistant pathogens necessitates the development of novel therapeutic agents, yet the de novo design of antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) is challenged by the vast combinatorial search space and the difficulty of balancing efficacy with toxicity. To address these limitations, we introduce a reinforcement learning framework that employs surrogate-guided self-play Monte Carlo tree search to explore the peptide landscape. By integrating surrogate models for predicted antimicrobial activity, HemoDL-predicted hemolytic propensity, and ESMFold structural confidence, the system performs multi-property computational optimization and candidate prioritization. In silico analysis demonstrated that the optimized peptides adopt amphipathic α-helical structures with high predicted folding confidence and possess favorable docking scores against Staphylococcus aureus resistance targets, including PBP2a and MurA. To assess the biological relevance of the computationally prioritized candidates, 16 peptides were synthesized and evaluated by agar dilution against a 37-strain bacterial panel over a concentration range of 0.25-64 μg/ml. AMP2, AMP7, and AMP9 achieved complete inhibition of at least one tested strain, corresponding to 3 of 16 synthesized candidates (18.75%). AMP12 and AMP13 showed partial growth reduction without complete inhibition within the tested range, whereas the remaining 11 candidates showed no complete inhibition. These findings quantify the current gap between surrogate-defined computational enrichment and assay-specific antibacterial activity. The strain-dependent experimental outcomes further indicate that surrogate, docking, and structural scores do not fully capture all determinants of antibacterial efficacy. The experimental assessment was limited to bacterial agar-dilution activity; mammalian-cell cytotoxicity, wet-lab hemolysis, and peptide-stability assays were not performed. In conclusion, this study establishes a computational framework for the design of bioactive peptides and provides structural insights for bridging the gap between deep learning predictions and experimental outcomes.

papers.title: GLAlign integrates single-cell multi-omics data via global manifold and local marker gene alignment.
papers.authors: Ba T, Hu M, Liu S, Zhang L, Chai L, Li Z, Gao C, Wang Y.
papers.abstract: Integrating heterogeneous single-cell multi-omics datasets remains challenging because different modalities are measured in distinct feature spaces and lack cell level pairing. Existing manifold alignment or feature conversion framework are often affected by weak cross-modality associations, geometric ambiguity, and overcorrection. Here we present GLAlign (Global manifold and Local marker gene Alignment), an optimization framework that jointly leverages global manifold structure and local marker gene information to integrate single-cell multi-omics data. GLAlign learns a shared latent space through a global objective comprising maximum mean discrepancy, distortion, and penalty terms, together with a local contrastive triplet loss guided by cross-modality marker gene overlap between independently inferred clusters. We demonstrate GLAlign's methodological contribution in extending the manifold alignment by biologically informed prior to ensure geometrically plausible and biologically correct alignments without requiring paired cells or manual cell type annotations. We evaluated GLAlign on simulated data and real datasets spanning PBMC scRNA-seq/scATAC-seq, mouse brain SNARE-seq, single-donor and multi-batch CITE-seq, and NCI-N87 scDNA-seq/scRNA-seq integration. Across the evaluated datasets, GLAlign achieved strong modality mixing and biological conservation, remained stable under moderate cell type imbalance and variations in clustering and marker information, and supported cross-modality label transfer and paired cell recovery. These results demonstrate that biologically structured coupling of global and local alignment provides an interpretable framework for heterogeneous single-cell multi-omics integration. GLAlign is freely available at https://github.com/Bateer-Bio/GLAlign.

papers.title: Biosemantic graph transfer learning for cross-patient cell type annotation and cell-cell interaction analysis in tumor single-cell RNA sequencing.
papers.authors: Li YC, Wong L, You HR, Wang XF, Wei MM, Wang L, Huang ZA, Huang YA, You ZH.
papers.abstract: The exploration of cellular heterogeneity within the tumor microenvironment (TME) via single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) is essential for understanding cancer progression and response to therapy. Current scRNA-seq approaches, however, lack spatial context and rely on incomplete datasets of ligand-receptor interactions, limiting accurate cell type annotation and cell-cell communication inference. This study addresses these challenges using a novel graph neural network model that enhances cell-type prediction and cell-interaction analysis. Our study utilized a dataset consisting of 49 024 cells from 19 patients across three cancer types: leukemia, breast invasive carcinoma, and colorectal cancer. The proposed scGSL model demonstrated robust performance, achieving an average accuracy of 84.83%, precision of 86.23%, recall of 81.51%, and an F1 score of 80.92% across all datasets. These metrics represent a significant enhancement over existing methods, which typically exhibit lower performance metrics. Additionally, by reviewing existing literature on gene interactions within the TME, the scGSL model proves to robustly identify biologically meaningful gene interactions in an unsupervised manner, validated by significant expression differences in key gene pairs across various cancers. The source code and data used in this study can be found at https://github.com/LiYuechao1998/scGSL.

papers.title: Community benchmarking of generative models for privacy-preserving synthetic bulk RNA-seq data generation.
papers.authors: Öztürk H, Afonja T, Jälkö J, Binkyte R, Rodriguez-Mier P, Lobentanzer S, Wicks A, Kreuer J, Ouaari S, Pfeifer N, Menzies S, Pentyala S, Filienko D, Golob S, McKeever P, Banerjee J, Foschini L, De Cock M, Saez-Rodriguez J, Fritz M, Stegle O, Honkela A.
papers.abstract: Background The synthesis of anonymized data derived from real-world cohorts offers a promising strategy for regulatory-compliant and privacy-preserving biological data sharing, potentially facilitating model development that can improve predictive performance. However, the extent to which generative models can preserve biological signals while remaining resilient to adversarial privacy attacks in high-dimensional omics contexts remains underexplored. To address this gap, the CAMDA 2025 Health Privacy Challenge launched a community-driven effort to evaluate synthetic and privacy-preserving data generation for bulk RNA-seq cohorts. Results Building on this initiative, we systematically benchmark 11 generative methods across two cancer cohorts (~ 1,000 and ~ 5,000 patients) over 978 landmark genes. Methods are evaluated across distributional fidelity, downstream utility, biological plausibility and empirical privacy risk, with emphasis on trade-offs between vulnerability to membership inference attacks and other evaluation dimensions. Expressive deep generative models achieve strong predictive utility and differential expression recovery, but are often more vulnerable to membership inference risk under the evaluated threat model. Differentially private methods improve resistance to attacks at the cost of reduced utility, while simpler statistical approaches offer competitive utility with moderate privacy risk and fast training. Conclusions Synthetic bulk RNA-seq quality is inherently multi-dimensional and shaped by trade-offs between utility, biological preservation and privacy. Our results indicate that model architecture drives distinct trade-offs across these axes, suggesting that model choice should align with dataset characteristics, intended downstream use and privacy requirements. Privacy risk should also be assessed using multiple complementary attack methods and, where possible, mitigated through formal differential privacy protection.

papers.title: PHI: a Galaxy-based workflow for reproducible prophage-host interaction analysis and standardized viral-genomics reporting.
papers.authors: Saraiva JP, Borim Corrêa F, Bernt M, Ghanem N, Nieto E, Brizola Toscan R, Wick LY, Chatzinotas A.
papers.abstract: Background Viruses that infect bacteria, known as bacteriophages or phages, are widespread in nature and play important roles in shaping microbial communities and ecosystem functions. Some phages can integrate into bacterial genomes as "prophages", where they may influence the biology of their host by carrying genes that affect metabolism, virulence, or environmental adaptation. Despite their importance, studying prophages and their interactions with bacterial hosts remains challenging because it typically requires combining many complex computational tools and can be resource-intensive. Results In this study, we introduce the Prophage-Host Interaction Toolkit (PHI), a user-friendly and automated workflow available through the Galaxy platform. PHI brings together multiple established tools into a single, reproducible pipeline that identifies candidate prophages, evaluates their quality, predicts host relationships, and characterizes key functional genes. Importantly, all results are summarized in an interactive report that simplifies interpretation. Applied to the MBARC22 mock community of 22 bacterial reference genomes as a workflow demonstration, PHI identified 41 candidate prophages across 14 hosts, including high- and medium-quality viral genomes. Most host genomes exhibited > 99% completeness and Conclusions By removing installation barriers and consolidating the outputs of multiple established tools, PHI lowers the barrier to advanced phage analysis, enabling both specialists and non-experts to explore phage-host interactions and their implications in areas such as microbiome research, biotechnology, and environmental science.

papers.title: A comprehensive analysis of CBER experience with AAV gene therapy IND submissions.
papers.authors: Bing S, Argaw T, Kaushal M, Mazor R.

papers.title: Massive atlas of brain region linked to a host of diseases is the most detailed yet.
papers.authors: Naddaf M.

papers.title: PANGEA: an integrated cell atlas across diverse biological contexts enables systematic profiling of multicellular responses in human diseases.
papers.authors: Kim S, Cheong S, Lee S, Kim Y, Xie R, Koh IG, La J, Hwa C, An H, Park J, An JY, Wang B, Park JE.
papers.abstract: Diseases affect multiple cell types within tissues, but the overall landscape of the multicellular responses in human diseases remains largely unexplored. Here we categorize the multicellular responses of human diseases based on a remapped atlas of human cells, PANGEA, incorporating 12.6 million cells acquired from a pipeline that automatically processes raw sequence files from public repositories. We constructed a hierarchical cell classification framework comprising 32 major cell types and 165 cellular subtypes. On the basis of this annotation framework, we explored an extensive atlas of human cells containing 46.5 million cells from 160 diseases across 48 organs and revealed core archetypes of human diseases repeatedly found across organs. We show that this cell atlas could also serve as a reference for unbiased analysis in spatial transcriptomics, revealing spatial features associated with immunotherapy responses. Collectively, our study provides foundational resources for cell ontologies, enabling cross-tissue comparisons of cellular features in human diseases.

papers.title: Open foundation models for clinical AI.
papers.authors: Bansal V.

papers.title: Epigenetic gatekeeping enables genome-scale horizontal gene transfer in eukaryotic cells.
papers.authors: Aoki R, Nishihara H, Sakamoto T, Sato Y, Kuramoto T, Fukuda M, Matsunaga TM, Uehara A, Slane D, Kawanishi Y, Mori S, Nagaoka D, Hirakawa M, Gao H, Maejima D, Minoura Y, Suto Y, Ishii K, Anthony CJ, Ishiyama S, Kato S, Inui Y, Wada N, Mogi Y, Yoshida Y, Matsuzaki M, Suzuki T, Kuroiwa T, Ohkawa Y, Ikawa T, Lister R, Maruyama S, Kimura H, Matsunaga S.
papers.abstract: Horizontal gene transfer drives rapid evolutionary innovation, yet well-substantiated cases are largely confined to prokaryotes. Eukaryote-to-eukaryote transfer remains exceptionally rare, and direct genome-scale demonstrations are absent. Here, inspired by endosymbiotic genome acquisition, we show that mammalian cells can initiate genome-scale horizontal gene transfer through phagocytic uptake of intact algal cells, albeit at a much lower frequency than cell fusion. Live-cell imaging captures the early nuclear appearance of transferred algal DNA after fusion, while genome sequencing and cytogenetic analyses reveal stable retention of chromosome-scale algal DNA in mammalian cells. Hybrid cells maintain more than 16 Mb of algal DNA, including intact chromosomes, as telomere-linked structures that persist for 95 generations without selection. Transferred algal DNA shows a progressive increase in DNA methylation together with enrichment of repressive histone modifications, forming heterochromatic domains that physically associate with host chromosomes. Notably, mammalian cells deficient in a de novo DNA methyltransferase show reduced stable establishment and retention of transferred algal DNA, supporting a gatekeeping role for DNA methylation in the stable accommodation of foreign genomes. Our findings reveal an epigenetic mechanism that contributes to the stable accommodation of large-scale foreign DNA between distantly related eukaryotes.

papers.title: A p32 family RNA editing factor acts in mitochondrial ribosome biogenesis.
papers.authors: Chauhan P, Sveráková-Škodová I, Wong JE, Říha J, Dedková J, Huber A, Müller L, Gerasimov ES, Zíková A, Yurchenko V, Gahura O.
papers.abstract: Biogenesis of mitochondrial ribosomes (mitoribosomes) in the unicellular parasite Trypanosoma brucei requires an exceptionally large toolkit of assembly factors, identified in stable precursors of large and small mitoribosomal subunits (mtLSU and mtSSU) by cryoEM. Here, using genetic modifications and proteomic characterization of the immunoprecipitated assemblosome, the earliest characterized mtSSU precursor, we determined that a cap of its distinctive protrusion of hitherto unknown composition consists of a p22 homotrimer. This protein was previously implicated in the uridine-insertion editing of the cytochrome c oxidase subunit II transcript. Our functional analysis confirmed this role but revealed that its ablation also causes a loss of mtSSU and a systemic reduction in mitochondrial translation, phenocopying the depletion of established mitoribosomal assembly factors. Consequently, the oxidative phosphorylation system and mitochondrial function are compromised. The p22 protein belongs to the p32 family. We showed that five of its six trypanosomal members are involved in mtSSU biogenesis. Notably, p32 proteins are associated with mitoribosomes in two other distant eukaryotic lineages. A eukaryote-wide mapping of p32 proteins documented that their presence correlates with the retention of mitochondrial genomes. Together, our findings redefine trypanosomal p22 as a dual-function coordinator of mitochondrial gene expression and reveal that the ancestral role of the p32 family is associated with mitochondrial translation.

papers.title: UC Irvine's BRAIN Initiative Cell Atlas Network (BICAN) Brain Procurement Program for the Center for Multiomic Human Brain Cell Atlas Project.
papers.authors: Berry JV, Tran BM, Wu G, Tan Z, Mendoza E, Kim MA, Arat Z, Lin PSH, Valenzuela L, Holmes TC, Virovka A, Thaxton M, Nguyen M, Stein S, Sigaroudi VR, De La Rosa A, Gawronski BJ, A Silva J, Gonzalez L, Wright S, Wood KA, Hui GK, Anousaya D, Gangeddula VR, Gama N, Gama J, Gross T, Bunney BG, Stein R, Sequeira PA, Mamdani F, Cartagena PM, Bunney WE, Lou J, Park HL, Wilson A, Brooks HM, Allhusen V, R Crawford J, Knight JM, Ren B, Ecker JR, Behrens MM, Keene CD, Stark CE, Head E, Yong WH, Monuki ES, Xu X.
papers.abstract: High-quality neurotypical postmortem human brain tissue is essential for constructing comprehensive human brain cell atlases, but it is difficult to obtain. Here, we describe the establishment of UC Irvine's Brain Procurement Program, a coordinated multi-institutional pipeline to collect and process neurotypical donor brains for multiomic mapping studies within the National Institute of Health (NIH) BRAIN Initiative Cell Atlas Network (BICAN) consortium. Through partnerships with the Orange County (OC) coroner's office, UC Irvine's Willed Body Program, UC Irvine's Medical Center (UCIMC), and the Children's Hospital of Orange County, we have developed standardized workflows encompassing donor identification, postmortem brain recovery and processing, region-of-interest dissection, neurotypical donor selection, and data management. Our experience demonstrates the feasibility of a community-based, multi-institutional procurement framework while highlighting challenges in recruiting neurotypical donors and ensuring demographic representation reflective of Southern California. We further identify opportunities to strengthen outreach and donation pathways. This program provides a scalable model for advancing population-reflective, high-quality human brain cell atlas efforts.

papers.title: ULK1 knockout increases recombinant transcript abundance and improves recombinant membrane protein expression.
papers.authors: Karlsson A, Dannemeyer M, Gunnarsson J, Thalén NB, Hicks J, Lundqvist M, Backmark A, Engberg S, Raynoschek C, Volk AL, Elgendy R, Munson MJ, Malm M, Roth RG, Rockberg J.
papers.abstract: Cell homeostasis depends on pathways balancing degradation and synthesis, including autophagy. Following a previous small-molecule screen, suggesting unc-51-like kinase 1 (ULK1) as a target affecting recombinant protein expression, we generated an ULK1 knockout (KO) Expi293 cell line. The KO cell line increased the expression of a secreted model protein by up to 1.7-fold, and transcriptomic analysis suggested downregulation of key macroautophagy-associated genes despite upregulated productivity-associated stress genes. Transcriptional upregulation of membrane organization and protein localization processes indicated a potential for membrane protein production. Production of three model membrane proteins in the KO cell line yielded up to a 2-fold increase, with the highest increase in the soluble fraction. Transcriptomic analyses suggested an increased recombinant transcript abundance, broader downregulation of autophagy, and weaker stress responses. These findings indicate that autophagy-associated pathways modulate cellular responses to recombinant protein production and point to ULK1-associated pathways for host-cell engineering, especially for enhanced membrane protein production.

papers.title: Population-scale integration of spatial omics networks for clinical prediction and biological discovery by SPIN.
papers.authors: Liu T, Ko E, Yang Y, Wu H, Unjitwattana T, Wang S, Kang J, Li Y, Garmire LX.
papers.abstract: Spatial omics enables the integration of high-dimensional molecular organization with clinical outcomes, yet incorporating spatial single-cell information into predictive models at the population scale remains challenging. We introduce SPIN (spatial predictive integration network), which integrates subject-specific, cell-type level, spatially informed co-expression or co-abundance networks for population-scale clinical prediction. Current implementation of SPIN includes three key modules: network construction, molecular-to-clinical prediction by Bayesian scalar-on-network regression with manifold learning (BSNMani), and visualization & interpretation module. In the Seattle Alzheimer's Disease Brain Cell Atlas (SEA-AD) multiplexed error-robust fluorescence in situ hybridization (MERFISH) transcriptomics cohort, SPIN achieved an accuracy of 0.81 for dementia-status prediction and revealed co-expression subnetworks with clear biological relevance. SPIN also achieved robust survival prediction in a breast cancer single-cell proteomics cohort (C-index = 0.78), identifying two survival-associated spatial proteomic subnetworks. In summary, SPIN is an interpretable tool for spatial-omics-based clinical outcome prediction at the population scale.

papers.title: Amyloid and tau display distinct patterns across Alzheimer's in anterior caudate.
papers.authors: Kana OZ, Postupna N, Agrawal A, Long B, Travaglini KJ, Gabitto MI, Lai HY, Mahoney JT, Xiao M, Bajwa T, Hulsey-Vincent H, Oyaizu SL, Mena GE, Hong J, Gelfand EC, Kaplan ES, Ariza J, Smith KA, McMillen DA, Chakka AB, Goldy J, Melief EJ, Barta S, Oyama A, Ruiz A, Pom CA, Ayala A, Bixby M, Huang A, Martin N, Cuevas NV, Olsen P, Nagra J, Chakrabarty R, Tieu M, Cardenas T, Torkelson A, Bertagnolli D, Guzman J, Ferrer R, Waters J, Grabowski TJ, Crane PK, Gatto NM, Miller JA, Hodge RD, Hawrylycz M, Keene CD, Lein ES, Close JL.
papers.abstract: The anterior caudate shows a pattern of Alzheimer's disease pathology that differs from the more extensively studied cortex. Across 41 donors, we found mostly diffuse amyloid beta plaques in gray matter and phosphorylated tau threads associated with white matter. Combining digital pathology with single-nucleus and spatial gene expression data, we detected no significant loss or gain in neuronal cell-type abundance with increasing pathology. However, we did observe increases in an FLT1+/IL1B+ microglial population with tau burden. Fast-spiking PTHLH-PVALB interneurons showed changes in genes related to ion channels, cellular trafficking, and phosphorylation. These findings offer a cellular-resolution reference for investigating how Alzheimer's disease affects subcortical brain regions.

papers.title: Tissue-to-bytes: A digital twin for single-cell omics data integration across BRAIN Initiative Cell Atlas Network.
papers.authors: Tao S, Li X, Huang Y, Abeysinghe R, Tong L, Lin S, Chou WC, Edgu-Fry E, Smith KA, Ng L, Cui L, Zhang GQ.
papers.abstract: The National Institutes of Health (NIH) BRAIN Initiative Cell Atlas Network (BICAN) requires coordinated management of scarce human brain tissue resources, standardized metadata, and transparent tracking of tissue-to-data transformations across distributed laboratories and centers. We present the Neuroanatomy-Anchored Information Management Platform (NIMP), a consortium-scale web-based application system developed to coordinate multimodal single-cell omics resource generation and maintain end-to-end provenance throughout the tissue-to-bytes life cycle. NIMP integrates donor registration, anatomical annotation, tissue allocation, sequencing workflows, quality assurance and quality control, and archive-data deposition within a unified data ecosystem infrastructure. Over 3 years of production-strength deployment, the platform has managed BICAN consortium's data and metadata for 762 human donors, 8,449 brain slabs, and 21,781 sequencing libraries across 11 laboratories, collectively supporting generation of more than 18 million single cells. NIMP provides a scalable and reusable platform for provenance-aware resource management, FAIR data generation, and future large-scale atlas and multi-network data coordination initiatives.

papers.title: Sub-second dopamine reinforcement shapes juvenile social play.
papers.authors: Chen X, Tao X, Zhong Z, Zhu F, Zhang Y, Wang Y, Wang M, Li Y, Sun L, Ouyang Y, Ding Z, An M, Zhao Y, Zhou J, Zhang R, Xiong W, Ji N, Li Y.
papers.abstract: Juvenile social play is critical for neurodevelopment, yet the neural mechanisms organizing moment-to-moment interactions remain elusive. Using social behavior sequencing (Social-seq)-an occlusion-robust 3D pose estimation and unsupervised clustering pipeline-we found that nucleus accumbens (NAc) dopamine was tightly coupled to sub-second social syllables during naturalistic interactions. In wild-type juveniles, males exhibited a sharper dopaminergic contrast between proactive play and forced submission than females did, consistent with sex-divergent play strategies. In Shank3-deficient autism models, this process was fundamentally corrupted: proactive play-evoked dopamine responses were abolished in males and significantly sign-inverted in females, with male-specific enhancements during non-social behaviors, driving social play deficits. A multi-agent reinforcement learning model parameterized by disrupted, play-related dopaminergic reinforcement values recapitulated mutant phenotypes. Closed-loop optogenetic stimulation of ventral tegmental area (VTA)-NAc dopamine projections, time-locked to proactive play, restored reciprocal play in Shank3-deficient rats. Sub-second dopaminergic reinforcement thus orchestrates naturalistic social behavior, providing a behaviorally contingent interventional framework for neurodevelopmental disorders.

papers.title: Harmonized brain ontology and 3D atlases for human, macaque, and marmoset basal ganglia.
papers.authors: Ding SL, Bhandiwad AA, Rosen BQ, Seeman SC, Long B, Johansen NJ, Bayindir U, Facer B, Fu Y, Halimi Y, Hou Y, Hu D, Huang M, Ikeda T, Lesnar P, Liu XP, Luo Z, Ray PL, Royall JJ, Schmitz MT, Uematsu A, Vezoli J, Yazdani F, Bakken TE, Freiwald WA, Hodge R, Kalmbach BE, Kennedy H, Kruse L, Mollenkopf T, Ng L, Osumi-Sutherland D, Thompson CL, Hayashi T, Hawrylycz MJ, Glasser MF, Van Essen DC, Zeng H, Lein ES.
papers.abstract: A major goal of the BRAIN Initiative Cell Atlas Network (BICAN) is to create a suite of foundational reference cell atlases and associated standards for human and nonhuman primate brains. Central to this goal is the creation of cross-species-harmonized cellular taxonomies and structural parcellations with formal ontologies that can be mapped onto 3D reference frameworks, bridging neuroimaging and cellular and histological resolutions. We describe an iterative approach, focused initially on the basal ganglia, to co-create structural and cellular ontologies for human, macaque, and marmoset brains and to map and refine structural parcellations into neuroimaging-based common coordinate frameworks. We create a Harmonized Ontology of Mammalian Brain Anatomy (HOMBA) to meet these needs. These references provide the framework for documenting and mapping all experimental sampling in BICAN, allowing analyses of cellular and molecular variation as a function of topographic position and enabling comparisons of cellular, molecular, and neuroimaging-based functional variation across species.

papers.title: An integrative single-cell epigenomic atlas annotates the regulatory genome of the adult mouse brain.
papers.authors: Wang Z, Zu S, Armand EJ, Loe TH, Rink JA, Wu W, Xie Y, Chang L, Zhu C, Johnson ND, Lee J, Willier JK, Cho S, Cao S, Barcoma AS, Emerson N, Liu H, Wang K, Saravanan B, Zhong G, Gibbs ZA, Gao X, Xu S, Guo D, Tu Z, Li YE, Ecker JR, Behrens MM, Ren B.
papers.abstract: Histone modifications underpin the cell-type-specific gene regulatory programs that drive the remarkable cellular diversity of the mammalian brain. Here, we jointly profiled four histone modifications and the transcriptome in 2.5 million nuclei from the adult mouse brain. By integrating these data with chromatin accessibility, DNA methylation, and three-dimensional genome organization, we constructed a unified epigenomic atlas spanning over 100 brain cell subclasses and assigned active, primed, and repressive chromatin states across 81% of the genome. Active chromatin states marked by combinatorial histone modifications better nominate candidate enhancers with functional support than chromatin accessibility alone, while H3K27me3- and H3K9me3-marked chromatin states delineate distinct modes of cell-type-specific gene repression. Finally, this multimodal resource enables the development of deep learning models that predict cell-type-specific epigenomic features and gene expression from DNA sequence, providing a comprehensive framework for annotating the brain regulatory genome and interpreting non-coding disease risk variants.

papers.title: Single-cell, multi-region profiling of the macaque brain across the lifespan.
papers.authors: Yang W, Watkins KL, DeCasien AR, O'Neill MB, Bohlen MO, O'Day DR, Smith EA, Duran M, Qiu C, Meleshko A, Vo A, Menke M, Calderon D, Cayo Biobank Research Unit, Sallet J, Higham JP, Martínez MI, Trapnell C, Starita LM, Montague MJ, Platt ML, Chiou KL, Shendure J, Snyder-Mackler N.
papers.abstract: Brain aging is a complex process with profound health and societal consequences. However, the molecular and cellular pathways that govern its progression, and inter- and intra-individual variation, remain poorly defined. We present a transcriptomic atlas of 5.3 million cells from 582 samples spanning 11 brain regions of 55 rhesus macaques (aged 0.5-21 years). We identify age-depleted and vulnerable neuronal populations and subtle, age-associated compositional differences in glia-detectable only at single-cell resolution. We chart convergent and divergent age-associated molecular signatures across regions and cell types, which include sex-specific signatures that could underlie biases in neurological disorders. These signatures overlap those of Alzheimer's disease (AD), which suggests that aging and AD share molecular roots that emerge at different ages and in region- and sex-specific windows of vulnerability. This work provides a temporal, regional, and sex-stratified atlas of the aging primate brain, offering insights into cell-type-specific vulnerabilities and regional heterogeneity with translational human relevance.

papers.title: A single-cell and spatial 3D multi-omic atlas of developing human basal ganglia.
papers.authors: Heffel MG, Xu H, Pastor-Alonso O, Li X, Baig MS, Ghoor RI, Li R, Kern C, Kum J, Zhang Y, Paino J, Rathore GS, Tsai MJ, Tai CY, Tucker G, Zhao Z, Hou A, von Behren Z, Bhade M, Li S, Sandoval K, Scholes J, Codrea F, Calimlim J, Liao EK, Leung G, Kim J, LeFevre A, Johnson R, Blanchard T, Eskin E, Flint J, Cotter JA, Pasaniuc B, Bintu B, Zhu Q, Mukamel EA, Ernst J, Paredes MF, Luo C.
papers.abstract: Human basal ganglia (BG) neurons and inhibitory interneurons originate in the ganglionic eminences (GEs), transient structures in the ventral prenatal brain. This study delineates the specification and maturation of GEs and GE-derived neurons using single-nucleus methyl-3C sequencing (snm3C-seq), spatial transcriptomics, and single-molecule chromatin + RNA imaging, and we found heterogeneous temporal progression across GE subregions. Spiny projection neurons (SPNs), the principal cells of the BG, acquire distinct subtypes through synchronized 3D-epigenomic remodeling, in contrast to the asynchronous maturation of other neuron types. Oligodendrocyte differentiation involves a transient short-range chromatin state during infancy, showing that the short-range and long-range chromatin conformations previously linked to terminal glial and neuronal fates can also be transient. The temporal cortex matured epigenomically faster than other cortical regions during this period. Lastly, SPNs were enriched in genetic risk for neuropsychiatric disease. Our study extends findings on unique 3D-epigenomic dynamics during human brain development.

papers.title: Circuit-aligned specialization of human basal ganglia astrocytes.
papers.authors: Fu Y, Kempynck N, Ding W, Turner MA, Garcia AD, Schmitz MT, Close J, Kapen I, Hewitt M, Seeman SC, Long B, Ding SL, Ho W, Mahoney JT, Mich JK, Levi BP, Klein A, Behrens MM, Ecker J, Aerts S, Johansen NJ, Hodge RD, Lein ES, Bakken TE.

papers.title: Spatial and regulatory organization of cell identity across the primate subcortex.
papers.authors: Dan S, Turner MA, DeBerardine M, Caceres L, Nieto-Caballero VE, Schembri J, Levandowski K, Cardenas C, Wang N, Li C, Basu S, Zheng H, Liu X, Höllt T, Feliciano J, Zhang Q, Nakamoto R, McMillen DA, Martin N, Cuevas NV, Olsen P, Nagra J, Campos J, VanNess MM, Waters J, Ransford S, Juneau Z, Hastings S, Barta S, Ruiz A, Ariza J, Raphael BJ, Zeng H, Lein ES, Lelieveldt B, Feng G, Long B, Krienen FM.
papers.abstract: Mammalian brain cell identity is shaped by intrinsic factors and external context. We present a spatially resolved transcriptomic and gene regulatory atlas of cell types across all subcortical regions in a primate, the common marmoset. Dense sampling and cross-species integration revealed spatially precise neuronal assemblies, including ones in complex midbrain and diencephalic structures. Chromatin accessibility and transcriptional identity are spatially tuned within and across subcortical structures; spatial gradients within hippocampal subfields are orchestrated by graded transcription factors acting through graded enhancers. The primate-expanded thalamic γ-aminobutyric acid (GABAergic) population shares transcriptional and regulatory syntax with conserved midbrain populations, reflecting an evolutionary adaptation compared with rodents. Similar regional expression across cell types can arise by distinct regulatory architectures, as observed in telencephalic astrocytes and neurons. Conversely, distant cell types can share regulatory programs despite divergent identities: striatal GABAergic spiny projection neurons and telencephalic glutamatergic neurons share a postsynaptic regulatory program despite divergent lineages, regions, and neurotransmitter identities.

papers.title: Single-cell multimodal atlas reveals regulatory programs in the human brain.
papers.authors: Xie Y, Chang L, Zhong G, Rink JA, Báez-Becerra CT, Armand E, Ding W, Li K, Bonne E, Indralingam HS, Lie A, Dong K, Loe T, Huang B, Wang Z, Barcoma AS, Willier JK, Knutson KW, Liu J, Cho S, Cao S, Russo KG, Young CK, Arzavala J, Sanchez Y, Bikkina A, Schenker-Ahmed N, Kern JC, Zhao Z, Klein A, Flores J, Tai CY, Olness J, Monell A, Moghadami S, Barragan C, Chen C, Owens W, Wang W, O'Connor C, Liem M, Marrin MV, Rose C, Alt SN, Emerson N, Osteen J, Lucero J, Zemke NR, Li D, Hodge RD, Wang T, Keene CD, Xu X, Zhu Q, Ecker JR, Behrens MM, Ren B.
papers.abstract: Direct measurement of chromatin states together with transcription is essential for understanding how cell-type-specific regulatory programs are established and maintained in the adult human brain. Here, we present a large-scale single-cell multimodal atlas by jointly profiling the transcriptome with active (H3K27ac) or repressive (H3K27me3) histone modifications across 18 adult brain regions. We targeted over 750,000 nuclei spanning 160 cell types and integrated these data with chromatin accessibility, DNA methylation, 3D genome architecture, and spatial transcriptomes. This framework resolved chromatin states for over 500,000 candidate regulatory elements, identified enhancer-gene links and regulatory programs, revealed Polycomb-associated ultra-long-range contacts, and uncovered brainwide epigenomic heterogeneity. We further developed a sequence-to-function model to predict cell-type-specific effects of candidate neurological disease variants. Finally, comparative analyses across species reveal conservation in active regulatory programs but divergence in repressive programs. Together, this study provides a comprehensive epigenomic reference for interpreting regulatory principles and epigenetic memory underlying human brain organization and disease.

papers.title: Multiscale spatial atlas of human basal ganglia cell types and communities.
papers.authors: Berackey BT, Tan Z, Wu G, Das SC, Li R, Esser B, Ye Q, Nafisi M, Park SS, Sequeira Mendieta PA, Berry J, Mamdani F, Zhu Q, Holmes TC, Li D, Wang T, Behrens MM, Ren B, Ecker JR, Bintu B, Xu X.
papers.abstract: The human basal ganglia comprise functionally varied nuclei, but their cell-type composition and spatial organization have not been comprehensively resolved. We generated a multi-region, subcellular-resolution spatial transcriptomic atlas by integrating multiplexed error-robust fluorescence in situ hybridization (MERFISH)+ and spatiotemporal enhanced-resolution omics sequencing (Stereo-seq) across four neurotypical donors. The datasets profiled ∼7.9 million cells across the caudate, putamen, nucleus accumbens, and globus pallidus, resolving 60 transcriptionally distinct cell types. We identify region-selective molecular and spatial diversification of spiny projection neurons and non-neuronal populations. Subcellular RNA localization captures somatic size and projection-inferred signatures, reflecting direct- and indirect-pathway topology. Cellular community analyses reveal astrocyte and oligodendrocyte subclusters enriched at striosome-matrix borders, while primate-expanded interneurons are confined to matrix territories. Cross-species comparisons reveal conserved and species-specialized organization, including orthologous striosome-matrix architecture and conserved dorsolateral-to-ventromedial transcriptional gradients. Together, this multi-centimeter-scale human basal ganglia atlas links cell types, spatial architecture, and subcellular transcript topography across scales.

papers.title: Single-cell analysis of chromatin state and transcriptome in the human basal ganglia.
papers.authors: Chang L, Li K, Xie Y, Zhong G, Rink JA, Báez-Becerra CT, Lie A, Indralingam HS, Loe T, Dong K, Gao X, Wang Z, Zu S, Kern JC, Zhao Z, Boone E, Flores J, Monell A, Olness J, Barragan C, Osgood E, Owens W, Schenker-Ahmed N, Zhang W, Liu D, Barcoma AS, Willier JK, Knutson KW, Russo KG, Liu J, Cho S, Arzavala J, Young CK, Sundaram GV, Manning AC, Sanchez Y, Bikkina A, Berry JV, O'Connor C, Liem M, Marrin MV, Rose C, Alt SN, Zhu C, Zemke NR, Ding W, Klein A, Fu Y, Johansen N, Bakken TE, Hodge RD, Keene CD, Lein ES, Li D, Zhu Q, Wang T, Xu X, Ecker JR, Behrens MM, Ren B.
papers.abstract: The basal ganglia are central to motor control, learning, emotion, and reward processing, and their dysfunction contributes to many neurological and psychiatric disorders. Here, we generated a single-cell multi-omic atlas of histone modifications and transcriptomes across eight basal ganglia regions from neurotypical human donors. This atlas resolved cell-type- and region-specific landscapes of active and repressive candidate cis-regulatory elements and delineated gene regulatory networks underlying cell identity. We found that the combinatorial expression of homeobox transcription factors provides distinctive molecular descriptors of neuronal cell identities in the basal ganglia. Integration with matched MERFISH spatial transcriptomics further uncovered regional heterogeneity in epigenomic and transcriptional programs. Finally, we used this atlas to interpret noncoding risk variants associated with neuropsychiatric disorders and to construct a deep-learning model that predicts gene regulatory activities and variant effects. Together, this work provides a multimodal regulatory framework for understanding human basal ganglia organization, evolution, and disease genetics.

papers.title: Multimodal single-cell epigenomic and 3D genome atlas of the human basal ganglia.
papers.authors: Ding W, Klein A, Báez-Becerra CT, Rink JA, Bartlett A, Wang R, Zeng Q, Castanon RG, Nery JR, Osgood E, Owens W, Petrella A, Chen C, Saldaña Acerbo A, Barcoma AS, Liu J, Russo KG, Knutson KW, Young CK, Willier JK, Barragan C, Arzavala J, Cho S, Altshul J, Chan D, Soma E, Luo J, Jain M, Velazquez S, Sundaram GV, Manning AC, Sanchez Y, Bikkina A, Fu Y, Komandur K, Doan E, Fu S, O'Connor C, Liem M, Marrin MV, Rose C, Alt SN, Berry J, Kern JC, Boone E, Tian W, Chen H, Xie Y, Wu Y, Hariharan M, Li K, Chang L, Johansen N, Zhang W, Zhao Z, Flores J, Tai CY, Olness J, Schenker-Ahmed N, Liu XP, Zhu Q, Kalmbach BE, Hodge RD, Bakken TE, Lein ES, Li D, Wang T, Xu X, Ren B, Behrens MM, Ecker JR.
papers.abstract: The basal ganglia (BG) underlie motor control, reward processing, and many neurological and psychiatric disorders, yet cell-type-resolved epigenomic and 3D genome maps of the human BG remain limited. Here, we present a multimodal single-cell atlas of DNA methylation (261,331 nuclei) and 3D chromatin conformation (229,286 nuclei) from eight subregions, harmonized under the BG consensus taxonomy and integrated with matched data across multiple regulatory layers. We identify millions of differentially methylated regions across cell types, enriched for distinct transcription factor motifs, and link them to disease-associated heritability. We characterize the POU6F2 + STR D2 SMYD2-HTR7 spiny projection neuron (SPN) subtype, with concordant signatures across multiple modalities, and reveal region-specific methylation and contact gradients. Integrative gene regulatory networks (GRNs) predict cell-type-resolved enhancer-promoter interactions, nominating candidate regulatory mechanisms for Parkinson's disease (PD) risk variants at SNCA. Finally, multiplexed error-robust fluorescence in situ hybridization (MERFISH) profiling combined with cross-species Patch-seq identifies a neuronal subtype, STR FS PTHLH-PVALB GABA, with electrophysiological differences across the striatal matrix-striosome (MS) boundary.

papers.title: Common variation of cell abundances and gene expression in the human striatum.
papers.authors: Burger SC, Nemesh J, Yoo O, Muratoglu E, Vanderburg C, Yuan J, Shakir K, Mello CJ, Gao H, Rayan NA, Finn E, Milidantri J, Mohsin A, Kim K, Drouin S, Budnik N, Goldman M, Bratchikov S, Fritch H, Genovese G, Hogan M, Catalini O, Kashin S, Rockweiler N, Wysoker A, Macaisa L, Reese L, Flowers K, Kraft AW, Fleming SJ, Coe M, Gunaratne R, Spina L, Fischer G, Crombie C, Kamitaki N, Macosko EZ, Ichihara K, McCarroll SA.
papers.abstract: The cellular and molecular bases of inter-individual variation in the human brain are not yet understood, particularly beyond the neocortex. Here, we describe cellular and gene-expression variation in the striatum and prefrontal cortex from single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) analysis of 3.9 million nuclei from 178 adult brain donors. People with more astrocytes, microglia, or oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs) in any one brain region tended to have this property in all gray-matter regions sampled. OPC proportions declined by 40% across ages 30-80 in the cortex and striatum. Age-associated gene-expression changes differed substantially across cell types. Donor age was predicted from RNA-expression patterns with a median absolute error of 6.6 years across cell types. Common genetic variants were associated with the expression of nearly 10,000 genes; these effects were mostly cell-type specific and distinguished striatal from cortical neurons. These open-access data provide a foundation for future studies of human brain variation and vulnerabilities.

papers.title: Mesoscale molecular architecture of the striatum across cell types and adult aging.
papers.authors: Kraft AW, Lee M, Gao H, Mohsin A, Rayan NA, Lawler AJ, Kim G, Milidantri J, Vanderburg C, Balderrama K, Nadaf N, Kumar V, Flowers K, Finn E, Shabet M, Muratoglu E, Yoo O, Shakir K, Nemesh J, Burger SC, Drouin S, Catalini O, Raj M, Budnik N, Reese L, McCarroll SA, Ichihara K, Macosko EZ.
papers.abstract: The human striatum governs diverse motor, cognitive, and affective behaviors yet lacks the obvious cytoarchitectural boundaries defining functional territories elsewhere in the brain. Using Slide-tags single-nucleus spatial transcriptomics, we profiled 1.1 million cells across 19 postmortem donors to uncover the striatum's spatial organization. These data revealed a consistent subdivision of the striatum into six zones, each defined by molecularly distinct populations of spiny projection neurons (SPNs) and featuring spatially coordinated neuron-astrocyte interaction networks. To determine their structural relevance, we generated a companion mouse spatial atlas that identified four homologous zones that aligned with territories defined by brain-wide afferent projections. Finally, imputing zonal identities onto a 131-donor single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) cohort revealed that dorsal zones exhibit the greatest age-related transcriptional change and that the expression differences defining zonation attenuate with age. This resource establishes a conserved mesoscale spatial framework for the mammalian striatum, linking single-cell molecular identity to structural connectomics and aging.

papers.title: Spatial transcriptomics reveals molecular organization of human and nonhuman primate basal ganglia.
papers.authors: Hewitt MN, Turner MA, Johansen N, McMillen DA, Dan S, DeBerardine M, Ruiz A, Huang M, Quon J, Fu Y, Kapen I, Barta S, Martin N, Cuevas NV, Olsen P, Nagra J, Campos J, VanNess MM, Ransford S, Juneau Z, Hastings S, Ching L, Kunst M, Basu S, Höllt T, Li C, Lelieveldt B, Yazdani F, Zhang Q, Levandowski K, Feng G, Rosen BQ, Glasser MF, Hayashi T, Garcia AD, Kana O, Maltzer ZM, Campagnola L, Jarsky T, Kruse L, Freiwald W, Keene CD, Van Essen DC, Ariza J, Waters J, Krienen FM, Bakken TE, Hodge RD, Ng L, Zeng H, Lein ES, Close JL, Long B, Seeman SC.
papers.abstract: The basal ganglia (BG) are interconnected subcortical nuclei with a complex topographical organization that orchestrate goal-directed behaviors and are implicated in neurodegenerative movement disorders. We generated a cellular-resolution spatial transcriptomics atlas of the BG in human, rhesus macaque, and common marmoset, sampling over one million cells in each species. By integrating spatial data with a cross-species consensus single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) cell-type taxonomy, this atlas reveals principles of molecular organization within and across structures. Extensive spatial sampling across the rostral-caudal axis illuminates complex, yet highly stereotyped, multi-axis gene expression gradients superimposed onto discrete compartments of the striatum. Additionally, we identify core-shell organization of the internal globus pallidus. This unified, cross-species spatial transcriptomics atlas will be a foundational resource for characterizing the molecular and functional organization of the BG and their roles in health and disease.

papers.title: Cross-species multiomic atlas of the primate basal ganglia.
papers.authors: Johansen NJ, Fu Y, Schmitz M, Dubuc A, Kempynck N, Wirthlin M, Garcia AD, Hewitt M, Turner MA, Seeman SC, Long B, Liu XP, Budzillo A, Dan S, DeBerardine M, Kapen I, Yanny AM, Ding W, Avola A, Barlow ST, Bertagnolli D, Bhandiwad A, Nieto Caballero VE, Caceres L, Casper T, Chakka AB, Chakrabarty R, Clark M, Daniel S, Eggermont J, Ferrer R, French L, Gloe J, Goldy J, Guilford N, Guzman J, Hirschstein D, Ho W, James K, Jones DL, Jungert M, Kannan M, Kedzierska KZ, Kroes T, Leytze M, Manning A, McCue R, Morrison C, Nguy B, Otto S, Pena N, Pham T, Phillips E, Rajagopal A, Rimorin C, Rivera AD, Rocha D, Sanchez R, Schau G, Schembri J, Shapovalova NV, Sherman J, Thijssen J, Tieu M, Torkelson A, Tran A, Vieth A, Wang Y, Yuan D, Close J, Daigle TL, Dalley R, Dee N, Ding SL, Fiabane E, Gouwens N, Huynh G, Lee BR, Levi BP, McMillen D, Miller JA, Mollenkopf T, Ng L, Ray PL, Sobieski C, Sorensen SA, Yao Z, Yazdani F, Freiwald W, Ecker JR, Lelieveldt B, Kalmbach B, Keene CD, Gillis J, Osumi-Sutherland D, Ting JT, Zeng H, Smith K, Krienen FM, Hodge RD, Lein ES, Bakken TE.
papers.abstract: The basal ganglia (BG) are conserved brain regions essential for motor control, learning, emotion, and cognition and are implicated in neurological and psychiatric disease, yet a unified cross-species taxonomy of BG cell types is lacking. We present a multiomic consensus atlas of 1.8 million nuclei from humans, macaques, and marmosets spanning eight BG structures, integrating gene expression, open chromatin, and spatial profiling. Alignment across species and to mouse and human whole-brain atlases identifies 61 homologous cell types conserved over 76 million years. Dorsal-ventral spatial identity is more conserved than D1/D2 receptor or striosome/matrix identity, and striatum (STR) D2 SMYD2-HTR7 spiny projection neurons have distinct molecular, electrophysiological, and morphological features. Cis-regulatory analysis reveals conserved sequence grammars that encode cell identity and inform viral targeting, and cell-type-resolved mapping localizes psychiatric and neurodegenerative risk to specific BG cell populations. This work provides a foundational resource for BG evolution, function, and disease.

papers.title: Decomposition of the S. aureus pangenome reveals evolving genetic repertoire associated with adaptation and virulence.
papers.authors: Chauhan SM, Palsson BO, Monk JM.
papers.abstract: Bacterial pangenomes are mosaics of vertically inherited chromosomal backgrounds and horizontally acquired mobile elements, yet existing analysis methods either assign each genome to a single phylogenetic group or treat genes independently, failing to resolve this composite architecture. Here, we show that non-negative matrix factorization decomposes the accessory pangenome of 1,398 curated Staphylococcus aureus genomes into 24 additive gene modules ("phylons") that cleanly separate lineage-defining components from mobile genetic element repertoires, achieving 90% reconstruction accuracy with 96% precision. The additive representation, where each genome equals a primary lineage phylon plus one or more mobilome phylons, recovers known biology (clonal complex structure, immune evasion cluster types) and reveals previously uncharacterized structure, including multiple horizontal transfer events linking the CC30 and hybrid ST239 pandemic lineages. Annotation-independent validation with geNomad confirmed that 75-96% of mobilome phylon gene instances physically reside within prophage regions across all 1,398 genomes, while coordinate-level analysis of the remainder revealed prophage boundary effects, chromosomally integrated elements, and composite mobilome architecture rather than false assignments. External validation on 966 independent draft genome assemblies yielded zero false-positive lineage assignments (mean AUC = 0.996) with no dependence on assembly quality, and mobilome phylons discriminated human from livestock hosts and methicillin-resistant from methicillin-susceptible isolates without retraining. A lightweight projection tool, phylon_assign, enables rapid classification of new genomes. The generalization of this framework from Escherichia coli and Enterobacter to Staphylococcus aureus - species with fundamentally different pangenome structures - establishes non-negative matrix factorization as a scalable, organism-agnostic approach for resolving the modular architecture of bacterial pangenomes.
