papers.title: Explainability in transformer-based models: methods, tools, and applications in natural language processing and bioinformatics.
papers.authors: Karimi NM, Rezaeian M.
papers.abstract: In recent years, Transformer-based models have become state of the art in natural language processing (NLP) and have achieved exceptional performance in a wide range of tasks. Their impact has extended to critical domains such as healthcare and bioinformatics. Transformer models are nonlinear and complex, making it challenging for researchers to understand different aspects of model performance and decision-making processes. Given the widespread use of these models in data processing, particularly in applications related to human health, the need for interpretable and transparent models has become essential. The goal of this paper is to provide a comprehensive review of explainability methods for transformer models, as well as the interpretability tools commonly used in NLP and bioinformatics. First, interpretable methods in different domains are broadly categorized. It then presents a focused discussion on strategies for explaining transformer-based models. By analyzing and comparing these methods, their strengths, applicability to transformers, and limitations are highlighted. As model complexity increases, understanding model behavior becomes more challenging. Explainability techniques can help address this gap and support tasks such as error diagnostics, model improvement, and other applications. Greater clarity in a model's decision-making process can increase user confidence. Interpretable models are particularly important in critical applications such as drug design, where they can support deeper investigation and facilitate new discoveries. Finally, this paper outlines potential directions for future research.

papers.title: CRAFT: an antigen-specific TCR generative model for conditional de novo design with physicochemical constraints.
papers.authors: Yang X, Li Z, Li Z, Zhang W, Zhang X, Yang T, Liu M, Li X.
papers.abstract: T-cell receptors (TCRs) are essential to adaptive immunity and mediate the recognition and elimination of malignant or infected cells through antigen-specific interactions. Despite the clinical progress of TCR-based immunotherapies, computational de novo design of antigen-specific TCRs remains difficult. The main difficulties include the complexity of peptide-major histocompatibility complex (pMHC)-dependent recognition, strict physicochemical requirements at the binding interface, and the small amount of paired training data available for model development. Current generative approaches depend largely on 1D sequence statistics and do not capture pMHC presentation context, interfacial physicochemical properties, and native receptor priors within a unified framework. We present conditional reconstruction of antigen fragments for TCRs (CRAFT), a decoupled generative model for pMHC-conditioned de novo design of antigen-specific TCR CDR3$\beta $ sequences under physicochemical constraints. With large-scale pretraining, CRAFT learns base representations that help reduce the limitations imposed by data scarcity. We further incorporate antigen-derived contextual information to guide antigen-specific TCR CDR3$\beta $ sequence design. The architecture comprises an antigen encoder (PrimeBERT) that captures the pMHC context and an autoregressive decoder (PrimeTCR) that preserves native receptor priors. The encoder and decoder are coupled through cross-attention and augmented with Atchley factor embeddings, allowing CRAFT to incorporate physicochemical constraints relevant to antigen-conditioned receptor design during sequence decoding. Across multiple evaluations, CRAFT demonstrates competitive sequence naturalness, together with favorable performance in specific binding, and predicted structural plausibility. Overall, CRAFT provides a computational framework for developing personalized tumor immunotherapies. It also holds potential to support clinical translation by enabling the efficient, targeted discovery of candidate TCRs.

papers.title: SnoDB 3.0: a specialized database featuring murine and human annotation and cross-species correspondence for the snoRNA community.
papers.authors: Montmartin S, Bergeron D, Song KS, Thiaw AB, Erkan Ş, Coderre S, Govone M, Meliane Z, Hedjam J, Durand S, Abou Elela S, Whipple A, Marcel V, Scott MS.
papers.abstract: Small nucleolar RNAs (snoRNAs) are a large, evolutionarily conserved family of non-coding RNAs that guide ribosomal RNA (rRNA) modifications. Recent years have seen growing interest in the biological and biomedical roles of snoRNAs, their guided rRNA modifications, and their alternative functions. snoDB is a specialized database that aggregates human snoRNA annotations and features, including genomic location, host gene, conserved motifs, protein and RNA interactors, expression levels, as well as rRNA target sites and modification levels. In this third release, we expand the database to include murine snoRNAs with an equivalent level of annotation, update human snoRNA host genes, RNA interactors and protein interactors, and introduce new tools to establish snoRNA and rRNA target cross-species correspondence. snoDB 3.0 is available at https://bioinfo-scottgroup.med.usherbrooke.ca/snoDB/.

papers.title: PANTHER: the protein tree and function resource in 2027.
papers.authors: Mi H, Ebert D, Muruganujan A, Thomas PD.
papers.abstract: PANTHER (Protein ANalysis THrough Evolutionary Relationships) is a comprehensive resource of phylogenetic trees of protein-coding gene families. Trees are manually annotated with Gene Ontology (GO) terms describing how protein functional characteristics were gained and lost over time along tree branches, and these evolutionary models are used to create GO annotations for protein-coding genes. Orthologs, paralogs, and xenologs are assigned based on the trees. Here, we describe updates to the PANTHER resource since our previous published report in 2022. Since that time, the content of the database has been systematically improved: GO annotations of the trees have been expanded to increase coverage of genes by 20%-100% depending on the organism; thousands of families have been revised and ~100 added; and the PANTHER release pipeline has been modified to improve stability of the trees across versions. The expanded annotations for all 131 genomes in the PANTHER trees can be downloaded or used for analyzing gene lists directly on the PANTHER website, and users can now generate tree-based GO annotations for any sequence file using InterProScan.

papers.title: KinaseMD 2.0: an updated database of kinase mutations and drug response.
papers.authors: Hu X, Lin S, Fu S, Zeng J, Xu Z, Zheng T, Wang T, Liu X, Huang P, Li Z, Liu T, Xu H.
papers.abstract: Kinase mutations can alter activity, inhibitor response and downstream phosphorylation signaling, particularly within four resistance-associated substructures: gatekeeper, G-loop, αC-helix, and A-loop. KinaseMD 2.0 (http://modinfor.com/KinaseMD/) updates the kinase-centered database in three areas. Integrating source-curated annotations with Dr. Kinase predictions expanded substructure annotations from 1162 to 13 522 and kinase coverage from 388 to 547. Updated pharmacogenomic and signaling layers contain 422 244 drug-response measurements, 1614 candidate drug-resistance evidence records, and 359 600 predicted phosphorylation-network rewiring events. The new Kinase Perturbation Evidence Mapping (KPEM) workflow combines LLM-based literature extraction from an initial collection of over 480 000 publications with standardized processing of 30 public drug-treatment phosphoproteomic datasets. It provides 23 757 kinase-level records of literature-reported evidence and 53 029 phosphoproteomic records across 5124 drug/agent categories and 1598 disease contexts, distinguishing reported phosphorylation evidence from inferred kinase-associated signaling responses. By linking resistance-associated substructures, cancer mutations, drug response, and phosphorylation signaling, KinaseMD 2.0 supports studies of drug-resistance mechanisms and kinase-inhibitor design and development.

papers.title: CATH and TED in 2026: expansion in the number and diversity of CATH superfamilies.
papers.authors: Edmunds NS, Sillitoe I, Miller D, Waman VP, Alvarez-Carreño C, Jones DT, Bordin N, Orengo C.
papers.abstract: CATH (https://www.cathdb.info) is a widely used bioinformatics resource that classifies protein structural domains from the wwPDB and integrates evolutionary, structural, and functional annotation alongside interactive visualization and analysis tools. CATH is recognized as a Core Data Resource by ELIXIR and a Global Core Biodata Resource by the Global Biodata Coalition. CATH continues to expand its coverage of protein structure space by integrating experimentally determined structures from the Protein Data Bank with the rapidly growing collections of predicted structures from the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database as part of The Encyclopedia of Domains, the new sister resource of CATH. We provide an update on advances in new homology detection protocols and automated workflows providing end-to-end domain annotation and classification for processing large-scale protein structural data.

papers.title: The Chemical Probes Portal-2026: expanding and enhancing this expert review-based public resource to sustain chemical probe selection and application in bioscience.
papers.authors: Sarper M, Sanfelice D, Chen Y, Chitsazi R, Gingrich PW, Antolin AA, Bellenie B, Brennan PE, Edwards A, Müller S, Al-Lazikani B, Workman P.
papers.abstract: The Chemical Probes Portal (https://www.chemicalprobes.org) is an open, international, resource empowering scientific robustness by supporting responsible research using chemical probes. The Portal informs best-practice in the selection and application of small-molecule chemical probes through expert review, manual curation, and community engagement. Used correctly, high-quality chemical probes are powerful, versatile research tools enabling the fundamental study of protein function, target validation, and development of new therapeutics. Conversely, the inappropriate selection and use of these chemical tools can compromise experimental interpretation, reliability, and translational impact, highlighting the need for trusted advisory resources. The Portal addresses this challenge, providing a unique collection of curated data, expert reviews, and related guidance. We describe significant developments to the Portal's content and infrastructure. We have substantially expanded the content, with curated probes increasing by 26% since our last update. We have significantly enhanced website functionality through implementation of new, more informative probe pages, improved search tools and enhancements in data accessibility, machine readability, and interoperability. Together, these developments strengthen the Portal as a trustworthy, user-friendly provider of expert-reviewed chemical probe information and an increasingly valuable source of gold-standard FAIR, accessible data in the era of AI-assisted information discovery, underpinning reliable bioscience research.

papers.title: A genome-wide association study and genetic risk score for age at diabetes diagnosis support beta-cell dysfunction in young-onset diabetes in Chinese.
papers.authors: Fan B, Tam CHT, Luk AOY, Lau ESH, Lim CKP, Shi M, Wan R, Cheung SHM, Fan Y, Ng ACW, Wu H, Yang A, Lui JNM, Lee HM, Chow E, Kong APS, Ozaki R, O CK, Yu G, Huang C, Wang MHT, Wong SYS, Lee EKP, Hu A, Yan D, Jia W, Lee KF, Siu SC, Hui G, Tsang CC, Lau KP, Leung JYY, Cheung EYN, Tsang MW, Kam G, Lau IT, Li JKY, Yeung VTF, Lau E, Lo S, Fung S, Cheng YL, Chow CC, Fan X, Chan TF, Yip KYL, Lok S, Yu W, Tsui SKW, Lan HY, Szeto CC, Tang NLS, Tomlinson B, Huang Y, So WY, Ma RCW, Chan JCN, Hong Kong Diabetes Biobank Study Group and TRANSCEND Consortium.
papers.abstract: Background We investigated genetic variations driving young age-at-diabetes-diagnosis (ADD) and developed a genetic risk score (GRS) to identify Chinese individuals at risk of young-onset diabetes (YOD with ADD Methods We performed genome-wide association studies (GWAS) for ADD with internal and external replication in 22,611 individuals with type 2 diabetes (T2D, 20% with YOD) and identified Chinese-prioritized loci by conditioning on the polygenic risk score (PRS) of ADD constructed from publicly available datasets. We constructed ADD-GRS using genome-wide independent variants (p Results We identified three independent signals at genome-wide significance (P Conclusions Both known and novel T2D loci contribute to ADD in Chinese people and may be used to detect high risk individuals for early intervention to prevent or delay onset of YOD.

papers.title: Epigenetic heterogeneity in breast tumours informs diagnosis and prognosis.
papers.authors: Furth N, Riemenschneider C, Arieli Y, Avni M, Povolotski MY, Yung H, Karagach S, Atrakchi O, Erez N, Salame TM, Noberini R, Durand A, Jouault G, Dassa B, Zerbib M, Oren R, Golani O, Bar-Zakai B, Mavor Y, Friedman-Eldar O, Kadar-Sfarad H, Gilron S, Givon-Madhala O, Ronel N, Abu-Rmilah F, Moshe I, Ish-Shalom S, Yosepovich A, Kaplan M, Bakalenik M, Dadiani M, Tryggvadottir R, Shatkin G, Hakobyan M, Kovacsovics A, Mackowiak SD, Arnold A, McLaughlin S, Andreishcheva E, Shinde A, Zhang J, Jones D, Nili Gal-Yam E, Geiger T, Bonaldi T, Feinberg AP, Meissner A, Vallot C, Ron G, Shema E.
papers.abstract: Breast cancer, the most diagnosed cancer among women, is stratified by gene expression patterns into luminal and basal-like subtypes, and the latter is associated with worse prognosis 1-3 . Recent advances in single-cell technologies have underscored the presence of intratumour heterogeneity, which poses substantial challenges in cancer treatment and achieving long-term disease-free survival 4-7 . Here we extensively profile epigenetic heterogeneity in a cohort of treatment-naive human luminal tumours, which were obtained directly after surgical resection. By applying a single-cell epigenetic approach based on cytometry by time-of-flight, we identify a recurrent subpopulation of basal-like cells in luminal tumours with a conserved epigenetic signature across patients. These basal-like cells, also identified by deconvolution of whole-genome DNA methylation patterns, are characterized by high expression of aggressive oncogenic traits and downregulation of hormone receptor signalling. Direct comparison of single-cell proteomic and genomic profiling of monomethylation and trimethylation of histone 3 on lysine 4 revealed that these marks are key features associated with loss of luminal identity. Finally, we highlight the potential of concomitant single-molecule profiling of histone modifications on cell-free nucleosomes in blood as an epigenetic liquid biopsy approach for early diagnosis of breast cancer. Moreover, the epigenetic basal signature measured in blood is linked to prognosis, which enables the identification of patients at increased risk for disease relapse.

papers.title: Evolutionary dynamics in the years preceding acute myeloid leukaemia.
papers.authors: Watson CJ, Poon GYP, MacGregor HAJ, Fonseca AVA, Apostolidou S, Damaskou A, Boniface C, Hackett S, Gentry-Maharaj A, Menon U, Blundell JR.
papers.abstract: Somatic evolution in ageing tissues underlies many cancers 1,2 . However, our quantitative understanding of the rules governing this pre-cancerous evolution remains incomplete. Here we exploit a unique collection of serial blood samples 3 , collected annually for up to a decade and beginning as early as 15 years before diagnosis of acute myeloid leukaemia, to provide a quantitative description of pre-cancerous evolutionary dynamics. Using deep duplex sequencing and evolutionary theory, we quantify the acquisition ages and fitness effects of the key driver events in acute myeloid leukaemia development. The first driver mutations are typically acquired in the first few decades of life, when the blood remains highly polyclonal. These early slow-growing clones subsequently acquire multiple further driver mutations that confer selective advantages up to 100-fold larger than the early drivers. These faster-growing clones harbouring multiple driver mutations can cause complete somatic sweeps of the blood decades before diagnosis, a feature strongly associated with future acute myeloid leukaemia. Our data show that the clonal dynamics of blood are consistent with a set of remarkably simple evolutionary rules that strike a balance between chance and determinism.

papers.title: Advancing multimodal tools to decode organoid complexity.

papers.title: Saturation genome editing of BRCA1 across cell types improves interpretation of variant pathogenicity.
papers.authors: Dace P, Forrester NM, Zanti M, Cubitt L, Terwagne C, Buckley M, van Veen EM, Wilson TS, Scaffidi P, Michailidou K, Findlay GM.
papers.abstract: Germline pathogenic BRCA1 variants predispose women to breast and ovarian cancer. Despite accumulation of functional evidence, over half of reported single-nucleotide variants in BRCA1 lack a definitive clinical interpretation. Furthermore, the consistency of variant effects across cell types remains largely unexplored. Here we performed saturation genome editing (SGE) of BRCA1 in HAP1 cells to score 4,113 previously unassayed variants. Additionally, we developed an SGE assay in human mammary epithelial cells (HMECs), allowing comparison of effects across cell lines, drug treatments and genetic backgrounds. We identified 538 variants impacting gene function through distinct mechanisms. HAP1 function scores discriminate between known pathogenic and benign variants with near-perfect accuracy. Intriguingly, however, nearly half of HAP1 loss-of-function variants scored neutrally in HMECs. We show that discordantly scored variants are hypomorphic and confer intermediate cancer risk. Overall, this work demonstrates how performing SGE across cell models improves the functional interpretation of rare variants.

papers.title: Independent interferometric observable confirms black hole shadow in M87.
papers.authors: Lai S, Thyagarajan N, Wong OI, Diakogiannis F.
papers.abstract: A new epoch for direct visualization of accretion dynamics near the event horizon of a black hole began when the Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration synthesized an Earth-sized aperture with millimetre radio interferometry and published the first reconstructed image 1-4 of a black hole shadow at the core of radio galaxy Messier 87 (M87). The image appeared as a ring-like structure, representing the gravitationally lensed and redshifted emission around the central supermassive black hole, M87*, located at the galactic nucleus. However, application of various data analysis and imaging heuristics resulted in divergent representations of M87* fine-scale features 3,5-7 , with some external analyses even challenging the fundamental ring-like morphology of the source 8,9 . Such difficulties arise as a consequence of the inherent sparsity of the very long baseline interferometry measurements, making interferometric image reconstruction an inadequately constrained problem. Moreover, the solution is sensitive to instrument calibration, post-processing algorithms and imaging hyperparameters. Here we apply an independent imaging algorithm that we have developed to the M87* dataset that is free from prescriptive morphological priors and founded on observables immune to instrument calibration errors. We reconstruct the black hole shadow image and unequivocally reproduce a ring-like morphology, with an angular diameter of 42.2 ± 1.5 μas corresponding to a black hole mass of 6.5 ± 0.5 billion solar masses assuming nominal scaling parameters, observed at an inclination angle of approximately 20° from the approaching jet.

papers.title: Genome-wide association study meta-analysis identifies susceptibility loci informing Ewing sarcoma etiology and potential mechanisms of risk.
papers.authors: Hubbard AK, Neyret-Kahn H, Müller-Nurasyid M, Löw D, Strauch K, Lee OW, Raduski AR, Yang T, Zhou W, Stratton EW, Jay O, Grossetête S, Song AJ, Dutta D, Hutchinson AA, Hicks BD, Manning M, Liu J, Boyce C, Hartmann W, Dirksen U, Kulozik AE, Metzler M, Krumbholz M, Teumer A, Völzke H, Völker U, Schiffman JD, Khan J, Hudson MM, Ness KK, Wang Z, Janeway KA, Lupo PJ, Spector LG, Huang WY, Moore SC, Chanock SJ, Grünewald TGP, Delattre O, Machiela MJ, Ewing Sarcoma Germline Genetics Group.
papers.abstract: Ewing sarcoma (EwS) is a rare, aggressive pediatric malignancy driven by FET::ETS family fusions (EWSR1::FLI1 in >85% of cases) with no established environmental risk factors. We analyzed 2,014 EwS cases and 10,525 cancer-free controls in a two-stage analysis that combined an international genome-wide association study and a case-parent trio study. The combined meta-analysis identified 18 variants at 14 susceptibility loci (9 novel and 5 replicated) with moderate effect sizes (odds ratios ≥ 1.25). Integrative analyses of the EwS loci revealed enrichment of enhancer-like GGAA microsatellites, with evidence for binding of the EWSR1::FLI1 fusion at most loci. EWSR1::ETS knockdown in EwS cell lines resulted in dysregulated genes at susceptibility loci related to skeletal/muscle development, RNA binding/processing, and chromatin regulation. Our findings provide insights into the inherited component of EwS, highlighting a genetic architecture in which common germline variation with moderate effects interacts with somatic EWSR1::FLI1 fusions to promote sarcomagenesis by dysregulating local genes.

papers.abstract: Wölbert et al. established a strategy that integrated conserved cell-type-specificity with conservation of transcriptional levels to identify robust signature genes. By leveraging evolutionary conservation as an additional dimension of cell identity, this strategy would facilitate cell identity annotation across species, particularly in non-model organisms and rare cell populations.

papers.title: Burst-to-burst information resetting in sequential rhythmic neural activity.
papers.authors: Sanchez-Martin P, Elices I, Garrido-Peña A, Garcia-Saura C, Levi R, Rodriguez FB, Varona P.
papers.abstract: In multiple neural systems, networks of bursting neurons generate and coordinate robust sequential rhythms, such as those observed in central pattern generators (CPGs) that control motor activity. In this paper, we combine electrophysiological experiments and biophysical models of the pyloric CPG to investigate cycle-by-cycle coordination resetting in sequential rhythms. In particular, we focus our analysis on the variability constraints of sequence intervals defined by the burst onset and offset time references, which structure the timing of the rhythmic CPG sequence cycle-by-cycle. We identified the conditions under which sequential dynamical invariants emerge as robust relationships between specific intervals within the same cycle, and when such relations reset at each cycle or extend between intervals of consecutive cycles. Our results help understand the mechanisms underlying the autonomous cycle-by-cycle sequential coordination and the relationships between intervals from consecutive cycles when a slow modulatory action establishes a common trend across the rhythm.

papers.title: Pepti-DrugPhAI: Multimodal AI-evaluator for functional pharmacokinetics and toxicity of peptides.
papers.authors: Bogdanova EA, Lukianov TF, Chernukhin AV, Shaytan AK.
papers.abstract: Peptide drugs exhibit exceptional selectivity for biological targets and high functional activity making them among the most promising therapeutic agents. However, unsatisfactory pharmacokinetic characteristics remain a critical barrier to their implementation. They often become the primary reason for the failure of promising candidates in preclinical and clinical trials. To address this issue, we present Pepti-DrugPhAI - a comprehensive algorithm for the precise prediction of the pharmacokinetics and toxicity of a wide range of peptide compounds. Unlike many existing solutions, the proposed algorithm is multimodal and can simultaneously process both SMILES representations of chemical structures and amino acid sequences. This ensures efficient processing not only of canonical peptides but also of non-canonical modifications, cyclic structures, and peptide-like small molecules. We also created an original dataset for model training integrating data from public databases and relevant scientific publications. The algorithm simultaneously predicts key parameters including membrane permeability (Caco-2 and PAMPA penetration), distribution and excretion (half-life, clearance, volume of distribution), as well as general and specific toxicity profiles (neurotoxicity, hemolytic activity). A key innovation of the study is the integration of functional pharmacokinetic scoring. The model not only predicts ADMET values but also calculates an adaptive suitability rating for a compound in the context of its specific biological activity. We have conducted a comparative analysis of various data encoding strategies implementing a stack of models ranging from classical machine learning methods to modern transformers and language models in classification modes. Results from testing on independent test sets demonstrate high prediction accuracy and interpretability of features making Pepti-DrugPhAI a powerful tool for more robust selection of promising peptide drug candidates. All data and the code are available in the GitHub repository at https://github.com/EABogdanova/Pepti-DrugPhAI.

papers.title: PhysInfer: A physics-constrained neural network for adaptive inference of transcriptional bursting from single-cell RNA-seq.
papers.authors: Zeng X, Zhang J, Li S, Wang H.
papers.abstract: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) has established that gene expression is driven by stochastic transcriptional bursting. However, inferring burst dynamics from static scRNA-seq snapshots is fundamentally constrained by parameter unidentifiability and model topology mismatch. Here, we propose PhysInfer, an unsupervised framework that integrates a physics-constrained neural network with adaptive model selection and parameter decoupling. A physics-informed loss function, combining stationary-distribution likelihood with zero-count anchoring, reparameterizes the optimization from unidentifiable microscopic rates to an interpretable macroscopic burst-quantity representation of burst size and burst frequency, thereby providing an interpretable parameterization for assessing practical recoverability in static data. Validation on synthetic data with known ground-truth parameters confirms high inference accuracy in low-to-medium activation regimes and shows that recovery of BS and productive BF becomes increasingly condition-dependent as the ON-state probability approaches saturation; under different recovery criteria, the condition-specific upper Pon limit for simultaneously recovering BS and productive BF varies with cell number and capture efficiency. Applied to a mouse embryonic fibroblast (MEF) dataset, PhysInfer reconstructs a transcriptional dynamic manifold across the 2,137-gene secondary BIC analysis set, showing cross-gene variation in fitted burst frequency and burst size. A model-specific stationary likelihood combined with zero-count anchoring improves robustness to zero-heavy observations. The adaptive topology module further identifies a distinct subset of genes with stable support for an effective sequential 3-state representation, revealing distributional structure beyond that captured by standard 2-state fitting. PhysInfer thus provides a robust, topology-adaptive, and interpretable solution for characterizing transcriptional kinetic patterns from static single-cell transcriptomic snapshots.

papers.title: Sphinx: An R package for adaptive spatial neighborhood modeling and functional analysis in spatial omics.
papers.authors: Yan M, Tan X, Liu Z, Zhang S, Du Y, Li H, Chen L, Xie L.
papers.abstract: Spatial omics enables analysis of tissue microenvironmental heterogeneity, but most spatial tools are optimized for transcriptomics and poorly suited to proteomics data. We developed Sphinx, an R package providing a comprehensive workflow for spatial proteomics, including preprocessing, cell annotation, adaptive spatial neighborhood modeling, and functional characterization. Importantly, it introduces an adaptive parameter selection framework guided by spatial statistical metrics and incorporates computational optimizations for large-scale datasets, enabling robust neighborhood modeling. Notably, Sphinx offers improved computational efficiency and scalability. Across lung adenocarcinoma, colorectal cancer, and mouse spleen datasets, Sphinx robustly identifies cell types and spatial functional units, including tertiary lymphoid structures. We also explored the application of Sphinx to paired high-resolution spatial transcriptomics datasets, illustrating its potential applicability. Sphinx provides a flexible and efficient framework for spatial proteomics, enabling robust characterization of spatial organization and tissue microenvironments.

papers.title: An antigen-specific protein language model guides CDR optimization for antibody design.
papers.authors: Ashraf FB, Paco K, Zebardast S, Zhang Z, Mooney R, Dávila Ojeda CJ, Mendivil MP, Alam RM, Chen E, Ogu I, Lay JA, Yang TY, Barroso da Silva FL, Johal M, Tolstorukov I, Sazinsky MH, Ray A, Lonardi S.
papers.abstract: The capacity of an antibody to recognize and bind an antigen with high specificity and strength (i.e., its binding affinity) is a key determinant in the design and optimization of neutralizing antibodies against pathogenic targets. Here we introduce Ab-Affinity, a fine-tuned protein language model (PLM) that predicts the binding affinity of an antibody against a target peptide within the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein. Cross-validation results shows that that Ab-Affinity outperforms other PLM-based affinity predictors when evaluated on a held-out validation and independent test sets. When integrated with a genetic algorithm and simulated annealing for sequence diversification and fitness optimization, Ab-Affinity enables the generation of candidate antibodies exhibiting over 100-fold improvement in predicted binding affinity relative to its parental (natural) antibody. More broadly, antibodies designed with Ab-Affinity attain higher predicted binding affinities than those produced by alternative mutational strategies, yielding synthetic antibodies with favorable predicted biophysical characteristics. Molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations for the strongest synthetic candidates indicate enhanced interactions and increased stability with the target peptide epitope within the spike protein. Experimental validation in vitro for a top-ranked candidate reveals an apparent increase in binding relative to its parental antibody. All model weights, source code, and analysis pipelines are publicly released to allow full reproducibility.

papers.title: FDTest: Fluctuation-dissipation theorem as a test for memory effects in brain dynamics.
papers.authors: Geli SM, Monti JM, Ponce-Alvarez A, Deco G, Sanz Perl Y.
papers.abstract: A central challenge in neuroscience is to understand how the brain flexibly balances local and distributed information processing to support diverse cognitive and conscious states. We hypothesize that a key signature of this balance is the presence of memory effects, which arise when a brain region's future activity depends not only on its current state, but also on past information fed back from the wider network. Here we introduce the FDTest, a method for assessing local memory effects in multidimensional systems by measuring violations of a generalized Fluctuation-dissipation theorem (FDT). We first apply this framework to whole-brain models fitted to human neuroimaging data, demonstrating that the brain's memory structure reflects its underlying connectivity. We then extend the analysis to individualized models of subjects during wakefulness and deep sleep. Memory effects are consistently stronger in wakefulness, indicating richer inter-regional dependencies and more integrated dynamics. These findings establish local memory as a dynamical marker of brain state and position the FDTest as a principled tool for probing the hidden structure of neural dynamics.

papers.title: RNA sequencing depth guidelines for the study of alternative splicing.
papers.authors: Chervontseva Z, Tsoy O, Hackl LM, Ameling S, Franzenburg S, Hoffmann M, Liv-Willuth L, Lee HK, Knabl L, Furth PA, Völker U, Hennighausen L, Baumbach J, Kacprowski T, List M.
papers.abstract: A key parameter in the experimental design of RNA-seq projects is the choice of sequencing depth. Considering a limited budget, one needs to find a trade-off between the number of samples and the sensitivity of the analysis, particularly concerning lowly expressed genes. While previous studies have proposed a lower bound for the comprehensive analysis of differential gene expression, for the analysis of alternative splicing, it has only been proposed for human adipose tissue. However, alternative splicing differs across tissues and conditions. We analyzed publicly available and newly generated deep-sequenced paired-end RNA-seq samples (between 150 and >500 million reads, read length 50-150 bp) from human buffy coat cells and diverse sets of tissues, including gluteal subcutaneous fat, heart, and hypothalamus. Our results show that the sequencing depth typically used in published cohorts is not sufficient to comprehensively capture the landscape of alternative splicing. This motivates the use of deeper sequencing or long-read technologies in future studies. Toward this goal, we offer guidelines and a website (https://sequencing-depth4splicing.com/) for choosing a suitable sequencing depth.

papers.title: The balance between R-loops and RNAPII occupancy determines the outcome of transcription-replication conflicts.
papers.authors: Tsirkas I, Lee CSK, Dovrat D, Singh N, Paleiov Z, Lalonde M, Sajid A, Straub T, Sergi SG, Bento F, Luke B, Aharoni A, Hamperl S.
papers.abstract: Maintaining genome integrity requires the precise coordination of replication and transcription. While R-loops are known to cause transcription-replication conflicts (TRCs), the precise nature of the barrier, whether it is the RNA:DNA hybrid itself, the stalled RNA Polymerase II (RNAPII), or a combination of both, remains elusive. Using live-cell imaging in yeast to monitor a single R-loop prone locus in real time, we demonstrate that wild-type replisomes traverse R-loop enriched transcription units with high efficiency. We find that while R-loops initially repress transcription, replisome passage prompts a robust recovery of transcription activity. Indeed, we discover that R-loops serve a critical regulatory function by suppressing excessive RNAPII occupancy. In an RNAPII mutant with high DNA affinity, the enzymatic removal of R-loops leads to a pile-up of RNAPII molecules, creating a barrier to replication, more severe than the R-loops themselves. Thus, our findings reveal a dual nature of R-loops: while they can be obstacles and repress transcription, they can also serve as a physiological buffer that prevents the formation of high-density RNAPII 'trains'. These findings establish that the precise regulation of both R-loop levels and RNAPII density is critical for preventing harmful TRCs and maintaining genome stability.

papers.title: Truncated APC regulates alternative splicing by interacting with DDX21 in colorectal cancer.
papers.authors: Lv Y, Huang C, Ling H, Xu S, Wang X, Cao J, Lin J, Dai M, Zou B, Jin X, Chen R, Wang F, Xie D.
papers.abstract: Truncating mutations in the adenomatous polyposis coli (APC) gene-a key driver of colorectal cancer (CRC) initiation-frequently lead to the production of a truncated APC protein (Trunc-APC). However, its post-transcriptional roles and oncogenic potential remain largely unexplored. Here, we demonstrate that Trunc-APC functions as an RNA-binding protein, directly associating with pre-mRNA via its N-terminal 1-169 amino acid region to regulate widespread alternative splicing (AS) in CRC cells. Specifically, Trunc-APC promotes exon inclusion in ARHGEF11, producing an oncogenic isoform that is associated with enhanced Bcl-xL/BAX complex formation and reduced apoptosis. Mechanistically, Trunc-APC interacts with the RNA helicase DDX21 and facilitates SF3B complex recruitment to pre-mRNA, thereby modulating splicing patterns. Notably, treatment with the splicing inhibitor Madrasin significantly reduced tumor burden in ApcMin/+ CRC mice, indicating strong antitumor efficacy. Collectively, these findings establish Trunc-APC as a novel regulator of alternative splicing and a promoter of CRC progression, and highlight the therapeutic potential of targeting the Trunc-APC/DDX21/SF3B axis in CRC.

papers.title: A RARγ-SMARCA5 chromatin-remodeling axis stabilizes AR luminal programs and opposes lineage plasticity in prostate cancer.
papers.authors: Wani SA, Hussain S, Mir KB, Gray JS, Nayak D, Tang H, Perez LM, Long MD, Siddappa M, Corey E, Nelson PS, McCabe CJ, Sucheston-Campbell LE, Freeman MR, Campbell MJ.
papers.abstract: In prostate cancer (PCa), epigenomic mechanisms drive resistance to androgen receptor (AR) signaling inhibitors, such as enzalutamide (enza). We tested whether retinoic acid receptor gamma (RARγ) shapes the epigenome to direct AR transcription, promote luminal identity, and limit enza resistance. RARγ restoration in enza-resistant 22Rv1 cells induced a large RARγ complex containing its coactivator TACC1 and the chromatin remodeler ISWI ATPase SMARCA5. RARγ restoration expanded and redistributed the AR cistrome toward active promoters, enhancers, and unique super-enhancers and increased the overlap with H3K27ac. RARγ restoration also increased SMARCA5 promoter-proximal binding that overlapped with G2/M-enriched AR cistrome, linking AR redistribution to cell cycle-associated chromatin engagement, including at luminal genes. In 22Rv1 and LNCaP C4-2 (also enza-resistant), RARγ restoration directed the AR transcriptome toward luminal differentiation. A miR-96 antagomir (targeting RARγ) mirrored the impact of RARγ restoration. RARγ antagonized the actions of the master lineage regulator ONECUT2 at the cistrome and transcriptome level and these antagonized genes were significantly associated with alternative lineages in murine PCa models of lineage plasticity and enza responsiveness and lineage plasticity in human PCa cohorts. These findings identify RARγ as a regulator of a chromatin remodeling mechanism that sustains luminal AR programs and opposes therapeutic resistance.

papers.title: Bipartite DNA-binding domain of transcription factor BCL11B binds clustered short DNA sequence motifs.
papers.authors: Lee J, Zhou J, Horton JR, Yu M, Muoghalu MD, Khan FA, Zhang X, Huang Y, Blumenthal RM, Zhang X, Cheng X.
papers.abstract: B-cell leukemia/lymphoma 11B (BCL11B), despite its name, is a key regulator of T-cell development, lineage specification, and T-cell malignancies. BCL11B contains a bipartite DNA-binding domain composed of two C2H2 zinc finger arrays: low-affinity ZF2-3 and high-affinity ZF4-6. These arrays recognize similar six-nucleotide motifs, TG(n)CC(n), as seven of the eight DNA base-contacting residues are conserved between them. The most conserved interactions involve the central GG dinucleotides, recognized by arginine and lysine residues at the key base-interacting positions of ZF3 and ZF5. We determined eight crystal structures of ZF2-3 bound to 12- or 20-base pair DNA duplexes containing either one or two binding motifs. The structures reveal that ZF2-3 recognizes DNA with remarkable configurational flexibility, binding motifs on either the same or opposite DNA strands with variable spacing in three relative orientations: head-to-tail (or tail-to-head), head-to-head, and tail-to-tail. Analysis of BCL11B ChIP-seq peaks revealed a strong enrichment of 1-bp-spaced, same-orientation TGACC(c/t) motif pairs. We also examined six neurodevelopmental disorder-associated missense variants affecting DNA base-contacting residues. Substitutions that replace bulky, positively charged arginine or lysine with smaller or hydrophobic amino acids weaken DNA-binding affinity and specificity, whereas substitutions between asparagine and lysine alter base recognition preferences.

papers.title: Strand-displacement amplification reduces structure-induced PCR bias and preserves structurally diverse aptamers during SELEX.
papers.authors: Jeong H, Jeong CB, Moon JY, Park D, Jung C.
papers.abstract: Stable secondary structures are important for aptamer folding and target recognition, but they can introduce structure-dependent amplification bias during Systematic Evolution of Ligands by Exponential Enrichment (SELEX), with G-quadruplexes (G4s) representing the most demanding case. Here, we introduce strand-displacement SELEX (SD-SELEX), which employs a polymerase with robust 5'→3' strand-displacement activity to improve the amplification of structured templates. Comparative analyses showed that SD polymerase efficiently amplified hairpin- and G4-forming templates, whereas Taq polymerase exhibited structure-dependent amplification variability. In parallel thrombin SELEX experiments, SD-SELEX achieved 37-fold greater structural preservation and 65-fold higher batch-to-batch reproducibility than Taq-SELEX over 11 rounds. High-throughput sequencing further showed that SD-SELEX maintained G4 motif representation and progressively enriched the known 15-mer thrombin-binding aptamer through round 8, after which it was gradually replaced by newly identified G4 variants, whereas Taq-SELEX progressively depleted these sequences. SD-SELEX also identified novel G4 aptamers with affinities comparable to that of the reference aptamer, whereas representative Taq-SELEX candidates generally showed weaker binding. A parallel selection against VEGF-165 showed the same divergence, with SD-SELEX retaining structurally complex sequences and a previously reported functional motif that were progressively lost under Taq. Thus, SD-SELEX primarily improves aptamer discovery by reducing structure-induced amplification bias and preserving structurally diverse functional candidates, rather than by substantially increasing affinity alone.

papers.title: MethMarkerDB 2.0: an expanded and functionally annotated database for cancer DNA methylation biomarkers.
papers.authors: Sun Y, Peng Z, Zhong L, Li Z, Hao Y, Zhou Q, Li G.
papers.abstract: Cancer-associated differentially methylated regions (DMRs) are promising biomarkers for cancer diagnosis, prognosis, and therapeutic response, but their biological significance and potential applications remain to be systematically explored across datasets. To support this, we released MethMarkerDB 2.0 (https://methmarkerdb.hzau.edu.cn/v2), which provides several improvements over the previous version: (i) Expands the data resource from 13 to 21 cancer types and from 658 to 1236 whole-genome methylome samples, comprising ∼5.6 million candidate DMRs and 6411 literature-curated biomarker records.(ii) Integrates 450K DNA methylation data from The Cancer Genome Atlas and Epigenome-Wide Association Study Atlas and transcript annotations into the "MethMarker Gene Search" module. These data provide complementary evidence from independent datasets and platforms and allow users to examine CpG-level information for individual DMRs. Additionally, cell-type-resolved reference methylation data allow users to check cellular-background methylation. (iii) Introduces four analysis modules to characterize DMR methylation patterns across age groups and spatial ecotypes, and connect DMRs with transcription factor binding evidence and cancer cell-line drug responses. Moreover, the "Methylation-Cas Designer" supports guide RNA design for methylation-sensitive restriction enzyme-Cas assays and targeted epigenome editing. In summary, MethMarkerDB 2.0 provides expanded resources, diverse functional analyses, and experimental design tools, facilitating the interpretation and application of cancer-associated DMRs.

papers.title: MobiDB in 2027: machine-actionable access to intrinsic protein disorder knowledge.
papers.authors: Piovesan D, Lamara A, Worth AM, Mehdiabadi M, Begue SC, Tosatto SCE.
papers.abstract: MobiDB (https://mobidb.org) integrates structural and functional annotations for intrinsically disordered proteins and regions across UniProtKB. The 2027 release strengthens semantic consistency, programmatic access, and reproducible reuse. A refined controlled vocabulary groups features in a hierarchical way and distinguishes evidence classes and types annotation sources as providers, methods, or aggregation rules. A new versioned REST API, along with a developed MCP server, enables scripts, workflows, and tool-using artificial intelligence systems to retrieve and combine evidence-bearing records through documented operations. The redesigned website applies the same vocabulary to protein entries, documentation, and cross-proteome statistics. Additional developments include standardized Nextflow production workflows, updated RING Protein Data Bank interaction processing, integration of Motif Map of the Proteome and Linear Motif mediated Protein-Protein Interaction Database annotations, and a release-aware catalogue of static datasets for large-scale analysis. Following the recent increase in reference proteomes in UniProtKB, MobiDB now provides a more representative estimate of long-disorder with a median residue coverage of 12.3% in eukaryotes, 1.9% in archaea, 1.7% in bacteria, and 3.4% in viruses; and protein prevalence of 48.7%, 11.9%, 11.2%, and 25.0%, respectively. Together, these developments make disorder knowledge easier to discover, relate to function, and reuse with explicit provenance.

papers.title: Beyond unseen entities: Auditable cold-start evaluation for drug interaction prediction.
papers.authors: Ru X, Wang Y, Zou Q, Niu M.
papers.abstract: Reliable generalization is essential for deploying drug-drug interaction (DDI) and drug-target interaction (DTI) models in drug discovery, pharmacovigilance, and clinical decision support. However, strong performance on random splits or weakly constrained evaluations may not reflect how well a model generalizes to new drugs, targets, or deployment conditions. In pairwise prediction, test instances may still resemble training examples in molecular structure, sequence, or network context. Such overlap can inflate performance estimates and make interpolation appear to be extrapolation. In this Perspective, we argue that cold-start evaluation should be treated as an auditable deployment claim. We organize common evaluation settings by their source and scope of novelty, ranging from random splits and entity-disjoint protocols to structure-level, temporal, domain-disjoint, and many-domain evaluations. The L0-L5 framework clarifies which deployment claim each setting is designed to test. Coverage, overlap, and distance quantify the resulting train-test discrepancy. We further provide a practical checklist for leakage control, validation alignment, candidate-pair construction, and domain-level risk reporting. This Perspective clarifies the boundaries and evidential scope of cold-start evaluation, providing a common basis for interpreting and comparing results across DDI and DTI studies.

Allele-selective targeting of uromodulin by antisense oligonucleotides reduces aggregates and kidney damage in a mouse model of autosomal dominant tubulointerstitial kidney disease.
papers.authors: Sjöström S, Mariniello M, Schiano G, Lake J, Botta S, Hill A, Hall J, Devuyst O.
papers.abstract: Autosomal dominant tubulointerstitial kidney disease (ADTKD) arises from gain-of-toxic-function mutations in the UMOD gene coding for uromodulin, the most abundant protein excreted in normal urine. Mutant uromodulin accumulates in the cells lining the thick ascending limb (TAL) of the loop of Henle, leading to intracellular aggregates, cellular stress, and kidney damage. Here, we demonstrate that an antisense gapmer oligonucleotide (ASO) designed against the representative c.553C > A (p.R185S) UMOD mutation produced allele-selective silencing of the mutant messenger RNA and protein in kidney cells. Short-term administration of a murine ASO analogue in the established Umod R186S/+ mouse model of ADTKD suppressed uromodulin and lowered tubular damage, whereas a non-targeting scrambled control was inactive. After a 4-week treatment, ASO accumulation in the Umod R186S/+ kidneys reached ∼320 000 copies per TAL cell, quantified using a sensitive splint-ligation assay. The ASO treatment suppressed premature mutant uromodulin and its toxic aggregates in Umod R186S/+ kidneys, whereas it had no effects on wild-type uromodulin in Umod +/+ kidneys. Notably, the ASO improved tubular function and decreased kidney tubulointerstitial inflammation in Umod R186S/+ mice. This work offers a roadmap for antisense therapy to treat ADTKD-UMOD and substantiates the therapeutic potential of ASOs in disorders of the kidney tubule.

papers.title: The anti-phage defense system GAPS4 is a double-edged sword that sensitizes bacteria to DNA-damaging agents.
papers.authors: Mahata T, Kanarek K, Haldar A, Ragavan RM, Shur G, Yehia R, Burstein D, Haitin Y, Qimron U, Salomon D.
papers.abstract: The arms race between bacteria and bacteriophages (phages) gave rise to multiple layers of antagonistic mechanisms, many of which remain unexplored. Here, we investigated the widespread anti-phage defense system GAPS4. We found that GAPS4 forms a heterotetrameric complex containing active PD-(D/E)xK phosphodiesterase domains. It is triggered upon sensing DNA damage, leading to genomic DNA degradation and cell suicide. We further demonstrated that this activation mechanism renders GAPS4 a double-edged sword, sensitizing bacteria to various DNA-targeting antibacterial agents. Collectively, our findings reveal a possible evolutionary trade-off between anti-phage defense and immunity against interbacterial antagonism.

papers.title: Cell-free expression and NGS-powered substrate profiling reveal a thermostable metagenomic meganuclease from an extreme environment with novel specificity.
papers.authors: Dorrazehi GM, Penner M, Athanasiou C, Boursinhac L, Mobarec JC, Webster CI, Papworth M, Hollfelder F.
papers.abstract: As an alternative to historical enzyme isolation, metagenomic databases (e.g. MGnify) provide information on vast unculturable microbial diversity, including extreme environments, and constitute an enormous source of functional proteins. Conservative mining of these data by close sequence homology alone tends to identify merely different versions of known enzymes. Here we present a discovery strategy for meganucleases based on wider capture of less homologous enzymes in metagenomic databases, and incorporating metadata with their homology. We use cell-free expression to bypass host incompatibility and the need for purification, along with deep sequencing for experimental assessment of substrate specificity and cleavage pattern, thereby circumventing classical gel-based profiling. Specifically, we discovered the temperature-stable (>55°C), intron-encoded LAGLIDADG meganuclease I-MG11 that recognizes a GC-rich 17 base pair sequence to generate 4-nt palindromic 3'-overhangs-the first monomeric meganuclease to produce such overhangs. Co-folding models of I-MG11 bound to DNA provide a structural context for enzyme-DNA interactions, highlighting differences from other monomeric LAGLIDADG meganucleases (e.g. I-SceI) shaped by InDels (insertion-deletions) in the DNA-binding region that may cause specificity changes. Our strategy streamlines general bona fide identification and annotation of meganucleases, while the unique properties of I-MG11 expand the toolbox of molecular genome engineering.

Transcription factor 3 cooperates with CXXC finger protein 1 to regulate histone H3K4 trimethylation and developmental competence in mouse oocytes.
papers.authors: Qiu YX, Zhang C, Cao LR, Liu BF, Chen Q, Yang WJ, He YL, Su YQ, Zhao H, Xie W, Fan HY, Li J.
papers.abstract: During oogenesis, the establishment of oocyte-specific gene expression relies on epigenetic and transcriptional remodeling. Both histone modifications and transcription factors are crucial for the oocyte to acquire developmental competence; however, the mechanisms involved remain incompletely understood. Here, we identify transcription factor 3 (TCF3), an E-protein family member, as a key maternal regulator of oocyte developmental potential. Oocyte-specific deletion of Tcf3 results in female infertility, characterized by impaired meiotic maturation and early embryonic arrest at the two-cell stage. These defects are associated with defective maternal mRNA clearance and disrupted establishment of the H3K4me3 landscape in maturing oocytes. Mechanistically, we demonstrate that TCF3 directs H3K4me3 deposition at target gene promoters through interaction with CXXC finger protein 1 (CXXC1), the core subunit of the SETD1 histone methyltransferase complex. Importantly, this TCF3-CXXC1 interaction depends on their DNA-binding activity, highlighting the specificity of TCF3 in coordinating with CXXC1 to regulate maternal target genes, such as Pabpn1l. Together, our findings uncover a transcription factor-driven mechanism of epigenetic reprogramming that is essential for the maternal-to-zygotic transition.

papers.title: Archaeal histones coordinate conserved DNA sequence motifs to promote CRISPR adaptive immunity.
papers.authors: Patel P, Treat AR, Gonzalez R, Rajaraman S, Cruga BN, Chinea EB, Onwuka A, Nguyen C, Terns MP, Santiago-Frangos A.
keywords: Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats
papers.abstract: Archaea and bacteria acquire resistance to viruses by integrating fragments of foreign DNA at the beginning of a CRISPR locus. In the archaeon Pyrococcus furiosus, histones bind the leader to promote specific integration at the first CRISPR repeat. However, it remains unknown whether archaeal CRISPR leaders contain conserved DNA sequence motifs required for integration. Here, we analyze 542 archaeal CRISPR leaders found across Thermococcales and Methanococcales. We identify 36 motifs found up to 500 bps upstream of archaeal CRISPR loci. Scrambling or truncating novel motifs or histone binding sites found 100-400 bps upstream of the P. furiosus CRISPR modestly decreases integration efficiency. However, mutation of motif T2, which overlaps with the proximal histone site and is adjacent to the CRISPR, ablates both histone-mediated and histone-independent integration. Mutations tiled across T2 reveal that a pyrimidine at position -3 of the leader is required for histone-independent integration, and basepairs -4 to -19 are required for histone-mediated integration. T2 is found in most Thermococcales, and a similar sequence is found in most Methanococcales leaders, suggesting this motif may be a broadly conserved element that facilitates CRISPR adaptive immunity across taxonomic orders. These data shed light on the sequence requirements for histone-mediated DNA integration.

papers.title: Microfluidic concatemer sequencing unveils cooperative and competitive enhancer clusters in gene regulation.
papers.authors: Chen Q, Zheng S, Li F, Shi Y, Li Z, Li X, Wang J, Xu B, Li X, Zhang Q, Zheng M, Zhang Z.
papers.abstract: Chromatin looping plays a pivotal role in eukaryotic gene regulation; however, technical limitations have hindered the comprehensive characterization of higher-order interactions among genomic loci. As a result, key questions, such as whether enhancers function cooperatively or competitively at the single-molecule and ensemble levels, remain largely unresolved. Here, we present Drop-t, a novel microfluidics-based method that enables systematic profiling of higher-order chromatin architecture at both the single-molecule and population scales. We demonstrate that Drop-t is not only resistant to common ligation-induced DNA entanglements, which frequently cause nanopore clogging, but also provides greater relevance for elucidating regulatory mechanisms compared to existing ligation-free approaches. Using Drop-t, we uncovered extensive, previously underappreciated non-specific enhancer-promoter interactions (EPIs) and showed that these may influence transcriptional variability by competing with specific EPIs. Notably, we identified two major gene classes, dictator genes and leader genes, based on whether their promoters are predominantly regulated by competitive or cooperative specific EPIs, respectively. Together, our findings established Drop-t as a powerful tool for decoding the higher-order organizational principles of chromatin architecture and their impact on transcriptional regulation and variability.

papers.title: Absolute quantification and profiling of cellular tRNAs by nanopore sequencing and a deep learning classifier.
papers.authors: Ueda H, Maeda M, Okada S, Noguchi R, Dasgupta B, Yamamoto R, Furuta M, Nishi A, Nagao A, Sakaguchi Y, Miyauchi K, Suzuki T.
papers.abstract: Transfer RNAs (tRNAs) link mRNA codons to amino acids during translation. Their abundance and modification states are dynamically regulated and influence translation efficiency, mRNA stability, and proteostasis. Accurate profiling of tRNAs is essential, but deep sequencing suffers from modification-induced biases during cDNA synthesis, while nanopore direct RNA sequencing (DRS) still faces challenges in accurate tRNA profiling. Here, we develop an end-to-end deep learning model, termed nano tRNA classifier, that directly uses nanopore-DRS ionic current signals to classify tRNAs without basecalling. The model achieves 98.2% classification accuracy with high read retention across all Escherichia coli tRNA species. Using an equimolar mixture of native tRNAs as a ground-truth reference, we correct read-count bias, enabling absolute quantification and profiling under diverse culture conditions. We further develop binary classifiers that detect specific tRNA modifications at the single-molecule level with high accuracy. This nanopore-based platform integrates accurate tRNA classification, absolute quantification, and single-molecule modification detection.

papers.title: LLM ensemble PREVIA predicts future PTSD risk from emergency department trauma narratives with expert-level accuracy.
papers.authors: Mueller V, Yadav J, Farnsworth A, Hilberdink CE, Gershov S, Oermann EK, Wall SP, Shalev AY, Schultebraucks K.
papers.abstract: Post-traumatic stress disorder affects numerous trauma survivors following emergency department discharge, making this encounter vital for early risk stratification. Yet emergency clinicians face severe time constraints, making existing screening tools impractical. We introduce PREVIA, a clinically-informed large language model ensemble, that predicts post-traumatic stress disorder risk from unstructured patient trauma narratives, collected in response to a routine-care question asked in the emergency department, by extracting early post-traumatic stress symptoms, peri-traumatic symptoms, risk, and protective factors. Within an ongoing longitudinal study, we included N = 145 patients across two New York City level-1 trauma centers within 24 hours of trauma and assessed post-traumatic stress disorder 1-month post-trauma. In this work, PREVIA accurately forecasts post-traumatic stress disorder (AUROC = 78.49% ± 5.75%, sensitivity=95.4% ± 3.99%, precision=46.76% ± 8.66%), performs comparably to an emergency clinician specialized in post-traumatic stress disorder on 30 randomly selected patients (PREVIA: AUROC = 84.39%, sensitivity=100.00%, precision=50.00%; clinician: AUROC = 83.86%, sensitivity=88.89%, precision=50.00%), and generates interpretable explanations without additional clinical burden. These initial findings support PREVIA's potential as a scalable emergency department screener for timely, targeted interventions, and warrant validation in larger, independent cohorts.

papers.title: Single-cell machine learning uncovers genetically anchored, cell-type specific programs of Alzheimer's disease.
papers.authors: Madduri AV, Ellis RJ, Lakhani CM, Bennett DA, Patel CJ.
papers.abstract: Univariate differential expression analysis dominates single-cell transcriptomic studies of Alzheimer's disease, yet marginal testing alone cannot resolve multivariate disease-associated structure or distinguish clinical from neuropathological signatures. Here we introduce TriSCOPE, a framework integrating multivariate predictive modeling, donor-aware differential expression, and pseudotime inference, applied to six Alzheimer's disease snRNA-seq datasets comprising ~4.2 million nuclei from 627 donors. Across six major brain cell types and 41 subclusters, we identify cell-type-specific predictively expressed genes that are largely non-overlapping with differentially expressed genes, revealing disease-relevant signals invisible to univariate approaches. Conditional GWAS-eQTL colocalization anchors a subset of these predictively expressed genes to inherited Alzheimer's disease risk loci, including 27 genetically supported gene-cell type pairs (among them ARL17B, JAZF1) with no significant differential expression. Integration across all three analytical branches nominates high-confidence convergent programs including astrocytic stress markers (such as GFAP, MT2A), neuronal signaling genes (like RASGEF1B, LINGO1, NRG1), and microglial and oligodendrocyte regulators (including SYTL3, SPP1, APOD). Comparison of clinical and neuropathological models reveals cell-type-specific divergence between cognitive and pathological Alzheimer's disease signatures. Key predictively expressed genes including ARL17B, LINGO1, and APOE replicate across independent cohorts, with cross-cohort generalizability confirmed across all three analytical branches of TriSCOPE.

papers.title: How far can you borrow? Divergence limits of cross-species Gene Ontology enrichment in non-model organisms.
papers.authors: Lee SG, Park C.
papers.abstract: Functional interpretation of omics data from non-model species almost always relies on borrowing Gene Ontology (GO) annotations from a model organism-often a distant one (Arabidopsis for plants, zebrafish or human for fish)-and running enrichment analysis on inferred orthologs. How far this practice can be pushed before the enrichment result degrades has never been quantified at the level practitioners use. We present the first systematic benchmark of the divergence-tolerance of cross-species GO-transfer enrichment, across six focal species spanning three eukaryotic kingdoms, each with 15-22 reference species tiling a continuous phylogenetic gradient. Set-level fidelity-measured as redundancy-robust Wang semantic similarity between transferred and experimental-truth enriched term sets-declines monotonically with distance, collapsing to chance at the clade boundary in some panels (fish, rice) while remaining well above it in others (insect, fungi, mammal) (half-collapse identity, ID50, ~40%-59%). At fixed distance, a richer reference raises recall but lowers precision, quantifying a long-recognized but unresolved trade-off. Conserved processes transfer reliably to distant references whereas taxon-specific processes do not, a pattern consistent across all six focal species tested. Whole-genome duplication degrades transfer only when ohnolog retention is high, showing up as sensitivity to the orthology method rather than a steeper decline. An independent, GO-free measure of expression conservation supports the curves in vertebrates. We condense these results into a focal-species × distance reliability guide and a step-by-step decision protocol that let researchers judge, before analysis, whether borrowed-GO enrichment can be trusted for their species and question.

papers.title: Impact of training data on deep learning-based RNA 3D structure quality assessment.
papers.authors: Adamczyk B, Szachniuk M, Antczak M.
papers.abstract: Accurate reference-free assessment of predicted RNA 3D structures is essential for large-scale RNA modeling, yet the impact of training data on deep learning-based quality predictors remains poorly understood. Here, we present a systematic cross-training analysis of three deep learning predictors for RNA 3D structure quality assessment, each originally developed on distinct training sets. By retraining each predictor on alternative (nonnative) datasets-including RNA3DQA, a new set created specifically for this project-and evaluating performance on independent RNA-Puzzles benchmarks, we systematically assess the relative contributions of model architecture and training data composition. Our results reveal pronounced differences in cross-dataset generalization, with predictors often performing better when trained on nonnative datasets than on their native ones. Notably, the impact of the training datasets varied across predictors, with RNA3DQA yielding the overall best accuracy and ranking stability results specifically for the ARES model. Native training sets yielded better performance for RNA3DCNN and lociPARSE. These findings demonstrate that the characteristics of the training data play a dominant, model-dependent role in shaping the performance and robustness of reference-free RNA 3D structure quality assessment methods. We conclude with practical recommendations for designing transferable training datasets and for benchmarking deep learning-based quality predictors in RNA structural bioinformatics.

papers.title: scYOU: a multi-scale yoked optimization and unsupervised framework for analysis of cellular heterogeneity and complex-associated protein module recovery.
papers.authors: Gan Y, Huang Y, Gong X.
papers.abstract: Advances in high-resolution proteomic technologies are enabling systematic characterization of cellular heterogeneity and protein functional programs at increasing depth. However, existing computational approaches typically focus on either cell-level organization or protein-level structure, lacking a unified framework that jointly models both entities. Here we present scYOU, a multi-scale yoked optimization and unsupervised framework that simultaneously captures cellular heterogeneity and protein functional organization through a dual-channel neural network architecture. scYOU learns cell and protein embeddings in parallel while coupling the two views through a supercell-constrained alignment strategy. Supercells are constructed based on high-order expression similarity and define grouping structures over cells. A dual-channel alignment objective is imposed at the reconstruction level, such that reconstructed expression profiles of cells within the same supercell are encouraged to converge, whereas those from different supercells remain separable. On the protein side, Gene Ontology-derived functional similarity priors regularize protein embeddings to preserve molecular biological consistency. Across diverse benchmark datasets, scYOU achieves strong and relatively consistent clustering performance together with improved embedding separability, while the learned protein representations support embedding-guided refinement of existing interaction networks and the recovery of complex-associated protein modules. These results establish scYOU as a structurally coupled, multi-level representation learning framework for proteomic data, and highlight the importance of jointly modeling cellular heterogeneity and protein functional modules within a unified computational paradigm. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/anchor-hue/scYou.

papers.title: Graphics processing unit-accelerated quantum simulation for molecular biology and drug discovery: algorithms, platforms, and emerging applications.
papers.authors: Chen YL, Lee OK.
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence has intensified the need for methods that describe molecular systems with quantum-mechanical accuracy. Gate-based quantum computing offers a principled framework for simulating electronic structure, molecular interactions, and biological processes at a fidelity inaccessible to classical force fields or density functional theory alone, yet scarce, noisy hardware limits direct experimentation. Graphics processing unit (GPU)-accelerated quantum simulation has emerged as a practical bridge, allowing quantum algorithms to be developed, validated, and benchmarked on classical infrastructure at 30-40 noiseless qubits, and far beyond where tensor-network methods apply. Unlike recent reviews organized around quantum machine learning (QML) or around hardware, this review is organized around the simulation layer itself and asks, for each domain, what can be established in simulation, what requires a quantum processor, and how the two connect in one hardware-agnostic workflow. We examine how the variational quantum eigensolver, quantum phase estimation, and sample-based hybrid schemes address electronic structure in small-molecule pharmacology; how quantum-enhanced conformational sampling complements AlphaFold; and how QML introduces alternative feature spaces for drug-target, structure-activity, and genomic modeling. We compile published GPU benchmarks, identify the molecular systems for which tensor-network simulation is and is not adequate, explain how GPU platforms accelerate error mitigation, and critically assess 2023-6 developments, including quantum-centric supercomputing, hybrid quantum Monte Carlo on trapped-ion hardware, protein binding-site prediction on utility-scale processors, below-threshold error correction, and a classically verifiable quantum-advantage claim. Framing GPU simulation as a near-term enabler rather than a final objective, the review offers a practical entry point for biological and pharmaceutical scientists.

papers.title: A recall-rescue fuzzy layer over paired Z-DNA Hunter scans for fast Z-DNA detection.
papers.authors: Petrovič M, Trenz O, Kledus F, Brázda V, Šťastný J.
papers.abstract: Accurate detection of Z-DNA-forming regions is limited by the trade-off between sensitivity and specificity in sequence-based methods. We present Z-DNA-Fuzzy Hunter 1.1.0-a fast and interpretable protocol that extends Z-DNA Hunter through a dual-scan strategy combined with a fuzzy expert layer. A permissive scan (model 2, minimum length 6 bp, threshold 30%) captures a broad candidate set, while a stringent scan (model 2, minimum length 10 bp, threshold 60%) provides high-confidence support. These outputs are integrated using fuzzy inference incorporating sequence signal, cross-scan support, genomic context, and bias penalties. On the audited 385-locus Shin analysis, the protocol achieves balanced accuracy 0.883 (recall 0.862, specificity 0.904), comparable with the published Z-DNABERT operating point, while alternative modes increase specificity to 0.973. The paired scans are combined by a transparent, configurable prioritization layer with an adjustable recall-specificity trade-off. The local workflow requires only a FASTA (Fast-All sequence alignment format), sequence and transcription start site annotation. The tool is freely available at https://github.com/mifo123/zdna-fuzzy-hunter.

papers.title: spaDWGCN: a spatial distance weighted graph convolution network for accurate spatial tissue structure identification.
papers.authors: Zou K, Wan R, Liu X, Pan Y, Shi J, Cao W, Yang F, Cheng Z, Zhu Q.
papers.abstract: The continuous development of spatial transcriptomics enables us to obtain gene expression matrices alongside spatial coordinate labels for cells or spots, providing tools for understanding spatial tissue microenvironments and spatially resolved cell-cell interactions. Although numerous methods have been developed to identify spatial tissue architecture, most of them adopt binary adjacency matrices that treat all neighboring cells equally, and few comprehensively incorporate distance information into both graph construction and feature representation. Here we introduce spaDWGCN, a spatial distance weighted graph convolutional network algorithm that takes cellular gene expression and microenvironment composition as inputs. This approach introduces fine-grained distance weighting at two levels: replacing the conventional 0-1 binary adjacency matrix with a distance-weighted adjacency matrix at the graph level, and substituting the neighbor count matrix with a distance-weighted microenvironment composition matrix at the feature level. Furthermore, spaDWGCN jointly models gene expression and microenvironment composition through separate graph convolutional network branches and trainable fusion, integrating transcriptional patterns with their local neighborhood context within a unified framework. Experiments on spatial transcriptomics multi-platform datasets, including MERFISH, STARmap, Stereo-seq, Slide-seqV2, and 10× Visium, demonstrate that this distance-weighted strategy achieves competitive performance in spatial domain identification and other downstream analyses.
