Structured multi-view relational learning for drug response prediction.
papers.authors: Wang Z, Li W, Xu J, Meng Y, Zhou H, Jin S.
papers.abstract: Drug response prediction (DRP) requires models that jointly characterize molecular drug structure and heterogeneous cellular states. Although recent deep learning approaches have integrated multi-omics profiles with drug representations, many treat omics views as parallel feature sources or merge them before relational modeling, which can weaken omics-view-specific cell-line relation structures. Here, we propose MulDR, a structured multi-view relational learning framework that preserves omics-view-specific cell-line relation structures before drug-conditioned cell-drug interaction. MulDR constructs separate relation structures for pathway activity, gene expression, mutation, and DNA methylation, learns view-specific relational cell representations, and uses complementary motif-level, geometry-aware molecular graph, and Morgan fingerprint drug representations to condition their fusion. With this design, cell-line similarity remains view-dependent until the interaction stage, rather than being prematurely compressed into a single feature or relation space. Extensive experiments show that MulDR consistently outperforms representative and recent baselines under the same evaluation protocol, reducing root mean square error by 6.07% relative to the strongest baseline. Cold-start evaluations on unseen drugs and cell lines further show that MulDR generalizes to previously unseen entities, while ablation studies show that removing either view-specific relational modeling or drug-conditioned fusion consistently compromises predictive performance. Together, these results suggest that preserving omics-specific cell-line relations before drug-conditioned interaction modeling provides an effective strategy for robust DRP.

papers.title: CalDyn: an advanced high-throughput automated algorithm for monitoring intracellular calcium dynamics and electrophysiological signals in patient-derived cells.
papers.authors: Sleiman Y, El Achkar G, Colombani S, Estève E, Reisqs JB, Kervella M, Goual L, Bounasri E, Ferreira MJ, Cupelli M, Torrente AG, Thireau J, Costa PF, Boutjdir M, Lacampagne A, Muchir A, Seyer P, Delanoë-Ayari H, Meli AC.
papers.abstract: Background Quantitative analysis of intracellular calcium and electrophysiological signals is challenging when signals exhibit baseline drift, low-amplitude events, irregular waveforms, or multicomponent transients. We developed CalDyn, a MATLAB-based graphical application for automated peak detection, waveform characterization, event classification, batch processing, quality control and data export. Methods CalDyn combines Savitzky-Golay filtering, LOESS-assisted derivative detection, optional baseline correction, waveform-boundary fitting and rule-based peak classification. It was evaluated on calcium recordings (healthy and disease-associated hiPSC-derived cardiomyocytes, hiPSC-derived neurons, primary skeletal myotubes), current-clamp action potentials and cardiac optical-mapping signals. Outputs were compared with PeakInspector, Clampfit and BV Workbench using paired and Bland-Altman analyses. Detection was assessed against 142 expert-annotated events and synthetic signals of known timing and amplitude. Results CalDyn achieved 94.4% sensitivity, 89.9% precision and an F1 score of 0.92. Performance peaked for healthy cardiomyocytes, paced myotubes and action potentials, with lower recall in arrhythmic cardiomyocytes and variable precision in neurons. CalDyn detected candidate low-amplitude diastolic and multicomponent Ca2+ events in arrhythmic cardiomyocytes, although the biological identity of CalDyn-only events was not independently confirmed. Comparisons with software revealed parameter-specific systematic differences, notably for rise rates and classifications. Action-potential measurements showed limited mean bias but non-negligible limits of agreement. In synthetic signals, amplitude error increased with noise and uncorrected drift, and timing error with low sampling rates. Detection remained stable across moderate parameter variation. Conclusions CalDyn provides an accessible, reproducible and versatile workflow for automated analysis of heterogeneous calcium and electrophysiological signals. With appropriate quality control, it offers a robust alternative to modality-specific tools.

papers.title: Germline dependence in protein language model retrieval of adaptive immune receptors.
papers.authors: Wang S, Sengupta A, Li S, Standley DM.
papers.abstract: Protein language models (PLMs) are increasingly used to represent adaptive immune receptors, yet their advantage over classical sequence comparison remains unclear. We benchmarked general and receptor-specific PLMs against classical sequence-comparison methods for antigen-specific nearest-neighbor retrieval across four B- and T-cell receptor databases. Using CDR3 sequences alone, classical methods consistently outperformed general PLMs: BLOSUM62 and Levenshtein exceeded ESM2 variants by 7-12 percentage points in retrieval accuracy. Among receptor-specific models, only SCEPTR and, on one database, TCR2vec matched these baselines, although both additionally encoded V-gene information. AntiBERTa2 and IgBert did not close the performance gap. Using full variable-domain sequences, alignment and PLM performance converged. Germline-reversion, region-masking, and V-gene control analyses indicated that this convergence largely reflected conserved germline-derived context, particularly V-gene identity, with limited evidence for improved extraction of antigen-specific information from the CDRs. Germline dependence also extended to SCEPTR and TCR2vec. Heavily mutated HIV-1 antibodies provided a setting-specific exception to this pattern. Random train-test splits yielded retrieval accuracy 15-28 percentage points higher than clone-aware splits, consistent with optimistic performance estimates due to clonal leakage. These findings emphasize the need for strong sequence-comparison baselines and explicit germline controls when evaluating immune-receptor representations and support clone-aware splitting as a minimum benchmark standard.

papers.title: Metapath-guided topology and domain knowledge fusion for predicting miRNA-drug-disease triplet resistance and sensitivity associations.
papers.authors: Sheng N, Gao L, Tang X, Liu Y, Huang L, Wang Y.
papers.abstract: Accurately predicting drug resistance and sensitivity is critical for understanding disease treatment mechanisms and improving therapeutic strategies. MicroRNAs (miRNAs) play essential roles in regulating drug response. However, existing computational methods mainly focus on miRNA-drug pairwise associations and overlook the disease-specific context. In this study, we propose a metapath-guided topology and domain knowledge fusion framework (MTDKF) for predicting miRNA-drug-disease triplet resistance (MRDR) and sensitivity (MRDS) associations. Specifically, we construct a triplet heterogeneous graph to model the interactions among miRNAs, drugs, and diseases. A metapath topology view encoder is designed to capture regulatory patterns between nodes. Additionally, a domain knowledge view encoder is introduced to incorporate sequence, structural, and semantic features of biological entities. These two views are further integrated to learn robust and discriminative representation. We manually curate two benchmark datasets from experimentally validated associations. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that MTDKF consistently outperforms state-of-the-art approaches across multiple evaluation metrics. Furthermore, case studies on two breast cancer drugs doxorubicin and tamoxifen demonstrate its potential in discovering novel miRNAs related to drug resistance and sensitivity under disease-specific contexts.

papers.title: Efficient and accurate mixed model association tool for single-cell eQTL analysis.
papers.authors: Zhou W, Cuomo ASE, Hu L, Xue A, Kanai M, Liu YC, Kang T, Kim Y, Rodriguez A, Madduri RK, Gorissen BL, Chau G, Senabouth A, Gordon MG, Perez R, Kathail P, Kim MC, Ye CJ, Krishna C, Xavier RJ, MacArthur DG, Powell JE, Daly MJ, Neale BM.
papers.abstract: Genetic effects on gene expression often vary across cell types, motivating expression quantitative trait loci (eQTL) mapping in single-cell RNA sequencing data. Existing approaches generally aggregate expression across cells, use Gaussian models poorly suited to read counts or do not scale. Here we show that SAIGE-QTL, a Poisson mixed model that directly models single-cell read counts, enables calibrated and computationally scalable eQTL mapping while accounting for donor-level and cell-level covariates and unequal numbers of cells per donor. In simulations and three single-cell datasets, SAIGE-QTL improved statistical efficiency and discovery of genes with significant eQTLs (eGenes) relative to pseudobulk methods and produced results consistent with existing single-cell models at substantially lower computational cost. In 1.2 million immune cells, SAIGE-QTL identified 48.8% more eGenes than pseudobulk analysis. SAIGE-QTL further enabled genome-wide trans-eQTL mapping and rare variant set-based testing, identifying rare variant associations independent of common eQTL signals. SAIGE-QTL therefore expands single-cell eQTL discovery across common, rare and trans-acting genetic variation.

papers.title: Redundancy maximization as a principle of associative memory learning in Hopfield networks.
papers.authors: Blümel M, Schneider AC, Neuhaus V, Ehrlich DA, Graetz M, Wibral M, Makkeh A, Priesemann V.
papers.abstract: Associative memory, traditionally modeled by Hopfield networks, enables the retrieval of previously stored patterns from partial or noisy cues. Yet, the local computational principles which are required to enable this function remain incompletely understood. To formally characterize the local information processing in such systems, we employ a recent extension of information theory-Partial Information Decomposition. It decomposes the contribution of different inputs to an output into unique information from each input, redundant information across inputs, and synergistic information that emerges from combining different inputs. Applying this framework to individual neurons in classical Hopfield networks we find that below the memory capacity, the information in a neuron's activity is characterized by high redundancy between the external pattern input and the internal recurrent input, while synergy and unique information are close to zero until the memory capacity is surpassed and performance drops steeply. Inspired by this observation, we use redundancy maximization at each neuron as an information-theoretic learning goal. This increases the network's memory capacity to 1.59, a more than tenfold improvement over the 0.14 capacity of classical Hopfield networks, and also outperforming recent state-of-the-art implementations of Hopfield networks. Overall, this work establishes redundancy maximization as a design principle for associative memories and opens pathways for new associative memory models based on information-theoretic goals.

papers.title: Microbiome-derived proline dipeptides underpin improved nitrogen utilization efficiency in dairy cattle.
papers.authors: Qi W, Chen X, Guo H, Zhu S, Zhou Z, Xu L, Yan Q, Gu FF, Liu JX, Sun HZ.
papers.abstract: Dairy production is constrained by low nitrogen utilization efficiency (NUE; milk N/intake N), leading to nitrogen losses and environmental pollution. Although the rumen microbiome is central to nitrogen turnover, the role of small peptides, a critical nitrogen pool, remains poorly understood. Here, we constructed a genome-resolved atlas of predicted small-peptide metabolism and integrated high-performance chemical isotope-labeling metabolomics with metagenomics in 30 dairy cows. Among 349 detected small peptides, proline-containing dipeptides were associated with higher NUE, together with an S15 peptidyl-peptidase with Xaa-Pro dipeptide-generating activity. In vitro rumen fermentation, metatranscriptomics and targeted quantification showed that proline-dipeptide accumulation coincided with transcriptional patterns consistent with nitrogen assimilation and amino acid biosynthesis. Bacterial incubation and heterologous expression confirmed that S15.001 hydrolyzed Xaa-Pro substrates. These findings identify a microbial proline-dipeptide axis associated with NUE and provide a basis for precision nutrition strategies targeting ruminal peptide metabolism.

papers.title: kinGEMs: A robust and scalable framework for resource-constraint models through stochastic tuning of deep learning-predicted kinetic parameters.
papers.authors: A Barghout R, Chiñas Serrano L, Sanchez-Lengeling B, Mahadevan R.
papers.abstract: The construction of accurate enzyme-constrained genome-scale models (ecGEMs) remains a critical challenge in systems biology, limited by sparse kinetic data and the need for biologically meaningful representations. This work presents an integrated framework combining CPI-Pred, a deep learning model to predict kinetic parameters (kcat) from sequence and compound embeddings, with kinGEMs, a pipeline to incorporate these uncertainty-aware parameters into ecGEMs for metabolic optimization. By leveraging representations at multiple scales, the approach captures sequence, structure, and kinetic data to enhance model generalizability and accuracy. Rigorous benchmarking demonstrates the framework's capability to predict growth rates and fluxes that are consistent with experimental observations and measured proteome fractions, reduce median flux variability by several folds, and yield better-constrained metabolic models by explicitly accounting for the uncertainty inherent in ML-predicted kinetic parameters. kinGEMs successfully generated ecGEMs for 93 models spanning a phylogenetically diverse set of organisms including Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria, mycobacteria, parasitic protists, fungi, and mammalian cell lines. These innovations breakdown the barrier to application of ecGEMs to non-model organisms and open new avenues for metabolic engineering and synthetic biology in more industrially relevant hosts.

papers.title: MultiMHC: a multiscale learning framework integrating sequence and residue contact topology for peptide-MHC binding prediction.
papers.authors: Chen W, Chi Y, Wang Y, Wu J, Wei M, Zhao W, Kang Y, Bai X, Chen S, Zhou Z, Zhou R.
papers.abstract: Accurate prediction of peptide-major histocompatibility complex (pMHC) binding is central to understanding antigen presentation and identifying T-cell epitopes in cancer immunotherapy. Although recent methods have achieved notable progress, most approaches rely predominantly on sequence-based features and only partially capture structural determinants of pMHC recognition. In this study, we present MultiMHC, a multiscale deep learning framework that integrates complementary sequential and biologically-informed residue contact topology for pMHC binding prediction. MultiMHC combines a recurrent neural network to model global sequence context with a graph-based representation to encode residue contact patterns derived from known pMHC binding interfaces. Features from these two pathways are subsequently fused to generate binding predictions across peptides of varying lengths. Benchmark evaluations show that MultiMHC achieves performance comparable to existing state-of-the-art methods, with particularly strong performance in ranking-based assessments. Moreover, evaluation on the Tumor Neoantigen Selection Alliance dataset showed that MultiMHC binding scores can enrich experimentally validated T-cell epitopes among top-ranked candidates, supporting its potential utility as an upstream binding-based filtering step in neoantigen discovery workflows. Together, these results highlight the value of incorporating residue interaction patterns and lightweight structural information into pMHC modeling and establish MultiMHC as a robust and extensive framework for antigen presentation analysis.

papers.title: Response to comments on "SpatialDG: a novel spatial domain identification method for spatially resolved transcriptomics data based on dual-graph neural network".
papers.authors: Wu J, Oshinjo A, Izzi V.
papers.abstract: We respond to concerns regarding reference-label-informed epoch selection in SpatialDG. We acknowledge this limitation and report a matched DLPFC reevaluation of SpatialDG and Spatial-MGCN under the same reference-label-independent checkpoint-selection rule, in which SpatialDG achieved the higher three-seed mean ARI on all 12 slices.

papers.title: HEDGEHOG: hierarchical evaluation of drug generators through rigorous filtration.
papers.authors: Ryabchenko DA, Gurevich P, Kadyrov SD, Frolova D, Fedisheva K, Shapeev AV, Nikolenko SA, Pak MA.
papers.abstract: Generative molecular models can support early drug discovery by proposing new candidate compounds de novo. In practice, useful candidates must balance target-relevant activity, physicochemical properties, and other multiparameter design constraints. However, standard metrics commonly used to evaluate molecular generators only weakly reflect whether the generated compounds are medicinally plausible and suitable for downstream computation. This can produce an incomplete view of model performance and inefficient use of computational resources. We introduce HEDGEHOG, a configurable six-stage evaluation framework that is constructed as a hit identification workflow: (i) preprocessing; (ii) physicochemical descriptor screening; (iii) structural alerts and graph-sanity checks; (iv) synthesis feasibility; (v) docking; and (vi) 3D pose and interaction checks. We evaluated $22$ generative models in a KRAS G12D case study, using three runs of $1000$ requested generation attempts per model. The models showed different patterns of attrition, and final survival ranged from zero to $127.0 \pm 18.1$ molecules per run. None of the standard metrics showed a significant association with final survival after correction for multiple testing. HEDGEHOG provides a reproducible framework for evaluating molecular generative models under defined screening criteria. The framework identifies stage-wise failure modes across generators and provides a practical basis for developing molecular generators better aligned with early drug discovery.

papers.title: SwimmingIndividuals: A high-performance agent-based model for marine ecosystems.
papers.authors: Woodstock MS, Mattern JP, Wu Z, Britten GL.
papers.abstract: Because they are based on established theory, mechanistic models are essential for projecting ecological responses to novel conditions. Yet mechanistic agent-based model (ABM) applications have often been limited by computational constraints. This paper introduces SwimmingIndividuals, an open-source ABM framework that advances our ability to simulate physiological processes, animal movement, higher trophic level marine ecosystem dynamics, and fisheries removals at large ecological scales. The software's key contributions are a suite of mechanistic sub-models governing the full life cycle of each agent, including visual prey detection, adaptive behaviors such as diel vertical migration (DVM), a flexible bioenergetics engine with three taxon-specific metabolic architectures, and a spatial pathfinding algorithm for habitat-seeking movement. These processes are made computationally tractable through a hybrid CPU/GPU architecture written in Julia. Unlike prior ABMs that use fixed perception radii or single-equation bioenergetics, SwimmingIndividuals enables emergent ecological dynamics across populations of superindividual agents. We demonstrate the framework through three Gulf of America simulations. The model reproduced DVM, cetacean diving patterns, size-based trophic shifts, and von Bertalanffy growth curves consistent with published King Mackerel stock assessments. Long-term simulations generated realistic population dynamics and quantified impacts of fishery harvest control rules across five fleets. SwimmingIndividuals provides a powerful, flexible, open-source platform for mechanistic marine ecosystem research and ecosystem-based fisheries management.

papers.title: Ten simple rules for a department chair.
papers.authors: Tomaska L.
papers.abstract: Department chairs occupy a pivotal position in the university. Teaching, research, graduate education, and much of the academic community's professional and administrative activity are organized at the departmental level. Yet, despite the importance of the position and the considerable challenges it entails, many scientists assume the role with little or no formal preparation for academic leadership. This paper is intended as a practical primer rather than a comprehensive guide to academic leadership. The proposed rules provide a framework that prospective and current department chairs can adapt to their own institutional circumstances, experience, and leadership style.

papers.title: Sequence-based coevolutionary prediction of species-specific interactomes.
papers.authors: Fernandez-Martin M, Pontes C, Ruiz-Serra V, Valencia A.
papers.abstract: Evolutionarily conserved protein-protein interactions (PPIs) reveal fundamental biological processes. However, predicting protein function solely from these interactions provides an incomplete picture of biological systems. Computational methods for predicting PPIs often struggle due to limited functional annotations in databases, making it difficult to fully understand unique biological systems. This study introduces ContextMirror2.0 (CM2.0), a coevolution-based method designed to address these limitations. Coevolutionary approaches, unlike supervised machine learning methods, do not rely on labelled datasets, proving valuable in addressing the scarcity of data for species-specific PPIs. Around 40% of CM2.0's top-1000 predicted PPIs for E. coli, S. enterica, and S. aureus are supported by experimental PPI databases. However, comparative analysis of the resulting functional communities further revealed both highly conserved interaction patterns and species-specific interactions. CM2.0 leverages coevolutionary information at the phylogenetic level to explore protein interaction dynamics and understand the functional consequences of species-specific variations. This information can inform further studies on the emergence of novel functions, adaptation to specific environments, and the development of targeted therapies.

papers.title: Nondisruptive 3D profiling of combinations of epigenetic marks in single cells.
papers.authors: Chen Y, Radda JSD, Alderman MH, Jin S, Cheng Y, Zhang Y, Liu M, Xiao AZ, Wang S.
papers.abstract: Advances in single-cell sequencing and spatial omics technologies have enhanced our understanding of diverse cellular identities, compositions, architectures and functions. However, the single-cell three-dimensional (3D) organization of the epigenome is still not well understood, due to an absence of spatial single-cell methods that allow high-resolution, locus-specific detection of combinations of epigenetic marks while maintaining 3D genome organization. Here we develop epigenetic proximity hybridization reaction (Epi-PHR), a nondisruptive image-based single-cell spatial epigenetic profiling technology. Epi-PHR detects combinations of epigenetic marks in situ at hundreds of gene targets within single cells while preserving 3D genome organization. Phased Epi-PHR combined with chromatin tracing reveals unexpected associations between epigenetic mark enrichment and chromatin folding of an imprinted gene cluster at the single-chromatin-copy level for the distinct alleles from different parental origins. We expect Epi-PHR will be broadly applicable in research requiring single-cell spatial epigenetic information, advancing our understanding of the combinatorial epigenetic code and its relationship with chromatin organization.

An information-theoretic framework for inferring T cell dynamics from single-cell RNA and T cell receptor sequencing.
papers.authors: Ceglia N, Salehi S, Sethna ZM, Elhanati Y, Freeman SS, Lyudovyk O, Burman B, Chow A, Zamarin D, DeWolf S, Shahid S, Bojilova V, Rusk N, Balachandran VP, McPherson A, Shah SP, Greenbaum BD.
papers.abstract: Single-cell T cell receptor (TCR) repertoire sequencing enables simultaneous profiling of gene expression and TCR sequences, providing a coregistered measure of T cell phenotypic diversity and clonal dynamics. However, principled probabilistic frameworks for joint modeling of clonotype and phenotype have remained limited. Here we introduce TCRi, a hierarchical Bayesian information-theoretic framework that infers the joint probability distribution between genetic clonotype and transcriptional phenotype from paired single-cell transcriptomic and TCR sequencing data. TCRi treats phenotype assignment as a probabilistic inference problem: a variational autoencoder embeds single-cell expression into a structured latent space, and a hierarchical Bayesian model learns clonotype-specific phenotype distributions through principled information-sharing across clonotypes, patients and covariates. From these distributions, TCRi computes information-theoretic quantities: clonotypic entropy, phenotypic entropy, phenotypic flux and mutual information between clonotype and phenotype. When TCRi was applied to four real-world datasets comprising 167,118 CD8 T cells from patients with cancer treated with anti-PD-(L)1 immune checkpoint blockade, mutual information emerged as a robust discriminator of therapeutic response.

papers.title: Single-cell atlas uncovers layer 4 heterogeneity and functional gradients in rhesus macaque visual cortex.
papers.authors: Günther DM, Batiuk MY, De Oliveira R, Petukhov V, Wunderle T, Dragicevic K, Buchholz CJ, Fries P, Khodosevich K.
papers.abstract: Non-human primates like rhesus macaques are pivotal models for decoding human visual cortex physiology and disorders. However, there is a lack of high-resolution transcriptomic atlases comparing distinct areas of the visual cortex in macaque. Here, we developed BrainSPACE, an innovative pipeline for rapid and precise brain tissue banking, to sample visual cortex areas: V1, V2, V4, MT, and TEO. We applied single-nucleus RNA-sequencing (snRNA-seq) to unravel neuronal diversity in BrainSPACE-banked V1 and V4 areas ( ~ 100,000 nuclei). We uncovered conserved GABAergic neuron profiles but stark area-specific diversity in principal neurons, featuring seven unique layer 4 subtypes in V1 and one in V4. Complementary smFISH validated transcriptional gradients across these areas, aligning with ventral and dorsal stream hierarchies. Gene ontology analyses highlighted plasticity-related pathways in unique layer 4 subtypes, with genes like NTNG1 and NLGN1 linked to neurodevelopmental disorders such as autism and schizophrenia. Our insights bridge molecular architecture to visual processing, offering an interactive atlas for community use. By revealing how layer 4 heterogeneity drives hierarchical specialization, our work advances primate brain mapping and informs therapeutic strategies for vision-related pathologies.

papers.title: Leveraging human pangenome for improved somatic variant detection.
papers.authors: Fu Q, Xin Z, Miao B, Zhang W, Kong N, Tang Z, Ruttenberg A, Albracht DC, Belter EA, Garza JE, Tomlinson C, Mehinovic E, Shen J, Zhuo X, Dong S, Johnson BK, Majewski MF, Palmer T, Jang HJ, Cheng Y, Li Z, Lawson HA, Lindsay T, Li D, Fulton R, Shen H, Jin SC, SMaHT Network Assembly/Pangenome Working Group, Macias-Velasco JF, Wang T.
papers.abstract: Somatic variant detection is technically challenging due to low variant allele fractions, the confounding presence of germline variation, and reference bias. Linear references, such as GRCh38, miss sample-specific variation, leading to misalignments and incorrect variant calls. Although telomere-to-telomere donor-specific assemblies (DSAs) accurately represent individual genomes, their application is limited by cost and technical barriers. Alternatively, the graph-based human pangenome provides a scalable framework to improve read alignment and perform genome inference. Here, we benchmarked somatic variant detection using GRCh38, graph-based pangenomes, and pangenome-inferred DSAs with a HapMap mixture dataset and the COLO829 melanoma cell line. Pangenome-guided alignment improves read mapping and somatic variant calling accuracy. Furthermore, personalized pangenomes partially reconstruct donor-specific genomic content, improving accuracy, reducing germline contamination, and enabling detection of events in loci absent or poorly represented in GRCh38. These findings demonstrate that graph-based and personalized pangenomes are effective strategies for enhancing somatic variant detection compared with GRCh38.

papers.title: TriTower-m6Am: A triple-tower heterogeneous deep learning architecture integrating semantic, sequential, and structural information for mRNA N6,2'-O-dimethyladenosine site prediction.
papers.authors: Xiong K, Jia J.
papers.abstract: Background N6,2'-O-dimethyladenosine (m6Am) is a cap-proximal mRNA modification deposited by PCIF1 (phosphorylated C-terminal domain (CTD)-interacting factor 1) at the first transcribed nucleotide of eukaryotic mRNAs. Knowing where m6Am sites sit would help explain how cells tune mRNA stability and translation, but current predictors typically depend on a single representation and do not jointly model multiple views of the same RNA sequence. Results We present TriTower-m6Am, combining semantic (RNA-FM, a pretrained RNA foundation model, with BellPooling), sequential (One-Hot BiLSTM, bidirectional long short-term memory), and structural (RGCN, a relational graph convolutional network, over the 41-nt window) representations of each RNA window. On an independent test set of 640 sequences, TriTower-m6Am reaches an area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.776 and a Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) of 0.425, against DTC-m6Am's AUC = 0.765 and MCC = 0.411, using 4.4 times fewer trainable parameters; at every matched specificity between 0.40 and 0.70 it recovers 1-7 more true sites out of 320 than DTC-m6Am. The AUC-weighted voting keeps every tower's contribution readable for any individual prediction. Analyses of the graph tower delimit its benefit to the relational aggregation of local backbone adjacency over sequence-derived node features: the edge-type ablation, the node-feature ablation, and a structure-permutation control agree that the specific RNAfold-predicted fold carries no attributable signal, and a probing analysis shows that per-base base-pairing status is largely recoverable from the sequence-derived RNA-FM embeddings (AUC = 0.72 vs. 0.65 from the raw sequence), so the fold annotation is substantially redundant with the semantic representation the ensemble already receives. Conclusions Combining semantic, sequential, and structural views of the same RNA sequence improves m6Am prediction beyond any single representation, and the ensemble's voting weights make each prediction auditable without a post-hoc explainer. Whether the triple-tower pattern transfers to other RNA modification prediction tasks remains to be tested in future work.

papers.title: Ten simple rules for a successful global health roundtable.
papers.authors: Uribe Guajardo MG, Rush A, Cunich M, Cravero K, Huckel Schneider C.
papers.abstract: Qualitative approaches play a critical role in global health research by capturing the social, political, and contextual dimensions that shape health outcomes. While interviews and focus groups are widely used, these methods are often time‑limited and project‑specific. Global health roundtables offer a complementary approach, providing a flexible and long-term platform for engaging diverse stakeholders-including researchers, practitioners, policymakers, and community representatives-in collective dialogue, knowledge exchange, and collaboration. When designed well, roundtables can support co‑production of knowledge, address complex system‑level challenges, and generate insights with relevance beyond a single event. Despite their growing use, practical guidance on how to design and run roundtables specifically for global health remains limited. In this article, we present ten simple rules for organising successful global health roundtables, drawing on existing literature, practice‑based experience, and examples from different geopolitical and health‑system contexts. The rules address key stages of the roundtable lifecycle, including topic selection, objective setting, inclusive participation, management of power dynamics, optimisation of engagement and commitment, ethical recognition of contributions, and translation of dialogue into meaningful outputs and sustained collaboration. Together, these rules provide an accessible framework to support researchers, practitioners, and policy actors in using roundtables as ethical, inclusive, and impactful tools for global health research, policy development, and practice.

papers.title: Social manipulations trigger shifts in group-level dominance patterns.
papers.authors: van der Marel A, Francis X, O'Connell CL, Estien CO, Carminito C, Moore VD, Hobson EA.
papers.abstract: Within dominance hierarchies, individuals often direct aggression based on their own rank and the rank of others. When many group members make the same rank-informed aggression decisions, a broader group-level "dominance pattern" can emerge which further structures aggression within the framework of the dominance hierarchy. However, whether groups can change their group-level dominance patterns over time, and what factors might drive these changes, are not well understood. We investigated aggression dynamics by experimentally manipulating captive groups of monk parakeets (Myiopsitta monachus) using targeted rank-based removals and reintroductions of group members to induce social instability. Dominance patterns often shifted after experimental perturbations but remained stable in their absence. The rank of the perturbed individual affected both individual aggression decisions and the shifts in dominance patterns observed. In particular, reintroductions of top-ranked birds led to marked changes in aggression and shifts in dominance patterns. Understanding the factors that shape these dynamics can help explain how animal societies respond to social disturbance.

papers.title: spOT-NMF: gene expression deconvolution via optimal transport with proximity-aware niche mapping for spatial transcriptomics.
papers.authors: Abdelkareem AO, Gill GS, Manoharan VT, Verhey TB, Morrissy AS.
papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics enables direct profiling of cellular organization within intact tissues, yet two challenges limit its full exploitation: accurate reference-free deconvolution of mixed expression signals (including species-admixed models such as xenografts), and lack of tools that can translate per-spot program usage values into spatial niches. We developed spOT-NMF, an optimal transport-based non-negative matrix factorization method that replaces standard reconstruction loss with the Wasserstein distance to disentangle mixed signals without requiring matched single-cell atlases. While the generalized OT-NMF factorization is applicable to any expression matrix, a proximity-based niche inference module further translates program co-usage from spatial transcriptomes into directional co-occurrence networks that define tissue compartments and their boundaries. Benchmarking across five gold-standard datasets spanning sub-cellular to multi-cellular resolutions, multiple platforms, and two-species admixture scenarios, spOT-NMF ranks first among reference-free methods, with particular advantage under the signal imbalance conditions characteristic of xenografts. We show that reference-free deconvolution recovers cell populations absent from matched single-cell atlases, highlighting the value of unsupervised analysis. Applied to glioblastoma xenografts and human colorectal cancer, spOT-NMF reveals spatially restricted interferon signaling, invasion routes, and CAF-tumor boundaries. spOT-NMF is available as an open-source Python package with GPU, CPU, and HPC support.

papers.title: Machine learning for RNA-small molecule interactions: methodologies, evaluation, and future directions.
papers.authors: Chen S, Huang Z, Wang Y, Li Y, Liu G, Tan YS, Wu M, Deng L.
papers.abstract: RNA is emerging as a compelling therapeutic target due to its rich structural diversity and central involvement in gene regulation, splicing, translation, and cellular signaling. Alongside advances in structural biology, computational approaches, especially machine learning and deep learning, have transformed the systematic analysis of RNA-small molecule interactions. In this paper, we provide a comprehensive survey of computational methods for RNA-small molecule interaction prediction, with a particular emphasis on three core tasks: binding site prediction, binding preference prediction, and binding pose prediction. We first summarize the data resources commonly used to support these tasks and outline molecular representations that capture RNA structural features and the chemical properties of small molecules. We then review a spectrum of computational approaches for the above three tasks, ranging from statistical methods and traditional machine learning to deep learning. We further evaluate representative methods for each task, providing insights into their respective strengths and limitations. Finally, we highlight open challenges in current research on RNA-small molecule interactions, including limited data availability, the black-box nature of the models, and the growing need for generative modeling. We discuss emerging directions such as data augmentation, model interpretability, and RNA-targeted small-molecule design as promising pathways to address these challenges and advance rational RNA-targeted drug discovery.

papers.title: Inferring causal networks for genomic trios with high-dimensional confounding variables.
papers.authors: Kvamme JM, Fu AQ.
papers.abstract: Causal structure inference under the principle of Mendelian randomization (PMR) enables the study of causal relationships between two molecular phenotypes (e.g. gene expression) by leveraging genetic variants as instrumental variables to impose constraints on edge direction. In practice, inference is often affected by numerous confounding variables, such as other genes, other processes and demographic variables, making it essential to robustly account for confounders. However, existing methods have limited ability to accommodate high-dimensional confounding. Here, we introduce Mendelian randomization for genomic networks (MRGN), a regression-based method under the PMR for inferring causal models in genomic trios from individual-level data while accounting for many confounders. MRGN extends beyond the canonical mediation model to distinguish among multiple causal relationships. By prioritizing conditional independence tests given the genetic variant and confounders, MRGN can detect causal relationships between phenotypes even when their marginal association is weak. Through extensive simulations, we demonstrate improved inference accuracy, robustness, and computational efficiency over existing approaches. We further apply MRGN to data from the Genotype-Tissue Expression Consortium to investigate how genetic variants may regulate gene expression in cis and trans.

papers.title: Identifying multi-omics spatial domains via masked autoencoder and diffusion-based latent regularization with SpaMEDM.
papers.authors: Zhou C, Lu M, Meng Y, Hu S, Zhu Y, Sun Y, Gu J, Tian Z, Yang F, Wang J, Li L.
papers.abstract: Spatial multi-omics data provide complementary molecular views of tissue organization. However, their integration remains challenging due to data sparsity, technical noise, and modality-specific distributions. Here, we present Spatial Masked autoEncoder and Diffusion-based Model (SpaMEDM), an end-to-end graph representation learning framework that augments a dual-attention graph-integration backbone with masked reconstruction and diffusion-based latent noise-prediction regularization. In the masked track, randomly masked spot features are recovered by leveraging modality- and graph-specific neighborhood information. In parallel, Gaussian perturbations are applied to modality-specific latent representations at randomly sampled noise levels, and a spatial-graph-informed network is trained to predict the injected noise. This diffusion-based objective is used exclusively during training to encourage robustness to latent perturbations, rather than to perform iterative reverse diffusion or sampling during inference. Furthermore, cosine-based paired-spot directional alignment and adjacency reconstruction encourage compatible cross-modality representations and preservation of the selected graph structure. SpaMEDM flexibly supports purely spatial, dual feature-spatial, and modality-specific feature-pruned spatial graph configurations. Evaluations across diverse spatial multi-omics datasets demonstrate competitive spatial-domain identification performance and produce integrated embeddings that facilitate downstream exploratory analyses.

papers.title: Metabolomics Subcenter (Met-SC): an integrated metabolomics database and analysis platform.
papers.authors: Wen L, Wang M, Zeng Z, Song S, Zhao W, Xu G, Liu X.
papers.abstract: The rapid growth of metabolomics data has increased the need for integrated storage, analysis, and reuse. Here, we present Metabolomics Subcenter (Met-SC) V1.0 (https://metabolomics.dicp.ac.cn/), an integrated database and platform for standardized data deposition, spectral-resource management, online analysis, and disease-focused knowledge mining. The deposition framework captures project, sample, pretreatment, and instrument metadata across chromatographic, capillary electrophoresis-mass spectrometry, and nuclear magnetic resonance workflows. Met-SC contains 7 756 867 reference spectra associated with 1 989 680 unique compounds and 73 014 049 unknown-feature spectra derived from diverse biological matrices and experimental conditions. Its web-based analysis module provides 27 functions for data preprocessing, quality-control visualization, and statistical analysis. Metabolism-centered knowledge graph for colorectal cancer (MetKG-CRC) comprises 108 679 biomolecular entities and 600 093 literature-supported evidence triples. By linking data deposition, spectral resources, analysis, and evidence-supported knowledge exploration in a single platform, Met-SC facilitates reproducible metabolomics data management and downstream discovery.

papers.title: The UCSC Genome Browser database: 2027 update.
papers.authors: Speir ML, van Baren MJ, Barber GP, Benet-Pages A, Birgmeier J, Casper J, Clawson H, Diekhans M, Fischer C, Gonzalez JN, Hinrichs AS, Lee CM, Nassar LR, Perez G, Raney BJ, Robinson J, Smith AD, Alde E, Kitiyakara B, Haussler D, Kent WJ, Haeussler M.
papers.abstract: Since 2000, the UCSC Genome Browser (https://genome.ucsc.edu) has served as a standard tool for visualizing and comparing annotations across thousands of genome assemblies. Users can browse and visualize a wide range of data types from gene annotations to regulatory regions and comparative genome alignments. Once the data view is configured, the Genome Browser image can be exported for use in publications. Beyond visualization, users can use our tools to compare and export the annotations for further analysis. This year's feature updates include the full release of a tool to copy annotations between related assemblies, QuickLift; feature additions to our data-hosting service HubSpace to enable live editing of configuration files; two new display configurability options: "My Annotations" and custom item coloring; and several improvements to genome assembly discovery and track management. Beyond these new features, 28 new annotation tracks have been added across three broad categories: variant databases and interpretation, gene regulation, and transcriptome and gene expression. These include ENCODE4 cCREs and other ENCODE4 regulatory annotations, variant frequencies and phased variants from national sequencing projects, and two massively parallel reporter assay tracks.

papers.title: GutBiomeDB: an integrated human gut microbiome database of 168 464 samples.
papers.authors: Zhai J, Liu BH, Guo LY, Li Y, Liu J, Su X, Cui R, Zheng D, Sun Y, Dai C.
papers.abstract: The gut microbiome plays an important role in maintaining human health. Despite the rapid growth of literature and publicly accessible data on the gut microbiome, a large-scale, well-curated database integrating a unified matrix with multiple analytical tools is still lacking. Here, we introduced GutBiomeDB, a comprehensive database and analysis platform for the human gut microbiome. GutBiomeDB contains 168 464 samples from 482 BioProjects, spanning 72 countries, 224 disease conditions, and seven life stages. To improve the reusability and accessibility of data, the uniformly processed taxonomic profiles generated by Abdill et al. were reused without reprocessing to construct a matrix of 4680 taxa and 3142 genera, and disease, life-stage, sex, and geographic metadata were manually curated by our team. Additionally, GutBiomeDB offers four tools for in-depth analysis: "Differential Analysis" for comparing diversity and abundance of user-selected cohorts and performing random-effects meta-analysis across projects; "Interaction Network" for comparing disease and healthy-control co-occurrence networks; "Lifecycle Atlas" for visualizing genus trajectories across seven life stages; and "Health Index" for searching similar samples and scoring uploaded genus profiles. GutBiomeDB serves as a versatile and valuable resource for advancing a broad spectrum of gut microbiome research and clinical relevance. GutBiomeDB is freely accessed at https://gutbiomedb.online.

papers.title: Ribocentre-FoldBridge: a comprehensive database bridging RNA chemical probing data and 3D structures.
papers.authors: Sun H, Hu L, Peng X, Zhang W, Lin J, Huang J, Zhang C, Huang L, Miao Z.
papers.abstract: RNA chemical probing generates nucleotide-resolved profiles in vitro and in cells, while X-ray crystallographic or cryo-electron microscopy models provide high-resolution structural models but remain comparatively low throughput. Aligning these experiments from different modalities may provide insights into RNA structure formation and molecular functions. Here, we present Ribocentre-FoldBridge (https://foldbridge.ribocentre.org/), an AI-assisted, curator-reviewed database linking curated chemical-probing profiles with experimentally determined 3D structures. This database catalogues 12 types of RNAs, linking 256 929 probing profiles across five experimental categories to 5321 structure-linked cases. It interactively visualizes the probing profiles that align with RNA secondary and tertiary structures at nucleotide resolution. We demonstrate probe-specific reactivity patterns across paired, unpaired, and solvent-accessible structural contexts. The database aims to provide a reproducible evidence layer for examining RNA structure-function relationships across heterogeneous experiments, and thus facilitate the development of new RNA structure or function prediction programs.

papers.title: GlyTouCan v4: a redesigned interface and expanded functionality for the international glycan structure repository.
papers.authors: Shiota M, Ono T, Matsubara M, Kimura N, Masding T, Tsukada N, Inoue K, Yamada I, Aoki-Kinoshita KF.
papers.abstract: GlyTouCan (https://glytoucan.org) is the international, species-neutral glycan structure repository that assigns stable, globally unique accession numbers to glycan structures independently of the experimental method used to determine them. Here, we describe GlyTouCan version 4, released on June 22, 2026, which introduces a completely redesigned user interface with substantially faster browsing and searching, including a new "archetype" view that groups registrations that differ only in the anomeric or ring form of the reducing-end residue together for clearer filtering of the >256,000 glycans now registered. Version 4 provides an improved graphical structure input, via the updated browser-embedded GlycanBuilder application, for both searching and registering structures. Users may now sign in with an ORCID ID in addition to a Google account, and all previously released v3 REST API endpoints remain fully backward compatible. Version 4 also introduces a framework for industry affiliates, providing a structured pathway for commercial organizations that work with or synthesize glycans, while all existing academic database-partner relationships are maintained. GlyTouCan remains freely available to all users without charge, login, or registration for browsing and searching. We also summarize the repository's data content, which spans >600 monosaccharide types and, judging from these, includes many glycans of probable bacterial or plant origin.

papers.title: scSpAS: an integrated single-cell and spatial atlas of transcript isoform regulation.
papers.authors: Chen L, Liu D, He Z, Xu Z, Li R, Yang Q, Gao Z, Xia R, Song J, He T, Wang Y, Lin JW, Chen L.

papers.title: BioImage Archive: bringing bioimaging data together.
papers.authors: Zulueta-Coarasa T, Yoldas A, Anita L, Babalola K, Bircan K, Cattavitello C, Clementel D, Ma M, Mandloi T, Marks D, Rookyard C, Sherwood F, Somasundharam S, Velasquez M, Weyand S, Hartley M.
papers.abstract: The BioImage Archive (https://www.ebi.ac.uk/bioimage-archive) is EMBL-EBI's flagship resource for life sciences image data. It serves as a deposition database for biological images across scales from near-atomic through to whole organisms, and across imaging modalities. The Archive's mission is to support the reproducibility of quantitative results based on imaging, support methods development including modern deep-learning-based approaches, and allow large-scale reanalysis of image data. Across the Archive's ecosystem, we provide access to over 11 PB of image data. Recent developments in underpinning infrastructure now allow interactive exploration, visualization, and streaming access to a subset of the Archive's data using the new OME-Zarr file format, and will ultimately provide access to all of EMBL-EBI's archived image data, including data from the Electron Microscopy Public Image Archive. Migration of all holdings and a unified submission system are in progress.

papers.title: SABIO-RK in 2027: enzyme kinetics data with modernized framework and enhanced data access.
papers.authors: Rey M, Wittig U, Hu X, Müller W.
papers.abstract: SABIO-RK (https://sabiork.h-its.org) is a publicly available database providing expert-curated information on biochemical reactions, kinetic parameters, enzymes, and experimental conditions. For over 20 years, it has served as a central resource for experimentally measured enzyme kinetic data, as required for modeling in systems biology, in enzymology research, and lately to train machine learning predictors or AI-driven data extractors. Here, we report on SABIO-RK's comprehensive redesign of its infrastructure and interfaces for improved usability and scalability. The updated system integrates data input, curation, and public access into a unified JSON-based framework with full version control for transparency and reproducibility. The new web interface offers streamlined navigation and enhanced search with over 60 fields. Browse functionality provides structured database overviews, while the Results Explorer allows interactive refinement of search results, which can now be saved and reused. A secure RESTful API enables open programmatic access, returning results in JSON, CSV, SBML, or EnzymeML formats. As of September 2026, the database contains 76 973 entries from 8149 publications, covering 10 375 reactions, 2315 enzymes (EC (Enzyme Commission) numbers), and 14 224 chemical compounds. The new SABIO-RK also improves the curation workflow, simplifies user feedback, and facilitates future community curation. Upcoming features include AI-driven literature recommendations, entity recognition, and the integration of visual search.

papers.title: Cellular and spatial continuum of TAM functional states governs immune exclusion and dictates immune checkpoint resistance in melanoma.
papers.authors: Chakraborty S, Corrales E, Godbole I, Madkhali N, Das T, Krolla C, Nystrom A, Meiss F, Rafei D, Bengsch B, Andrieux G, Boerries M.
papers.abstract: Background Immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) therapy has transformed melanoma treatment, yet many patients either fail to respond or develop resistance after an initial response. The cellular and spatial determinants within the tumor microenvironment (TME) that underlie these divergent ICI therapy outcomes remain poorly defined. Here, we aimed to characterize the immune composition and spatial organization of the TME associated with ICI response and resistance. Methods We integrated public scRNA-seq data (N = 32) with in-house spatial transcriptomics and imaging mass cytometry from an independent melanoma cohort (N = 6) to achieve high-resolution spatial profiling of the TME. This multimodal approach allowed us to map cellular heterogeneity within discrete spatial neighborhoods. To validate our findings, we constructed a scRNA-seq derived signature-matrix and deconvoluted a bulk RNA-seq cohort (N = 334). Clinical associations were assessed using Kaplan-Meier survival analysis, Cox hazard models, and a machine-learning classifier. Results We identified a distinct tumor-associated macrophage (TAM) state, termed lipid-associated TAMs (LA-TAMs), characterized by conserved lipid metabolic programs and tumor-specific adaptations in glycolysis under hypoxic conditions. Deep spatial multi-omics profiling revealed divergent immune architectures associated with treatment outcomes. In non-responder patients, LA-TAMs colocalized with sparsely distributed TIM3⁺ exhausted CD8⁺ T cells within an immune-excluded TME. In contrast, responder patients harbored interferon-primed CCL4 + TAMs (IFN-TAMs) spatially associated with Granzyme B⁺ activated CD8⁺ T cells, reflecting an immune-active microenvironment. These findings define contrasting macrophage-centered immune neighborhoods linked to ICI response. Interestingly, patients with LA-TAM-enriched neighborhoods were consistently non-responders or progressed during follow-up, irrespective of the presence of IFN-TAM neighborhoods. Lastly, we constructed a single-cell-derived signature matrix that estimates TAM fractions from bulk RNA-seq data and revealed LA-TAM abundance as a robust, independent predictor of poor ICI response and survival in a validation cohort. Conclusions Our study defines the spatial landscapes of TAM-heterogeneity in melanoma and identifies LA-TAM neighborhoods as an important feature of ICI resistance. Although patients span a continuum of TAM-centered immune states, the presence of LA-TAM is likely to diminish the beneficial effects of IFN-TAM-associated immune activation. Finally, our proposed Melanoma-TME-derived signature-matrix provides a translatable framework to robustly predict ICI response and resistance.

papers.title: Integrated single-nucleus and spatial transcriptomics define tumour cell metaprograms and tumour microenvironment organisation in choroid plexus tumours.
papers.authors: Klötergens A, Inserte C, de Faria FW, Verma A, Schüftan E, Roy R, Banerjee V, Albert TK, Lu IN, Kordes U, Obrecht-Sturm D, Thomas C, Kerl K.
papers.abstract: Background Choroid plexus tumours (CPTs) are rare intraventricular brain neoplasms derived from choroid plexus epithelium, predominantly affecting young children. They include benign choroid plexus papilloma (CPP), atypical CPP (aCPP), and malignant choroid plexus carcinoma (CPC) and segregate into three DNA-methylation subgroups: paediatric A (pedA), paediatric B (pedB), and adult. Methods To resolve subtype-specific biology, we performed single-nucleus RNA sequencing on 43 CPTs and integrated 12 non-neoplastic foetal, paediatric, and adult choroid plexus references, complemented by spatial transcriptomics in a subset of 16 tumour sections and 2 normal choroid plexus samples. Results Tumour embeddings and correlation analyses demonstrated that CPTs cluster by methylation subtype rather than WHO grade, revealing epigenetically driven relationships despite divergent histology. We identified 10 tumour metaprograms spanning epithelial differentiation, ciliogenesis, proliferation, extra cellular matrix remodelling, and stress responses. PedA and adult tumours showed relatively homogeneous program distribution dominated by differentiation or ciliation states, whereas pedB tumours exhibited marked heterogeneity with selective enrichment of hypoxia, interferon signalling, early stress response, and TGF-β signalling. Spatial mapping revealed consistent anticorrelation of these programs with ciliogenesis and differentiation programs, suggesting stress-associated dedifferentiation. Elevated stress and hypoxia scores correlated with poorer survival. PedB tumours showed enrichment of interferon- and lipid-associated myeloid populations, that carried pro-angiogenic signatures. They were spatially co-localised with hypoxic and interferon I expressing tumour areas, that were predicted to interact with myeloid cells via immunosuppressive cues, shaping a pro-angiogenic, pro-tumour environment. Conclusions This study identifies stress- and hypoxia-associated dedifferentiation programs that are selectively enriched in pedB tumours, correlate with poor clinical outcome, and antagonise multiciliogenesis and epithelial differentiation. Their spatial co-localisation with immunosuppressive, pro-angiogenic macrophage populations links developmental arrest to microenvironmental remodelling and aggressive behaviour. These findings provide a biologically grounded framework for risk stratification and highlight hypoxia, angiogenesis and macrophage polarisation as candidate therapeutic targets in high-risk CPTs.

papers.title: YEASTRACT+: the 2026 update with focus on global quantitative transcription regulation data and metabolic engineering applications.
papers.authors: Coutinho L, Paulo L, Couceiro D, Val T, Oliveira J, Costa IV, Zolotareva M, Matos M, Fernandes M, Mupueleque M, Sá-Correia I, Teixeira MC, Monteiro PT.
papers.abstract: YEASTRACT+ (http://yeastract-plus.org/) is a tool for the analysis, prediction, and modelling of transcription regulatory data at gene and genomic levels in yeasts. It incorporates three integrated databases: YEASTRACT, PathoYeastract, and NCYeastract, focused on Saccharomyces cerevisiae, pathogenic yeasts, and non-conventional yeasts of biotechnological relevance, respectively. In this release, YEASTRACT+ offers upgraded information on transcription regulation for 13 yeast species, extending the database to two additional yeasts of the basidiomycota phylum, the pathogenic yeast Cryptococcus neoformans, and the biotechnologically relevant Rhodotorula toruloides. A dramatic upgrade in the quality of the data provided occurred, as regulatory associations between transcription factors (TFs) and target genes are now associated with quantitative assessment. Quantitative impact of TFs on gene expression levels enabled the construction and release of two additional analytical tools: quantitative rank by TF, for the prediction of the most relevant TFs underlying a given transcriptomics dataset; and metabolic engineering based on integrating the quantitative impact of TF expression into genome-scale metabolic models. Altogether, this release of YEASTRACT+ provides unparalleled access to massive, curated, quantitative data associated with gene expression control in 13 yeast species, and a set of tools to enable its full exploitation towards fundamental, biotechnological, and health-related applications.

papers.title: LncRNAfunc 2.0: an evidence-integrated knowledgebase for regulatory and functional interpretation of lncRNAs in cancer.
papers.authors: Yang M, Li J, Lu X, Liu J, Zhou X, Zhao L, Wu X, Xu Y.
papers.abstract: Long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) play diverse regulatory roles in cancer, yet their functional interpretation remains largely based on molecular associations and computational predictions, while experimentally derived evidence is fragmented across heterogeneous resources. Here, we present lncRNAfunc 2.0, an updated knowledgebase for systematic functional interpretation of cancer lncRNAs through multi-source evidence integration. Compared with the previous version, lncRNAfunc 2.0 reprocesses pan-cancer data from The Cancer Genome Atlas, incorporates normal-tissue and cancer-cell-line contexts from GTEx and CCLE, substantially expands binding and interaction evidence, and introduces perturbation evidence for lncRNAs and their regulators. These resources are integrated with association-based analyses and computational predictions as complementary evidence for interpreting lncRNA-associated regulatory relationships. lncRNAfunc 2.0 organizes functional knowledge into six biological dimensions: dysregulation, upstream regulation, lncRNA-mediated mRNA regulation, transcript remodeling, protein regulation, and tumor phenotypes. This framework connects regulatory determinants of lncRNAs with their downstream molecular relationships and phenotypic associations, including mRNA regulation, alternative splicing, protein regulation, survival, molecular and immune phenotypes, and drug response. Overall, lncRNAfunc 2.0 provides an evidence-integrated framework for exploring context-dependent lncRNA functions and regulatory mechanisms across cancers. lncRNAfunc 2.0 is freely available at https://lncrnafunc.xu-bioinfo.com/.

papers.title: OrganiZymeDB: a comprehensive database of enzyme stability and function in the presence of organic solvents.
papers.authors: Debruyne R, Pucci F.
papers.abstract: Low enzymatic tolerance to organic solvents is a major bottleneck for the development of industrial biocatalysis, since many substrates have limited water solubility, thus requiring the use of organic solvents for substrate solubilization and process economic viability. Yet, despite decades of experimental research in this field, no public resource currently exists that systematically collects and curates these data, limiting their accessibility and reuse for large-scale analyses and for the development and validation of computational methods. To address this gap, we present OrganiZymeDB (https://organizymedb.org/), a comprehensive, manually curated database of 28,121 experimental measurements of enzyme stability and function in the presence of organic solvents, compiled from 646 publications and covering 704 distinct proteins. Each entry is extensively annotated with the experimental conditions, including assay type, solvent identity and volume fraction, assay solution composition, pH, temperature, substrate(s), product(s), and enzyme production method, as well as the protein 3D structure and cross-links to other databases. OrganiZymeDB will assist both experimentalists, by providing straightforward access to solvent-compatibility data for enzymes of interest, and computational scientists, by providing a well-curated dataset to develop and evaluate methods for predicting enzyme solvent tolerance, ultimately enabling the design of robust industrial biocatalysts.

papers.title: R-loopBase v2.0: species- and cell type-resolved quantitative R-loop maps and R-loop regulatory resources.
papers.authors: Gu R, Hu J, Gao Y, Yang H, Lin R, Zhong X, Zhang KX, Li W, Hu Q, Wei L, Xing Z, Chen JY.
papers.abstract: R-loops are non-canonical nucleic acid structures implicated in diverse cellular processes and diseases. We previously developed R-loopBase to address the pressing challenges of inaccurate R-loop maps and the limited understanding of the R-loop regulatory network. However, R-loopBase provided only human R-loop maps with categorical confidence and did not account for cell type specificity. These limitations, coupled with the emerging R-loop profiling technologies and advances in R-loop regulatory mechanisms, have motivated the development of R-loopBase v2.0 (https://rloopbase.nju.edu.cn). After uniformly re-analysing 358 R-loop mapping datasets generated by 16 technologies, we introduce a quantitative R-loop scoring framework that assesses genome-wide R-loop confidence in human, demonstrating strong concordance with known R-loop biology. We further extend the framework to specific cell types and mouse, fruit fly, and yeast. In parallel, we substantially expand the collection of R-loop regulators across species, enabling the inference of changes in R-loop homeostasis. Building on these expanded datasets, we implement several new interactive features and analytical tools, including an expanded multi-species genome browser, deep learning-based R-loop prediction, R-loop homeostasis analysis, and a streamlined data download portal. We anticipate that R-loopBase v2.0 will serve as an enhanced, up-to-date one-stop resource for the R-loop research community.

papers.title: GlycoPOST: expanding glycomics data sharing to glycoproteomics through the updated MIRAGE guidelines.
papers.authors: Takahashi Y, Wang Z, Noguchi R, Seno A, Aoki-Kinoshita KF, Okuda S.
papers.abstract: GlycoPOST (https://glycopost.glycosmos.org) is a public mass spectrometry (MS) data repository for submitting and sharing glycan-related raw MS data along with structured experimental metadata, in accordance with the Minimum Information Required for A Glycomics Experiment (MIRAGE) guidelines. As of 1 September 2026, GlycoPOST hosts 602 projects containing 7.6 TiB of data, of which 445 are publicly available. In this update, we implemented major updates to GlycoPOST, expanding its scope from glycomics to glycoproteomics by incorporating the recent revisions published on the MIRAGE MS guidelines, in addition to enabling users to filter "presets," which are units for metadata in GlycoPOST, by keywords and last update date. The newly introduced concept of "project type" enables each GlycoPOST submission, referred to as a "project," to be classified according to whether it contains glycomics or glycoproteomics data. This makes it easier to select reusable metadata profiles (presets) by displaying only categories relevant to the experimental field. Furthermore, with the introduction of a project type specifically designed for glycomics-assisted glycoproteomics experiments, it is now possible to register data and metadata from both glycomics and glycoproteomics within a single project. These updates will promote standardized data sharing and reanalysis across glycomics and glycoproteomics using GlycoPOST.

papers.title: iGPSC-DB: a comprehensive database for an inferred single-cell genetic perturbation atlas.
papers.authors: Wang P, Chen Z, Zhang Y, Kang A, Xing J, Wang X, Xu L, Lu S, Song X, Guo Q, Xu Y, Li F.
papers.abstract: Genetic perturbation-induced transcriptional reprogramming drastically remodels tumor cellular phenotypes and tumor microenvironment crosstalk. Unraveling the heterogeneous cellular responses to genetic perturbations is essential for the mechanistic dissection of tumors and the discovery of therapeutic targets. Here, we present iGPSC-DB (https://bio-bigdata.hrbmu.edu.cn/iGPSC-DB), a database designed to infer connections between tumor microenvironmental cells and diverse genetic perturbation events and to dissect the heterogeneous cellular responses to these perturbations. iGPSC-DB curates associations linking 178 114 perturbation events that target 7407 genes to 9 249 080 single cells from 1580 samples across 88 cancer types. iGPSC-DB also provides seven user-friendly tools for retrieving and analyzing: (i) inferred associations between genetic perturbation events and cells/cell types; (ii) the inferred perturbation-associated effects of perturbations on cellular functions, developmental trajectories, and cell-cell communication within the tissue microenvironment; (iii) the combined effects of different perturbations on cells, facilitating the design of combination therapeutic regimens; (iv) the impact of different perturbations on the differentiation trajectories and functional states of malignant cells; and (v) the association between perturbed target genes and clinical survival outcomes. iGPSC-DB will serve as a valuable resource to advance single-cell-resolution research on gene functions, regulatory mechanisms, and the discovery of tumor therapeutic targets.

papers.title: Decoding the regulatory programs governing glioblastoma plasticity.
papers.authors: Saraswat M, Rueda-Gensini L, Heinzelmann E, Gracia T, Memi F, de Jong G, Straub J, Schloo C, Hoffmann DC, Jung E, Kindinger T, Masclef L, Weigel B, Lim B, Tuschmann F, Weil S, Gould O, Mair R, Mikulik K, Rohbeck M, Wick W, Winkler F, Bayraktar OA, Stegle O, Mall M.
papers.abstract: Glioblastoma is incurable and resistant to therapy despite genomic stability under treatment 1-8 , suggesting that non-genetic cellular plasticity is a central driver of progression. Whether such plasticity reflects stochastic state switching or is governed by predictable gene regulation has remained unclear 9-13 . Here we introduce scDORI (single-cell deep multi-omic regulatory inference)-a deep-learning framework that infers enhancer-driven gene-regulatory networks at single-cell resolution-and apply it to single-nucleus multiome profiles of more than one million cells from primary glioblastomas. Integrating computational inference with systematic perturbation screens across patient-derived models, we show that a structured regulatory program with an asymmetric interplay of activators and repressors governs cellular plasticity in glioblastoma. The resulting transition landscape is hierarchical and predictable, but permits cross-lineage trajectories that are absent from normal neurodevelopment. Within this landscape, low-plasticity states such as the neuronal-like state are not stable differentiation end points but actively maintained configurations, stabilized by a network of safeguard repressors that silence alternative fates. We identify MYT1L as the dominant member of this network, and show that it binds to and represses master regulators of every alternative state to consolidate neuronal-like identity. MYT1L restricted plasticity even under standard-of-care therapy and suppressed tumour growth and invasion in vivo. Conversely, loss of MYT1L reactivated plasticity and accelerated malignant features, indicating that low-plasticity identity requires continuous repression. These findings reframe malignant cell state stability as a balance between activation and continuous repression, and nominate safeguard repressors as candidate therapeutic targets that are distinct from differentiation-inducing activators, with potential relevance across cancers in which phenotypic switching drives therapy resistance.

papers.title: A spatiotemporal cancer cell trajectory underlies glioblastoma heterogeneity.
papers.authors: de Jong G, Memi F, Gracia T, Lazareva O, Gould O, Solomou G, Aivazidis A, Dave M, Zhang Q, Jensen M, Rifaioglu AS, Barros-Silva JD, Eckert S, Zhou D, Wood Y, Tuck E, Er S, Rademaker K, Petryszak R, Marshall H, Roberts K, Trinh AL, Rai S, Shaw T, Oszlanczi A, Powell H, Mazin P, Makarchuk S, Chang Y, Kania K, Jin L, Tudor C, Chan HM, Johnson H, Rumney B, Anderson H, Halliwell J, Pereira VB, Katsirea Z, Mamun I, Mulas I, Quaegebeur A, Briggs M, Cox J, Lee JTH, Rueda-Gensini L, Saraswat M, Seferbevoka Z, Young A, Patel M, Porter T, Gerstung M, Prete M, Prigmore E, Mall M, Bulstrode H, Saez-Rodriguez J, Briscoe J, Rowitch DH, Mair R, Behjati S, Stegle O, Bayraktar OA.
papers.abstract: Cancer cells show highly heterogeneous and plastic states in glioblastoma, an incurable brain tumour 1-5 . However, how these malignant states arise and whether they follow defined cellular trajectories across tumours is poorly understood. Here we generated a deep single-cell and spatial multi-omic atlas of human glioblastoma that pairs transcriptomic, epigenomic and genomic profiling of 12 tumours across many regions. We identify that glioblastoma heterogeneity is driven by spatially patterned transitions of cancer cells from developmental-like states towards those defined by a glial injury response and hypoxia. This cellular trajectory regionalizes tumours into distinct tissue microenvironments and manifests in a molecularly conserved manner across tumours as well as genetically distinct tumour subclones. Consistently, using a new deep-learning framework to map cancer cell states jointly with clones in situ, we show that tumour subclones are finely spatially intermixed through glioblastoma tissue microenvironments. We validate this cellular trajectory by using somatic mutation-based hierarchies in vivo and an experimental patient-derived organoid model ex vivo. Finally, we show that this cancer cell trajectory is intimately linked to myeloid heterogeneity and unfolds across regionalized myeloid signalling environments. Our findings define a stereotyped trajectory of cancer cells in glioblastoma and unify glioblastoma tumour heterogeneity into a tractable cellular and tissue framework.

papers.title: Venousization enables angiogenesis in the absence of VEGFR signalling.

papers.title: Faint exoplanets detected using computational approach to remove glare from stars.
Longitudinal single-cell profiling of breast tumors highlights immune and epigenetic mechanisms associated with sensitivity to aromatase inhibitors.
papers.authors: Altinönder I, Winton V, Quý KL, Fongaard M, Bjørnstad PM, Agustsdottir EES, Geisler SB, Seyedzadeh M, Buvarp UC, Lyngra M, Frigessi A, Lambrechts D, Kristensen V, Mathelier A, Greiff V, Geisler J, Tekpli X.
papers.abstract: Estrogen receptor (ER)-positive breast cancer treatment is based primarily on endocrine therapy. To dissect mechanisms of sensitivity to aromatase inhibitors in ER-positive breast cancer, we profiled tumor biopsies from 25 patients during neoadjuvant therapy using single-cell RNA sequencing, immune receptor sequencing and enhancer activity mapping. Malignant cells with high ER signaling and elevated activity of enhancers with ER binding sites were sensitive to treatment. Resistance was associated with androgen receptor signaling, dedifferentiation and epithelial-mesenchymal transition. Poor responders preferentially used the androgen receptor cis-regulome under treatment pressure. The baseline tumor microenvironment was associated with tumor downstaging. Poor responders exhibited a 'hot', yet ineffective immune landscape enriched for naive lymphoid and undifferentiated myeloid cells. Good responders showed an active immune microenvironment with sustained clonal expansion of T cells. Our longitudinal single-cell analyses elucidate the genetic, cellular and epigenetic mechanisms driving sensitivity and resistance to neoadjuvant aromatase inhibition in ER-positive breast cancer.

papers.authors: Kim H, Schuster ALR, Andara K, Bachini M, Carpten JD, Claus EB, Colditz GA, Craig DW, Diehl D, Ding L, Drake BF, Fields RC, George S, Ip-Toma C, Janeway K, Kwan BM, Lenz HJ, Mack JW, Pecos R, Salmi L, Sussman AL, Trent J, Van Allen E, Verhaak R, Willman CL, Bridges JFP, Participant Engagement and Cancer Genome Sequencing (PE-CGS) Network.

papers.title: Systematic screen of RNA binding proteins that enhance circular RNA translation.
papers.authors: Lu QY, Wang SQ, Ye YW, Wei T, Yang Y, Wei HY, Wang Z.
papers.abstract: Translatable circular RNAs (circRNAs) have emerged as a promising alternative to conventional mRNA therapy due to their improved stability that results in a prolonged expression window. The translation of circRNAs is mainly driven by internal ribosome entry site (IRES) or IRES-like elements, which is tightly regulated by various trans-acting RNA binding proteins (RBPs). Here we develop a cell-based system to systematically screen RBPs that enhance translation of circRNAs, identifying 68 proteins as putative activators of noncanonical translation. These translation activators are involved in a broad range of biological processes including RNA processing, ribosomal biogenesis, and translation initiation. We further design a machine learning algorithm to extract common sequence features of these activators and predict more potential RBPs with translation activator activities. The newly identified and predicted activators are subsequently validated to promote the IRES-mediated circRNA translation in a context-dependent fashion. Overall, this study provides new insights into IRES-related trans-acting factors and expands the toolbox for engineered RBPs in RNA synthetic biology.
