papers.title: Bayesian efficient coding.
papers.authors: Park IM, Pillow JW.
papers.abstract: The efficient coding hypothesis, which proposes that neurons are optimized to maximize information about the environment, has provided a guiding theoretical framework for sensory and systems neuroscience. More recently, a theory known as the Bayesian Brain hypothesis has focused on the brain's ability to integrate sensory and prior sources of information in order to perform Bayesian inference. Although pieces of a connection between these two hypotheses have appeared in prior work, a general formulation that treats the optimality criterion as an arbitrary functional of the posterior distribution - and thereby admits both information-based and other objectives within a single framework - has remained largely implicit. Here we make this formulation explicit, developing a Bayesian theory of efficient coding that defines Bayesian efficient codes in terms of four basic ingredients: (1) a stimulus prior distribution; (2) an encoding model; (3) a capacity constraint, specifying a neural resource limit; and (4) a loss functional, quantifying the desirability or undesirability of various posterior distributions. Classic efficient codes arise as the special case in which the loss functional is the posterior entropy, leading to a code that maximizes mutual information, but alternate loss functionals give solutions that differ dramatically from information-maximizing codes. Within this framework we introduce covtropy, a novel family of losses defined on posterior distributions and parameterized by a single exponent, and use it to show that decorrelation of sensory inputs - optimal under classic efficient codes in low-noise settings - can be disadvantageous for objectives that penalize large errors. We then reanalyze Laughlin's seminal data on contrast coding in the blowfly large monopolar cell, and find that the measured response nonlinearity is better explained by minimizing Lp reconstruction error with p = 1/2 than by information maximization, overturning a forty-year-old interpretation. Bayesian efficient coding thus enlarges the family of codes that are optimal under different objectives and provides a more general framework for understanding the design principles of sensory systems.

papers.title: Shapley fields reveal mosaic chemotopic organization in the mouse Olfactory bulb across diverse chemical feature sets.
papers.authors: Milićević N, Burton SD, Wachowiak M, Itskov V.
papers.abstract: Neural representations in the olfactory bulb (OB) remain poorly understood compared to well-established coding principles in other sensory systems. This difficulty arises because a natural coordinate system for olfactory stimulus space has not yet been identified, complicating the characterization of neural receptive fields analogous to those in other sensory modalities. Moreover, the extent to which these tuning properties are spatially organized within the OB remains unclear. To advance our understanding of the olfactory coding, we introduce an interpretable method of Shapley fields, as an olfactory analog of retinotopic receptive fields. Shapley fields are spatial distributions of chemical feature importance for the tuning of OB glomeruli. We used this tool to investigate chemotopy in the OB with diverse sets of chemical features using widefield epifluorescence recordings of the mouse dorsal OB in response to stimuli across a wide range of the chemical space. We found that Shapley fields reveal a weak chemotopic organization of the chemical feature sensitivity of dorsal OB glomeruli. This organization was consistent across animals and mostly agreed across very different chemical feature sets: (i) the expert-curated PubChem database features and (ii) features derived from a Graph Neural Network trained on human olfactory perceptual tasks. This chemotopy involved at least three chemical feature dimensions, rather than one or two dominant properties. Moreover, we found that the principal components of the Shapley fields corresponded to single commonly accepted chemical classification groups. This implies that these chemical groups could have been identified purely from the mouse olfactory responses. Our findings suggest that Shapley fields may serve as a chemical feature-agnostic method for investigating olfactory perception.

papers.title: Hematotoxicity: the hidden legacy of CAR T cell therapy.
AI-based precision prognostics and therapy personalization for childhood brain tumors.
papers.authors: Stefan S, Amann AS, Smith KS, Boniolo F, Larsson I, Pfitzer EC, Li Q, Robinson GW, Harter PN, Lotter W, Northcott PA, Hovestadt V.
papers.abstract: Accurate prediction of patient outcomes remains a critical challenge in oncology, in particular for childhood brain tumors, in which treatment decisions need to carefully balance risk of tumor recurrence and death against severe therapy-induced sequelae. Here, we developed MANTIS (methylation profiling and artificial neural networks for time-dependent individualized survival predictions), a precision artificial intelligence (AI) tool for medulloblastoma and ependymoma outcome prediction built on genome-wide DNA methylation array data from 2,786 patients. MANTIS generates individualized survival probabilities over a 10-year period and achieves concordance indices as high as 0.80 ± 0.07, significantly exceeding the predictive accuracy of current clinical indicators. Extending MANTIS to estimate individualized treatment effects identifies ~60% of patients with average-risk medulloblastoma without a significant survival disadvantage (P = 0.683) when treated with less intensive craniospinal irradiation doses, which is associated with improved neurocognitive outcomes. In conclusion, our study establishes a foundation for AI-based precision prognostics and therapy personalization in childhood brain tumors and offers a blueprint for similar initiatives in other cancer types.

papers.title: A framework for genome-wide characterization of DNA methylation and variant effect prediction.
papers.authors: Mao W, Chen KM, Park CY, Theesfeld CL, Troyanskaya OG.
papers.abstract: DNA methylation plays a critical role in many essential biological processes, including transcriptional regulation, genomic imprinting, chromosomal maintenance, genomic stability and development, and has phenotypic and disease impacts. However, genome-wide characterization of methylation patterns across cell types and tissues remains a major challenge. Here, to address this, we present a framework that enables systematic genome-wide analysis of methylation and sequence-based prediction of context-specific methylation effects of variants. Our data-driven discovery of methylation classes reveals context-dependent roles for methylation across tissues, cell types and regions of the genome. The framework also includes Wreath, a deep learning-based sequence model specifically designed to accurately predict the context-dependent impact of any genetic variant on methylation. These developments leverage a compendium that harmonizes disparate methylation profiles from disparate studies including over 90 tissues and cell types. Using Wreath, we systematically characterized the impact of noncoding pathogenic variants on tissue-specific methylation, generating mechanistic hypotheses for individual regulatory variants. We make the full framework, including the compendium, the methylation classes and the model, available for use by the community.

papers.title: GATA transcription factors coordinate developmental progression in the arabidopsis root.
papers.authors: Denyer T, Solansky P, Herrmann A, de Martino F, Symeonidi E, Brösamle V, Timmermans MCP.
papers.abstract: Proper organ development requires the coordination of cell type-specific differentiation programs with general maturation processes through precise spatiotemporal gene regulation. In plants, where RNA polymerase pausing is not well established, alternative mechanisms must ensure this coordination. Here, using single-cell resolution transcriptomic and chromatin accessibility data, we reconstruct developmental trajectories of the Arabidopsis root ground tissue to investigate these mechanisms. We describe phased transcriptional landscapes governing the transition from stem cell to early differentiation, in which chromatin accessibility marks the activation of key developmental regulators. A major transcriptional switch in the late meristematic zone, underpinned by extensive chromatin remodeling, drives the transition from cell division to differentiation. Leveraging machine learning to examine integrated transcriptomic and chromatin accessibility trajectories, we identify GATA transcription factors (TFs) as central coordinators of this switch; a role we validate experimentally. We show that the GATA TFs sit at the tipping point of a feedback-driven bistable system that integrates inputs from auxin and cytokinin to balance proliferation and differentiation, ensuring temporal precision in root development at both the tissue and organ scales.

papers.title: Iterative computational and rational design generates diverse PET hydrolases for plastic depolymerization.
papers.authors: Norton-Baker B, Fram B, Thadani NN, Komp E, Su Y, Storment OO, Murphy NP, Lim S, Erickson E, Rollins N, Gado JE, Shearer CA, Mathews II, Truebridge I, Llases M, Bahl CD, Sarangi R, Marks DS, McGeehan JE, Sander C, Beckham GT, Gauthier NP.
papers.abstract: Evolutionary relationships among homologous enzymes can be leveraged to introduce large numbers of amino acid substitutions for improved functional properties. Here, we combine evolution-informed design (EVdesign) with rational design to engineer improved poly(ethylene terephthalate) (PET) hydrolases (PETases). Designs derived from multiple PETases reveal strong parent-dependent differences in success and performance, with Thermobifida fusca TfCut2 emerging as the most design-amenable scaffold. Increasing sequence diversification reduces the number of active enzymes but broadens performance variance, enabling discovery of high-performing outliers. Four rational mutations overcome a thermostability bottleneck in TfCut2 and this variant provides a robust scaffold for iterative EVdesign, which further improves activity. Overall, we experimentally test 603 designs from eight parent PETases. More than 400 variants containing 12-68 substitutions were able to depolymerize PET, nearly all outperforming their parent enzymes, and many approach benchmark LCC-ICCG performance in partial conversion assays. These results establish EVdesign as a robust strategy for generating diverse, high-activity enzymes.

papers.title: Multi-platform framework for mapping somatic retrotransposition in human tissues.
papers.authors: Wang S, Bae M, Wang J, Zhao B, Nguyen K, Mallett S, Switzenberg JA, Losh SJ, Sexton CE, Miao B, Dong S, Zeng X, Wang Z, McDonald TL, Mumm C, Gadde RK, Tariq AM, Chen Z, Feng WC, Burn A, Park J, Chu C, Shen H, Wang T, Urban AE, Zhu X, Li H, Burns KH, Chun HE, Park PJ, SMaHT MEI Working Group, Boyle AP, Mills RE, Zhou W, Lee EA.
keywords: Somatic Mosaicism, Mobile Element Insertions, Retrotransposition, Benchmarking, Long-read Sequencing, Transposon-targeted Sequencing, Multi-platform Sequencing, Donor-specific Genome Assembly, Line-1 Source Tracing, Haplotype Phasing
papers.abstract: Mobile element insertions (MEIs) shape the human genome in both germline and somatic tissues. While inherited MEIs are well characterized, identifying somatic MEIs (sMEIs) in non-cancer tissues remains challenging due to their low allelic fraction and repetitive nature. Here, we present an integrative framework for sMEI mapping that leverages modern sequencing technologies and analytical innovations. We first benchmarked sMEI detection methods, demonstrating advantages of long-read and MEI-targeted sequencing for ultra-rare events, and established an effective cross-platform integrative approach using a mixture of well-established cell lines. Haplotype phasing and donor-specific genome assemblies further refined sMEI calls by distinguishing germline and false signals in in silico tumor-normal mixtures. We also developed a source-tracing approach based on sequence variation within MEIs, expanding the catalog of active source elements beyond traditional transduction-based inference. Applying this framework to benchmark donor tissues, we detected rare somatic L1 insertions in all four tissue types examined, revealing structural and source diversity. Our work provides a foundational framework and biological insight into somatic retrotransposition in the human body.

papers.title: Toward comprehensive maps of somatic mosaic mutations.
papers.authors: Jia P, Ye K.
papers.abstract: The Somatic Mosaicism across Human Tissues Network has established complementary benchmarks for somatic mutation detection, extended mutation analysis into underexplored genomic regions, and highlighted chromatin states as potential records of cellular history. These studies show that detection performance depends on reference representation, benchmark quality, and experimental design, requiring careful calibration when integrating technologies.

papers.title: Folding without glutamine: Proteome-scale removal of a canonical amino acid.
papers.authors: Garciarrubio A, Ramos-Cerrillo B, Morett E, Segovia L.
papers.abstract: All known life uses a canonical alphabet of 20 amino acids, yet which residues are structurally essential remains untested at proteome scale. Isoleucine was recently eliminated from ribosomal proteins in Escherichia coli, establishing that amino acid alphabet reduction is feasible. Here we ask whether an entire amino acid can be eliminated from a proteome, and develop a computational framework to identify the best target. Using two independent approaches - ProteinMPNN structure-based probabilities and multiple sequence alignment conservation - we define "keep-score" as the fraction of positions where the native residue is optimal. Both methods converge on an unexpected candidate: glutamine has the lowest keep-score, with proline and glycine the highest - counter to substitution-matrix intuition. Glutamine's low keep-score is not explained by a single obvious substitute; glutamate is preferred in only 14% of replacements. Removing this target proteome-wide, we replaced every glutamine across 4,148 proteins with ProteinMPNN-optimal alternatives and modeled the resulting sequences with AlphaFold2. The recoded proteome maintained native-like structures: 85.5% of models exceeded a TMscore of 0.8, indistinguishable from the 85.9% baseline for rebuilt native sequences. Orthogonal validation - ESMFold predictions, Rosetta energy calculations, and conformational ensemble comparisons - revealed no evidence of systematic misfolding attributable to glutamine removal. As a consistency check, a glutamine-free TEM-1 β-lactamase designed with ProteinMPNN conferred ampicillin resistance in E. coli, indicating fold preservation can extend to biological function. Evolutionary evidence further supports these findings: 24% of E. coli proteins have glutamine-free orthologs in prokaryotic genomes, and glutamine ranks lowest in keep-score in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. These results show that an entire amino acid can be removed from a proteome with folds broadly preserved, establishing keep-score as a general framework and glutamine as the primary candidate for recoding. Crucially, this reflects a computational analysis of structural replaceability, not a demonstration of biological dispensability.

papers.title: The influence of ensemble size and composition on the performance of combined real-time COVID-19 forecasts.
papers.authors: Becker F, Sherratt K, Bosse NI, Funk S.
papers.abstract: During infectious disease outbreaks, short-term forecasts can play an important role for both decision makers and the general public. While previous research has shown that combining individual forecasts into an ensemble improves accuracy and consistency, practical guidance for organisers of multi-model prediction platforms on how to construct an ensemble has been scarce. In particular, it is not entirely clear how ensemble performance relates to the size of the underlying model pool, a relevant question when relying on voluntary contributions from modelling teams that face competing priorities. Furthermore, the exact composition of an ensemble forecast may influence its performance. Ensembles can either include all models equally or, alternatively, discriminate based on past performance or other characteristics. Using data from the European COVID-19 Forecast Hub we investigated these questions, with the aim of offering practical guidance to organisers of multi-model prediction platforms during infectious disease outbreaks. We found that including more models both improved and stabilised aggregate ensemble performance, while selecting for better component models did not yield any particular advantage. Diversity among models, whether measured numerically or qualitatively, did not have a clear impact on ensemble performance. These results suggest that for those soliciting contributions to collaborative ensembles there are more obvious gains to be made from increasing participation to moderate levels than from optimising component models.

papers.title: Global sensitivity analysis for stochastic models of infectious diseases: Re-emergence of yellow fever virus in the Americas as a case study.
papers.authors: Kornetzke N, Wearing HJ.
papers.abstract: Emerging infectious diseases are a persistent public health threat that challenge deterministic, mechanistic modeling approaches. Because outbreaks initially start with a low number of infected hosts, their dynamics are highly stochastic, making traditional deterministic methods, e.g., ordinary differential equations, unable to qualitatively or quantitatively capture the transmission dynamics. In place, stochastic models are used, such as Markov chain models, but these models present their own challenges. Often, to infer a quantity of interest with stochastic models, we need to sample the model's distribution many times over, introducing an additional source of noise to our analysis. This additional noise makes the inference of our quantity of interest more difficult and computationally expensive. Here, we show how novel tools from the field of uncertainty quantification can be used to efficiently separate these two channels of noise, allowing us to make rigorous statistical inferences about processes important for disease emergence. We illustrate these techniques with a model of yellow fever virus spillover in the Americas, a virus that has seen rapid re-emergence amongst multiple hosts and vectors in South America over the last decade. We show that only a handful of parameters' uncertainties greatly affect variation in cumulative disease incidence. In particular, uncertainty in patch connectivity and non-human primate latency has the greatest impact on the variation of cumulative disease incidence of yellow fever virus across patches.

papers.title: PhenX Toolkit: a knowledgebase that enables consistent data collection and facilitates cross-study analysis and data reuse.
papers.authors: Huggins W, Hendershot TP, Marazita ML, Bakalov VD, Ceger P, Cook B, Cox LA, Ives C, Nelms MD, Quattrone W, Reeve TC, Williams DN, Hamilton CM.
papers.abstract: The PhenX (consensus measures for Phenotypes and eXposures) Toolkit (https://www.phenxtoolkit.org/) is a publicly available knowledgebase of well-established, broadly validated measurement protocols recommended for use in genomic, clinical, translational, and epidemiological research involving human participants. Consistent use of PhenX protocols, including questionnaires, bioassays, and physical assessments, improves the rigor, transparency, reproducibility, and comparability of research data. The Toolkit was recently highlighted in the National Institutes of Health (NIH) implementation plan, "Leading in Gold Standard Science," as an example of efforts to advance reproducible biomedical research. The Toolkit currently includes 1010 protocols spanning a wide range of diseases, exposures, and study designs. Content development is guided by the scientific community through a consensus-based process involving expert Working Groups, community input, and strategic oversight from the PhenX Steering Committee. Collaborations with NIH Institutes have expanded Toolkit content in priority areas, including substance use and cardiovascular disease. The PhenX Toolkit enhances study design and supports implementation of selected protocols. PhenX also collaborates with resources that facilitate data collection (REDCap), data standards (LOINC), and data repositories to promote interoperability and cross-study analyses. To date, the Toolkit has been recommended in 711 NIH funding opportunities and cited in >1300 publications. Future directions are discussed.

papers.title: A catalog of transcriptome genetic regulation in a consanguineous Middle Eastern biobank.
papers.authors: Naeem H, Diboun I, Siddig Z, Ghorbani M, Hassan S, Farhad R, Moosa S, Abouelhassan R, Tauro M, Razali RM, Iqbal M, Aliyev E, Vempalli FR, Hashmi MA, Massih AA, Mathew R, Mattei V, James N, Mathew LS, Silcock L, Wang K, Bedognetti D, Tomei S, Chaussabel D, Fakhro KA, Montgomery SB, Mokrab Y.
papers.abstract: Ancestry-specific genetic mapping of transcriptome regulation is pivotal for understanding genome function, especially in underrepresented consanguineous populations. Here we characterized 1,882 Qatar Biobank participants, integrating blood RNA sequencing, whole-genome sequencing and phenotypic data across 45 clinically relevant traits. We cataloged ~7 million significant quantitative trait loci (QTLs), both short and structural variants, impacting gene expression, isoform usage, splicing and allele-specific expression, uncovering 1,379 novel eGenes. Fine-mapping resolved 29,953 high-confidence, independent causal loci including 24% previously unreported as well as those with effect alleles showing significant divergence across global populations, while 1,371 were absent from public databases. Leveraging elevated autozygosity, we found that causal variants are depleted from runs of homozygosity, consistent with purifying selection, while recent autozygosity increased the burden of homozygous regulatory variants. We identified QTLs with recessive deleterious effects on 10 Mendelian disease genes and homozygous QTLs causing extreme outlier expression in 66 genes including dosage-sensitive ones. Colocalization analysis revealed 58 causal variants acting on 20 clinically relevant phenotypes, implicating novel genes including ATP6V0B and RQCD1 in metabolic and blood disorders. These findings establish this QTL catalog as a valuable Middle Eastern resource for genome interpretation and genomic medicine.

papers.title: Clonal hematopoiesis and cytopenias following CAR19 therapy.
papers.authors: Hamilton MP, Phillips N, Noordenbos T, Boegeholz J, Sugio T, Sworder BJ, Alig SK, Good Z, Schroers-Martin JG, Tamaresis J, Esfahani MS, Lu Y, Olsen M, Liu CL, Ehlinger Z, Desai M, Muffly L, Negrin RS, Arai S, Johnston L, Lowsky R, Meyer E, Rezvani A, Shizuru J, Weng WK, Shiraz P, Sidana S, Bharadwaj S, Smith M, Dahiya S, Sahaf B, Frank MJ, Mackall CL, Diehn M, Kurtz DM, Miklos DB, Alizadeh AA.
papers.abstract: CD19-directed chimeric antigen receptor T cell therapy (CAR19) improves survival in relapsed/refractory large B cell lymphoma compared with immunochemotherapy with intent for autologous hematopoietic cell transplantation (autoHCT). However, major toxicities include prolonged cytopenias, infection and secondary hematologic malignancies. Here, to investigate these complications, we studied patients with lymphoma receiving CAR19 and compared clinical outcomes to propensity-matched autoHCT-treated controls. CAR19-treated patients exhibited impaired immune reconstitution and increased infection. Bone marrow analysis showed that prolonged post-CAR cytopenias are associated with clonal cytopenias of undetermined significance and interferon-mediated inflammation. Clonal hematopoiesis (CH) commonly expanded following CAR19 infusion and was associated with impaired immune reconstitution and treatment-related myeloid malignancy (tMN). Post-CAR tMN was molecularly and clinically comparable to post-autoHCT tMN. Single-cell DNA analysis revealed mostly independent CH clones, while CAR integration into CH-mutant T cells occurred frequently and may drive expansion and persistence. Together, these findings implicate CH expansion and marrow inflammation in key CAR19-associated toxicities.

papers.title: Structural basis for N-glycopeptide preference in an infant-derived Bifidobacterium bifidum PNGaseA.
papers.authors: Bakshani CR, Caulton SG, Taleb V, Ojuri TO, Coughlan K, Montesa A, Pérez-Latorre A, Merino P, Kozak RP, Çakaj S, Bottacini F, Lovering AL, van Sinderen D, Hurtado-Guerrero R, Crouch LI.
papers.abstract: N-glycans are abundant nutrient sources for human gut bacteria, which deploy peptide: N-glycosidases to release them from glycoproteins. Breast milk is comprised of a high proportion of N-glycosylated bioactive proteins that can be accessed by infant colonic microbes. Here, we biochemically and structurally characterize a PNGaseA-family enzyme from infant-associated Bifidobacterium bifidum LMG13195. This enzyme acts on a broad range of N-glycan structures but shows a marked preference for N-glycans attached to glycopeptides rather than to denatured or native proteins, highlighting a specialized route for N-glycan acquisition in infant-associated Bifidobacterium species. Structures of the apo enzyme, an unliganded E236Q mutant, and a D107N-E236Q complex with a G2-peptide reveal a canonical two-β-sandwich PNGase core plus an additional ten-strand β-sheet cradle and are the first structures of this superfamily. Comparison of these states, combined with molecular dynamics simulations, indicates that glycopeptide binding is coupled to β-sheet cradle-loop movements that close against β-sandwich 1 over the peptide C terminus. The complex defines recognition of the two core GlcNAc residues and the central mannose, reveals that peptide contacts are concentrated around the +2 Thr residue of the NXT sequon, and positions the scissile amide at the active site. These findings, together with mutational and computational analyses, provide a structural basis for N-glycopeptide preference by linking glycopeptide binding to cradle closure and catalysis, thereby expanding the host-glycan nutrient landscape accessible to infant-gut Bifidobacterium species.

papers.title: Reconstructing the single-cell spatiotemporal dynamics of glioblastoma invasion.
papers.authors: Mangukiya HB, Skeppås M, Lasses Armatowski A, Uppman I, Hallin L, Kruse F, Nordquist C, Kundu S, Berglund M, Malik AA, Krona C, Jörnsten R, Nelander S.
papers.abstract: Glioblastoma invasion into healthy brain tissue remains a major barrier to effective treatment, but the dynamic single-cell behaviors underlying this process remain difficult to measure across patient models. Here, we introduce GlioTrace, an ex vivo imaging and computational framework for real-time tracking of glioblastoma invasion in patient-derived xenograft brain slices. Combining whole-specimen confocal microscopy with machine learning-based morphology classification and probabilistic modeling of state transitions, GlioTrace reconstructs how tumor cells switch between invasion phenotypes and how these dynamics are shaped by local tissue context and therapy. Across six patient-derived models, GlioTrace reveals that invasion plasticity is patient-specific, spatially organized, and modulated by vascular proximity and microglial interaction. Targeted therapies selectively alter phenotype composition and transition probabilities, whereas standard-of-care treatment enriches a highly motile, transition-connected branching state consistent with a treatment-tolerant invasive phenotype. Thus, GlioTrace makes glioblastoma invasion a measurable dynamic process for comparing patient-specific treatment responses in living brain tissue.

papers.title: HuBMAP Data Portal: a resource for multimodal spatial and single-cell data of healthy human tissues.
papers.authors: Turner ML, Smits TC, Liaw TS, Honick B, Shirey B, Choy L, Akhmetov N, An S, Betancur D, Bordelon D, Burke K, Cao-Berg I, Conroy J, Csonka C, Cuda P, Donahue S, Fisher SA, Furst D, Hanna E, Hardi J, Kakar T, Keller MS, Lange D, Li X, Ma Y, McWilliams A, Money A, Morgan R, Mörth E, Muerto J, Musen MA, Nic E, O'Connor MJ, Phillips GA, Ropelewski AJ, Sablosky R, Saripalli S, Sibilla M, Simmel D, Simmons JA, Tang X, Welling J, Yuan Z, Hemberg M, HuBMAP Consortium, Ruffalo M, Silverstein JC, Blood PD, Gehlenborg N.
papers.abstract: The NIH Human BioMolecular Atlas Program (HuBMAP) Data Portal ( https://portal.hubmapconsortium.org/ ) serves as a comprehensive repository for multimodal, multi-scale spatial and single-cell data from healthy human tissues. As of August 2026, the portal hosts 9,316 public datasets from 26 data types spanning 29 organ classes across 501 donors. Portal infrastructure and user interfaces support data search and discovery, visualization, and analysis directly in web browsers. These capabilities include metadata- and data-driven search, collaborative Workspaces with access to high-performance compute, and interactive Vitessce visualizations across non-spatial, 2D, and 3D spatial datasets. Data-type-specific uniform processing pipelines and rigorous quality control processes ensure comparability of results across laboratories, organs, and donors, while externally processed community-contributed datasets provide complementary perspectives. Here we describe portal functionality, infrastructure, and design, and highlight its role as a platform for large-scale spatial single-cell research across diverse data types, organs, and scales.

papers.title: SpatioCAD: Context-aware graph diffusion model for pinpointing spatially variable genes in heterogeneous tissues.
papers.authors: Wen H, Shen Q, Zhang S.
papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics enables comprehensive characterization of tissue architecture, and the identification of spatially variable genes (SVGs) is a critical step for defining region-specific molecular markers and uncovering spatially regulated mechanisms across diverse biological contexts. However, most existing methods for SVG detection overlook cell density variations, a major confounding factor in complex tissues such as tumors, where heterogeneous cellularity frequently introduces false-positive calls. Here we present SpatioCAD, a computational framework that explicitly decouples genuine spatial expression patterns from confounding effects driven by cellularity. SpatioCAD introduces a graph diffusion model that inherently incorporates cell-density-aware conditions to simulate expression propagation, supporting the identification of SVGs across a broad range of expression levels. Systematic evaluations on simulated datasets demonstrate its superior statistical power and specificity. Applied to breast cancer, lung cancer, and glioma datasets, SpatioCAD identifies functionally diverse SVGs, including low‑abundance transcripts with established roles in tumor progression, while also recapitulates biologically meaningful tissue architecture features. Importantly, SpatioCAD is fast and scalable to large tissues.

papers.title: Direction-selective retinal ganglion cells encode motion direction uniformly, despite having discretely distributed cardinal preferences.
papers.authors: Paris C, Hubert F, Franke F, Marre O, Chalk M, Ferrari U.
papers.abstract: On-Off direction-selective retinal ganglion cells (DS RGCs) exhibit broad tuning curves, responding robustly to motion aligned with or near their preferred direction. These cells comprise four major subtypes, each tuned to motion along one of the four cardinal axes: nasal, superior, temporal, or inferior. However, natural stimuli can move in any direction, and it remains unclear whether intermediate directions are encoded less effectively, or whether this cardinal organization nevertheless supports uniform direction encoding. Here, we combined previous electrophysiological recordings of DS cells presented with a moving light bar stimulus with an information-theoretic measure, the Stimulus Specific Information, to estimate the directional sensitivity of small populations of recorded neurons. This analysis revealed that DS RGC populations are uniformly sensitive across all directions of motion. We then asked whether the observed homogeneous sensitivity was a consequence of DS RGCs maximizing the average stimulus information. Simulations with artificially modified tuning curve widths revealed that DS cells prioritize avoiding pronounced drops in sensitivity over maximizing the average transmitted information. This property reduces large deficits in sensitivity for certain directions, thereby limiting potential "blind spots" in the encoding of motion. More generally, our results raise the possibility that maintaining a high minimum sensitivity could be one factor influencing the organization of sensory representations.

papers.title: Traction force microscopy using temporal information.
papers.authors: Hamaoka K, Kusakari K, Tanimoto H.
papers.abstract: Traction force microscopy is a simple, non-invasive method that can quantify cellular contact forces at the cell-substrate interface. It solves an inverse problem of determining the force field from measured substrate deformation. Because this problem is ill-posed with a large condition number, it is necessary to suppress the amplification of measurement noise during inversion. Previous studies have employed algorithms such as regularization or filtering that utilize spatial information to discriminate noise and true signals. Here, we propose an alternative approach that utilizes temporal information of the system. This method employs Kalman filter, a simple data assimilation algorithm in time series analysis, to recover the force field. Using numerically generated data, we show that the method is more accurate than standard algorithms including L2-regularization and is effective at filtering out temporal noise. Using experimental data on locomoting cells, we demonstrate that the method can reliably infer time-varying cellular traction forces. We also demonstrate two extensions of the proposed method: incorporation of additional knowledge and direct inference of low-dimensional force characteristics. These practical advantages will motivate the use of proposed framework for analyzing dynamic cell mechanics.

papers.title: The promiscuity and degeneracy of ten unique RNA base-pairing rules can determine the success of adaptive RNA evolution.
papers.authors: Goldbach L, Martin NS, Wagner A.

papers.title: MAGE: an efficient algorithm for identifying Maximal Age-indexed GEne sets.
papers.authors: Çalış M, Altuntas V, Kahveci O, Hiram Guzzi P, Veltri P, Kahveci T.
papers.abstract: Aging alters transcriptional regulation in a tissue- and time-specific manner, reshaping gene regulatory networks and shifting regulatory influence dynamics. Traditional in silico influence maximization methods often rely on static gene expression snapshots and fail to capture gene-to-gene influence variations over time. To address this, we introduce the Age Index, a network-based metric that quantifies time-varying gene influence. We define the Maximal and Minimal Age Index Problems (MAP$^{+}$ and MAP$^{-}$) as the tasks of identifying gene sets with the highest and lowest Age Index, and prove these problems are NP-hard. To solve them, we develop MAGE (Maximal Age-Index Algorithm), a stochastic method that iteratively constructs gene sets by prioritizing genes likely to optimize the Age Index. MAGE identifies statistically significant gene sets at the genome scale, with strong literature support, highlighting its potential to uncover age-sensitive regulatory mechanisms.

papers.title: HiCP2GAN: a plug and play foundation model-based GAN for Hi-C enhancement.
papers.authors: Olowofila S, Oluwadare O.
papers.abstract: The 3D organization of chromatin shapes gene regulation and cellular function, and Hi-C has become the primary technique for mapping chromatin interactions genome-wide. However, high-resolution data remain costly and scarce, leaving many studies with sparse contact maps that limit downstream analysis. Deep learning methods, especially generative adversarial networks (GANs), have shown promise for enhancing low-resolution Hi-C data, but most existing GAN-based approaches rely on custom discriminators trained from scratch, which can yield unstable training and limited generalization. Hi-C foundation models pretrained on large-scale data capture rich, transferable representations of chromatin structure, yet their use as discriminators within adversarial enhancement frameworks had not been explored. We introduce HiCP2GAN, a plug-and-play GAN that employs a pretrained Vision Transformer-based Hi-C foundation model as its discriminator. The discriminator was pretrained on 118 million Hi-C patches across diverse species and cell types, providing biologically meaningful gradients for adversarial supervision. The framework is generator-agnostic: any compatible Hi-C resolution enhancement architecture can serve as the generator, enabling fair comparison across methods. The encoder phase of the foundation model was adapted as a discriminator backbone, finetuning the first few layers from the input while freezing the deeper transformer layers to preserve pretrained knowledge while allowing task-specific adaptation. Experiments across various cell lines show that HiCP2GAN outperforms traditional GAN-based methods in most settings and improves the reconstruction quality and biological reproducibility of existing Hi-C enhancement models in most evaluated cases. HiCP2GAN is publicly available at https://github.com/OluwadareLab/HiCP2GAN.

papers.title: IsoPrism predicts isoform usage from short-read transcriptomes through structure-guided competitive allocation.
papers.authors: Yan P, Liu J, Cui X, Liu X, Shi L, Cheng L.
papers.abstract: Short-read (SR) single-cell and spatial transcriptomics characterize gene expression but provide limited resolution of within-gene isoform usage. Here we present IsoPrism, a structure-guided competitive allocation framework that predicts isoform proportions from gene-level expression. IsoPrism combines individual expression and local expression context with transcript structural annotations, using shared iterative updates to preserve non-negative, gene-normalized proportions. Joint supervision from individual long-read (LR) counts and group-level isoform usage enables prediction in samples without matched LR measurements. Across five transfer scenarios derived from three paired transcriptomic resources, IsoPrism achieved the highest mean dominant isoform accuracy, compositional similarity, and cluster-level allocation correlation among eight evaluated methods. Ablation analyses supported complementary contributions from structural queries, expression context, iterative allocation, and dual-resolution supervision. Applied to a developing mouse cortex atlas, IsoPrism identified stage- and cell-type-associated isoform-usage patterns, including variation in the predicted relative usage of two Pkm transcripts. IsoPrism enables isoform-usage analysis of SR transcriptomes by transferring information from paired LR references, extending the analytical value of existing single-cell and spatial gene-expression atlases.

papers.title: ADInteractome: discovering Alzheimer's disease-associated gene interactions from single-nucleus RNA-seq data through neural interaction states.
papers.authors: Wu Y, Maurya N, Yang Y, Chen W, Wang G, Liu Z, Hu X, Zheng WJ, Xu Z.
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a prevalent neurodegenerative disorder characterized by amyloid $\beta $ plaques and tau tangles, yet its molecular mechanisms remain elusive. Advances in single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) have provided profound insights into the cellular heterogeneity of AD-associated brains. In this study, we introduce ADInteractome, an interpretable artificial intelligence framework designed to discover gene interactions associated with AD directly from the internal state of neural networks trained on the snRNA-seq data of brain cells. The method is based on the intuition that if a neural network can accurately classify cells from AD and non-AD donors based on their snRNA-seq data, then its internal interaction states, reflecting interaction patterns within the gene expression data, are informative for identifying biologically meaningful gene interactions. Applied to a large-scale snRNA-seq dataset from the Seattle Alzheimer's Disease Brain Cell Atlas, ADInteractome reveals cell-type-specific and AD-associated gene circuits supported by existing literature. The results were further supported by our virtual knock-out and knock-in experiments, a novel concept to probe our findings through a data-driven approach. Compared with traditional co-expression network methods, it achieves stronger enrichment for known AD-associated gene interactions and uncovers novel interaction patterns. These findings highlight the potential of interpretable AI approaches for elucidating complex molecular interactions in neurodegenerative disease.

papers.title: Multi-omics survival prediction under modality incompleteness via dynamic modality graphs and product-of-experts fusion.
papers.authors: Xie W, Zhang H, Yang J, Yu K, Li W.
papers.abstract: Multi-omics data integration provides rich complementary information for cancer survival prediction, yet modality incompleteness is pervasive in real-world medical data and undermines the stability and applicability of existing models. To address this challenge, we propose DMG-PoE, a robust learning framework for multi-omics survival prediction. The framework introduces a dynamic modality graph (DMG) that propagates complementary information across modality nodes to compensate for missing inputs, combined with an uncertainty-aware product-of-experts (PoE) fusion mechanism that adaptively weights each modality by its estimated precision, and a consistency-constrained training strategy that stabilizes predictions across varying modality subsets. Systematic evaluation on the SurvBoard benchmark across 10 TCGA cancer types and seven omics modalities demonstrates that DMG-PoE achieves the highest average C-index under both the standard setting (complete-modality training/testing) and the missing-augmented setting (training additionally includes real incomplete samples and nonclinical modality dropout, with complete-only testing); controlled per-modality masking experiments validate effective test-time recovery in 22/24 cancer-modality combinations, and cross-cohort transfer with only two of seven modalities available further confirms generalization under severe input restriction.

papers.title: AxialTAD: an axial contrast architecture for TAD boundary prediction from Hi-C.
papers.authors: Choi WY, Rhee JK.
papers.abstract: Topologically associating domains (TADs) are fundamental units of 3D chromatin organization, and accurate identification of TAD boundaries from Hi-C contact matrices remains an active challenge. Recent deep learning approaches have advanced substantially, but these rely on increasingly large architectures, raising the question of how much of this capacity boundary-centric analysis requires. Here we propose AxialTAD, a compact deep learning model centered on an Axial Contrast Module (ACM) that explicitly encodes directional contrast in contact intensity along the row and column axes of local Hi-C patches, an operator aligned with the geometric signature of TAD boundaries. Evaluated on four human cell lines (GM12878, HeLa-S3, IMR-90, K562) within cell lines and under leave-one-cell-out generalization, AxialTAD performed comparably with a recent convolutional neural network (CNN)+Transformer baseline (deepTAD) while using 76%-80% fewer trainable parameters (113K-137K versus 571K). A parameter-matched conventional CNN achieved similar F1 to AxialTAD in the human 25 kb experiments. When trained and evaluated within each of two mouse datasets, AxialTAD outperformed both this control and deepTAD. Orthogonal validation against CTCF and cohesin ChIP-seq supported the biological plausibility of the predicted boundaries. These results indicate that, within the range of architectures examined, a large architecture is not necessary to reach this level of boundary prediction.

papers.title: Domain-aware enzyme classification via multiple instance learning.
papers.authors: Xiao Q, Ye Y, Tang H.
papers.abstract: Motivation Accurate Enzyme Commission (EC) number prediction is fundamental to protein function annotation and metabolic pathway reconstruction. Recent methods based on protein language model embeddings or 3D structure have improved EC prediction, but important limitations remain. Whole-sequence embeddings can dilute local functional signals, such as catalytic residues and functional domains, whereas structure-based methods depend on accurate protein structures and are therefore difficult to apply broadly. Results We present MIL-BC, a multiple instance learning framework for EC prediction that models each protein as a bag of domains rather than a single sequence-level object. This design is motivated by the observation that enzymatic function is often determined by constituent functional domains instead of the full-length sequence alone. Domain instances are generated automatically using our DCTdomain algorithm, avoiding dependence on curated domain annotations. MIL-BC aggregates domain-level evidence into protein-level EC predictions and assigns interpretable weights to domains that contribute most strongly to each prediction. We further combine the domain embedding with global embedding in MIL-BC+. MIL-BC+ achieved F1 improvements of 0.03-0.17 over the sequence-based baseline on all four test sets. The largest gains were observed for proteins with multiple enzymatic functions, where domain-level modeling better separates mixed functional signals. These results show that domain-centric multiple instance learning is an accurate and interpretable strategy for enzyme classification. By improving EC prediction without requiring structural data or curated domain labels, MIL-BC provides a scalable framework for large-scale protein function annotation. Availability and implementation Code is available as a GitHub repository at https://github.com/omics-ai/enzyme-mil.git.

papers.title: TRACER: twin-contrastive learning for fine-grained and rare spatial domain identification in spatial transcriptomics.
papers.authors: Liu Q, Lu X, Song B, Wei Q, Feng W, Guo K, Wang J, Zhou M, Zhao Y, Wang G.
papers.abstract: Motivation Fine-grained and rare spatial domains are difficult to identify in spatial transcriptomics because they contain few spots, show subtle transcriptional differences, and are strongly influenced by neighboring regions. Results We present TRACER, a twin-contrastive learning framework that integrates a graph convolutional autoencoder with neighborhood-aware instance-level and cluster-level contrastive learning. By jointly preserving local spatial continuity and enhancing domain separability, TRACER achieved competitive and generally robust performance compared with representative spatial domain identification methods across multiple spatially resolved transcriptomic datasets, including human dorsolateral prefrontal cortex generated by 10× Visium, mouse brain datasets generated by STARmap, osmFISH, and BARISTAseq, and human breast cancer. TRACER recovered major cortical and anatomical structures, improved the identification of rare or transitional domains in the mouse somatosensory cortex, and revealed candidate functionally distinct small domains within a broadly annotated breast cancer region. Availability and implementation The source code of TRACER is available at https://github.com/luxin-heart/TRACER.

A haplotype reference panel constructed from 490,319 UK Biobank genomes improves genotype imputation for global populations.
papers.authors: Wienbrandt L, Prieß C, Schmöhl M, Neff V, Gretsova M, Torres G, Wacker EM, Franke A, Ellinghaus D.
papers.abstract: Here we constructed a genotype imputation reference panel from whole-genome sequencing data from 490,319 UK Biobank (UKB) participants 1 and enabled both standalone and cloud-based phasing and imputation through EagleImp 2 and EagleImp-RAP within the UK Biobank Research Analysis Platform. The UKB reference panel achieves lower phasing switch error rates than the widely used TOPMed r3 panel (133,597 individuals) for all global superpopulations except AMR and for 25 of 26 1000 Genomes Project subpopulations. Imputation accuracy, measured by MAE, improved for 4 of 5 superpopulations and 12 subpopulations for variants with minor allele frequencies down to 0.01%. Estimated squared correlation further improved across all 5 superpopulations and 22 subpopulations, with the largest gains in East and South Asian populations. Reimputation of COVID-19 genome-wide association study datasets from Italy, Germany, Spain and Norway 3,4 demonstrated that common-variant imputation remains unsaturated, enhancing the discovery of genome-wide significant loci and improving fine-mapping resolution.

papers.title: SiSaNA: a Python-based command line interface for single-sample network analysis.
papers.authors: Newman NK, Belova T, Kuijjer ML.
papers.abstract: Motivation Reconstructing and analyzing single-sample regulatory networks has proven useful for understanding mechanisms of regulatory biology and its disruption in disease but traditionally required a fair amount of programming experience and work from the user. Results Here, we present Single-Sample Network Analysis (SiSaNA), a workflow that removes the need of prior programming experience and allows for single-sample regulatory network reconstruction and analysis, all via a command line interface. Using example input files, we walk the user through a tutorial on how to run the SiSaNA pipeline, interpret the results, and obtain high-quality figures summarized in a single HTML file as output. Availability and implementation SiSaNA is freely available to install with pip via the Python Package Index. It is additionally available on GitHub at https://github.com/kuijjerlab/sisana. Example input files can be found at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17190642.

papers.title: Advancing morphological profiling with self-supervised learning through comparative insights into representation learning of cellular perturbations.
papers.authors: Abdelmoula WM, Albuquerque T, Jaensch S, Pati P, Van Dyck M, Allen SJ, Zhang L, Mansi T, Liao R.
papers.abstract: Self-supervised learning (SSL) enables scalable, label-free foundation models (FMs) that learn task-agnostic representations directly from images, bypassing cell segmentation and feature engineering inherent to classical morphological profiling. We present a large-scale evaluation of SSL FMs for image-based phenotypic profiling, covering contrastive (DINO), masked-based generative (MAE, iTPN) and hybrid (DINOv2) learning mechanisms, pretrained on all unannotated chemical perturbations from the Joint Undertaking for Morphological Profiling-Cell Painting (JUMP-CP) dataset (119,876 compounds, ~1.77 million images, 7 laboratories). Here we show that top-performing SSL models outperformed CellProfiler in compound-replicate retrieval on the held-out JUMP-Target2 set (302 annotated compounds, P ≤ 0.001). DINO and DINOv2 generalized across diverse perturbations and cell types, outperforming CellProfiler with 31-37% gains in site-averaged mean average precision for mechanism-of-action retrieval on EU-OPENSCREEN Bioactives (2,464 compounds), and consistently surpassing masked-based models across all benchmarks. This study provides a systematic assessment of SSL approaches for advancing morphological profiling and offers pretrained FMs to accelerate drug discovery.

papers.title: PRIDA: cross-domain protein-RNA interaction prediction based on biological language models and conditional domain-adversarial learning.
papers.authors: Zhou Y, Li J, Liu S, Wang Z, Liu R, Zhu Z, Zhu T, Zhang J.
papers.abstract: Motivation The interaction between RNA and proteins is a complex process that involves atom-level details and dynamic changes. Accurate prediction of protein-RNA interactions helps researchers to develop protein-targeted small nucleic acid drugs. However, the scarcity of protein-RNA complexes and experimental data limits the ability of existing data-driven supervised learning methods to learn latent patterns, leading to limited performance. Results In this study, we propose PRIDA (Protein-RNA Interaction prediction based on Domain-Adversarial learning), a protein-RNA interaction framework that combines bilinear attention with conditional domain-adversarial learning. Powered by pretrained protein and RNA language models, PRIDA improves interaction prediction under protein-level distribution shifts and limited labeled data. By integrating PRIDA with Monte Carlo Tree Search, we apply it to a virtual screening pipeline to generate RNA aptamer candidates for specific target proteins. Experimental results show that PRIDA achieves state-of-the-art performance in cross-domain protein-RNA interaction prediction and provides effective guidance for RNA aptamer virtual screening. Availability and implementation The data and source code of the proposed method are available at GitHub (https://github.com/zhouyyang/PRIDA) and Zenodo (https://zenodo.org/records/23644677).

papers.title: Verix: a toolkit for benchmarking and harmonization of complex structural variants.
papers.authors: Rohlicek C, Battistella E, Maheshwari A, Cui T, Huang B, Gao Y, Popic V.
papers.abstract: Summary Complex structural variants (CSVs) represent a critical yet under-characterized class of large-scale genomic rearrangements. CSV discovery requires not only the accurate detection of individual breakpoints but also their assembly into a single, structurally resolved CSV event. However, CSV method development is currently limited by a diagnostic gap: existing SV evaluation frameworks are designed for single-interval or single-junction SVs and cannot quantify multi-breakpoint CSV reconstruction fidelity or systematically distinguish between different types of reconstruction errors, such as over-segmentation or collapse of independent breakpoints. Here we present Verix, a comprehensive toolkit designed for the fine-grained evaluation and integration of CSVs. Verix introduces granular diagnostic metrics that enable researchers to thoroughly characterize CSV predictions and stratify performance based on breakpoint sensitivity, precision, and structural integrity. In addition to pairwise callset-to-truthset comparisons, Verix also provides an intra- and inter-callset harmonization module for generating consensus calls for a single tool's output or across disparate discovery pipelines. As such, Verix provides the infrastructure needed to rigorously evaluate and reconcile CSV calls, accelerating the standardization of CSV discovery in both research and clinical settings. Availability and implementation Verix is available under the MIT license at https://github.com/PopicLab/verix and https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22998063.

papers.title: Tandem repeat variation shapes immune cell type-specific gene expression.
papers.authors: Tanudisastro HA, Cuomo ASE, Weisburd B, Welland M, Spenceley E, Franklin M, Xue A, Huang HL, Bowen B, Fan J, Dong OA, Henry A, Allen PC, Wing K, Tang O, Gray M, Reis ALM, Margoliash J, Kurtas NE, Pullin JM, Lee AS, Brand H, Harper M, Bobowik K, Silk M, Miniter A, Marshall J, Bakiris V, Madala BS, Uren C, Bartie C, McCloy RA, Senabouth A, Dashnow H, Fearnley L, Martin-Trujillo A, Dolzhenko E, Qiao Z, Grieve SM, Nguyen T, Ben-David E, Chen L, Farh KK, Talkowski ME, Alexander SI, Siggs OM, Gruenschloss L, Nicholas HR, Piscionere J, Simons C, Wallace C, Gymrek M, Deveson IW, Hewitt AW, Figtree GA, de Lange KM, Powell JE, MacArthur DG.

papers.title: Rare and common genetic variants shape single-cell immune gene expression.
papers.authors: Cuomo ASE, Spenceley E, Tanudisastro HA, Bowen B, Henry A, Huang HL, Xue A, Zhou W, Welland MJ, Bryen SJ, Dong OA, Lee AS, Pullin JM, Wing K, Tang O, Gray MP, Franklin M, Harper M, Silk M, Bobowik K, Stuckey A, Marshall J, Bakiris V, Uren C, McCloy RA, Madala BS, Miniter A, Bartie C, Neavin DR, Qiao Z, Ben-David E, Chen L, Farh KK, Grieve SM, Nguyen T, Wallace C, Piscionere J, Siggs OM, Nicholas H, de Lange KM, Hewitt AW, Figtree GA, MacArthur DG, Powell JE.
papers.abstract: Understanding the genetic basis of gene expression can shed light on the regulatory mechanisms underlying complex traits and diseases 1,2 . Single-cell-resolved measures of RNA levels and single-cell expression quantitative trait loci have revealed genetic regulation that drives cell states and types across diverse tissues 3 . Here we describe phase 1 of TenK10K, which leverages single-cell RNA sequencing data from more than 5 million cells across 28 immune cell types, along with matched whole-genome sequencing data from 1,925 individuals. This provides power to detect associations for rare and low-frequency genetic variants that have largely been uncharacterized in their impact on cell-specific gene expression. We map the effects of both common and rare variants in a cell-type-specific manner using a recent method that increases power by modelling single cells directly rather than aggregated 'pseudobulk' counts. We identify putative common regulatory variants for 83% of all 21,404 genes tested and cumulative rare-variant signals for 47% of those genes. We explore how genetic effects vary across cell types and states, develop a framework to determine the degree of single-cell expression quantitative trait loci cell-type specificity and show that about half of the effects are observed only in one or a few cell types. By integrating our results with functional annotations and disease information, we further characterize the likely molecular modes of action for many disease-variant associations. Finally, we explore the effects that genetic variants have on gene expression across continuous cell states, and effects that vary cell-state abundance directly.

papers.title: Genetic variants shape single-cell chromatin accessibility and disease risk.
papers.authors: Xue A, Fan J, Dong OA, Huang HL, Chen L, Allen PC, Spenceley E, Sagi-Zsigmond E, Bowen B, Henry A, Cuomo ASE, Tanudisastro HA, Qiao Z, Dorans E, Ben-David E, Farh KK, Hu L, Liu YC, Neavin DR, Lee AS, Senabouth A, Bartie C, McCloy RA, Chin V, Zhou W, Price AL, de Lange KM, Figtree GA, Hewitt AW, MacArthur DG, Powell JE.
papers.abstract: Understanding how genetic variation shapes gene regulation at single-cell resolution is crucial for elucidating complex disease mechanisms 1 , but has been limited by the lack of large-scale single-cell multi-omics data 2-4 . Here we present single-cell assay for transposase-accessible chromatin with sequencing of 3.5 million peripheral blood mononuclear cells from 1,042 donors with matched whole-genome sequencing. Across 28 immune cell types, we tested 440,996 chromatin accessibility peaks and identified 243,225 chromatin accessibility quantitative trait loci (caQTLs) at 100,483 peaks, 60% of them cell-type specific. Rare variant analysis identified 38,161 associated peaks, with predicted transcription factor-binding disruption implicated at individual loci. Colocalization with expression QTLs (eQTLs) from single-cell RNA sequencing data (5.4 million peripheral blood mononuclear cells) 5 defined 28,834 candidate cis-regulatory elements. Across genome-wide association studies for 16 diseases and 44 blood traits, caQTLs colocalized 4.5-22.6% more signals than eQTLs alone. Cell-type-specific and tissue-specific context, distal effects and multi-causal-variant models raised genome-wide association study-eQTL concordance from approximately 16% to approximately 65%. Cell state further modulates genetic effects, with 27% of over 200,000 caQTL-cell-state interactions lacking a main effect. At the inflammatory bowel disease risk gene ADCY7, accessibility effects varied with genotype and G protein-mediated pathway activity in CD4 + T cells. A graph neural network trained on both eQTL and caQTL layers inferred peak-gene links in unpaired multiome data with up to 17.2% higher accuracy than QTL-agnostic data, uncovering 128 additional transcription factor-target pairs (22% increase). Together, these results show that genetic variants shape chromatin accessibility in a cell-type-specific and cell-state-specific manner, influencing immune function and disease risk.

papers.title: Population-scale single-nucleus multi-omic profiling of skeletal muscle reveals extensive context-specific genetic regulation.
papers.authors: Varshney A, Manickam N, Orchard P, Tovar A, Ventresca C, Zhang Z, Feng F, Mears J, Erdos MR, Narisu N, Nishino K, Rai V, Stringham HM, Jackson AU, Tamsen T, Gao C, Yang M, Koues OI, Welch JD, Burant CF, Williams LK, Jenkinson C, DeFronzo RA, Norton L, Saramies J, Lakka TA, Laakso M, Tuomilehto J, Mohlke KL, Kitzman JO, Koistinen HA, Liu J, Boehnke M, Collins FS, Scott LJ, Parker SCJ.

papers.title: Starlng: STability Analysis of coRegulated 'Nests' of Genes.
papers.authors: Munteanu A.
papers.abstract: Motivation Single-cell assays (both single and multi-omics) represent the state-of-the-art for detailed characterization of cell phenotypes, a task frequently initialized with the identification of groups of genes linked to well-defined, stable subpopulations of cells. Gene expression covariation patterns are simplified precursors of Gene Regulatory Networks (GRNs) and play a crucial role in inferring causality and dynamics within GRNs. However, current gene clustering methods struggle to capture spatial organization and relationship dynamics along developmental trajectories, while remaining vulnerable to noise and algorithmic stochasticity. Results Expanding on the ClustAssess framework, which shifted the cluster-centric assessment of populations of cells to an element-centric perspective, we propose to assess the covariation induced by gene graph clustering. The Starlng (abbrev) framework provides an optimized, interactive environment for the identification of the filtered modules. The pipeline identifies the stable configuration of clustering parameters and robust gene modules (nests of genes), followed by the removal of the outlier clusters based on the pseudotime variance. We illustrate Starlng on the identification of reliable, reproducible communities of genes, as well as reveal unbiased hierarchical relationships between higher level cell clusters and more granular subgroups of genes. Availability and implementation Starlng is implemented in R and freely available at https://github.com/Core-Bioinformatics/Starlng.

papers.title: rustybam: a composable toolkit for alignment analysis and visualization with SafFire.
papers.authors: Mirchandani C, Vollger MR.
papers.abstract: Summary We present rustybam, a Rust-based command-line toolkit for CIGAR-aware manipulation of PAF and BAM alignments, and SafFire, a browser-based tool for interactive genome comparison visualization with annotation overlays. rustybam's composable subcommands provide overlap resolution, coordinate liftover, alignment splitting at structural variants, scaffolding, and identity statistics. Availability and implementation Both tools are open source under the MIT license. rustybam is available via Bioconda (https://anaconda.org/bioconda/rustybam), crates.io, and GitHub (https://github.com/vollgerlab/rustybam). SafFire is hosted at https://vollgerlab.com/SafFire/ with source code at https://github.com/vollgerlab/SafFire. Archived versions are available on Zenodo: rustybam (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.4654875) and SafFire (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.5765964).

papers.title: CSK-DDI: compensating structural incompleteness with knowledge graph world knowledge for drug-drug interaction modeling.
papers.authors: Wang J, He Y, Ma T, Song B.
papers.abstract: Motivation Drug-drug interaction (DDI) prediction is critical for drug safety, yet existing methods suffer from structural incompleteness in drug representation. Motif and molecular graph encodings capture local substructures and global topology but remain confined to the closed structural space of individual molecules, lacking cross-entity and contextual information and leading to limited generalization, especially in cold-start scenarios. To address this issue, we propose CSK-DDI (Compensating Structural Incompleteness with Knowledge Graph World Knowledge for Drug-Drug Interaction Modeling), a multimodal framework that jointly encodes motif-level chemical patterns, molecular graph topology, and biomedical knowledge graph (KG) context as complementary drug representations. The KG encodes drugs' contextual positions and relational semantics through multi-entity and multi-relation connections, providing global cross-entity and cross-semantic information that complements structural representations. The resulting fusion captures local chemical patterns, global topology, and biomedical context in a unified embedding. Results CSK-DDI employs a cross-attention mechanism to enable multi-view interaction among motif, molecular graph, and KG representations, producing unified structure-aware and context-aware drug embeddings. To improve robustness under sparse conditions, the model further incorporates a cold-start-oriented representation enhancement strategy. Experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate consistent improvements over state-of-the-art methods, with particularly notable gains in cold-start scenarios. Availability and implementation Source code and data are available at https://github.com/cgwcbz2/CSK-DDI and on Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21415769.

papers.title: Continuous mass photometry by single-molecule trapping.
papers.authors: Loewenthal D, Asor R, Thorpe S, Peters JS, Zouboulis KC, Kaplan M, Thiele JC, Bardzil J, Helmi S, Burnap SA, Tan TK, Struwe WB, Benesch JLP, Kukura P.
papers.abstract: The dynamic choreography of biomolecular interactions underpins the processes of life, but its direct observation remains challenging. Here we introduce continuous mass photometry, enabling hour-long, mass-resolved observation of individual biomolecules tethered to supported lipid bilayers, their complexes and interactions, with up to sub-kilodalton mass precision and millisecond temporal resolution. Our approach represents a quantitative time-resolved single-molecule measurement modality for studying complex biomolecular mechanisms in action.
