papers.title: Multi-view state-space modeling for zero-shot circRNA-miRNA interaction prediction.
papers.authors: Wei MM, Wang L, Huang YA, Huang ZA, Hu PW, You ZH.
papers.abstract: Motivation CircRNA-miRNA interactions (CMIs) play regulatory roles in human diseases and provide clues for therapeutic target discovery. However, most existing prediction methods rely on circRNA-miRNA pairs and overlook disease-level regulatory contexts, which limits their ability to characterize cross-pathway dependencies in zero-shot inference. Results We propose MV-S2M, a multi-view state-space modeling framework that integrates molecular attributes to enhance relational reasoning, enabling zero-shot CMI prediction. Specifically, MV-S2M performs structure-aware diffusion to enrich molecular priors and constructs disease-mediated semantic subgraphs. It then incorporates state-space modeling to capture long-range dependencies and view-specific regulatory patterns. The learned multi-view representations are fused through a linear projection and fed into an MLP for CMI prediction. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that MV-S2M achieves state-of-the-art performance under both zero-shot and conventional settings. Cold-start evaluations reveal distinct generalization behavior across different unseen-entity settings. Case studies illustrate the contribution of meta-path-guided semantic subgraphs to CMI prediction. Availability and implementation The code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/591286260/MV and https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22858403.

papers.title: Ernie-Switcher: RNA foundation model-guided design of programmable RNA devices in a navigable landscape.
papers.authors: Lei X, Li R, Liu Y, Huang J, Yang Y, Li R, Liu S, Wang P, Jiang H, Xiong W.
papers.abstract: Motivation Recent advances in biological foundation models have enabled new opportunities for data-driven molecular engineering. However, designing programmable RNA devices remains challenging because of the vast, nonlinear sequence-structure-function landscape. Here, we present Ernie-Switcher, a deep learning framework built upon the RNA foundation model (RNAErnie), comprising three coupled components: (i) integration of RNAErnie-derived sequence-phenotype representations for realistic design generation and filtering, (ii) characterization of RNA landscape navigability as a theoretical basis for sequence optimization, and (iii) incorporation of biophysical constraints to maintain optimization trajectories within biologically plausible bounds. Results We validated Ernie-Switcher using RNA toehold switches. Theoretically, the observed lower bound on threshold navigability (86.4%) of the RNA landscape supports the theoretical feasibility of RNA switch sequence optimization. Experimentally, the optimized toehold switches achieved ON/OFF expression ratios of up to 35-fold in Escherichia coli. Collectively, RNAErnie-guided sequence optimization provides a scalable strategy for engineering high-performance RNA devices. To facilitate broad adoption, we deployed Ernie-Switcher as a freely accessible web platform. Availability and implementation The Python code and pre-trained models are available at https://github.com/zhutiblah/Ernie-Switcher and are archived on Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21859277. The RNA toehold switch design platform is available at https://ernie-switcher.bioinformatics-syn.org/.

papers.title: GBZ-base and GAF-base: indexed pangenome file formats.
papers.authors: Sirén J, Paten B, Human Pangenome Reference Consortium.
papers.abstract: Motivation Existing pangenome file formats are designed for batch processing. Graphs must be loaded into memory, and alignment files must be read sequentially. Indexed file formats that can be used directly from disk would be more appropriate for interactive applications. Results We propose GBZ-base and GAF-base-SQLite-backed file formats comparable to GBZ and GAF. GBZ-base supports efficient extraction of local subgraphs, and GAF-base lets us extract all alignments to the subgraph. Additionally, GAF-base is smaller than any other file format for sequence-to-graph alignments. Availability and implementation From https://github.com/jltsiren/gbz-base and https://crates.io/crates/gbz-base under the MIT license.

papers.title: SomatiX: accurate and efficient somatic SNV detection from matched tumor-normal long-read DNA sequencing.
papers.authors: Liu Z.
papers.abstract: Motivation Accurate somatic single-nucleotide variant (SNV) calling from matched tumor-normal long-read DNA sequencing remains challenging because sequencing errors, variable tumor purity, tumor-in-normal contamination, and low variant allele fractions (VAFs) can obscure tumor-specific signals. Although recent deep-learning methods have improved long-read somatic variant calling, robust low-VAF detection and efficient genome-scale analysis remain important methodological challenges. Results We present SomatiX, a deep-learning method for somatic SNV detection from matched tumor-normal long-read DNA sequencing data, built on an allele-aware pileup representation. In comprehensive cancer benchmark analyses across diverse cell-line datasets, sequencing contexts, VAF bins, and minimum variant-supporting read thresholds, SomatiX outperformed DeepSomatic and ClairS in F1 score across most Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT) benchmark conditions and achieved competitive performance on Pacific Biosciences (PacBio) data. Across the held-out chromosome 1 cancer cell-line benchmarks, at the threshold of ≥3 variant-supporting reads and a VAF ≥0.05, SomatiX achieved mean F1 scores of 0.986 for ONT data and 0.988 for PacBio data. SomatiX showed particularly strong performance for low-VAF SNVs in ONT data while using a compact model and achieving the fastest runtime among the evaluated tools. Availability and implementation SomatiX is available at https://github.com/colinliuzelin/SomatiX and archived at Zenodo under DOI: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22062438. The repository includes source code, trained models, and benchmarking scripts.

papers.title: Large-scale semantic indexing of Spanish biomedical literature using contrastive transfer learning.
papers.authors: You R, Huang T, Wang Z, Liu Y, Zhou H, Zhu S.
papers.abstract: Motivation The exponential growth of biomedical literature has made automatic indexing essential for advancing biomedical research. While automatic indexing has made strides in English biomedical literature, there has been limited research on non-English biomedical texts due to insufficient high-quality training data. Results We propose BERTDeCS, a novel deep learning framework for automatically indexing Spanish biomedical literature using contrastive transfer learning. BERTDeCS utilizes a multilingual BERT (M-BERT) to generate multi-language representations and adapts M-BERT for Spanish biomedical literature domain through contrastive learning. Additionally, BERTDeCS enhances its semantic indexing capabilities on Spanish biomedical literature by leveraging enriched English annotated literature in MEDLINE through transfer learning. Experimental results on Spanish datasets demonstrate that BERTDeCS outperforms state-of-the-art indexing methods, achieving top performance in the MESINESP and MESINESP2 Tasks on medical semantic indexing in Spanish within the BioASQ challenge. Additional experiments on Portuguese provide preliminary evidence that BERTDeCS can transfer to a closely related language sharing substantial lexical and biomedical terminology with Spanish. Availability The source code is available at https://github.com/yourh/BERTDeCS and at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23212468.

papers.title: AbLWR: a context-aware listwise ranking framework for antibody-antigen binding affinity prediction via positive-unlabeled learning.
papers.authors: Xu F, Huang ZA, He H, Song Y, Liu W, Zhang D, Hu Y, Wu J, Tan KC.
papers.abstract: Motivation Accurate prediction of antibody-antigen binding affinity is fundamental to therapeutic design and the rapid response to evolving pathogens. However, current computational approaches predominantly formulate this as a point-wise regression task. This paradigm struggles to discriminate subtle affinity differences among highly homologous variants and lacks the global context necessary to effectively prioritize top-tier candidates. Furthermore, the field is severely constrained by label sparsity. Although sequence data is abundant, experimentally verified affinities are scarce, leaving a massive pool of unverified antibody-antigen structural interactions unexploited by standard supervised paradigms. Results We propose AbLWR (Antibody-antigen binding affinity Listwise Ranking), a novel framework that reformulates the conventional affinity regression task as a listwise ranking problem to directly optimize candidate prioritization. To mitigate label sparsity, AbLWR incorporates a Positive-Unlabeled (PU) learning mechanism, leveraging a dual-level contrastive objective and meta-optimized label refinement to distill robust structural representations from vast unlabeled data. To accommodate antigenic variation, we employ a homologous antigen sampling strategy coupled with a Multi-Head Self-Attention (MHSA) module, which explicitly models inter-sample dependencies within training lists to capture subtle affinity nuances. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that AbLWR significantly outperforms state-of-the-art sequence-, structure-, and complex-based baselines. It improves the Full Rank Accuracy (FRA) by approximately 8% compared to the strongest baseline in randomized cross-validation, and exhibits strong robustness in out-of-distribution scenarios involving distinct antigen and antibody clusters. Case studies on Influenza Viruses and Human Interleukin-33 further validate its practical utility. Specifically, AbLWR successfully tracks affinity drops caused by antigenic drift and immediately captures optimal binders in simulated wet-lab screening. Availability Source code and datasets are freely available at https://github.com/Josie-xufan/AbLWR.

papers.title: BioHarness: substrate-aware evidence assembly for biomedical question answering across literature, knowledge bases, and biological atlases.
papers.authors: Xiao M, Qin C, Chen J, Cheng Y, Zhou Y, Zhu H.
papers.abstract: Motivation Biomedical question answering often requires evidence beyond topically retrieved literature, including gene alias resolution, database identifier normalization, and atlas-derived biological measurements. However, existing retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems typically follow a fixed workflow and lack an explicit mechanism for deciding when retrieved text is sufficient, when biomedical entity mapping is needed, or when executable evidence assembly over structured measurements should be invoked. This motivates a substrate-aware large language model (LLM) harness that selectively assembles sufficient evidence by combining literature retrieval, biomedical entity mapping, and access to atlas-derived measurements. Results We introduce BioHarness, an LLM harness for staged biomedical evidence assembly across literature retrieval, biomedical entity-mapping resources, and atlas-derived structured measurements. Across 22 123 biomedical QA items spanning seven answer formats, BioHarness improves the pooled score from 62.2 to 67.2 over the strongest baseline. Ablations, case studies, and backbone-scaling analyses show that these gains arise from repairing evidence-substrate mismatches through reranking, entity grounding, and structured measurement access, rather than from indiscriminately invoking more reasoning steps, retrieving additional literature, or relying on a particular answer-model scale. Comparisons with the frontier models and harness show that BioHarness, despite using an open-weight backbone with only 3B active parameters, approaches frontier-level performance on selected literature QA tasks and outperforms frontier harnesses without web access on biomedical identifier and locus lookup. Availability and implementation The source code, reproducible benchmarking scripts, and processed benchmark data required to reproduce all results in this study are publicly available under an open-source license, together with the exat configuration, model versions, and decoding settings used in our experiments. In addition, we developed a prototype web demo (https://xcompass.scimatrix.cn/) that illustrates how BioHarness can be used in an interactive biomedical QA setting.

papers.title: LRP2: a proteogenomics pipeline for long-read informed protein isoform analysis and discovery.
papers.authors: Schertzer MD, Lewandowski JT, Watts EF, Rosenow W, Mehlferber MM, Jeffery ED, Adamson SI, Bruand J, Tseng E, Neelamraju Y, Garrett-Bakelman FE, Dolzhenko E, Knowles DA, Sheynkman G.
papers.abstract: Summary Most human genes produce multiple RNA isoforms, yet it remains unclear which isoforms are translated into stable, functional proteins. Long-read RNA sequencing resolves full-length transcript structures and, when paired with mass spectrometry, can provide empirical evidence of isoform translation. Despite this opportunity, comprehensive workflows integrating isoform discovery, open reading frame prediction, peptide identification, and protein inference remain limited, leaving users to handle these steps piecemeal. Here, we present LRP2, a modular, end-to-end long-read proteogenomics pipeline built in Nextflow. LRP2 scales transcript discovery to hundreds of samples via PacBio's latest Isocall tool, removes technical artifacts with SQANTI QC, generates and classifies predicted proteomes via CPAT and SQANTI Protein, performs multi-group differential expression and usage analysis via edgeR, DRIMSeq, and a long-read adaptation of LeafCutter, and integrates protein-level evidence from DDA and DIA MS data through FragPipe. For cross-dataset comparison of novel isoforms, LRP2 employs deterministic splice junction, coordinate-based isoform identifiers. Used as an integrated pipeline, LRP2 enables the detection of novel peptides and improves protein isoform inference to confirm protein isoform translation. Availability and implementation LRP2 is freely available as a modular Nextflow pipeline at https://github.com/sheynkman-lab/LRP2 (v2.0.0, archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22795865). LRP2 supports Docker, Apptainer/Singularity, and Conda environments with GENCODE references.

papers.title: From SELEX to sequencing: uncovering enriched aptamers with next-generation sequencing and bioinformatics.
papers.authors: Girbas MG, Müller J, Schlensak C, Avci-Adali M.
papers.abstract: Motivation The combinatorial chemistry process called systematic evolution of ligands by exponential enrichment (SELEX) enables the selection of aptamers against different targets. The integration of next-generation sequencing (NGS) into SELEX workflows represents a powerful strategy to enhance the identification and prioritization of target-binding aptamers. In this study, we present an optimized computational approach for the NGS-based analysis of enriched aptamer pools generated through SELEX. It encompasses sequencing library preparation, sequence data preprocessing, clustering, multiple sequence alignment, phylogenetic analysis, and secondary structure prediction. Results To identify target-specific aptamers, two comparative analysis strategies were implemented. In the first strategy, sequences detected in the negative selection pool were removed from the positive selection pool to eliminate nonspecific binders, resulting in six distinct sequence clusters. In the second approach, all sequences were retained, and cluster distributions were compared between the positive and negative selection pools, identifying seven clusters in the positive and six in the negative pool. Phylogenetic relationships and structural predictions enabled the selection of promising candidates, which were prioritized based on secondary structure, sequence abundance, and genetic distance from nonspecific binders. Binding specificity was assessed through dot blot assays, confirming that the selected aptamers exhibited strong specific binding to the target protein. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of the NGS-guided workflow for aptamer discovery and highlight its value in streamlining candidate selection for downstream functional validation. Availability and implementation The data underlying this article will be shared on reasonable request to the corresponding author.

papers.title: Benchmarking segmentation methods for spatial transcriptomics.
papers.authors: Martínez-de-Morentin X, Khan SA, Maillo A, Lehmann R, Kiani NA, Lagani V, Gomez-Cabrero D, Tegner J.
papers.abstract: Cell segmentation is a critical yet under-standardized step in spatial transcriptomics, directly affecting cell identity assignment, spatial organization and downstream biological interpretation. Despite rapid advances in spatial transcriptomics technologies, systematic evaluations of segmentation methods across platforms and biological contexts remain limited. Here we benchmark 11 image-based, transcriptomics-based and multimodal segmentation methods across 15 datasets generated by 5 spatial transcriptomics technologies, spanning 12 human and mouse tissue types. We introduce biologically informed evaluation metrics that quantify segmentation quality, transcript recovery, cell composition, morphology, expression purity and spatial organization. Benchmarking reveals substantial variation in performance across datasets, technologies and evaluation criteria, highlighting trade-offs among segmentation completeness, transcriptomic fidelity and biological interpretability. Cross-technology analyses further demonstrate that segmentation choice critically shapes downstream analyses, including cell-type specificity, transcript contamination and ligand-receptor inference. Together, our unified Nextflow pipeline provides a scalable foundation for standardized evaluation of segmentation and method selection in spatial transcriptomics.

papers.title: Near-complete assembly of wild emmer wheat unveils centromere reorganization during polyploid evolution.

papers.title: Co-regulation confounds direction of genetic effects in transcriptome-wide association studies.

papers.title: High false sign rates in transcriptome-wide association studies.
papers.authors: Gerlach PA, Milind N, Spence JP, Pritchard JK.
papers.abstract: Transcriptome-wide association studies (TWAS) are widely used to identify genes involved in complex traits and to infer the direction of gene effects on traits. However, despite their popularity, it remains unclear how accurately TWAS recover the true direction of a gene's effect on a trait. Here we estimate the false sign rate of TWAS for plasma proteins, leveraging the expectation that increased gene expression should generally increase protein expression. We then extend this framework to complex traits, where loss-of-function burden tests provide the expected direction of effect. In both analyses, we observe high discordance with expectations, with TWAS showing a false sign rate of 23% for plasma proteins and 33% for complex traits. We propose that much of the sign discordance arises when expression quantitative trait loci in non-trait-relevant tissues tag haplotypes associated with traits in genome-wide association studies via distinct, tightly linked regulatory variants, yielding spurious TWAS associations with the correct genes but with unreliable direction of effect. These findings show that TWAS-based direction-of-effect estimates should be interpreted with caution and raise concerns about the reliability of TWAS more broadly.

papers.title: CauTrigger: deciphering biological system state transitions by hierarchical causal decomposition.
papers.authors: Zhang C, Cai D, Aihara K, Chen L.

papers.title: Tracing causal cascades underlying biological state changes.
OpenDVP: an experimental and computational framework for community-empowered deep visual proteomics.
papers.authors: Nimo J, Fritzsche S, Valdes DS, Trinh M, Pentimalli T, Klingeberg M, Schallenberg S, Klauschen F, Herse F, Florian S, Rajewsky N, Coscia F.
papers.abstract: Deep visual proteomics (DVP) is an emerging approach for cell-type-specific and spatially resolved proteomics. However, its broad adoption has been constrained by the lack of an open-source end-to-end workflow within a community-driven ecosystem. Here we introduce openDVP, an experimental and computational framework for accessible and scalable DVP. OpenDVP combines open-source image analysis tools (MCMICRO, QuPath and napari) with scverse formats (AnnData and SpatialData) for multiomics integration. It provides two workflows: a fast-track pipeline requiring no image analysis expertise, and an artificial intelligence-powered pipeline incorporating state-of-the-art methods for image preprocessing, segmentation and spatial analysis. We apply openDVP across three archival tissue studies (human placenta, early stage lung cancer and locally relapsed breast cancer), integrating spatial single-cell phenotypes with exploratory proteomic measurements. Finally, we introduce deep proteomic profiling of cellular neighborhoods as a scalable approach for spatial discovery proteomics.

papers.title: Genome-wide detection of genotype-environment interactions at biobank scale with fastGxE.
papers.authors: Ning C, Zhou X.
papers.abstract: Traditional genome-wide association studies have primarily focused on detecting main genotype effects, often overlooking genotype-environment interactions (GxE), which are essential for understanding context-specific genetic effects and refining disease etiology. Here we present fast genotype-environment interaction analysis (fastGxE), a scalable and effective genome-wide GxE method designed to identify genetic variants that interact with environmental factors to influence traits of interest. fastGxE controls for polygenic effects, polygenic interaction effects and noise heterogeneity; it remains robust to the number of environmental factors involved in GxE interactions; and it ensures scalability for genome-wide GxE analysis in large biobank studies, achieving speed improvements of 32.98-126.49 times over existing approaches. We illustrate the benefits of fastGxE through extensive simulations and an in-depth analysis of 32 physical traits and 67 blood biomarkers from the UK Biobank. In real-data applications, fastGxE identifies 7 genomic loci associated with physical traits, including 4 novel ones, and 18 genomic loci associated with blood biomarkers, 12 of which are novel. The new discoveries highlight the dynamic interplay between genetics and the environment, uncovering potentially clinically relevant pathways that could inform personalized interventions and treatment strategies.

papers.title: Genome-wide analyses identify 60 loci associated with liver triglyceride content.
papers.authors: Jamialahmadi O, Mowlaei S, Gelev KZ, Mancina RM, Flagiello V, Kozlitina J, Pajukanta P, Valenti L, Romeo S.
papers.abstract: We performed a large-scale genome-wide association study meta-analysis of magnetic resonance imaging-derived liver triglyceride content across 71,488 European-ancestry participants from the UK Biobank, approximately doubling the sample size of previous genome-wide association studies 1 . We identified 60 independent loci, including 31 not previously reported, and estimated the single nucleotide polymorphism-based heritability of liver triglyceride content at 25%. Integrative fine-mapping and gene-prioritization analyses nominated candidate effector genes for 48 loci. Of the 31 newly identified variants, 14 were validated in meta-analyses of clinically diagnosed metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (42,163 cases and 1,646,254 controls). People in the highest versus lowest decile of a polygenic risk score for liver triglyceride content had 2.71-fold higher odds of cirrhosis and 7.47-fold higher odds of hepatocellular carcinoma. Plasma proteins associated with the liver triglyceride polygenic risk score were enriched for metabolic remodeling and inflammatory pathways, with liver-enriched protein signatures increasing and visceral adipose signatures decreasing with higher genetic risk. Together, these findings refine the genetic architecture of liver triglyceride content, linking polygenic susceptibility to downstream metabolic and inflammatory pathways and providing insights into the genetic basis of steatotic liver disease.

papers.title: XenoMix: estimating mouse content from DNA methylation data of Patient-Derived Xenograft models.
papers.authors: Esmaeelpour N, Mücke O, Altun G, Cornick J, Capone M, Sotillo R, Llamazares-Prada M, Plass C, Scherer M.
papers.abstract: Summary DNA methylation microarrays enable cost-effective, high-throughput profiling of human and mouse samples and are widely used to study epigenetic alterations in cancer. Patient-Derived Xenograft (PDX) models complement this approach by preserving primary tumor characteristics while enabling in vivo studies of drug response and therapy resistance. However, it remains difficult to quantify mouse DNA contamination in PDX DNA methylation data generated using microarrays. We present XenoMix, a light-weight computational tool for quantifying mouse DNA contamination directly from DNA methylation data in PDX models. XenoMix leverages the high sequence homology between human and mouse genomes to detect and quantify unexpected signal contributions originating from mouse DNA. Using ground truth mixtures, XenoMix achieved Pearson's correlation coefficients higher than 0.99. When applied to PDX data, we identified varying levels of mouse contamination originating from biological and technological variability. XenoMix establishes a critical quality control step in DNA methylation analysis of PDX models, and we show that the estimated contamination can be incorporated as a confounding variable in downstream analyses. Availability and implementation XenoMix is available as a standalone R package from https://git.dkfz.de/b370/scepigen/XenoMix and as a module in the RnBeads software package.

papers.title: Integrating complementary datasets for constructing microbiome-metabolome-disease pathways.
papers.authors: Fang L, Ye C, Wang Y.
papers.abstract: Motivation Microbiome-metabolome-disease pathways play a central role in host health, but studying them is limited by the data available. Large clinical microbiome cohorts often lack metabolomic measurements, while multi-omics studies with paired profiles are typically small or incompletely phenotyped. Combining such complementary datasets is challenging: the metabolite is not measured in the clinical cohort, microbiome data are high-dimensional and compositional, and log-ratio analyses depend on an arbitrarily chosen reference taxon. Results We propose a framework that integrates a large target cohort that has microbiome and outcome data with a smaller external study that has paired microbiome-metabolome profiles. A high-dimensional structural equation model jointly links the microbiome, the metabolome, and the disease outcome. It allows for unmeasured confounding and groups microbes into functional categories. We address compositionality with the additive log-ratio (ALR) transformation, estimate parameters by penalized two-stage least squares, and test metabolite-disease associations with a regularized permutation test. A novel multiple-reference procedure treats each microbe in turn as the ALR reference. It combines the resulting P-values with the Cauchy combination test and classifies microbes by stability selection, which makes inference robust to the choice of reference. In simulations, the method controls the type I error rate, and its power increases with both target and external sample sizes. An application to inflammatory bowel disease, integrating the FRAN and iHMP cohorts, reveals biologically interpretable microbiome-metabolome-disease links. Availability and implementation The method is implemented in the R package MMDP, freely available at https://github.com/lei-fang-stat/MMDP.

papers.title: The landscape of gene loss and missense variation across the mammalian tree informs on gene essentiality.
papers.authors: Liao C, Ye R, Ivankovic F, Fu JM, Walters R, Lowther C, Valkanas E, Churchhouse C, Samocha KE, Lindblad-Toh K, Karlsson E, Hiller M, Talkowski ME, Neale BM.
papers.abstract: Patterns of gene and sequence preservation across species provide insight into gene essentiality under natural selection. Here we developed two interspecies constraint metrics across 462 mammalian species: Gene Identity Score of Mammalian Orthologs (GISMO), which quantifies gene loss weighted by evolutionary distance to humans, and GISMO-mis, which measures missense constraint using the ratio of missense to synonymous variation across mammals. Both metrics are strongly correlated with human loss of function, missense and dosage constraint derived from large-scale sequencing studies, yet are largely independent of coding sequence length. GISMO and GISMO-mis identify essential genes missed by existing human-only metrics, particularly short genes. Genes in the most constrained deciles are enriched for rare variant associations in disorders linked to reduced fecundity, including schizophrenia, autism and neurodevelopmental disorders, and show strong enrichment for common variant heritability. These deciles also exhibit reduced copy number variation, consistent with dosage sensitivity. In addition, GISMO improves prioritization of recessive disease genes and captures signatures of homozygous selection across the mammalian tree. Taken together, GISMO and GISMO-mis leverage deep mammalian evolution to provide complementary, length-robust measures of gene essentiality that strengthen disease-gene prioritization and illuminate the selective forces shaping human biology.

papers.title: Imputation of fluid intelligence to increase power for gene discovery.
papers.authors: Benjamin DJ.

papers.title: Multiancestry conditional and joint analysis applied to GWAS summary statistics.
papers.authors: Wang X, Wang Y, Yang J, Visscher PM, Wray NR, Yengo L.
papers.abstract: Conditional and joint (COJO) analysis of genome-wide association study (GWAS) data is a standard post-GWAS analysis for identifying statistically independent associations. Although GWAS meta-analyses are increasingly conducted across multiple ancestry groups, the optimal strategy for multiancestry COJO analysis remains unclear. Here we introduce Manc-COJO, a method for multiancestry COJO analysis. Simulations and real-data analyses show that Manc-COJO improves detection of independent association signals while reducing false positives compared with single-ancestry COJO implemented in genome-wide complex trait analysis (GCTA) and its ad-hoc multiancestry adaptations. We also introduce Manc-COJO:FIX, a follow-up algorithm to identify ancestry-specific independent associations. The C++ implementation of Manc-COJO is over 120-fold faster than GCTA-COJO and supports linkage disequilibrium references derived from either individual-level genotype data or pre-computed matrices, facilitating analyses when data sharing is limited.

papers.title: Distilling direct effects via conditional differential gene expression analysis.
papers.authors: Gu J, Skelton A, Staley J, Popson P, Peng L, Song X, Knowles J, He Z.
papers.abstract: Motivation Differential gene expression (DGE) analysis is foundational for interpreting RNA sequencing data, but it conflates direct biological effects with correlations propagated through gene co-expression. Across three RNA sequencing datasets (including a genome-scale perturb-seq experiment), we find that only a small fraction of differentially expressed genes have direct effects on the trait of interest, while the majority are undirected or passengers whose associations are mediated through other genes. Results To distinguish direct effect genes, we introduce conditional differential gene expression (CDGE) analysis, a framework that tests for conditional rather than marginal association between each gene and the trait of interest. Implemented via the GhostKnockoff procedure with lasso regression, CDGE delivers false discovery rate control, operates on summary statistics from existing DGE pipelines, and accommodates batch effects. The genes identified by CDGE mediate the effects of most other differentially expressed genes and show stronger enrichment for known protein-protein interactions and biological pathways than DGE-identified genes. These results suggest that the field has been systematically over-interpreting DGE outputs, and that distinguishing direct from mediated effects is essential for prioritizing genes for functional follow-up and therapeutic development. Availability and implementation To facilitate public access to knockoff-based CDGE analysis, we have developed the R package "KnockoffCDGE" as an integrated implementation, which is freely available at https://github.com/GuJQ5/KnockoffCDGE (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23241517).

papers.title: Multi-immersion oblique plane microscope (miOPM): a reconfigurable platform for high-resolution light-sheet fluorescence microscopy.
papers.authors: Chen B, Millett-Sikking A, Chang BJ, Gałecki S, Daetwyler S, Jiou J, Monistrol J, Shen Q, Zhou F, Lin HY, Jenkins E, Stein MC, Marlar-Pavey M, Sturm G, Li AL, Tang Q, Feng BY, Diaz U, Chen Y, Shalizi A, Gillich A, Friedman JR, Tomer R, Marshall WF, Shahmoradian S, Dean KM, Fiolka R.
papers.abstract: Light-sheet fluorescence microscopy (LSFM) enables gentle, rapid and efficient volumetric imaging of biological specimens. Despite its potential, LSFM has fragmented into multiple variants, each narrowly optimized for specific samples or imaging regimes, limiting its broad applicability. Here we introduce the multi-immersion oblique plane microscope (miOPM), an adaptable LSFM platform for high-resolution imaging ranging from subcellular dynamics to whole organisms and cleared tissues. miOPM supports seamless interchangeability of oil, water and air objectives and maintains diffraction-limited performance across a refractive index range of 1.33 to 1.51. It is compatible with standard sample mounting, current clearing protocols and high-throughput 3D imaging. We leverage miOPM to image diverse biological specimens at multiple spatial scales. By expanding the adaptability and ease of use of LSFM, miOPM is poised to democratize advanced 3D imaging.

papers.title: AmpliconSuite: an end-to-end workflow for analyzing focal amplifications in cancer genomes.
papers.authors: Luebeck J, Liefeld T, Wong IT, Huang E, Kim F, Dameracharla B, Chan M, Ahuja R, Fetter K, Khatri D, Zhu K, Tabor T, Schreyer D, Prasad G, Gnanasekar A, Raeisi Dehkordi S, Spandau S, Adamaszek M, Kenkre R, Agashe T, Torvi D, Giurgiu-Kraljič M, Kim S, Kim H, Bailey P, Verhaak RGW, Deshpande V, Reich M, Mischel PS, Mesirov JP, Bafna V.
papers.abstract: Here we present AmpliconSuite, a toolkit for focal amplification analysis from cancer whole-genome sequencing that identifies extrachromosomal DNA (ecDNA), breakage-fusion-bridges and other amplification modes. Its ecContext module categorizes ecDNA structures to understand formation mechanisms. Validation across 175 metaphase fluorescence in situ hybridization-probed genes in 72 models demonstrated accurate predictions. Analysis of 6,506 patient pan-cancer samples revealed ecDNA-mediated oncogene co-amplification preferences. To democratize data sharing, we created AmpliconRepository, a community-contributable platform, enabling investigation of results across >15,000 publicly hosted samples.

papers.title: A pangenomic method for establishing a synthetic somatic variant resource in HapMap mixtures.
papers.authors: Kong N, Tang Z, Ruttenberg A, Macias-Velasco JF, Li Z, Casey E, Zhang W, Miao B, Xin Z, Fu Q, Park H, Zhuo X, Mehinovic E, Belter E, Tomlinson C, Garza JE, Dong S, Johnson B, Majewski MF, Palmer T, Cheng Y, Lindsay T, Schedl T, Li D, Shen H, Fulton R, SMaHT Network Assembly/Pangenome Working Group, Wang T, Jin SC.
papers.abstract: Somatic mosaicism is widespread in human biology and disease, yet robust benchmarks are scarce. The Somatic Mosaicism across Human Tissues (SMaHT) Consortium mixed six HapMap cell lines to create artificial somatic variants spanning 0.25%-16.5% variant allele fractions. We developed a technology-agnostic method that builds pangenome graphs from individual assemblies to create unified benchmarking sets: >6 million single-nucleotide variants, >1.8 million small insertions/deletions, >49,000 structural variations, and 10,000 mobile element insertions across autosomes and mitochondrial chromosomes. We validated the variants using ultra-deep simulated reads and developed a binomial-based model to estimate coverage requirements for variant detection. Evaluating multiple callers showed that telomere-to-telomere CHM13 alignment improves structural variant detection and offers advantages in difficult-to-map regions compared to GRCh38. Low-allele-fraction variant detection remained particularly challenging in repeat-rich genomic regions and falsely duplicated genes. This accurate, versatile resource enables systematic evaluation of somatic variant detection technologies.

papers.title: Detecting low-allele-fraction mosaic mutations: A multi-institution benchmarking with cell-line mixtures.
papers.authors: Ha YJ, Maziec D, Markowski J, Georges SJ, Parmalee NL, Berselli M, Coorens THH, Dong S, Gardiner S, Kalra D, Li D, Miao B, Musunuri R, Xue L, Yu Z, Walker K, Anderson L, Au NYT, Cibulskis C, Doddapaneni H, Grochowski CM, Jensen DM, Lindsay T, Loy K, Narayan A, Narzisi G, Ou J, Pham MM, Runnels AM, Stergachis AB, Sutherlin LM, Wang T, Jin H, Feng WC, Zhang Y, Veit AD, Kim CT, Chun HE, SMaHT Network Single Nucleotide Variant (SNV) Working Group, Ardlie K, Fulton RS, Germer S, Gibbs RA, Marth GT, Bennett JT, Park PJ.
papers.abstract: Mosaic mutations in normal tissues occur at low variant allele fractions (VAFs), complicating detection. To benchmark variant-calling strategies, the SMaHT Network created a cell-line mixture (1:49) and produced ultra-deep short- and long-read whole-genome sequencing data across five centers (170×-470× per center). We assembled a reference set of mosaic SNVs and indels, cross-validated with long-read data to expose short-read limitations. We also partitioned the genome by mappability to examine the impact of genomic context, added a negative reference set, and accounted for culture-derived mutations. When seven institutions applied twelve pipelines, callsets were largely discordant across tools and replicates, partly reflecting stochastic sampling of low-VAF mutations in biological replicates. For SNVs with VAFs above 2%, sensitivity and precision approached 80% at ≥300×, with little gain from additional sequencing. This work establishes a framework and best practices for reliably detecting low-VAF mutations in non-cancer tissues and provides a valuable resource for the community.

papers.title: Revisiting batch effect correction: a structured problem formulation and novel solutions.
papers.authors: Harrar A, Shaham U.
papers.abstract: Motivation Existing methods for batch effect removal often suffer from an ill-defined problem formulation and rely on unverified assumptions, limiting their robustness and generalizability. This study proposes a principled approach to systematically address these limitations. Results We present two novel methodologies for removing systematic batch effects: an unsupervised approach based on independent component analysis and a supervised approach using a domain adaptation technique. Both methods are grounded in rigorous mathematical principles. Our approaches outperform existing methods across multiple datasets. Availability and implementation The implementation of our methods, including all code, datasets, experimental workflows, and supplementary material, is available in Python and has been made publicly accessible on GitHub: https://github.com/shaham-lab/revisiting-batch-effect-removal.

papers.title: LoL-align: sensitive and fast probabilistic protein structure alignment.
papers.authors: Reifenrath L, van Kempen M, Kim G, Kim SH, Radnezhad M, Gilchrist CLM, Mirdita M, Steinegger M, Söding J.
papers.abstract: The ubiquitous availability of protein structures permits replacing sequence alignment with more accurate and sensitive structure alignment algorithms. LoL-align maximizes a local log-odds score for proteins to be homologous, given their intra-protein C α - C α distances. Here we show that LoL-align is markedly more sensitive in detecting remote homologs than TM-align and Dali on single- and multidomain benchmarks and achieves better alignment quality at 5-20 × their speed. LoL-align is fully integrated into Foldseek.

papers.title: MassNet: billion-scale AI-ready mass spectral corpus empowering scalable deep learning in proteomics.
papers.authors: A J, Zhang X, Zhang X, Wei J, Zhang T, Deng Y, Liu P, Nie Z, Yu Y, Chen Y, Dong N, Gao Z, Sun S, Guo T.
papers.abstract: Here we present MassNet, inspired by large-scale data corpora of text and images; MassNet is an artificial intelligence (AI)-ready data corpus for mass spectrometry (MS)-based proteomics. The corpus contains 1.5 billion tandem MS spectra from high-quality data-dependent acquisition (DDA) MS data across 35 species. Approximately 1.7 million peptide precursors are from human samples. We further present an AI-ready DDA data format called Mass Spectrometry DDA Tensor (MSDT) for compact and standardized storage, curation and reuse of data from multiple sources, which can be optionally converted to a Lightning Memory-Mapped Database for accelerated input/output in deep learning. On the basis of MassNet, we develop XuanjiNovo, a nonautoregressive transformer model that leverages a curriculum learning strategy for de novo peptide sequencing. XuanjiNovo achieves 38.35-143.57% improvement over state-of-the-art methods on human Astral data. MassNet also supports additional downstream tasks, including retention time prediction and PSM rescoring. MassNet represents a foundational MS-based proteomics data resource, marking a critical milestone for AI proteomics research.

papers.title: Microenvironment awareness pragmatic analysis for generative enzyme function reasoning.
papers.authors: Hao J, Yan K, Liu B.
papers.abstract: Motivation Accurate enzyme function annotation is critical for interpreting rapidly expanding sequence data, yet experimental methods are costly and low-throughput, while computational approaches face two key limitations. Most existing methods are discriminative models confined to known EC labels, making it difficult to generalize to emerging enzymatic activities under cold-start conditions. Moreover, they typically treat enzymes as isolated molecular entities and overlook microenvironment factors such as optimal pH and temperature, which provide important contextual clues for functional annotation. Results This study proposes Microenvironment awareness pragmatic analysis for generative enzyme function reasoning, a generative framework that integrates microenvironment as pragmatic context into enzyme function reasoning. By fine-tuning the large language model on a newly constructed Enzyme Microenvironment Database, the model learns to infer microenvironment from sequence and then reason function within that context, generating EC labels with explicit reasoning chains. Multi-task enzyme microenvironment prediction imputes missing pH and temperature values to complete the Enzyme Microenvironment Database. On public benchmark dataset, Microenvironment Awareness Pragmatic Analysis for Generative Enzyme Function Reasoning achieves an absolute F1 improvement of 0.1068 over the state-of-the-art GraphEC model. Under cold-start conditions, the model generates reference-worthy function labels, demonstrating its practical utility for emerging enzymatic activities. Availability and implementation The source code and data of MPA-EC can be accessed at https://bliulab.net/MPA-EC, https://zenodo.org/records/22152329 and https://github.com/bliulab/MPA-EC.

papers.title: Near-infrared photochromic miniprotein enables photoacoustic molecular imaging of acute inflammation and intracellular antigens.
papers.authors: Oliinyk OS, Xu Y, Luo J, Tokarchuk KO, Manoilov KY, van de Klashorst J, Eyring MP, Wang ME, Chen M, Song P, Hickey JW, Yao J, Verkhusha VV.
papers.abstract: Using near-infrared photoswitchable photochromic genetically encoded probes, differential photoacoustic tomography (PAT) enables deep-tissue imaging with high resolution and sensitivity; however, current bacteriophytochrome-based probes are bulky multidomain proteins exceeding 55 kDa, which constrains their use for designing PAT molecular reporters. Here we engineer rsmiRFPnano, a compact cyanobacteriochrome-derived photoswitchable PAT probe. With a molecular weight below 19 kDa, rsmiRFPnano efficiently incorporates biliverdin, exhibits high extinction coefficients in both photochromic states and demonstrates robust performance in live cells. We established rsmiRFPnano-based reporters for NF-κB and AP-1 pathways, which display low basal activity and strong activation-dependent responses. These reporters effectively visualized acute inflammation using noninvasive PAT in vivo, further validated through cellular-level spatial omics mapping. We then created photoswitchable nanobody probes, rsNIR-Fbs, stabilized upon antigen binding and rapidly degraded otherwise, enabling selective photoacoustic immuno-imaging of intracellular antigens in vivo. Together, these results establish rsmiRFPnano as an ultracompact and versatile platform for molecular PAT.

papers.title: Reconstruction of contact signals from repeated elements with Hicberg.
papers.authors: Gradit S, Ortion S, Larrous P, Delouis M, Koszul R, Cournac A.
papers.abstract: Throughout evolution, genomes have acquired various repetitive elements, such as transposons, ribosomal DNA, duplicated genes, and tandem repeats. These sequences pose significant challenges to current high-throughput sequencing pipelines, which generate short reads that cannot be unambiguously mapped to reference genomes. We present an innovative algorithm, Hicberg, designed to leverage reads typically discarded by standard pipelines. Hicberg employs statistical inference coupled with probability distribution computation to accurately infer missing 3D contacts of repetitive elements within a genome from paired omic data, such as Hi-C data. Our results demonstrate that Hicberg provides new insights into the potential impact of repetitive elements on the spatial organization of genomes. Notably, we observed the positioning of molecular motors that create chromosomal loops associated with certain transposons in yeast. These findings underscore the importance of an integrative approach to better understand genomic complexity and pave the way for deeper explorations of repeated elements.

papers.title: The divergent 3D genome landscapes of aging and neurodegenerative mouse models.
papers.authors: Kashuk E, Smirnov D, Eremenko E, Tsitrina A, Kriukov D, Golova A, Kaluski-Kopatch S, Khrameeva E, Toiber D.
papers.abstract: Chromatin structure is essential for gene regulation and genome stability, as neurons must preserve their 3D genome organization throughout life. This structure gradually deteriorates with aging and is further disrupted in neurodegenerative diseases. To investigate whether aging and neurodegeneration share early chromatin changes or diverge, we perform Hi-C on cortical neurons from adult, aged, and brain-specific SIRT6 -knockout (S6-KO) mice and compare them to the previously published Hi-C data sets from a CK-p25 Alzheimer's disease model stratified by γH2AX levels. All models show early features such as weakened interactions between chromosomes in expanded nuclei, A- to B-compartment shifts, and loss of architectural loops. However, aged neurons retain TAD prominence, short-range interactions, and enhancer-promoter loops, whereas pathological models showed reduced TAD prominence, shorter loops, and disorganized A-B mixing. These changes correlate with increased DNA damage. Our findings suggest that aging represents a "primed" state, in which chromatin regulation begins to erode, but further stressors like DNA damage are associated with progression toward neurodegenerative breakdown.

papers.title: Identity-by-descent captures shared environmental factors at biobank scale.
papers.authors: Marsico F, Buonaiuto S, Amos-Abanyie EK, Chinthala LK, Mohammed A, Zahr R, Regeneron Genetics Center, Rooney RJ, Williams RW, Davis RL, Finkel TH, Brown CW, Vacca M, Prins P, Colonna V.
papers.abstract: Genealogical ties leave traces beyond shared genetic material: relatives tend to share environmental exposures and cultural practices that persist across generations. Here, using genomic and electronic health record data from 13,143 individuals in the Biorepository and Integrative Genomics, we apply a hierarchical community detection algorithm that groups individuals into four major communities and 17 subcommunities based on the proportion of their genome shared identity-by-descent (IBD). This approach captures a fine-scale demographic structure beyond traditional ancestry classifications. By integrating neighborhood-level geographic data with census-derived environmental metrics, we reveal unequal exposure to environmental stressors between subcommunities, which correlates with differential rates of health conditions, including elevated respiratory condition prevalence in subcommunities under greater pollution burden. Through an interventional mediation analysis we find that a substantial part of the excess subcommunity-level risk remains unexplained by measured environmental factors alone, consistent with a contribution of unmeasured shared exposures captured by IBD-based grouping. Subcommunity-level disparities persist in sensitivity analyses adjusting for self-reported race, indicating that IBD-based clustering captures health-relevant information beyond demographic categories commonly used as proxies for social determinants of health. We implement an open-source dashboard for interactive exploration of IBD-defined communities, disease prevalence, and environmental exposures. Together, we demonstrate that IBD-based clustering jointly captures genetic and environmental determinants of health, offering a scalable framework for precision health and population genetics that translates biobank data into actionable insights.

papers.title: Micronuclear ecDNA constrains tumor cell fitness and is associated with favorable patient survival.
papers.authors: Brückner L, Xu R, Tang J, Gnanasekar A, Herrmann A, Wong IT, Zhang S, Tu F, Pilon M, Kukalev A, Pardon K, Sidorova O, Atta J, Yu Q, Montuori G, Pradella D, Ilić M, Suina K, Novais-Cruz M, Kaltenbach S, Treue D, Giurgiu-Kraljič M, Herzog S, Hollinger AS, Wittstruck N, Fernandez M, Wolozyn N, Becker F, Louma VR, Yan X, Schmargon R, Dörr JR, Gamlin D, Lehmann A, Gürgen D, Richter M, Dubois F, Simeoni F, Pennycook BR, Hamilton A, Lindemann RK, Dawes C, Balmus G, Hero B, Fischer M, Bafna V, Verhaak R, Wahl G, Liu Y, Koche RP, Papathanasiou S, Medema R, Spanjaard B, Ventura A, Pombo A, Huang W, Scheer M, Werner B, Chang HY, Mischel PS, Henssen AG.
papers.abstract: Extrachromosomal DNA (ecDNA) contributes to cancer genome instability by enabling high-copy oncogene amplification and genetic intratumoral heterogeneity. Micronuclei (MNs) are common in chromosomally unstable cancers, yet their role in ecDNA-driven tumors remains unclear. Here we investigate how ecDNA damage, mitotic segregation and MN formation are linked. We find that ecDNAs are a major source of MNs following their damage, particularly under replication stress. Replication stress promotes mitotic ecDNA clustering, asymmetric inheritance, mis-segregation into MNs and reduced transcriptional output. Single-MN sequencing reveals that multiple distinct ecDNA species coalesce within individual MNs. Cells inheriting ecDNA + MNs display impaired proliferative capacity and are more likely to undergo cell death. In patients with MYCN-amplified neuroblastoma, higher frequencies of ecDNA + MNs at diagnosis are associated with improved overall survival. Together, these findings identify ecDNA mis-segregation as a mechanism that limits tumor fitness, highlighting mitotic ecDNA retention as a potential therapeutic vulnerability.

papers.title: TL-iGeneCombo: transfer learning for individual sample specific gene combination effect prediction and selection in cancer cells.
papers.authors: Gökbağ B, Wang L, Yang C, Shen Y, Zhang P, Cheng L, Li L.
papers.abstract: Motivation Identifying effective gene combinations is critical for developing combinatorial cancer therapies. Synthetic lethality (SL) has been widely used to characterize genetic interactions based on cell viability, but predictive models are often limited by the availability of combinatorial double-knockout (CDKO) data for individual cancer cells. How to borrow information from CDKO experiments in other cancer cells to improve prediction in a targeted cancer cell remains an important challenge. Results We investigated the CDKO effects of paired genes using both SL as an indirect measure and gene combination effect as a direct measure. We developed TL-iGeneCombo, a transfer learning approach, to borrow data from CDKO experiments in other cancer cells for the prediction of SL and gene combination effect in a targeted cancer cell. Applying TL-iGeneCombo improved the accuracy of SL classification by 19% and increased the Spearman correlation of gene combination effect scores by 29%. Using data and models built from the first CDKO experiment in a prostate cancer cell, 22RV1, we further designed gene pairs for a second CDKO experiment in the same cell. It validated the superior prediction of gene combination effect, but not SL prediction. Availability and implementation The software is freely available at https://github.com/BirkanGokbag/TL-iGeneCombo under the GNU General Public License v.3.0.

papers.title: Tangermeme: a toolkit for understanding cis-regulatory logic using deep learning models.
papers.authors: Schreiber J.
papers.abstract: Deep learning models have achieved state-of-the-art performance at predicting diverse genomic modalities, yet their promise for biological discovery lies in how they are used after demonstrating their predictive performance. Here we describe the functionality of tangermeme, a highly optimized toolkit for 'everything-but-the-model' when it comes to genomic deep learning, and demonstrate how tangermeme can be used to distill the learned cis-regulatory patterns from models into human-interpretable insights.

papers.title: Validation and analysis of 12,000 AI-driven CAR-T designs in the Bits to Binders competition.
papers.authors: Kosonocky CW, Abel AM, Feller AL, Cifuentes Rieffer AE, Woolley PR, Lála J, Barth DR, Gardner T, Bits to Binders Competitors, Ekker SC, Ellington AD, Wierson WA, Marcotte EM.
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) methods for proteins have advanced rapidly, improving structure prediction and design, particularly for de novo binders. However, most evaluations emphasize binding affinity rather than higher-order biological function. We present Bits to Binders, a global competition evaluating de novo binder design in the context of chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells. Teams from 42 countries submitted 12,000 designs of 80-amino acid de novo minibinders targeting human CD20 as CAR binding domains. Designs were screened by pooled CAR-T proliferation, identifying 707 designs exhibiting significant CD20-specific enrichment, with team hit rates from 0.6% to 38.4%. Top-performing candidates were validated as individual constructs, measuring CD20-specific proliferation, expansion, cytokine production, and targeted cell lysis. We identified common design methodologies and factors correlated with DNA synthesis, expression, and target-specific T cell activation which nearly double the success rates when applied as a retrospective filter. We release this dataset as an open resource, with practical recommendations to support more effective AI-driven binder design.

papers.title: Accurate and well-powered case-control analysis of spatial molecular data.
papers.authors: Reshef YA, Sood L, Curtis M, Rumker L, Stein DJ, Palshikar MG, Nayar S, Filer A, Jonsson AH, Korsunsky I, Raychaudhuri S.
papers.abstract: As spatial molecular data grow in scope, there is a pressing need to identify disease-associated spatial structures. Current approaches typically make restrictive assumptions such as representing tissue regions by abundances of discrete cell types and samples by abundances of discrete niches; this risks overlooking important signals. Here we introduce variational inference-based microniche analysis (VIMA), a method combining deep learning with principled statistics to discover disease-associated spatial features with greater flexibility and precision. VIMA trains an ensemble of variational autoencoders to summarize the contents of every small tissue patch in a dataset via numeric 'fingerprints'. It uses these to define many data-dependent, overlapping 'microniches' and meta-analyzes them to identify microniches whose abundance correlates significantly with case-control status. We confirm VIMA's calibration, power and spatial accuracy in simulations. We then apply VIMA to spatial datasets spanning three diseases and spatial modalities, recapitulating known biology and identifying new spatial features of disease.

papers.title: Flexible discovery of disease-associated tissue structures.
Imputation of fluid intelligence scores reduces ascertainment bias and increases power for analyses of common and rare variants.
papers.authors: van den Berg DM, Malawsky DS, Huang W, Danecek P, Walter K, Kalantzis G, Wade I, Palmer D, Birney E, Verweij KJH, Smit DJA, Lindsay SJ, Hurles ME, Abdellaoui A, Martin HC.
papers.abstract: Studying the genetics of intelligence provides insight into the neurobiology of cognitive function and rare neurodevelopmental conditions. Here we integrated fluid intelligence (FI) tests across different UK Biobank measures and imputed FI for unmeasured individuals, increasing the sample size from ~270,000 to >455,000. We show through extensive validation that the imputed phenotype genetically resembles measured FI, although some noncognitive signal likely remains. Combining measured and imputed FI increases the number of independent significant common SNP associations from 390 to 550 and reduces the ascertainment bias introduced by FI test participants being, on average, more educated. Rare variant analyses identify 26 significantly associated genes (false discovery rate < 1%), including 8 without strong prior evidence of involvement in intelligence or neurodevelopmental conditions, which replicate in aggregate in external cohorts. Our results demonstrate that imputed intelligence can boost power for genetic discovery and support its use to help discover new neurodevelopmental condition-associated genes.

papers.title: Times are changing but order matters: transferable prediction of small-molecule liquid chromatography retention times.
papers.authors: Kretschmer F, Harrieder EM, Witting M, Böcker S.
papers.abstract: Liquid chromatography is a predominant technology for the separation of small molecules. Hundreds of retention time prediction models have been published over the past decades, yet truly transferable prediction (requiring no training data from the target chromatographic system) remains an open challenge. Unfortunately, retention times may change massively, even for nominally identical chromatographic conditions. Retention order is considerably more conserved; but even retention order may change if chromatographic conditions vary. Here we present 2-step, a two-step method for the prediction of retention times in reversed-phase chromatography. In the first step, a machine-learning model predicts a retention order index, taking into account chromatographic conditions. In the second step, we map predicted indices to absolute retention times. Disentangling these two tasks finally enables transferable retention time prediction across chromatographic conditions and compound classes, without requiring any target-system training data. Our 2-step method outperforms existing methods that were trained on the target dataset. Finally, we systematically study what chromatographic conditions result in notable changes of retention order.

papers.title: Single-cell profiling and genetic regulation of alternative polyadenylation in the human brain.
papers.authors: Nan J, Boix CA, Shi S, Fan X, Ni J, Wang K, Shuai X, Ding K, Wu P, An Y, Sun N, Hou L, Chen K, Huang X, Li C, Akay L, Louderback K, Nawaid H, Park YP, Fu X, Liu C, Li X, Yin Y, Mo W, Yang Z, Ma W, Hu X, Bennett DA, Kellis M, Tsai LH, Sunyaev S, Li J, Xiong X.
papers.abstract: Alternative polyadenylation (APA) has a central role in regulation of the fate of mRNA and exhibits high variability in the brain and in neurons. However, brain APA regulation has not been mapped at cell type resolution, and the genetic control of APA in brain cell types and its contribution to genetic disease have remained unclear. Here we report a single-cell atlas of APA of the aged human brain across 2 million cells from 379 human postmortem brains across individuals with and without Alzheimer's disease (AD). We show that APA provides an independent mechanistic layer for understanding gene regulatory changes in AD, as genes with APA alterations are distinct from those with expression changes but often converge to similar pathways, including microglial activation and microtubule transport in neurons. We integrate APA variation with whole-genome sequencing to identify cell-type-resolved 3' untranslated region quantitative trait loci (3'aQTLs) for 4,288 genes. We find that 3'aQTLs preferentially colocalize with pQTLs over eQTLs. Across 17 brain traits and diseases, we identify 168 GWAS loci dependent on 3'aQTLs, of which only 17.5% are shared with eQTLs. These include PLEKHA1 and APOC2 for AD, PAK6 and AP3B2 for schizophrenia, NDUFA13 for bipolar disorder, MTCH2 for multiple brain traits, and SNCA, the top locus in Parkinson's disease. We show that 3' untranslated region choice alters SNCA mRNA localization within the cell, consistent with the observation that the SNCA risk locus acts in an eQTL-independent manner in neurons and oligodendrocytes. Our results provide a cell-type-specific foundation to interrogate the cis and trans regulation of APA and to understand the contribution to disease heritability of this key post-transcriptional layer.

papers.title: Disease-associated loci share properties with response eQTLs under common environmental exposures.
papers.authors: Lin W, Li M, Allen O, Burnett J, Popp JM, Stephens M, Battle A, Gilad Y.
papers.abstract: Many disease-associated genetic variants likely exert context-dependent regulatory effects that are underrepresented in healthy, steady-state adult tissues. To investigate gene regulation across diverse environmental and cellular contexts, we exposed heterogeneous differentiating cultures from 51 human induced pluripotent stem cell lines to nicotine, caffeine, or ethanol and profiled 1.4 million cells by single-cell RNA sequencing. We identified hundreds of response expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs) across diverse cell types, as well as dynamic regulatory effects that vary along differentiation trajectories. In contrast to baseline steady-state eQTLs and similar to disease risk loci, response eQTLs are enriched in distal enhancers and regulate genes under strong selective constraint, contain complex regulatory landscapes, and display diverse biological functions. Response eQTLs also coincide with disease-associated loci not explained by baseline steady-state eQTLs. These findings indicate that interpreting disease-associated loci will benefit from studying gene-by-environment interactions across diverse biological contexts.

papers.title: Single-cell multiomics across nine mammals reveals cell-type-specific regulatory conservation in the brain.
papers.authors: Anderson AG, Rogers BB, Barinaga EA, Loupe JM, WaMaina E, Johnston SQ, Limbo HL, Gardner EA, Moyer AJ, Gross AL, Martin DR, Thyme SB, Rizzardi LF, Myers RM, Cooper GM, Cochran JN.
papers.abstract: Understanding gene regulation in the brain is essential for defining the genetic basis of neurologic disease. Cis-regulatory elements (CREs) regulate gene expression, but their function and evolution depend on sequence and cis- and trans-regulatory context. We generated single-nucleus RNA- and ATAC-seq data from cortex across nine mammalian species and identified cell-type-specific candidate CREs. We developed a multidimensional conservation framework integrating sequence, chromatin accessibility, and enhancer-gene associations. Massively parallel reporter assays in human neural progenitor cells and neurons measured activity of conserved and human-specific CREs, while CRISPR interference validated enhancer function at conserved loci, including FAM181B. Motif enrichment identified transcription factors distinguishing conserved from evolved CREs. Linkage disequilibrium score regression showed that conserved and human-specific CREs were enriched for neuropsychiatric GWAS risk, whereas neurodegenerative risk was restricted to conserved elements. These findings define functional dimensions of enhancer conservation and reveal how regulatory evolution shapes brain biology and disease susceptibility.

papers.title: Control of ice thickness in cryo-EM via confinement.
papers.authors: Zheng L, Song J, Zhao X, Cao J, Xu J, Wang Z, Zhang C, Sun W, Chen B, Gao X, Liu H, Yang J, Xu Y, Sun L, Dai Z, Wei X, Liu N, Peng H, Wang HW.
papers.abstract: Achieving thin ice with optimal thickness is a prerequisite for successful cryo-EM analysis of embedded macromolecules. Despite decades of effort, precise control of ice thickness in cryo-EM remains a major challenge. Here we reveal that the intrinsic instability of sub-100-nm liquid film, a previously overlooked determinant before vitrification, plays a critical role in controlling ice thickness. We found that well-designed graphene reservoirs can confine liquid film to an optimal thickness and overcome the limitations posed by liquid film instability, achieving precise control of ice thickness with robust reproducibility and large-area uniformity. These graphene reservoirs demonstrate superior liquid retention capabilities than conventional techniques, enabling tunable ice thickness through reservoir depth modulation. Moreover, this approach yields uniform confined ice in graphene sandwiches with controllable thickness and high efficiency, facilitating cryo-EM imaging of a broad range of macromolecule particles with high contrast, reduced motion and improved orientations for more robust high-resolution reconstruction.

papers.title: Genome-wide mapping of common and rare variant effects on adiposity across childhood.
papers.authors: Kentistou KA, Sundfjord J, Karimi R, Kaisinger LR, Hofmeister RJ, Fragoso-Bargas N, Lupu AE, Zhao Y, Tadross JA, Steuernagel L, Dowsett GKC, Lockhart S, Brüning JC, Liu J, Cortes A, Lo Y, Davitte J, Clement L, Havdahl A, Andreassen OA, Bratland E, Lam BYH, O'Rahilly S, Yeo GSH, Njølstad PR, Kutalik Z, Day FR, Vaudel M, Perry JRB, Ong KK, Johansson S.
papers.abstract: Our understanding of the genetic architecture of obesity is primarily based on studies of adults, with sparser data from childhood. Here, we conducted age-stratified genetic association studies against objectively measured (n = 62,276) or recalled childhood adiposity-related traits (n eff = 599,924), identifying 624 common variants associated with childhood adiposity, with one-third having no concordant association with adult body mass index. Signals linked to the leptin-melanocortin pathway (BSX, GNAS, LEPR and PCSK1) and incretin signaling (GIPR and GLP1R) showed childhood-specific effects on adiposity. Single-nucleus RNA sequencing data identified childhood-specific adiposity-regulating cell populations in the arcuate nucleus and mammillary bodies, indicating neurocircuits that regulate adiposity specifically during childhood. Finally, sequencing in 479,615 individuals uncovered rare protein-coding variation in ADCY3, CALCR, MC4R, MRAP2, POMC and MYH13, exhibiting stronger associations in childhood than in adults. Our findings suggest that childhood provides a more sensitive window for the study of key endocrine and neuropeptide pathways that regulate energy balance.

papers.title: Dissecting functional regulatory convergence over 160 million years of therian evolution.
papers.authors: Shukla N, Cook LE, Vespasiani DM, Pask AJ, Gallego Romero I.
papers.abstract: Understanding the molecular mechanisms underpinning convergent traits can provide insight into the predictability of the evolutionary process. The thylacine, an extinct marsupial carnivore, has been long known to have a very similar craniofacial morphology to that of eutherian canids, despite having diverged ≈160 million years ago. Using a massively parallel reporter assay (MPRA), we test the regulatory potential of a set of previously identified highly conserved craniofacial enhancers that showed convergent sequence acceleration in thylacine and wolf (TWARs). We compare orthologous sequences from six different taxa, including outgroup taxa with nonconvergent craniofacial phenotypes (Tasmanian devil and giant panda) and ancestral reconstructions for marsupial and placental carnivores (Dasyuromorphia and Carnivora). Dense 10 bp tiling allowed us to thoroughly examine features associated with activity, including percentage GC content and transcription factor binding motifs turnover. We identify marked conservation of levels and patterns of regulatory activity across all six taxa, as well as multiple cases of differentially active TWARs within each clade, with both thylacine and wolf driving functional divergence. However, evidence of convergent divergence relevant to craniofacial biology is limited to a TWAR with reduced activity in both the thylacine and wolf near the developmental gene LMO4 Ultimately our findings suggest that shared gene regulatory potential is not a feature of these convergently accelerated regions in the thylacine and wolf.

papers.title: Spatial genome organization in nematodes with programmed DNA elimination.
papers.authors: Simmons JR, Xue T, McCord RP, Wang J.
papers.abstract: Programmed DNA elimination (PDE) is a notable exception to genome integrity. In many nematodes, PDE is initiated by DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs), leading to chromosome fragmentation and subsequent DNA loss. However, the mechanism of nematode programmed DNA breakage remains largely unclear. In the human and pig parasitic nematode Ascaris ( Ascaris lumbricoides and Ascaris suum ), no conserved motif or sequence structures are present at chromosomal breakage regions (CBRs), suggesting the recognition of CBRs may be sequence independent. Using Hi-C, we reveal that Ascaris CBRs engage in three-dimensional (3D) interactions before and during PDE, indicating that physical contacts between break regions may contribute to PDE. The 3D interactions are established in both Ascaris male and female germlines, demonstrating inherent genome organization associated with the CBRs and to-be-eliminated sequences. In contrast, in the unichromosomal horse parasite Parascaris univalens , transient pairwise interactions between neighboring CBRs that will form the ends of future somatic chromosomes are observed only during PDE. We find that Ascaris PDE, which converts 24 germline chromosomes into 36 somatic ones, induces specific compartmentalization changes. Parascaris PDE generates the same set of 36 somatic chromosomes, and the 3D compartment changes following PDE are consistent between the two species. Overall, we suggest that CBRs are associated with the boundaries of distinct 3D genome domains. These domains partition the retained and eliminated DNA into separate spatial compartments. We also demonstrate that following PDE, the 3D genome reorganization of the somatic chromosomes in these nematodes is evolutionarily and developmentally conserved.

papers.title: Pre-diagnosis plasma cell-free DNA reveals early signatures of prostate and breast cancer risk up to eight years prior to clinical detection.
papers.authors: Cheng N, Ouellette TW, Skead K, Singhawansa A, Elliott M, Cescon DW, Bratman SV, De Carvalho DD, Soave D, Awadalla P.
papers.abstract: Genome-wide cell-free DNA (cfDNA) methylation profiling of 491 pre-diagnosis breast and prostate cancer plasma samples, some collected up to nine years before diagnosis, identifies early cancer-associated epigenetic alterations and predictive signatures. Differentially methylated regions were enriched in regulatory and repetitive elements and reflected cancer-tissue- and immune-cell-associated DNA methylation patterns. Logistic regression models trained on discovery set samples showed that cfDNA silencer-region methylation robustly predicted future prostate cancer, with high-risk individuals exhibiting a 3.55-fold increased hazard of developing prostate cancer. Enhancer hypermethylation modestly predicted incident breast cancer but strongly distinguished established late-stage breast cancers, with high-risk individuals showing a 2.3-fold increased hazard. These results highlight cfDNA methylation as a promising biomarker for early cancer risk prediction and surveillance.

papers.title: Concentrating cell-type-specific transcriptional signatures in bone marrow from interspecies comparisons.
papers.authors: Wölbert LC, Busa VF, Danson AF, Fernández Torices S, Sood S, Lammers F, Knoch J, Ball M, Fotopoulou F, Rodríguez Correa E, Schneider A, Coraggio F, Kuck A, Del Prete S, Claudino N, Koch ML, Cleland JP, Jayarajan J, Pilz F, Borgers H, Jolly A, Höfer T, Milsom MD, Essers MAG, Odom DT.
papers.abstract: Cell-type definition is commonly achieved using marker genes. Because cell types are broadly conserved across evolution, marker genes are identifiable via interspecies comparisons. We generated single-cell RNA sequencing datasets of bone marrow niche and hematopoietic progenitor compartments from four mouse species. Using these data, we developed a strategy that adds conservation of transcriptional levels to existing approaches that identify marker genes using conserved cell-type specificity. The resulting "signature gene" lists contain both well-known and underexplored bone marrow markers. Signature genes capture cell identities and thus can robustly discern homologous cell types in diverse tissues of evolutionarily distant species. Unbiased benchmarking assessments demonstrated that our signature genes are comparable or superior to larger, less-conserved gene lists. Last, we confirm our framework's versatility and robustness using published datasets from another tissue and mammalian order. Thus, combining conserved cell-type specificity and transcriptional levels is a powerful, widely applicable strategy to distill profoundly descriptive signatures.

papers.title: Nanopore sequencing identifies high-frequency somatic structural variations in laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma genomes.
papers.authors: Liu X, Xia L, Qiao Y, Li Y, Huang Y, Yue B, Liang X, Yang X, Zhang H, Zhang J, Chen X, Xie D, Liu J.
papers.abstract: Laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma (LSCC) is an aggressive cancer associated with poor quality of life. Understanding the somatic mutations in its genome is crucial for elucidating its occurrence and progression. Although somatic structural variations (SVs) have been documented in LSCC, conventional short-read sequencing lacks the sensitivity to effectively detect high-frequency SVs, variants that play a crucial role in tumorigenesis, shared across multiple samples. Here, we present SomaGauss-SV, a somatic SV detection workflow leveraging nanopore long-read sequencing data. Benchmarking against five paired tumor cell line data sets shows SomaGauss-SV consistently achieves a balanced high precision and recall. SomaGauss-SV applied to 15 paired LSCC tumor-blood samples uncovers a comprehensive SV landscape and reveals a significant positive correlation between somatic deletion burden and smoking intensity. Furthermore, a high-frequency somatic simple repeat expansion is identified in 28/39 (71.79%) of LSCC patients, which upregulates the expression of genes TP53BP2 and FBXO28 through spatial proximity. These findings underscore the potential of long-read sequencing and SomaGauss-SV for uncovering recurrent somatic SVs in LSCC, providing valuable resources for biomarker discovery.

papers.title: Uhrf1 loss disrupts CTCF-associated chromatin organization during early mouse embryogenesis.
papers.authors: Kurowski A, Zhu B, Sun Y, Sargunas P, Jain N, Chan A, Hadri L, Shi Y, Walsh MJ, Ma S.
papers.abstract: UHRF1 is a chromatin-binding protein essential for maintaining DNA methylation and histone modification states, yet its integrated role in vivo remains incompletely understood. To define its function, we generated conditional Uhrf1 knockout embryonic stem cells (ESCs) and embryos. Uhrf1⁻ / ⁻ ESCs exhibited near-complete loss of 5mC and 5hmC but maintained pluripotency, whereas Uhrf1-null embryos developed normally until E8.5 and then failed to develop further by E9.5, phenocopying Dnmt1 loss. Single-cell multi-omic (ME-seq) profiling of E8.5 embryos revealed impaired lineage stabilization, widespread hypomethylation, and disrupted chromatin architecture. Uhrf1 loss was associated with altered CTCF-associated chromatin signal, broad remodeling of chromatin contacts, altered cis-regulatory relationships, and reduced predicted BMP-related ligand-receptor communication, particularly within neural crest populations. These findings identify Uhrf1 as a central regulator that tightly couples DNA methylation maintenance to 3D genome organization during gastrulation, thereby, directing early lineage specification and positioning Uhrf1 as a pivotal mediator of epigenetic information transfer during early embryogenesis.

papers.title: Acute priming using elevated fluid viscosity recovers young-like single-cell surveillance behaviors in aged human T cells.
papers.authors: Dance YW, Amitrano A, Macaluso NC, Min C, Thompson LT, Saffron AM, Ge Z, Smith IM, Ezenwanne C, Milcik N, Fennell A, Pyndell KA, Szczesny C, Langdon J, Ursitti JA, Ward CW, Stroka KM, Walston JD, Sun SX, Konstantopoulos K, Phillip JM.
papers.abstract: Aging is a complex biological process often characterized by increased vulnerability to disease, infection, and death. This increased vulnerability is mechanistically linked to a progressive and functional decline of the immune system. In humans, aged T cells lose their ability to effectively surveil complex microenvironments, thereby decreasing their capacity to clear infections, eradicate diseases, and maintain physiological homeostasis. However, specific mechanisms by which aged T cells lose this capacity to surveil remain unclear. Here, we profile three core characteristics of T cell surveillance at single-cell resolution, specifically migration, deformability, and sensing.
