papers.authors: Chen YJ, Chiu YH, Liu CK, Hsu H, Wang KC, Lian GT, Chen YA, Lin SW, Yen HY, Li HW, Chi P.
papers.abstract: Replication fork reversal is a central response to replication stress, yet how a SNF2 translocase coordinates the distinct mechanical steps required for this reaction remains elusive. Here, we define the mechanism by which ZRANB3 catalyzes fork reversal using biochemical, biophysical, and single-molecule approaches. ZRANB3 binds fork DNA as a monomer at the junction, establishing the minimal functional unit required for activity. Mechanistically, ZRANB3 combines ATP-dependent localized duplex opening with ATP-independent strand annealing to facilitate four-way junction formation, followed by directional branch migration that supports long-range fork reversal. Single-molecule fluorescence analyses further demonstrate that monomeric ZRANB3 is sufficient to drive fork reversal. Together, these findings define how ZRANB3 integrates distinct DNA remodeling activities within a single enzyme to catalyze fork reversal.

papers.title: RIFTT: Robust Identification of Fusion genes in Tumor Transcriptomes.
papers.authors: Kerbs P, Latzko L, Mansmann U, Unger K, Greif PA, Vosberg S.
papers.abstract: Background Fusion genes serve as crucial biomarkers for cancer diagnosis, prognosis, and therapy, yet many detection tools lead to high false-positive rates and poor consensus. We developed RIFTT, a pipeline for Robust Identification of Fusion genes in Tumor Transcriptomes which integrates Arriba and FusionCatcher, two state-of-the-art fusion callers, together with novel scoring metrics (Promiscuity Score, Fusion Transcript Score, and Robustness Score). Results Benchmarking on TCGA-LAML, BeatAML, and LL-100 datasets demonstrated RIFTT's ability to reduce the number of candidates by up to 95% compared to single callers. At the same time, it preserves high-confidence events, outperforming both the nf-core/rnafusion pipeline and an Arriba/FusionCatcher consensus approach. RIFTT also identified novel high-evidence candidates, including a previously unreported recurrent fusion in acute myeloid leukemia. Conclusion Packaged in a Singularity container for ease of use across computing environments, RIFTT provides standardized visual and annotated tabular outputs to support downstream analysis in research workflows and clinical molecular diagnostics. RIFTT is freely available at https://github.com/pkerbs/RIFTT .

papers.title: PSHIC reveals allele-specific chromatin organization by phasing-free structural modeling.
papers.authors: Liu W, Wang X, Zhang Y, Pan G, Li S.
papers.abstract: Resolving the distinct 3D chromatin architectures of parental chromosomes is critical for understanding diploid genome function, but many haplotype-resolved Hi-C contact-map methods remain constrained by their reliance on phased single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs). This dependency treats reconstruction as a simple tag-and-sort problem, leading to massive data loss, extreme fragility to phasing errors, and inapplicability in SNP-sparse contexts. We introduce PSHIC, a computational framework that reveals this hidden chromatin organization by employing phasing-free structural modeling, directly from aggregated Hi-C data. PSHIC models chromosomes as continuous manifolds and solves the inverse problem of finding two homolog-specific structures whose combined contacts best explain the observed data. Comprehensive simulations across varying sequencing depths, SNP densities, and phasing error rates demonstrate that PSHIC consistently outperforms established methods, achieving superior accuracy (SCC ≥ 0.987), loop detection (F 1 ≥ 0.952), and structural fidelity (DER ≤ 0.04). Applications to real human and mouse Hi-C datasets show that PSHIC recovers known allele-associated features in X-chromosome inactivation, genomic imprinting, and regulatory networks. Results align with orthogonal experimental approaches including 3D DNA-FISH, 4C-seq, and ChIA-PET. PSHIC democratizes diploid chromatin analysis by enabling robust reconstruction in non-model organisms and other SNP-limited or poorly phased contexts.

papers.title: TransGram for heterogeneity-aware transcriptome reconstruction from long read RNA-Seq data.
papers.authors: Ren Z, Qi J, Han R, Guo S, Li J, Liu M, Li G, Yu T.
papers.abstract: The advancement of long-read RNA sequencing technologies leads to a bright future for transcriptome analysis. Reconstructing alternative isoforms from long-read RNA data is crucial in transcriptomic studies and poses computational challenges. In this research, we study the heterogeneity of current long reads RNA-seq data, and categorize the sequencing data into two types according to the fraction of the alternative splicing events appeared in the extracted reliably supported sub-path of the splicing graph. Leveraging the heterogeneity, we develop TransGram, an algorithm to reconstruct transcriptome from long RNA-seq reads, which employs the traditional assemble strategy to reconstruct the transcript-representing paths within the splicing graph, and incorporates a machine-learning-based model trained on splice graph-derived features to eliminate false positive transcripts. TransGram supports both annotation-free and annotation-guided modes. Comprehensive evaluations across multiple datasets and conditions demonstrate that TransGram consistently outperforms widely used tools StringTie2, IsoQuant, Bambu, and ESPRESSO, in terms of precision and recall.

papers.title: RhoA Y42C drives cell plasticity and PD-1-mediated immune evasion of diffuse gastric cancer.
papers.authors: Ko KP, Kim S, Jang J, Seo Y, Zou G, Zhang J, Jun S, Morrow B, Ajani JA, Park RJ, Lo YH, Curran MA, Hyunki K, Park JI.
papers.abstract: Diffuse gastric cancer (DGC) is an aggressive gastric cancer subtype with a poor prognosis. The RHOA Y42C mutation is recurrent in DGC, but its independent oncogenic role is unclear. Next-Generation Sequencing of 431 DGC cases revealed that most RHOA mutations occurred without CDH1 alterations. Using genetically engineered gastric organoids, we show that Rhoa Y42C , along with Kras G12D and Trp53 loss (RKP), induces DGC, independently of Cdh1 loss. Single-cell and spatial transcriptomics reveal that RKP tumors exhibit mucinous histopathology and a specific lineage trajectory from Aqp5 + cells to Muc1/Muc4 + cells. RKP tumors create an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment where AREG, transactivated by RhoA Y42C-YAP1, causes T cell exhaustion via PD-1 upregulation. Unlike E-cadherin loss-associated DGC, RKP tumors are highly susceptible to PD-1 blockade. Additionally, the RHOA Y42C mutation correlates with PD-1 upregulation in human DGC samples. These findings redefine the oncogenic role of RhoA Y42C, confirming its sufficiency for DGC development and suggesting PD-1 inhibition as a viable therapeutic option for DGC patients carrying this mutation.

papers.title: Physical determinants of reliable RNA-ligand binding prediction revealed by P-RISE.
papers.authors: Li H, Deng Y, Jiang Z, Gu X, Jiang D, Cao D.
papers.abstract: RNA-targeted small-molecule discovery is challenged by the scarcity of experimentally characterized RNA-ligand complexes and by the limited transferability of current computational approaches across chemically diverse systems. Here we present P-RISE, a physics-grounded framework for RNA-ligand binding prediction, and use it to identify the physical determinants underlying reliable performance. Systematic evaluation of force fields, ionic environments, dielectric treatments, and entropy corrections reveals three coupled requirements: preservation of RNA-binding pocket integrity under ion-sensitive conditions; an effective electrostatic error cancellation regime enabled by an elevated internal dielectric constant; and an empirically observed coupling between entropy correction and solvent modeling. Integrating these features, P-RISE provides stable affinity ranking, physics-grounded delineation of its physicochemical applicability domain, accurate metal ion site localization, and improved binding pose discrimination relative to established RNA docking and scoring approaches. Crucially, benchmarking against AlphaFold3 reveals that co-folding models, optimized for structure generation rather than energetic ranking, benefit from an explicit physics-based evaluation layer. Furthermore, diverse machine-learning comparisons demonstrate that purely data-driven methods lack stability and generalization in this data-poor regime. Ultimately, P-RISE provides a mechanistic understanding of RNA-ligand modeling, serving as a principled physical baseline that defines reliable prediction boundaries, and guides future data-driven integration.

papers.title: RNA viruses can exploit self-cleaving ribozymes for translation initiation.
papers.authors: López-Galiano MJ, Rueda O, Chiba S, Forgia M, Navarro B, Cervera A, Babaian A, Di Serio F, Turina M, de la Peña M.
papers.abstract: Small self-cleaving ribozymes are catalytic RNAs discovered in viroid-like agents, which are replicating circular RNAs (circRNAs) postulated as relics of a prebiotic RNA world. In the last decade, however, small ribozymes have also been detected across the tree of life, from bacterial to human genomes, and more recently, in unusual circRNA viruses. Here we report the conserved occurrence of diverse small ribozymes within the linear genomes of typical single- and double-stranded RNA viruses infecting fungi and plants. We identified type I hammerhead ribozymes in the 5'-UTRs of chrysovirids and fusarivirids, displaying self-cleaving activity in vitro and in vivo. Similar hammerhead, as well as hepatitis delta and twister ribozymes, occur in diverse megabirna-, hypo-, fusagra-, toti-, or tombus-like viruses. The ribozymes appear as isolated motifs within the UTRs or as tandem pairs that encompass small RNA segments (186-399 nt) resembling Zetavirus-like sequences. In vivo characterization of the 5'-UTR from a fungal chrysovirus revealed that its RNA self-cleaving activity is essential for protein translation initiation. Analogous experiments in plants with diverse ribozyme motifs confirmed that self-cleaving activity alone can induce cap-independent translation. We conclude that RNA self-cleaving activity, historically linked to the rolling circle replication of viroid-like circRNAs, appears to be co-opted by some linear RNA viruses for translational roles.

papers.title: A multi-center, single-arm, phase 2 trial of dasatinib in T follicular helper cell lymphomas.
papers.authors: Suma S, Sakata-Yanagimoto M, Suehara Y, Ara T, Goto H, Usuki K, Izutsu K, Yamaguchi M, Fukuhara N, Sakaida E, Ohmachi K, Uehara A, Matsue K, Kimura S, Nagai H, Maruyama D, Nishimoto M, Takeuchi K, Nakamura N, Terauchi T, Fujisawa M, Abe Y, Makishima K, Hattori K, Sakamoto T, Kurita N, Nishikii H, Yoshino F, Yoshida K, Hashimoto Y, Kaneta T, Ogawa S, Keino N, Gosho M, Hosokawa H, Steidl C, Hashimoto K, Chiba S.
papers.abstract: T follicular helper cell lymphomas (TFHL) harbor activating T cell receptor (TCR) signaling mutations and epigenetic alterations, such as TET2 mutations. Here, we conduct a multi-center, single-arm, phase 2 trial of the tyrosine kinase inhibitor dasatinib in patients with relapsed/refractory TFHLs (jRCT2031190079). The primary outcome is the overall response rate (ORR) according to CT-based Lugano criteria 2014. Key secondary endpoints include ORR in RHOA-mutated patients and progression-free/overall survival. The main inclusion criteria consist of TFHL diagnosis and relapse following at least 1 prior chemotherapy regimen. Key exclusion criteria encompass central nervous system involvement, history of other malignancies, and receipt of chemotherapy or radiotherapy within 4 weeks. Nineteen patients are enrolled, with 18 receiving dasatinib and 17 evaluable for efficacy. Median age is 73 years, 50% are female, and angioimmunoblastic T cell lymphoma is the predominant subtype (n = 13). Dasatinib yields a 23.5% ORR, below the prespecified 30% endpoint. Treatment-related adverse events occur in 61.1% of patients (n = 11). Patients harboring TCR signaling mutations, especially those with RHOA p.G17V, achieve a 36.4% ORR, whereas no responses are observed in mutation-negative cases. Exploratory single-cell RNA sequencing reveals interferon-γ/tumor necrosis factor-enriched tumor microenvironments and peripheral expansion of cytotoxic T cell clones in responders. Conversely, early progression correlates with a high TET2 mutation burden in non-malignant immune cells, including CD8 + T cell subsets. While the primary outcome is below the prespecified endpoint, our exploratory findings implicate immune dysfunction involving TET2 mutations in limiting the therapeutic benefit of dasatinib.

papers.title: A model of brain function to predict tau across Alzheimer's disease and related disorders.
papers.authors: Corriveau-Lecavalier N, Zhang G, Botha H, Barnard LR, Wiste HJ, Dicks E, Gogineni VR, Lee J, Sintini I, Senjem ML, Schwarz CG, Cogswell PM, Johnson DR, Gunter JL, Kamykowski MG, Graff-Radford J, Ramanan VK, Fields JA, Machulda MM, Stricker NH, Boeve BF, Lowe VJ, Kantarci K, Knopman DS, Whitwell JL, Josephs KA, Petersen RC, Jack CR, Jones DT, or the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative.
papers.abstract: We developed a machine learning framework grounded in a computational model of brain function and FDG-PET imaging to predict Alzheimer's disease (AD)-type tau across AD and related disorders (ADRD). The model was trained on 1088 research participants spanning normal aging and ADRD with FDG-PET and flortaucipir-PET (FTP-PET). Validation was conducted in: (1) a longitudinal subset of the training cohort (n = 215), (2) Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (n = 295), and (3) a heretogeneous clinical cohort (n = 264; n = 28 with FTP-PET). Results showed that the model accurately predicted FTP-PET when applied at the participant-level (R 2 ~ 0.34-0.71). It performed well in clinical scenarios, including classification of low versus high tau stages (79-95% accuracy) and prediction of tau in a heterogeneous clinical cohort without FTP-PET. These findings advance the understanding of the relationship between neurodegeneration and AD-type tau and provide a framework for estimating AD-type tau across ADRD.

papers.title: AI-accelerated scalable synthesis of nanocrystals for cost-effective photovoltaics.
papers.authors: Zhao X, Zhao C, Jin L, Zhang X, Li D, Zhu W, Li H, Li Y, Wu T, Yuan J.
papers.abstract: Metal halide perovskite nanocrystals (PNCs) are promising candidates for next-generation optoelectronics. However, their commercial application necessitates low-cost synthesis and processing methods that surpass conventional lab-scale techniques. To address this, we report a ligand triggered room-temperature injection (LTRI) method that initiates nanocrystal nucleation by tuning precursor reactivity with addition of short-chain octanoic acid (OcA). Subsequently, integrating automation synthesis and machine learning, we further develop an efficient AI-accelerated framework towards fast and target synthesis of the FAPbI 3 (FA: formamidinium) PNCs. Leveraging machine learning modeling, we identify that the critical size and distribution of FAPbI 3 PNCs can be effectively optimized by tuning the feed ratio of OcA to the precursor formamidinium acetate. Furthermore, our LTRI method is fully compatible with flow-synthesis system for scale-up production, enabling a substantial reduction in production cost to US$2.16 g -1 , significantly lower than the widely adopted hot-injection method (US$118.81 g -1 ). For practical application, we achieve a power conversion efficiency of 19.37% in photovoltaic applications with significant enhancement in device stability, matching the highest reported results for nanocrystal-based solar cells.

papers.title: Embryonic origin of cancer in newborn twins.
papers.authors: Walkowiak B, Baskind S, Dave M, Balasubramanian P, Anderson N, Kennedy J, Oliver TRW, Verma R, Depani S, Hannam S, Watson T, Rampling D, Straathof K, Palm L, Hutchinson JC, Lee-Six H, Slater O, Behjati S.
papers.abstract: Studying monozygotic twins who present with identical cancers informs on the developmental origins of childhood tumours. Here, we perform whole genome sequencing on multiple tumour, normal, and placental samples to reconstruct the phylogeny of a soft tissue cancer that spread in utero between monozygotic twins. We demonstrate the origin of the tumour from one twin and time its diversification and transplacental spread to the other twin, showing that the spread occurred only once. This generalisable and scalable approach additionally allows us to dissect the earliest stages of twinning, revealing unexpected asymmetrical contributions of embryonic lineages to the placenta and each twin and challenging the classical model of twinning.

papers.title: Region-specific generation and retention of acetylated cohesin shape the genome-wide pattern of sister chromatid cohesion.
papers.authors: Shimizu MI, Bando M, Yoshimura A, Sakata T, Nishiyama T, Shirahige K, Sutani T.
papers.abstract: Sister chromatid cohesion depends on ESCO2-mediated acetylation of the cohesin subunit SMC3, yet how this modification is established and maintained across the genome remains poorly understood. Here, we examined the chromatin-binding dynamics of ESCO2 and its enzymatic activity using quantitative ChIP-seq of human cells synchronously progressing through S phase. ESCO2 bound broadly along chromosomes without forming discrete peaks and preferentially localized to transcriptionally inactive regions, but was not confined to H3K9me3- or H3K27me3-enriched heterochromatin. Consistent with this binding pattern, ESCO2-dependent SMC3 acetylation showed a similarly broad distribution in these regions. In contrast, ESCO1, a paralog of ESCO2, primarily mediated SMC3 acetylation at cohesin peak sites. Notably, most of the broadly distributed, ESCO2-dependent SMC3 acetylation generated during S phase was progressively lost from chromatin after replication, whereas the fraction that persisted into late G2 accumulated in domains enriched for the repressive H3K27me3 modification. Our work identifies selective post-replicative retention of acetylated cohesin as a previously unappreciated step in shaping the genome-wide architecture of sister chromatid cohesion.

papers.title: Integrator complex removes lesion-stalled RNA polymerase II after transcription-coupled repair to facilitate transcription restart.
papers.authors: Blom CMA, Gómez-Vázquez E, van Sluis M, Marteijn JA.
papers.abstract: Gene transcription by RNA Polymerase II (Pol II) is highly vulnerable to transcription-blocking DNA lesions (TBLs), which, if unresolved, induce transcription stress leading to cellular decline and aging. TBLs are removed by transcription-coupled nucleotide excision repair (TC-NER). TC-NER is initiated when Cockayne syndrome group B protein recognizes lesion-stalled Pol II and promotes TC-NER complex assembly. This complex recruits TFIIH for lesion verification, followed by incision and repair to enable transcription restart. Many TBLs stall Pol II within its active site, shielding the lesion from repair and requiring Pol II processing to expose it. However, whether this occurs through Pol II backtracking or release from the DNA, and the regulatory mechanisms involved, remain poorly defined. Here, we identified the Integrator complex as a key factor in lesion-stalled Pol II processing. Interaction proteomics revealed Integrator recruitment to late-stage TC-NER complexes. Integrator's endonuclease core promotes efficient transcription recovery after TBL induction, without affecting lesion removal by TC-NER. Live-cell imaging and chromatin retention assays demonstrated that Integrator facilitates Pol II release from DNA following TC-NER. Collectively, these findings support a two-step mechanism for Pol II clearance during TC-NER, wherein TFIIH-mediated backtracking exposes the lesion for repair, followed by Integrator-mediated Pol II release to restore transcription.

papers.title: Queuosine-modification dependent histidyl tRNA fragment promotes cell-type dependent proliferation.
papers.authors: Zhang W, Chew BJ, Matuszek Z, Huang S, Frietze LR, Tran HAV, Katanski CD, Foo M, Dai Q, Pan T.
papers.abstract: tRNA fragments (tRFs) are natural, small non-coding RNAs produced by endogenous ribonucleolytic cleavage of tRNAs. tRFs play a role in many biological pathways, including regulation of cell proliferation. Specific tRNA modifications affect tRF biogenesis. Queuosine (Q) modification occurs at the wobble anticodon nucleotide of 4 mammalian tRNAs and protects these tRNAs from fragmentation. Here, we investigated cell-type and tRNA Q-modification dependencies on mammalian cell proliferation. We found that Q-modified tRNA can either increase, decrease, or make no difference in proliferation. Proliferation decreased in MCF7, a breast cancer cell line, when tRNAs were Q-modified and dependent on the modification enzyme complex, QTRT1/2. MCF7 proliferation increases upon the transfection of Q-modification-dependent tRFHis or decreases upon knockdown of endogenous tRFHis. Consistent with Q-dependent proliferation reduction, polysome profiling showed decreased translation efficiency of ribosomal proteins. Finally, protein pull-down of MCF7 lysates using tRFHis identified Musashi RNA-binding protein 2 (Msi2) as a tRFHis-binding protein. Msi2 knockdown reduced the Q-modification-dependent or tRFHis dependent cell proliferation effect. Our results illustrate a highly cell-type-dependent proliferation effect of tRNA Q-modification, suggesting multi-faceted mechanisms in studying this ubiquitous tRNA modification.

papers.title: PoolParty: streamlined design of DNA sequence libraries in Python.
papers.authors: Liu Z, Cordero A, Kinney JB.
papers.abstract: Background Computationally designed DNA sequence libraries are essential components of massively parallel reporter assays (MPRAs), deep mutational scanning (DMS) experiments, and other multiplex assays of variant effect (MAVEs). They are also increasingly used in silico to analyze genomic AI models. Designing these libraries, however, remains tedious and error-prone due to the scarcity of purpose-built software. Results Here we describe PoolParty, a Python package that streamlines the design of complex oligo pools using a simple but flexible API. In PoolParty, each library is represented by a computational graph that can be specified in just a few lines of code. Over 50 built-in operations cover nucleotide- and codon-level mutagenesis, motif insertion, barcode generation, and more. PoolParty automatically generates informative names for each sequence and provides "design cards" detailing how each sequence was generated. Visualization methods let users quickly audit library content and inspect the underlying graph. PoolParty thus transforms oligo pool design from a tedious task requiring custom functions and scripts into a structured, transparent, and reproducible process. Conclusions PoolParty streamlines the design of DMS, MPRA, and other multiplex assay libraries, and the design cards it provides can help researchers systematically probe and interpret genomic AI models. PoolParty can also be extended to support new assays and analysis strategies as they emerge.

papers.title: A multimeric pore complex in the poxvirus core revealed by integrative structural analysis.
papers.authors: Liu J, Schäfer S, Lehnung S, Baumann LM, Mühlberg L, Steiner C, Schreiber M, Linder M, Welsch S, Liu F, Bogdanow B, Krijnse Locker J, Turoňová B.
papers.abstract: It has long been known that poxviruses transcribe more than a hundred early mRNAs within their viral core, yet how these transcripts exit the core remains unknown. Here, we combine cryo-electron tomography with deep-learning-based particle picking, subtomogram averaging, cross-linking mass spectrometry, and AlphaFold3 modeling to resolve the molecular architecture of a long-sought pore within the poxvirus core. The pore is formed by a heteromeric assembly of the viral proteins E8, E6, and L3, which together create a hollow hexameric tube spanning both the core wall and the surface-exposed palisade layer. Within the pore channel, we observe a rod-like density consistent with the viral RNA helicase I8, which may contribute to the release of the newly synthesized viral mRNAs from the core. We further observe a state of the pore lacking the outer and basal rings under transcription conditions. Together, our findings identify the structure and dynamics of a candidate mRNA-release pore within the surface layer of a double-stranded DNA virus and suggest that it may form part of the poxvirus transcription machinery.

papers.title: Genomic surveillance meets clinical practice: rule-based individualized treatment prediction for gonorrhoea using SensiTyper.
papers.authors: Golparian D, Sánchez-Busó L, Unemo M.
papers.abstract: Extensively drug-resistant (XDR) Neisseria gonorrhoeae strains threaten the current empirical gonorrhoea treatment. We designed and analytically validated SensiTyper, a rule-based framework that predicts antimicrobial susceptibility from whole-genome sequencing data and generates susceptibility-guided individualized treatment recommendations. SensiTyper was applied to 13,701 gonococcal genomes from 68 countries in 1928-2024, including cultured isolates and clinical molecular samples, and benchmarked predictions against previous genomic and phenotypic data. Susceptibility predictions for ceftriaxone, ciprofloxacin, spectinomycin, and zoliflodacin had 98.9-100% sensitivity and specificity. Azithromycin susceptibility predictions had 92.5% sensitivity and 97.1% specificity, and gepotidacin susceptibility prediction 100% sensitivity, but 0% specificity, illustrating that low-level phenotypic gepotidacin resistance is not caused by the only known resistance determinants (GyrA A92T plus ParC D86N). The SensiTreat module integrates antimicrobial susceptibility profiles into sequential treatment logic, providing susceptibility-guided individualized treatment recommendations while also enabling alternative stewardship strategies prioritizing, e.g., ciprofloxacin. SensiTyper flags XDR isolates for expert follow-up, test-of-cure and comprehensive contact tracing. In conclusion, SensiTyper is a robust and adaptable approach for gonococcal antimicrobial susceptibility prediction, individualized gonorrhoea treatment and antimicrobial stewardship.

papers.title: Enzymes can activate and mobilize dense biomolecular condensates across scales.
papers.authors: Dindo M, Metson J, Ren W, Chatzittofi M, Yagi K, Bevilacqua A, Fukuhara E, Sugita Y, Golestanian R, Laurino P.
papers.abstract: Biomolecular condensates have so far been studied in terms of their structural, compositional, and functional properties. However, condensate enzymatic activity - a key aspect of cellular metabolism - remains unexplored due to the complexity of the system. In this study, using a combination of experimental, computational and theoretical techniques, we have discovered that the non-equilibrium activity which originates from catalytic reactions couples with the environment through various feedback mechanisms across five orders of magnitude of length scales. We observe that condensed enzymes catalyze more rapidly in the presence of crowding proteins and show that the increased enzymatic activity within these droplets stems from the emergence of lower-energy protein conformations induced by the highly crowded environment. Despite the crowding in the environment of the droplet, which might suggest an effective increase in its overall viscosity, we find that it becomes more agile, as evidenced by the observation of enhanced diffusion and macroscopic flow, due to the enzymatic activity. These findings shed light on the dynamic interplay between enzymatic activity, composition and crowding in condensates, and their roles on the mobility and accessibility of various functional units in these environments, expanding our understanding of liquid-liquid phase separation in metabolically active conditions.

papers.title: Degeneracy in neuronal bifurcation landscapes: Equivalent bifurcation sequences across distinct parameter sets.
papers.authors: Cafaro G, Bernard C, Hashemi M, Depannemaecker D.
papers.abstract: Degeneracy, the capacity of structurally distinct systems to achieve similar functions, is a fundamental property of living organisms, enabling adaptability and resilience. Neurons can maintain stable activity patterns despite substantial variability in ion channel expression, highlighting how different intrinsic configurations can produce equivalent electrophysiological behaviors. Previous studies have shown that neuronal activity emerges from the interaction between intrinsic membrane properties and ionic concentration dynamics. However, how degeneracy is organized within the dynamical landscape of neurons and how different degenerate configurations respond to external perturbations remain poorly understood. Here, we investigate how distinct biophysical parameter sets generate equivalent bifurcation sequences and how their resilience changes under ionic modulation. Using a minimal neuron model with three variable conductances, we systematically explore how variations in extracellular potassium concentration, representing physiological and pathological conditions, reshape neuronal dynamics. We show that distinct conductance configurations occupy structured regions of parameter space that support the same bifurcation pathways, leading to equivalent activity regimes such as bursting, seizure-like activity, and depolarization block. However, these degenerate configurations exhibit different sensitivities to extracellular perturbations, revealing that functional equivalence under fixed conditions does not imply equivalent robustness. To quantify this effect, we introduce resilience as a measure of the threshold at which a given conductance configuration transitions into a specific activity regime under external ionic changes. Our results demonstrate that degeneracy extends beyond the coexistence of multiple solutions: degenerate configurations form structured landscapes with distinct trajectories under environmental modulation. This framework provides a quantitative approach to investigate how intrinsic variability influences neuronal vulnerability and resilience across different dynamical states.

papers.title: ATP-independent entropy-driven dsRNA unwinding by DDX3X revealed by coarse-grained simulations and deep learning.
papers.authors: Wang K, Ren CL, Ma YQ.
papers.abstract: DEAD-box RNA helicases (DDXs) are traditionally known as ATP-dependent motors that unwind double-stranded RNA (dsRNA). Recent experiments, however, show that some DDXs promote dsRNA unwinding even in the absence of ATP, raising a fundamental question about the physical mechanism underlying ATP-independent strand separation. Here, we develop a minimal, physics-based coarse-grained RNA model and incorporate weak, specific interactions between DDX3X and dsRNA, revealing the inherently stochastic nature of unwinding events. The unwinding process must overcome an energy barrier, but thermal fluctuations and entropy gain provide a driving force for RNA remodeling. We identify that dsRNA separation proceeds through rare yet obligatory strand-displacing intermediates facilitated by DDX3X. By combining deep learning-assisted analysis, we further rank the contributions of different entropic components, revealing hydrogen bonding as the dominant factor, followed by base stacking and then the backbone conformation. These findings reveal a previously unrecognized physical mechanism for RNA duplex unwinding and offer an effective framework for studying RNA remodeling kinetics.

papers.title: Coupled beta and high-frequency oscillations emerge from synchronized bursting in a minimal model of the parkinsonian subthalamic nucleus.
papers.authors: Sheheitli H, Johnson LA, Wang J, Aman JE, Vitek JL.
papers.abstract: Local field potentials (LFPs) recorded from the subthalamic nucleus (STN) in Parkinson's disease (PD) exhibit a distinctive multiscale spectral signature: exaggerated beta-band oscillations (13-30 Hz) coupled to high-frequency oscillations (HFOs, 200-400 Hz), with HFO amplitude being phase-locked to the beta cycle. This phase-amplitude coupling (PAC) has been identified as a promising biomarker of the parkinsonian state, yet no biophysical model has explained how it emerges, what determines the HFO frequency, or how HFOs can exist without beta modulation in the medicated STN. Here we show that a heterogeneous population of excitatory Izhikevich neurons with recurrent coupling produces three dynamical regimes: (i) asynchronous tonic firing, (ii) asynchronous bursting, in which neurons burst individually producing broadband HFO power but without coherent population-level PAC, and (iii) synchronous bursting, which gives rise to beta-HFO PAC. The regimes are governed by two biophysically interpretable parameters that capture complementary effects of dopamine depletion: one reflecting changes in intrinsic neuronal excitability, the other reflecting changes in synaptic coupling strength. The transition from asynchronous to synchronous bursting in this model emulates the emergence of pathological STN neuronal activity in the parkinsonian state. HFO peak frequency varies continuously across the two-parameter landscape, suggesting a possible mechanism of the clinically observed shift from slow (200-300 Hz) to fast (300-400 Hz) HFOs between medication states. The character of the synchronization transition depends on baseline excitability, ranging from a sharp co-emergence of bursting and synchrony at low excitability to a decoupled transition at intermediate excitability, where the bursting fraction saturates while the population synchronization continues to increase with coupling. The asynchronous-to-synchronous bursting transition and the beta-HFO PAC in the STN population also arise in an extended version of the model with reciprocal coupling to an inhibitory population of globus pallidus externa (GPe)-like neurons, with the beta frequency varying with the delay in the synaptic coupling between the two populations. The model generates testable predictions for future clinical and experimental studies, provides a numerical dissection of how mesoscopic LFP features could map onto microscopic neuronal dynamics, and serves as a computational building block for future circuit-level models that may inform brain stimulation strategies tailored to the patient-specific dynamical state of the STN.

papers.title: Interpretable embeddings of speech explain and enhance the brain encoding performance of audio models.
papers.authors: Shimizu R, Antonello RJ, Singh C, Mesgarani N.
papers.abstract: Speech foundation models (SFMs) are increasingly hailed as powerful computational models of human speech perception. However, since their representations are inherently black-box, it remains unclear what drives their alignment with brain responses. To remedy this, we built linear encoding models from six interpretable feature families: mel-spectrogram, Gabor filter bank features, speech presence, phonetic, syntactic, and semantic features, and contextualized embeddings from three state-of-the-art SFMs (Whisper, HuBERT, WavLM), quantifying electrocorticography (ECoG) response variance shared between feature classes. Variance-partitioning analyses revealed several key insights: First, the SFMs' alignment with the brain can be mostly accounted for by their ability to learn and encode simple interpretable speech features. Second, SFMs exhibit a systematic trade-off between encoding of brain-relevant low-level and high-level features across layers. Finally, our results show that SFMs learn brain-relevant semantics which cannot be accounted for by lower-level speech features, with this capacity increasing with model size and context length. Together, our findings suggest a principled approach to build more interpretable, accurate, and efficient encoding models of the brain by augmenting SFM embeddings with interpretable features.

papers.title: Ten simple rules for teaching practical AI to health data teams.
papers.authors: Just E, Tan AC.
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has rapidly entered the healthcare discourse, often framed through the lens of frontier models, generative systems, and transformative potential. Yet for many healthcare data teams, the practical path from curiosity to capability remains unclear. Concerns about data privacy, regulatory compliance, brittle systems, and misaligned expectations frequently stall progress before meaningful experimentation can begin. This paper presents ten simple rules for teaching practical AI to healthcare data teams, grounded in real-world data, privacy-first experimentation, and system-level thinking. Drawing on hands-on training experiences and existing educational and methodological literature, we argue that AI education in healthcare must prioritize workflows over models, systems over components, and institutional capability over isolated technical success. These rules are intended to help educators and organizational leaders move teams beyond the AI hype cycle toward building trustworthy, sustainable, and context-aware AI systems that matter.

papers.title: Data analysis of experimentally solved nucleosome arrays reveals heterogeneous features.
papers.authors: Portillo-Ledesma S, Li Z, Franowicz E, Schlick T.
papers.abstract: Atomic-resolution nucleosome array structures have provided invaluable information on eukaryotic genome packing. Although these arrays are often obtained for regular fibers with designed sequences, such information complements in vivo genome organization data and modeling studies. Here, we analyze such systems with a focus on chromatin organization. We highlight both robust and unique features, as well as suitable average values for coarse-grained modeling, such as the relative orientation and positioning of neighboring nucleosomes, and opening of the linker DNA. Our associated web resource (https://www.biomath.nyu.edu/chromstruct/) shares these collected systems and provides tools for their analysis. The heterogeneous features exhibit a wide range of geometrical properties that depend on linker DNA length, core histone protein variants, auxiliary protein binding, and fiber interdigitation. Yet experimental fiber geometries can be reproduced reasonably using average parameters, as demonstrated here by simulations with our mesoscale model for regular fibers and as reported separately for life-like systems with epigenetic marks. Such analysis may also be useful for modular design of chromatin fibers. The structural characterization of these chromatin building blocks provides new insights into the regulation of chromatin architecture and has implications for the modular design of chromatin fibers.

papers.title: Dynamic phosphorylation of TCOF1 controlled by CK2 and PPM1D regulates nucleolar condensation and RNA polymerase I activity.
papers.authors: Palkova N, Palek M, Brodinova M, Chalupova Z, Storchova R, Jasprova J, Talacko P, Cmarko D, Macurek L.
papers.abstract: The nucleolus is a membrane-less organelle essential for ribosomal DNA (rDNA) transcription and ribosome biogenesis, yet the mechanisms regulating its dynamic assembly remain incompletely understood. Here, we identify the phosphatase protein phosphatase magnesium-dependent 1 delta (PPM1D) as a key regulator of the nucleolar architecture via dephosphorylation of the scaffold protein TCOF1. By combining super-resolution microscopy and domain mapping, we show that PPM1D localizes to the nucleolus through a conserved motif at the C-terminus. Phosphoproteomic analysis and structural modeling revealed that PPM1D targets casein kinase 2 (CK2)-phosphorylated sites within the low-complexity repeat domain of TCOF1, which impacts its interaction with RNA polymerase I (Pol I), immobilization in the fibrillar centres, and nucleolar condensation. Disruption of the phosphorylation balance by loss of PPM1D or inhibition of CK2 leads to nucleolar disorganization and reduced rDNA transcription. Finally, we demonstrate that pharmacological inhibition of PPM1D sensitizes cells to RNA Pol I inhibitors, in both p53-dependent and -independent contexts. Together, we uncover a reversible phosphorylation switch that governs TCOF1 dynamics and its nucleolar function, with potential implications for targeting ribosome biogenesis in cancer.

papers.title: The HELLS-MCM5 axis coordinates transcription-replication dynamics to preserve genomic integrity in ALK-negative anaplastic large cell lymphoma.
papers.authors: Mallia S, Gambarelli G, Vitale E, Manicardi V, Salviato E, Chiaro PD, Vezzani R, Donati B, Torricelli F, Zanelli M, Tameni A, Tamagnini I, Puccio N, Neri A, Ciarrocchi A, Fragliasso V.
papers.abstract: The chromatin remodeler HELLS acts as a pleiotropic guardian of genomic integrity, orchestrating critical processes from DNA replication to DNA damage repair. In anaplastic large cell lymphoma (ALCL), HELLS functions as a transcriptional sentinel, fine-tuning chromatin accessibility and RNA polymerase II kinetics to sustain the oncogenic transcriptional landscape essential for lymphomagenesis. Here we show that HELLS preserves genomic stability and sustains ALK-negative ALCL proliferation by preventing transcription-replication conflicts. HELLS acts as a global regulator of R-loop homeostasis while transcriptionally sustaining MCM5, a core subunit of the replicative MCM2-7 complex, which locally restrains replication-transcription collisions at actively transcribed loci. Mechanistically, HELLS loss reduces MCM5 levels, triggering aberrant firing of origins within transcriptionally active regions and consequent collisions between replication forks and the transcription machinery. Being positioned distally from R-loop-enriched sites, HELLS and MCM5 cooperate to preserve genome integrity, with MCM5 acting as the effector that delivers locus-specific protection against replication-associated genomic instability. Pharmacological or genetic disruption of this axis increases R-loop burden and drastically reduces the survival of ALK-negative ALCL cells, providing a rationale for combination therapy. Collectively, the HELLS-MCM5 module emerges as a master coordinator of transcription-replication dynamics and a novel therapeutic vulnerability in aggressive lymphomas.

papers.title: Structural probing of RNA hairpins quantifies protein occupancy on RNA and links it to function in human cells.
papers.authors: Thurm AR, Nguyen TH, Torres Campos JD, Mansfield M, Bintu L, Hagler LD.
papers.abstract: RNA structures that form inside living cells govern processes ranging from translation to RNA decay, many of which are controlled by RNA-binding proteins (RBPs). Because RBP specificity can depend on both RNA sequence and folding, traditional pulldown-based methods often obscure the structural context of bound RNAs. Here, a quantitative framework based on dimethyl sulfate mutational profiling and sequencing was established to directly measure RNA structure and RBP binding in human cells at single-nucleotide resolution. Applied to a 1600-member MS2 hairpin library, this approach revealed that RNA folding is the strongest determinant of MS2 coat protein (MCP) recognition in the MS2-MCP system, requiring formation of a stable hairpin and a consensus loop sequence, with stem length or GC content contributing primarily through their effect on hairpin folding. An in-cell occupancy model was derived to quantify fractional binding from structural readouts. Complementary systems using degron-tuned MCP and a downregulatory MCP fusion demonstrated binding behavior under subsaturating protein concentrations and showed that inferred occupancy quantitatively predicts RNA degradation efficiency. Together, these results establish a quantitative strategy for measuring RBP-RNA specificity and affinity directly in cells, using the MS2-MCP system to link RNA structure, protein occupancy, and regulatory outcome.

papers.title: XYcellAtlas: a cell-type- and spatial-resolved pan-cancer atlas of sex-biased and Y chromosome loss-associated molecular signatures.
papers.authors: Fan T, Shi X, Zhang L, Shi L, Lv W, Zhu Z, Tan J, Zhang L, Teng H, Sun Z.
papers.abstract: Sex is a critical determinant of cancer susceptibility, clinical prognosis, and therapeutic response. Sex chromosome aberrations, particularly somatic loss of the Y chromosome (LOY) in male malignancies, exert profound impacts on transcriptional regulation, tumor immune microenvironment remodeling, and malignant progression, highlighting an urgent demand for comprehensive integration of single-cell and spatial omics profiles dissecting sex-biased and LOY landscapes across human cancers. Here, we developed XYcellAtlas (http://www.xycellatlas.top/), an integrative database for integration and multidimensional visualization of sex disparities and LOY features across human tissues at single-cell transcriptomic, epigenomic, and spatial-transcriptomic resolutions. This resource aggregates data from 6764 patient samples covering 18 cancer types, eight precancerous lesions, and 21 tissue origins, encompassing over 25.8 million single cells and one million spatial-transcriptomic spots. Leveraging random forest classifiers trained on normal tissue datasets, XYcellAtlas quantifies cell-type-specific LOY frequencies across cell types. Furthermore, it systematically catalogs sex-biased and LOY-associated molecular alterations, including differentially expressed genes, chromatin peaks, core transcription factors, as well as their functional annotations and dysregulatory signatures within malignant cells and the tumor microenvironment. In summary, XYcellAtlas provides a unified, all-in-one analytical platform enabling researchers to query, inspect, quantify, and visualize sex-associated and LOY-derived multi-omics features underlying tumor evolutionary processes.

papers.title: STRAND: a comprehensive subcellular-resolved spatial transcriptome RNA architecture and navigation database.
papers.authors: Wu Z, Huo Y, Xu W, Li X, Li T.
papers.abstract: Subcellular RNA localization serves as a critical regulatory layer governing cellular polarization, local translation, and functional compartmentalization. Recent advances in high-resolution spatial transcriptomics have provided unprecedented opportunities to resolve these intracellular architectures at single-molecule resolution. However, relevant datasets are dispersed across studies and repositories, vary substantially in processing procedures and standards, severely limiting their cross-study reuse. To bridge this gap, we present STRAND (Subcellular-Resolved Spatial Transcriptome RNA Architecture and Navigation Database), a curated data resource and analysis platform for the automated harvesting, quality control, and interpretation of subcellular spatial transcriptomics data. Through an agent-assisted curation pipeline, STRAND has assembled 35 subcellular-resolution datasets from six major platforms, covering 17 tissue types in human and mouse and totalling ∼4.9 billion transcript coordinates. Building upon this standardized data resource, STRAND provides an analytical workflow spanning cell segmentation evaluation, cell-type annotation, RNA localization/colocalization pattern annotation, and subcellular compartment inference. Two case studies demonstrate that STRAND successfully identifies established RNA localization patterns in cultured cell lines and detects drug-induced RNA relocalization in cardiomyocytes. STRAND is openly available at https://strand.phasep.pro.

papers.title: ENdb 2.0: an updated database of experimentally supported enhancers.
papers.authors: Xu M, Zhang G, Wang Q, Chen Y, Song C, Liu J, Guo B, Zhou J, Li C.
papers.abstract: Enhancers are cis-regulatory elements that control gene expression during development, cell differentiation, and disease. Genome-wide studies have mapped large numbers of candidate regulatory elements, but experimentally supported enhancer information remains dispersed across primary studies and experimental systems. Here, we present ENdb 2.0 (http://www.licpathway.net/ENdb/index.php), an updated, manually curated database of experimentally supported enhancers. Compared with ENdb 1.0, the major updates are (i) literature coverage through 2026 and five species: Homo sapiens, Mus musculus, Drosophila melanogaster, Danio rerio, and Rattus norvegicus; (ii) 4831 enhancer evidence records, including 2793 enhancer-TF-target-gene records involving 496 TFs and 1070 target genes; (iii) expanded curation of genomic coordinates, experimental evidence, enhancer type, regulatory state, biological condition, tissues, cell sources, cell types, and diseases, covering 169 tissues, 1255 cell sources, 415 cell types, and 226 diseases; and (iv) biological search, genome browsing, pathway enrichment analysis, agent-assisted query, and structured data download. ENdb 2.0 links experimentally supported enhancer regions with regulatory factors, target genes, biological conditions, and supporting experiments across physiological and disease states.

papers.title: dictyBase 2026: a reimplementation of the Dictyostelium model organism database on minimal infrastructure.
papers.authors: Mendieta MJ, Dodson RJ, Basu S, Chisholm RL, Scaglione KM.
papers.abstract: Dictyostelium discoideum is a model organism used to investigate a wide array of biological processes including chemotaxis, cell motility, phagocytosis, multicellular development, and autophagy. Many of its genes have human orthologs implicated in disease, making it a useful model organism for studying conditions ranging from cancer to neurodegeneration. dictyBase has served this community for two decades as a home for genomic data, protocols, a stock center, and community news. Here we describe a complete reimplementation of dictyBase as a self-contained service that uses static data files rather than a database server. Each gene record gathers curated function, human-disease context, developmental expression, and protein structure in a single webpage. The site also provides tools for sequence search, genome browsing, enrichment analysis, and experimental design. The complete Dicty Stock Center catalog of 7055 strains and 1265 plasmids is included, and both can be ordered from the site. New literature is curated by an author-in-the-loop pipeline. A language model drafts the annotations, the authors of the paper correct them, and a curator approves them. Analyses can be run on curator-approved annotations alone or extended to include those still awaiting review. dictyBase is freely available at https://dicty.org.

papers.title: DiseaseCIO: a multi-omics atlas for characterizing clinical intervention outcomes across diverse diseases.
papers.authors: Zhai R, Ma T, Su M, Wang H, Li J, Xing J, Huang X, Yu P, Qiu J, Liu T, Xiao X, Li Y, Gu Y, Zhang Y.
papers.abstract: Heterogeneity in clinical intervention outcomes across patients is a major barrier to precision medicine. The integration of multidimensional high-throughput omics can help reveal the molecular basis of differences in clinical interventions and provide insights into outcome prediction, prognostic stratification, regulatory patterns, and resistance mechanisms. We present DiseaseCIO (Disease Clinical Intervention Outcomes, http://db.edbc.org/DiseaseCIO/), a database that integrates microbiome, transcriptome, and epigenome data with human disease intervention outcomes. It is designed to characterize the molecular landscape associated with disease intervention outcomes at the individual patient level. DiseaseCIO encompasses 42 798 pretreatment samples from 94 disease states, covering 510 treatment regimens involving 377 pharmacological and non-pharmacological interventions. These samples comprise four types of specimens collected from eight sampling locations. Using the customized iMOD workflow for multi-omics data processing, we generated 20 categories of molecular features and identified >1.84 million candidate feature-outcome associations. DiseaseCIO also provides interactive tools for differential analysis, prognostic evaluation, cross-omics correlation analysis, and cross-cohort integrative analysis of multidimensional features as well as enrichment analysis and signature construction for user-submitted feature sets. DiseaseCIO provides a molecular-level resource for exploring intervention outcome heterogeneity across diseases and identifying candidate multi-omics biomarkers associated with treatment response and prognosis.

papers.title: ARIEL: an openly accessible database of experimental RNA-ligand binding affinities paired with 3D structures.
papers.authors: Zeyadah MOR, Alqahtani AJ, Fliti SA, Akhtar N, Sharma S, Petta A, Cavallo L, Oliva R, Chawla M.
papers.abstract: RNA is an increasingly attractive target for small-molecule therapeutics, yet the rational design and computational modelling of RNA-binding small molecules are constrained by the scarcity of experimentally measured binding affinities linked to 3D structures. Here we present ARIEL (Affinity Resource for Interactions of RNA and Ligands), an openly accessible, manually curated database that pairs experimentally determined dissociation constants (Kd) of RNA-ligand complexes with the corresponding experimental structures. We screened 6954 RNA-containing structures from the Protein Data Bank, extracted 2843 complexes with a small ligand, and manually curated the associated primary literature to retrieve the corresponding Kd values. This yielded a nonredundant dataset of 278 RNA-ligand complexes with experimental affinities, including 179 unique ligands bound to 171 different RNA targets, with Kd values spanning nine orders of magnitude (-log Kd 2.1-11.0). Each entry also provides the Kd measurement method and conditions, full literature provenance, ligand physicochemical descriptors, and binding-pocket annotations, with direct cross-links between structures, ligands and source publications. ARIEL will be maintained through regular, versioned releases; it is freely available at https://aocdweb.com/BioTools/ARIEL/.

papers.title: Assessment of LLMs on basic bioinformatics tasks requiring multi-step reasoning and code writing.
papers.authors: Rajesh V, Blumberg M, Jain S, Siwo GH.
papers.abstract: Motivation Large Language Models (LLMs), AI agents and co-scientists promise to accelerate scientific discovery across fields ranging from chemistry to biology. Bioinformatics- the analysis of DNA, RNA and protein sequences plays a crucial role in biological research and is especially amenable to AI-driven automation given its computational nature. Here, we assess the bioinformatics capabilities of popular general-purpose LLMs on a set of tasks covering basic analytical questions that include code writing and multi-step reasoning in the domain. Results Utilizing questions from Rosalind, a bioinformatics educational platform, we compare the performance of the LLMs on 104 questions relative to expert ground truth and 68,760 humans with varying levels of expertise. Among the frontier LLMs evaluated (GPT-5.2, GPT-4o, GPT-3.5, Llama-3-70B, Llama-4 and Claude Sonnet 4.6), GPT-5.2 exhibited top performance, providing correct answers for 80/104 (77%) questions followed by Claude Sonnet 4.6. LLM performance varied widely depending on the biological categories of questions. While the latest generation of frontier LLM models showed overall improvements in performance, their performance in specific categories of biological questions was lower than first generation models. Overall, LLMs performance mirrored that of humans with lower performance in tasks in which humans had low performance and vice versa. However, LLMs also failed in some instances where most humans were correct and, in a few cases, LLMs excelled where most humans failed. To the best of our knowledge, this presents the first assessment of general purpose LLMs on basic bioinformatics tasks in distinct areas relative to both expert and non-expert ground truths. Availability and implementation The complete analysis was implemented in Python; all code is available at https://github.com/SiwoResearch/lllm-bioinformatics. Supplementary information Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

papers.title: Multikingdom and functional gut microbiota markers for cholangiocarcinoma.
papers.authors: Rao B, Liu S, Cui G, Jiang J, Li N, Hu J, Sun R, Li A, Zhang R, Lu H, Wen P, Xue J, Aji T, Wang H, Chen X, Zheng S, Yu Z, Ren Z.
papers.abstract: Background While the association between gut microbiota and cholangiocarcinoma (CCA) has been explored, existing research has been limited to bacterial components. The alterations in non-bacterial members (fungi, archaea, and viruses) and their functional characteristics in CCA remain unclear. This study aimed to comprehensively characterize the multi-kingdom gut microbiota and functional profiles in CCA patients and develop a non-invasive diagnostic model. Methods We performed metagenomic sequencing on 700 fecal samples collected from three distinct regions in China, comprising 289 CCA patients, 312 healthy controls, and 99 hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) patients. Multi-kingdom microbial composition and functional profiles were analyzed. We integrated multiple machine learning algorithms to generate 117 distinct modeling schemes for constructing and screening the optimal CCA diagnostic model. The model was validated across three independent cohorts and tested for specificity against HCC. We also benchmarked the model against established diagnostic approaches by reviewing 15 CCA clinical practice guidelines/consensus statements and their cited evidence and by evaluating model detection in CA19-9-positive and CA19-9-negative patients. Results Extensive alterations were identified in CCA patients across multi-kingdom and functional layers, including 198 archaeal, 154 bacterial, 78 fungal, and 120 viral species, as well as 278 genes, 99 pathways, and 151 carbohydrate-active enzymes (CAZymes). A panel of 21 multi-kingdom and functional markers demonstrated superior diagnostic accuracy with an average AUC of 91% across three validation cohorts, outperforming any single-kingdom model. The model exhibited high specificity in distinguishing CCA from HCC, achieving an AUC of 99.74% with a false positive rate of 11.11%. Benchmarking supported a complementary role as a noninvasive screening aid, the model showed pooled sensitivity and specificity of 96.2%, and 78.5%, respectively, and detected 97.6% of CA19-9-negative CCA cases. Conclusions This study represents the first comprehensive characterization of multi-kingdom gut microbiome and functional markers in cholangiocarcinoma. Gut multi-kingdom and functional microbial signatures represent a promising noninvasive tool that may aid the screening and early identification of cholangiocarcinoma in high-risk populations, complementing existing diagnostic approaches.

papers.title: Structural basis of voltage gating in a partially activated K+ channel.
papers.authors: Agrawal R, Mendoza Uriarte R, Pinto-Anwandter BI, Thomas T, Blachowicz L, Koh YH, Bezanilla F, Perozo E, Roux B.
papers.abstract: To understand the process of voltage activation in Kv channels, we determined the cryo-EM structure of the Shaker channel ILT mutant (V369I, I372L, S376T), known to partially decouple the gating charge movement of the voltage sensing domain (VSD) and the opening of the pore domain (PD). The structure captures an intermediate state in which the VSD is only partially activated while the gate of the PD remains closed. Combined with computational modeling based on AlphaFold2 predictions and molecular dynamics simulations, we show that the VSD activation is transduced to the PD via a dynamic shift in the population equilibrium of the S4-S5 linker between two metastable positions, thereby providing the basis for electromechanical coupling between the two domains.

papers.title: Characterization of chemoresistant cell populations improves risk stratification and therapy prediction in pediatric acute myeloid leukemia.
papers.authors: NajafPanah MJ, Stevens AM, Krueger MJ, Rochette M, Sandhu S, Kim L, Chiu HS, Epps J, Somvanshi S, Zorman B, Rodriguez Martinez M, Rapsomaniki M, Unger S, Becher B, Yi JS, Man TK, Redell MS, Sumazin P.
papers.abstract: Most pediatric acute myeloid leukemia (pAML) patients achieve complete remission after chemotherapy, yet nearly 40% ultimately relapse and die from their disease. High risk cases are typically referred for stem cell transplantation (SCT) in first remission, but because SCT is associated with substantial toxicity and cures after relapse are rare, accurate risk prediction is critical. Here, we show that combining the detection of chemoresistant cell populations, inferred from single-cell transcriptomic profiles of paired diagnosis-relapse samples, and cytogenetic biomarkers at diagnosis with measurable residual disease after induction chemotherapy, substantially improves risk prediction. This approach identifies a patient subgroup comprising 20% of the patients who do not undergo SCT, with a 5-year event-free survival below 40%, and accounting for nearly half of all deaths in this population. Molecular characterization of these cell populations reveals therapeutic vulnerabilities and potential targeted treatment strategies for high-risk pAML, providing a framework for precision oncology diagnosis and intervention.

papers.title: Evaluating generative models for structure-based drug discovery from de novo design to lead optimization.
papers.authors: Cao D, Fan Z, Yu J, Chen M, Jiang X, Sheng X, Wang X, Zeng C, Luo X, Teng D, Zheng M.
papers.abstract: Advances in protein structure prediction have created opportunities for structure-based drug design, yet translating structural knowledge into actionable small-molecule ligands remains difficult. Existing benchmarks often use simplified datasets and computational surrogates that poorly capture the heterogeneity and constraints of real-world drug discovery. We introduce MolGenBench, a comprehensive benchmark for de novo molecular generation and hit-to-lead optimization built on a large, structurally diverse dataset. Evaluation of 17 leading methods reveals persistent limitations, including weak virtual-screening performance, limited coverage of target-specific bioactive space, frequent high-risk structural motifs, poor target awareness, and reduced generalization to unseen proteins. Although some models improve three-dimensional conformation generation, they still struggle to produce active molecules reliably. MolGenBench provides standardized data, metrics, and analyses that connect structural prediction with practical molecular design and guide the development of more effective structure-based generative models.

papers.title: Untargeted screening of drug-like compounds using high-throughput metabolomics uncovers inhibitors of key biological pathways.
papers.authors: Sarvin N, Kantorovich R, Chakraborty S, Procaccia S, Lev Y, Sarvin B, Rutenberg A, Fokra M, Shemer S, Shlomi T.
papers.abstract: Metabolomics has demonstrated immense potential in elucidating mechanisms of action and off-target effects of known drugs. Here, we propose that metabolomic screening of cellular response to treatment with drug-like compounds can uncover clinically relevant inhibitors - driven by the extensive catalog of metabolic pathways implicated in human diseases. We developed a high-throughput LC-MS metabolomics pipeline paired with a computational Graph Neural Network for target deconvolution, and applied it to screen a library of 1,020 drug-like compounds in cultured cells in vitro. The screen revealed four drug-like compounds targeting key disease pathways, including inhibitors of purine and pyrimidine biosynthesis and an inducer of glutathione metabolism; validated via comprehensive metabolic assessments and growth rescue experiments. In a muscle atrophy model, driven by redox imbalance, the glutathione metabolism inducer reversed atrophy markers and restored protein content. Our scalable pipeline can be readily expanded to screen thousands of compounds, paving the way for the discovery of clinically relevant metabolic inhibitors.

papers.title: Single-cell imaging of the lytic phage life cycle in bacteria.
papers.authors: Wedd C, Li R, Yunusov T, Smith A, Hardo G, Hunter M, Mohan AK, Majed R, Fusco D, Bakshi S.
papers.abstract: Upon infecting a bacterial cell, a lytic bacteriophage commandeers the host's resources to replicate, before lysing the cell to release new virions. As phages are obligate parasites, each stage of the infection process depends on the physiological parameters of the host cell. Given the inherent physiological variability within a population of genetically identical bacterial cells, we ask how the phage infection dynamic reflects such heterogeneity. Here, we introduce a time-lapse imaging assay for investigating the dynamics of individual infection steps by a single T7 phage on a single bacterium. This high-throughput, time-resolved assay enables us to monitor the infection progression simultaneously in multiple cells, uncovering substantial heterogeneity at each step and revealing correlations between infection dynamics and the physiological state of the infected cell. Simulations of competing phage populations reveal that heterogeneity in infection dynamics can significantly impact phage fitness, highlighting it as a potential evolutionary driver of phage-bacteria interactions. A record of this paper's transparent peer review process is included in the supplemental information.
