papers.title: From 16S rDNA-seq count data to microbial interactions: A comprehensive benchmark of co-occurrence network inference methods.
papers.authors: Mariotto P, Baldan M, Di Camillo B, Baruzzo G.
papers.abstract: The study of the ecological interactions within microbial communities is crucial for gaining deeper insights into community ensemble and evolution, enabling targeted modification of the community's functionality. Many inference approaches have been developed to derive ecological associations. Here, we focus on co-occurrence computational methods, in which associations are inferred from metagenomic abundance data by measuring the statistical dependence between species counts across different sampled populations. The limitations in culture-based experiments have hindered the ability to assess these methods' validity, leading to scarce application in metagenomics studies. To provide a comprehensive assessment of network inference method performance, we benchmark 18 different computational approaches across a broad spectrum of experimental scenarios. We use synthetic 16S rDNA-seq count data generated from known underlying interaction networks, enabling systematic and controlled evaluation. The benchmark spans scenarios varying in numbers of species and samples, sample richness, sequencing depth, and interaction network structure. We evaluated the performance of the methods both in terms of accuracy of the inferred network, using various metrics from binary classification theory and metrics coming from network science, and in terms of computational burden. We found that methods have valid results only in a restricted, and often unrealistic, field of application, whereas their effectiveness diminishes with more realistic simulation parameters. Our findings highlight the limits of the co-occurrence-based approach and the need for further development in microbial ecological association inference.

papers.title: Taxonova: Deep learning enables fast and confidence-aware microbiome species-level amplicon classification.
papers.authors: Kakabra K, Patel S, Temko A, Claesson MJ.
papers.abstract: Accurate species-level taxonomic classification of microbial amplicon sequences remains challenging due to the difficulty of resolving subtle variations within conserved ribosomal regions. Traditional similarity-based methods struggle with short amplicons and sequences with poor database representation. No existing method performs robustly across the full spectrum of amplicon lengths, limiting applicability across diverse sequencing platforms and variable-region targets. We present Taxonova, a deep learning framework for both short- and long-read ribosomal amplicons. Evaluated across physical and biome-simulated mock communities representing seven biomes (via the accompanying benchmark tool Taxobench), Taxonova attains species-level F-measures of 0.76-1.00 (median 0.94) for short-read and 0.82-0.99 (median 0.97) for long-read amplicons spanning 250 bp to 4,900 bp, reduces the species-level abundance-estimation error (L1 norm) by a median of 0.52 to 1.50 depending on amplicon region, and has a species-level false-positive rate that is a median of 16.2 × 10-4 lower than that of the other classifiers. Species-level assignment is expected to be most reliable for well-characterised communities, such as human-associated microbiomes. To demonstrate real-world applicability, we also compared amplicon-derived taxonomic profiles to paired shotgun whole-genome sequencing from gut, soil and vaginal microbiomes; Taxonova achieves the strongest species-level concordance (Jaccard) in all three studies, with a species-level Jaccard index 0.009 to 0.022 higher than that of the next-best classifier across both high- and low-complexity communities. Taxonova runs at a throughput of roughly 100 sequences per second on a single CPU core, making it suitable for routine deployment in research settings.

papers.title: Cd47 deficiency in mouse brain under excitotoxic stress.
papers.authors: Kiamari M, Perna A, Santoro M, El Ariss A, Berson E, Zhao J, Gajera CR, Fox EJ, Montine KS, Aghaeepour N, Montine TJ.
papers.abstract: CD47, a transmembrane protein with well-established immune and neurodevelopmental roles, was recently identified as an abundant presynaptic protein in humans, non-human primates, and mice. To investigate how Cd47 influences neuronal stress and injury, we performed single-nucleus RNA sequencing of hippocampi from wild-type (WT) and Cd47 knockout (KO) mice exposed to kainic acid (KA) at convulsive (KA25; 25 mg/kg) or subconvulsive (KA3; 3 mg/kg) doses. Integrating cell-type annotations with Weighted Gene Co-expression Network Analysis (WGCNA) revealed distinct neuronal and glial gene modules whose co-expression structure differed by genotype and by KA exposure. Notably, certain modules showed KA-associated changes in co-expression structure only in Cd47-deficient cells. Enrichment analyses of these modules highlighted translational, bioenergetic, and synaptic gene sets. Comparing transcriptome-wide distributions using Wasserstein distance demonstrated that vehicle-treated KO cells most closely resembled WT cells exposed to KA3, of all fifteen pairwise comparisons. These findings suggest that Cd47 loss shifts the hippocampal transcriptome toward a state resembling mild excitotoxic stress, implicating Cd47 as a candidate regulator of neuronal stress adaptation and providing a hypothesis for testing that role.

papers.title: WinPopLDdecay: a hardware-adaptive and reproducible reimplementation of PopLDdecay with a graphical interface.
papers.authors: Zhao B, Zhang C, Gong ZK, Hu Z, Chen ZH, Li C, He W, Tan C.

papers.title: Metal-ion coordination drives active-site remodeling for backsplicing in circularly permuted group II introns.
papers.authors: Zhang J, Yao Y, Ma J.
papers.abstract: Circularly permuted (CP) group II introns are self-splicing ribozymes that undergo a sequential branching and backsplicing reaction to yield branched introns and circular exons (circRNAs). While the initial branching step is structurally characterized, the mechanistic principles that govern the subsequent large-scale active-site remodeling and stringent metal-ion specificity required for backsplicing remain poorly understood. Here, we present a series of high-resolution cryo-EM structures of the CP group II intron from Gluconacetobacter diazotrophicus PAL5 (Gdi-1), capturing the ribozyme at discrete stages along the branching -to- backsplicing pathway under distinct ionic conditions. Comparative analyses under K+/Mg2+, K+/Ca2+, and Cs+/Mg2+ conditions demonstrate that productive backsplicing relies on ion-specific coordination networks that govern 3' splice site (3'SS) docking and catalytic center formation, revealing the precise metal-ion-coordinated conformational rearrangements and dynamic splice-site exchange mechanisms. Crucially, we identify a previously unrecognized, highly selective monovalent cation-binding site, K3, that structurally couples the γ-γ' interaction to reassembly of the heteronuclear four-metal core, thereby promoting productive second-step active-site formation. Together, these findings establish a structural basis for metal-ion-dependent active-site remodeling during group II intron catalysis and provide mechanistic insights into metal-ion selectivity in circRNA biogenesis.

papers.title: Biobank-scale self-supervised genotype pretraining yields transferable representations for human genetics.
papers.authors: Sheng C, Du H, Shen H, Dai H, Song F, Li X, Chen K.
papers.abstract: Biobank-scale genotyping has created unprecedented cohorts for human genetics, yet the field still lacks scalable methods for learning transferable representations from largely unlabeled individual-level genotype data. Here, we introduce SNPBERT, a self-supervised transformer pretrained on genotypes from 485 923 UK Biobank participants using masked rsID prediction. SNPBERT embeddings recovered known population structure across UK Biobank and three external datasets, performed comparably to principal component analysis, and supported the identification of ancestry-informative marker SNPs. Fine-tuning with an attention-based multiple-instance head generated disease-specific risk scores that provided complementary information beyond conventional polygenic risk scores. The relative increase in Nagelkerke's R2 ranged from 0.7% to 3.3%, and independent associations were observed for seven of the eight chronic diseases examined. In celiac disease, attention prioritization recapitulated major histocompatibility complex signals while elevating variants in CCHCR1 and NOTCH4 relative to genome-wide association study (GWAS) ranking. These results support biobank-scale genotype pretraining as an early step toward foundation modeling for individual-level genotype data.

papers.title: The Mycobacterium tuberculosis Ku C-terminus orchestrates LigD activity through domain-specific interactions.
papers.authors: Sowa DJ, Huang J, Marwaha A, Subramaniam A, Doubleday C, Warner MM, Byun JA, Melacini G, Andres SN.
papers.abstract: Bacterial non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) is a key DNA double-strand break (DSB) repair pathway that relies on the Ku-LigD complex to alleviate genomic instability. The Mycobacterium tuberculosis Ku C-terminus has been highlighted for its role in LigD recruitment to DSBs and stimulation of LigD ligase activity. However, it remains unclear how the Ku C-terminus interacts with and potentially influences other LigD activities. Here, we combine NMR spectroscopy, structural modelling, and mutational analysis to define the interaction interface between the Ku C-terminus and LigD. We identify critical residues in Ku (E246, V248, S258, K260, and N266) and the LigD polymerase (D162, V194, R198) and ligase (D522, K579, L580) domains that mediate this interaction. Functional assays reveal that Ku stimulates LigD ligase activity through contacts with both polymerase and ligase domains, while Ku attenuates template-dependent polymerase activity, contrasting previous studies in Pseudomonas aeruginosa homologs. Disrupting the Ku-LigD interface, either through Ku or LigD mutations, abolishes ligase stimulation and restores polymerase activity, highlighting a dual regulatory mechanism. Our data supports a model where Ku's C-terminal region forms a bipartite interface with LigD to balance repair activity. These findings provide mechanistic insight into the Ku-LigD repair mechanism and uncovers species-specific differences in bacterial NHEJ.

papers.title: mobileRNA: an integrative, automated tool for accurate identification of mobile RNA molecules based on multiple genome mapping.
papers.authors: Jeynes-Cupper K, Tomkins M, Morris RJ, Catoni M.
papers.abstract: RNA molecules can act as intercellular signals, with evidence of transport for both messenger RNA (mRNA) and small RNA over long distances. Such molecules that move from the cell in which they originated are termed mobile RNA. In grafted plants, when different genotypes are joined together, the movement of RNAs between tissues can be revealed by approaches that exploit natural polymorphisms between the genomes involved. However, current methods suffer from a high level of technological noise, and the lack of standardized approaches makes it challenging for researchers to robustly identify mobile RNA molecules. Here, we introduce an automated pipeline, mobileRNA, which uses a multi-genome approach based on simultaneous alignment of RNA sequencing data to merged reference genomes. We validated our approach using simulated grafting combinations and compared to other methods. When applying mobileRNA to real data, we find poor overlap to existing mobile mRNA annotations, consistent with recent studies that question the reliability of previously reported mobile mRNAs. Introducing a genome mappability index as a criterion for the likely success of detecting mobile RNAs, we find that SNP-based or two-step mapping approaches are inherently limited due to errors and poor mappability compared to cross-species grafting with large evolutionary distances.

papers.title: The 7SK small nuclear ribonucleoprotein links the cell responses to transcription and replication stress by promoting replication fork reversal and homologous recombination.
papers.authors: Bowry A, Wilson C, Kelly RDW, Wilkins RJ, Walker AK, Varghese CS, Alshatti ZAM, Murphy-Hollies S, Morris JR, Egloff S, Kanhere A, Petermann E.
papers.abstract: The 7SK small nuclear ribonucleoprotein (7SK-snRNP) releases positive transcription elongation factor b to sustain RNA polymerase II (RNAPII) activity during transcription stress. Many conditions that block transcription also cause replication stress, and 7SK-snRNP components have potential roles in transcription-replication conflicts and double-strand break (DSB) repair. Here, we investigate roles of 7SK-snRNP components in replication stress responses. We report that 7SK-snRNP promotes replication fork slowing in response to agents that cause both replication and transcription stress. Our data suggest that 7SK-snRNP facilitates RAD51-mediated replication fork reversal rather than transcription-replication conflicts. 7SK-snRNP also promotes RAD51 recruitment to replication-associated DSBs or post-replicative gaps under conditions of transcription stress and supports homologous recombination at direct DSBs. In contrast, 7SK-snRNP components are not required for RAD51 recruitment in response to hydroxyurea. Our data support that LARP7 functions during replication stress independently of its interaction with BRCA1, and that LARP7 and HEXIM1 promote survival of replication stress. 7SK-snRNP components are not recruited to stressed replication forks, and RNAPII inhibition phenocopies loss of these proteins. Our data support a model where 7SK-snRNP modulation of RNAPII activity helps facilitate several RAD51 functions under transcription stress conditions, thereby connecting the cell responses to transcription and replication stress.

papers.title: EWSR1 associates with the 40S ribosomal subunit and represses translation to maintain endoplasmic reticulum homeostasis.
papers.authors: Hassoun ZEO, Ongena L, Condé L, Galvan B, Fettweis G, Lion M, Soin R, Bruyr J, Lemaitre F, Thiry M, Mariavelle E, Claes M, Blomme A, Menschaert G, Dehairs J, Kruys V, Gueydan C, O'grady TM, Swinnen JV, de Breyne S, Ohlmann T, Twizere JC, Habraken Y, Dequiedt F.
papers.abstract: FET family proteins (FUS, EWSR1, and TAF15) have garnered significant attention due to their involvement in oncogenic fusions and mutations in various cancers and neurodegenerative disorders. Although these highly conserved RNA-binding proteins are widely described as multifunctional regulators of gene expression, their precise molecular functions remain incompletely understood. Here, we uncover a previously unrecognized role for EWSR1 as a selective translational repressor in cancer cells. EWSR1 specifically targets mRNAs involved in lipid metabolism and endoplasmic reticulum (ER) homeostasis. Loss of EWSR1 disrupts ER morphology and impairs activation of the unfolded protein response of the ER (UPRER). Mechanistically, EWSR1 represses translation upon association with target mRNAs, and its conserved region spanning two arginine-glycine-glycine (RGG) boxes contributes to association with the 40S ribosomal subunit. These findings define a novel role for EWSR1 in post-transcriptional gene regulation and suggest that perturbations in its translational activity may underlie the pathogenesis of FET-associated diseases.

papers.title: Exploring DNA movement through the application of droplet-based high-efficiency chromatin conformation capture (DropHiChew) and loop velocity.
papers.authors: Zhang C, Xie Y, Tan C, Chen Z, Cao H, Guo M, Zhao L, Weng Z, Tang C.
papers.abstract: This study presents a novel approach to understanding DNA movement dynamics. Chromatin conformation plays a crucial role in controlling gene expression and cellular processes, with abnormalities linked to diseases like cancer and genetic disorders. ​Current single-cell chromatin conformation methods face limitations in cost-effectiveness, accessibility, and capturing dynamic genome architecture.​​ Therefore, we develop ​DropHiChew, a droplet-based, highly efficient chromatin conformation capture method employing 10× Genomics single-cell systems for user-friendly, cost-effective implementation. Combined with our ​loop velocity algorithm-which estimates the speed and direction of cell development by quantifying chromatin movement-this approach accurately gauges the trajectory of DNA motion and cellular states even at shallow sequencing depth (50k contacts per cell). Validation demonstrates its applicability across biological systems, including HEK293T, spermiogenesis, and embryonic development. The integration of DropHiChew and loop velocity offers potential for diverse applications in chromatin capture studies. This paradigm provides a dynamic perspective on genome organization for disease modeling, cellular differentiation, and developmental biology.

papers.title: DNA defense systems become a fitness liability during plasmid conjugation.
papers.authors: Martinson JNV, Song LCT, Rubin BE.
papers.abstract: Horizontal gene transfer via conjugative plasmids is a major driver of bacterial evolution. While antibiotic exposure selects for the resistance genes carried by some plasmids, much uncertainty remains about how plasmids persist and spread in microbial communities in the absence of such external selection. Here, we show that conjugative plasmid transfer selectively reduces the fitness of non-permissive recipients through the process of lethal zygosis: a phenomenon in which repeated Type IV Secretion System (T4SS) engagement damages recipients that fail to establish the plasmid. We found that this contact-dependent antagonism effectively clears a niche for plasmid donors by turning recipients' DNA defenses into a liability. Blocking establishment of the plasmid RK2 with CRISPR-Cas or restriction-modification caused strong fitness defects in Escherichia coli recipients by preventing expression of plasmid-encoded exclusion genes and leaving cells exposed to repeated T4SS engagement. We leveraged this insight to resolve an obstacle in bacterial editing by developing transposon vectors that co-deliver exclusion genes, increasing the efficiency of gene editing by orders of magnitude. Our results reveal the role of "coercive assimilation" in horizontal gene transfer, exposing a tradeoff where the advantage of bacterial immunity to foreign DNA is counterbalanced by increased susceptibility to lethal zygosis.

papers.title: TTPdb: a comprehensive database of targeted therapeutic peptides.
papers.authors: Zhang Y, Li X, Lu W, Mou M, Yuan P, Yang N, Li X, Zhang Z, Wang Y, Zhou Z, Zhou Y, Fu Y, Wang L, Zuo Z, Liu M, Zhu F, Liu J, Zhang Y, Jia Q.
papers.abstract: Targeted therapeutic peptides (TTPs) represent a promising therapeutic modality that bridges the gap between small-molecule drugs and macromolecular antibody-based therapeutics by combining high target specificity, superior tissue permeability, and controllable synthesis. Recent advances in chemical modification and computational design have accelerated the clinical translation of TTPs across diverse therapeutic areas, generating multidimensional data that encompass pharmaceutical profiles, structural binding insights, and structure-activity relationships. However, these data remain fragmented across disparate sources, and no dedicated platform exists to systematically integrate them for mechanistic exploration or rational peptide engineering. Here, we present TTPdb, a specialized database that consolidates comprehensive information on TTPs. TTPdb compiles 5366 TTPs (106 approved, 229 clinical, and 5031 preclinical or investigative), which span >600 disease types and are annotated with 3D structures, binding interactions, and physicochemical properties. TTPdb further catalogs peptide structural modifications and pharmacological mechanisms while establishing associations among peptides, targets, and diseases. TTPdb incorporates a multidimensional search module that supports universal keyword queries, structured conditional filtering, and FASTA-based sequence homology searches, with peptides, targets, and diseases as the primary search entities. As a valuable resource for rational peptide design and optimization in AI-driven biomedical research, TTPdb is freely accessible at https://idrblab.org/TTPdb.

papers.title: ProPepBA: a binding affinity database for canonical and chemically modified protein-peptide interactions.
papers.authors: Venkatachalam S, Gromiha MM.
papers.abstract: Protein-peptide interactions play a crucial role in various biological processes, including cell signaling, immune responses, and host defense. The strength of these interactions is quantified by binding affinity, which is essential for understanding peptide recognition, uncovering biological mechanisms, and facilitating the design of peptide-based drugs. Although thousands of experimentally determined protein-peptide binding affinities are available, the information is scattered throughout the literature, making it difficult to use for systematic analysis and computational modeling. Moreover, existing databases for protein-peptide binding affinities have limitations, such as small data size, lack of experimental conditions, and mutation information. To bridge this gap, we developed ProPepBA, a comprehensive database of experimentally determined protein-peptide binding affinities that has been meticulously curated. The current version includes 3962 binding affinity data for canonical peptides sourced from approximately 500 research articles/patents, along with 608 records for chemically modified peptides, including phosphorylation, acetylation, methylation, and terminal modifications. Each entry is provided with information on protein and peptide, thermodynamic parameters, experimental conditions, and literature references. Additionally, the entries are cross-linked to databases such as UniProt, PDB, AlphaFoldDB, and PubMed. ProPepBA offers a user-friendly web interface with advanced search options, enabling efficient data retrieval. By integrating experimental binding affinity data with sequence, structural, and thermodynamic information, ProPepBA serves as a valuable resource for exploring sequence-structure-affinity relationships, development of computational tools, and discovering high affinity peptide binders to facilitate peptide-based drug design. The database is freely accessible at https://web.iitm.ac.in/bioinfo3/ProPepBA.

papers.title: MitImpact 4: a genome-wide resource for the interpretation of coding and non-coding mitochondrial DNA variants.
papers.authors: Giovannetti A, Napoli A, Liorni N, Petrizzelli F, Biagini T, Gasbarrini A, Caputo V, Mazza T.
papers.abstract: Mitochondrial DNA variants are a frequent cause of inherited disease, yet their computational interpretation has focused almost exclusively on the 13 protein-coding genes. Variants in tRNA and rRNA genes, which carry a disproportionate share of the known pathogenic alleles, have remained a diagnostic blind spot, because their effect depends on RNA structure rather than on protein sequence and few dedicated predictors exist. MitImpact 4 removes this asymmetry. The database now covers all 49 704 single-nucleotide variants that can occur in the mitochondrial genome and reports their functional consequence, phylogenetic conservation, local mutational constraint, and population frequency in gnomAD, HelixMTdb, and ToMMo. Missense variants are annotated with APOGEE 2 and with newly added predictors, including AlphaMissense, ESM1b, VARITY, and LIST-S2, while tRNA and rRNA variants receive predictions from nAPOGEE, our RNA-specific model, alongside MitoTIP and PON-mt-tRNA. For both classes, scores are accompanied by posterior probabilities of pathogenicity that can be used within the ACMG/AMP framework for mitochondrial DNA. Clinical annotation from ClinVar and MITOMAP, including ClinGen expert-panel classifications, is integrated in a redesigned interface that also annotates user-submitted VCF files. MitImpact 4 is freely available at https://mitimpact.mcb2lab.org.

papers.title: MetabHub: an integrative platform for plasma nuclear magnetic resonance metabolomics using mediation analysis, disease prediction, and risk stratification.
papers.authors: Yuan J, Gong X, Diao C, Ren J, Wang Y, Bao A, Jin Z, Zhang X, Cao C, Li C.
papers.abstract: Plasma nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) metabolomics offers a scalable molecular readout linking genetic variation, environmental exposure, and clinical physiology to future disease risk. Existing resources typically address metabolite-disease associations, metabolite quantitative trait loci, or prediction separately, with limited support for integrated mediation and longitudinal risk stratification. MetabHub (https://www.metabhub.net) is a web-based resource built from individual-level UK Biobank data, comprising 364 795 European participants, 251 plasma NMR traits, 129 clinical measurements, 54 environmental exposures, genome-wide variants, and 57 incident diseases. It maps sex-combined and sex-specific associations across measurements, exposures, genotypes, metabolites, and diseases, yielding 2 950 764 significant associations. Using two-step screening and natural effect models, MetabHub identifies 1 886 224 significant clinical measurement, environmental factor, and genotype mediation pathways. It also provides metabolite-based prediction models for incident disease using penalized logistic regression, XGBoost, LightGBM, and multilayer perceptron, together with an online interface for applying pre-trained models to user-uploaded profiles. Model-derived metabolomic risk scores are further evaluated using Cox regression and survival stratification over ~14 years of follow-up. Global search, interactive visualization, downloadable tables, prediction, and stratification modules support mechanistic discovery and metabolomics-informed precision prevention.

papers.title: OpenAntigens: a structure-aware database for antigen construct design across the human cell-surface and secreted proteome.
papers.authors: Teixeira AAR, Zhu H, Kothiwal D, Cao R, Mills A.
papers.abstract: Choosing which region of a protein to express remains poorly standardized in antibody discovery, recombinant reagent generation, structural biology, and computational binder design. For human cell-surface and secreted proteins, this requires reconciling topology, processing, predicted, and experimental structure, modifications, interaction partners, orthologs, paralogs, and cross-reactivity risk before ordering DNA. OpenAntigens is a free, no-login database of construct-design reports for 5328 human secreted, GPI-anchored, single-pass, and multipass proteins. It integrates UniProt topology, AlphaFold pLDDT and PAE, PDB precedent, InterPro and Pfam domains, mouse and cynomolgus orthologs, paralog and family context, Open Targets disease associations, partner and assembly context, and BLAST searches. It provides 55 305 construct suggestions spanning full design regions, PDB-backed boundaries, annotated domains, pLDDT/PAE-derived regions, and membrane-expression options, plus 148 722 sequence-similarity hits to help choose constructs and assess cross-reactivity. For targets with compatible AlphaFold models, the interactive designer links sequence, structure, pLDDT, and PAE, allowing users to revise boundaries and export species-equivalent sequences with real-time cysteine and modification warnings. OpenAntigens places reproducible construct suggestions, comparative context, and browser editing in one workflow, reducing manual reconciliation across resources. OpenAntigens is available at openantigens.org.

papers.title: scMRdb: a comprehensive resource for cell-type-resolved Mendelian randomization of complex traits.
papers.authors: Pan S, Wang Z, Jia P.
papers.abstract: Mendelian randomization (MR) is a powerful analytical approach to infer putative causal links between gene expression and human disease, using genetic variants as instrumental variables to mitigate confounding and reverse causation. However, existing MR resources predominantly rely on bulk-tissue expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs), which mask cell-type-specific transcriptional effects by averaging expression across cellular populations. Furthermore, cell-type-resolved causal evidence from single-cell eQTL (sc-eQTL) MR analyses remains fragmented across individual studies with inconsistent workflows, prohibiting standardized cross-cell-type comparisons. Here we present scMRdb (https://ngdc.cncb.ac.cn/scmrdb), a comprehensive resource for cell-type-resolved MR of human complex traits and diseases. scMRdb harmonizes 5206 genome-wide association study (GWAS) summary statistics of European and East Asian ancestry with 585 sc-eQTL datasets spanning 11 tissues and cell systems, including 110 cell types. A uniform pipeline evaluates all gene-trait pairs via MR followed by Steiger directionality testing. Significant associations are assessed by colocalization, and results are stratified into six confidence tiers with integrated drug-target annotation. scMRdb enables systematic recovery of candidate causal genes supported by cell-type-resolved regulatory evidence that is often diluted or obscured in bulk-tissue analyses. We expect scMRdb to serve as a user-friendly portal for generating cell-type-informed mechanistic hypotheses and prioritizing actionable therapeutic targets for complex human diseases.

papers.title: BacMap 3.0: a comprehensive knowledgebase of annotated bacterial genomes.
papers.authors: Kruger R, Kyes M, Oler E, Saha S, Han S, Poelzer J, Wakoli J, López-Hernández Y, LeVatte M, Berjanskii M, MacKay S, Kovur P, Fitzsimmons CJ, Cahill JF, Wishart DS.
papers.abstract: BacMap 3.0 (https://bacmap.ca) is a comprehensive, freely accessible resource integrating 23 524 bacterial and archaeal species, 32 866 genomes, >100 million genes, 1756 primary metabolic pathways, and 45 284 metabolites within one interactive platform. Despite the extraordinary growth of bacterial and archaeal genome sequencing, relevant data remain distributed across numerous specialized databases, impeding comprehensive genome-to-function analysis. While existing microbial resources generally emphasize genome annotation, taxonomy, metabolic pathways, or phenotypes separately, BacMap 3.0 unifies these complementary information layers within an organism-centred framework. It resolves this fragmentation by consolidating genomic, functional, structural, metabolic, phenotypic, ecological, and phylogenetic information into richly detailed, organism-specific "BacCards". Each BacCard combines an interactive genome map with extensive annotations covering bacterium-specific taxonomy, physiology, morphology, metabolism, protein structures, pathways, and metabolites. To facilitate data exploration, BacMap 3.0 supports taxonomic and phenotype-based browsing, chemical structure searches, interactive genome visualization, as well as gene, genome, 16S RNA, and protein BLAST searches. Building on earlier releases devoted primarily to genome visualization, BacMap 3.0 increases organismal coverage by >13-fold and transforms BacMap into an integrated bacterial knowledgebase for genome-to-function investigation across multiple biological scales. By bringing diverse biological information together in a single searchable environment, BacMap 3.0 offers a powerful platform for comparative genomics, microbiome research, infectious disease investigation, and biotechnology with a goal of accelerating the interpretation of microbial diversity, biology, and function.

papers.title: Connectome simulations identify a central pattern generator for fly walking.
papers.authors: Pugliese SM, Chou GM, Abe ETT, Turcu D, Lancaster JK, Tuthill JC, Brunton BW.

papers.title: Perinatal elimination of genetically aberrant human cortical neurons.
papers.authors: Shao DD, Zhao Y, Brew J, Adla Y, Ghosh U, Viswanadham VV, Luquette LJ, Zhao S, Kriz AJ, Qian X, Taketomi T, Coy S, Santagata S, Miller M, Tsuruta F, Park PJ, Walsh CA.
papers.abstract: Human neurons are postmitotic and long-lived, requiring precise genomic regulation. Normal neuronal function is highly dosage-sensitive, with copy number variants (CNVs) and heterozygous point mutations associated with a host of neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric conditions 1-4 . Here we investigated somatic CNVs arising in single neurons to understand the dynamic processes that shape the normal neuronal genetic landscape. Altogether, we sequenced 2,357 single neurons from human postmortem brain from fetal to postnatal life. Two single-cell whole-genome sequencing approaches-Tn5-transposase-based amplification (1,526 neurons, 16 individuals) and primary template amplification 5 (831 neurons, 12 individuals)-showed that an average of 25.9% [12.7-46%] of prenatal cortical neurons have highly aberrant genomes, that is, widespread CNVs involving multiple chromosomes. This proportion reduced by about 4.5-fold after birth across the two single-cell whole-genome sequencing approaches (Fisher meta-analysis P = 3.5 × 10 - 6 ). Neurons with widespread CNVs were mainly eliminated perinatally, timed roughly parallel to periods of programmed cell death 6 , whereas neurons with smaller CNV burdens declined slowly in frequency with postnatal age. CNVs in surviving neurons were depleted for dosage-sensitive genes and genes involved in neurodevelopmental disorders (hypergeometric test P < 0.05), suggesting selective elimination of neurons with these CNVs. Analysis of 44,861 nuclei with single-nucleus assay for transposase-accessible chromatin (snATAC) and single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) showed that neurons with high CNV burdens exhibited abnormal synaptic gene expression, suggesting that abnormal synaptic gene regulation contributes to neuronal elimination. Elimination of defective neuronal genomes might represent an important developmental genome quality-control process that may be vulnerable in neurodevelopmental disease, and suggests purifying selection during human neurodevelopment.

papers.title: T and B cells recognize splicing-derived neutrophil neoantigens in lupus.
papers.authors: Najjar R, Wang X, Shaikh F, Wang N, Le E, An J, Pourshamsi M, Mustelin C, Moadab F, Mirabile-Brightman S, Montero L, Zavala KS, Gureghian V, Cervantes G, Van den Bogaerde SJ, Adhikari S, Pogorelyy MV, Thomas PG, Schoenberger SP, Mustelin T.

papers.title: An mRNA-lipid nanoparticle vaccine against H5N1 influenza virus protects lactating dairy cows from infection.
papers.authors: Santos JJS, Souza CK, Zanella GC, Goulart DB, Arruda B, Boggiatto P, Palmer MV, Snyder CA, Kristula MA, Dickens C, Webb TL, Atkinson RK, Dadonaite B, Dwivedi G, Alameh MG, Hunter CA, Murphy LA, Bloom JD, Weissman D, Althouse GC, Baker AL, Hensley SE.

papers.title: An engineered, compact Cas12m variant for multiplexed gene activation in vivo.
papers.authors: Zhang H, Yang L, Liu Y, Han D, Li Y, Lin J, Wang B, Hu J, Zhang Y, Zhang Y, Li J, Wei S, Liu S, Li T, Zhong N, Zhang G, Zhou X, Shi L, Huang J, Yang H, Tan G, Zhou Y, Li G.

papers.title: CopilotJ: a conversational multi-agent system for intelligent and efficient bioimage analysis.
papers.authors: Lu Z, Yuan Z, Chen Y, Chen Z, Qiu Z, Ren H, Sun L, Wang Y.

papers.title: Cellular-resolution three-photon ultra-deep imaging (TrUDI) of neuronal population activity at 2-mm depth in the mammalian brain.
papers.authors: Santra K, Barber K, Logiacco F, Frechou MA, Bellafard A, Liou JY, Vaziri A.

papers.title: Aptamer-mediated multivalent endogenous ADAR1 recruitment for highly efficient RNA editing.
papers.authors: Zhu H, Zhou Y, Huang R, Wang YF, Hu Y, Wang L, Jin JH, Ye Q, Liu X, Wang ZG, Xie HY, Li JB, Pang DW, Liu SL.

papers.title: Thyra: bridging mass spectrometry imaging and SpatialData for unified multimodal analysis.
papers.authors: Visvikis T, Hendriks TFE, Vierdag WM, Marconato L, Heeren RMA, Cuypers E.

papers.title: Computational modeling and preclinical evaluation support targeting somatic instability for Huntington's disease treatment.
papers.authors: Simpson BP, Ranum PT, Leib DE, Tecedor L, Giovenco RC, Huerta-Ocampo I, Hundley AA, Smith N, Fluta CM, Cali CP, Benoit J, Soper JC, Connelly J, Yohrling GJ, Ghoroghchian PP, Cha JJ, Davidson BL.
papers.abstract: Genetic modifiers of Huntington's disease (HD) disease onset and progression implicate somatic instability (SI) of the expanded CAG repeat as a key pathogenic driver, with MSH3 emerging as a therapeutic target. Here, we generated a computational model that uses HD patient data to infer therapeutic effects of reducing SI and in parallel designed an artificial miRNA to lower MSH3 mRNA (miMSH3) after delivery with AAV-DB-3, a previously described medium spiny neuron (MSN)-targeting AAV capsid variant. AAV-DB-3.miMSH3 achieved 48-94% MSH3 mRNA reduction in MSNs of nonhuman primates (NHPs), which when applied to predictive modeling predicts 50-120 % slowing of HD progression as measured by change from baseline in the composite Unified Huntington Disease Rating Scale. Additionally, AAV-DB-3.miMSH3 reduced SI reduction by up to 46% in HdhQ111 mice. Cumulatively, the preclinical experimental data and the computational model support the translational potential of AAV-DB-3.miMSH3 as a disease-modifying therapy for HD.

papers.title: Strand- and replication timing-dependent functions of DNA polymerase η in human DNA replication.
papers.authors: Bainbridge LJ, Masuda Y, Minamisawa T, Takahashi M, Kaneko K, Masutani C, Daigaku Y.
papers.abstract: Efficient DNA replication requires coordinated use of replicative and error-prone polymerases, which provide flexibility at the cost of mutagenesis. DNA polymerase η (Pol η) tolerates UV-induced lesions via translesion synthesis (TLS), but may contribute more broadly to DNA synthesis. Using polymerase usage sequencing (Pu-seq), we map Pol η activity genome-wide during unperturbed replication in human cells. Pol η preferentially participates in lagging strand replication, as in budding yeast. This bias requires direct PCNA interaction, suggesting stochastic engagement of PCNA-bound intermediates at replication forks. Pol η usage also varies across S phase, with PCNA ubiquitylation-dependent enrichment in late-replicating domains. In cancer genomes, characteristic Pol η mutations are enriched in late-replicating regions and correlate with RAD18 expression, linking PCNA ubiquitylation to Pol η-mediated mutagenesis. Thus, Pol η usage is biased by strand and replication timing during unperturbed replication and may contribute to mutational burden in human genomes.

papers.title: Individualised electrophysiological neural field models for the assessment of thalamocortical function in disorders of consciousness: A multicentre study.
papers.authors: Cóngyǔ L, Tewarie PKB, Alnagger NLN, Mindlin I, Van der Lande GJM, Belloli L, Laureys S, Naccache L, Rohaut B, Thibaut A, Annen J, Gosseries O, Núñez P, Sitt JD.
papers.abstract: Understanding the neural mechanisms underlying disorders of consciousness (DoC) remains a major challenge, particularly in distinguishing limited awareness in minimally conscious state (MCS) and complete unawareness in unresponsive wakefulness syndrome, also coined vegetative state (UWS/VS). In this multicentre study, we fitted a biophysically informed corticothalamic neural field model to high-density EEG data from two large independent datasets, comprising 203 UWS patients, 270 MCS patients and 74 healthy controls. We then used the fitted parameters to simulate EEG time series on a per-subject basis and compared empirical and simulated complexity metrics. The model reliably captured the spectral features across different states of consciousness and revealed reduced corticothalamic integrity in DoC patients that was more pronounced in UWS than in MCS, supporting the mesocircuit hypothesis. Furthermore, the simulated EEG reproduced the complexity patterns of the empirical recordings, with permutation entropy emerging as a sensitive marker capable of distinguishing between MCS and UWS for both real and simulated time series.

papers.title: Modeling reaction-diffusion processes in simplified to complex astroglial branchlet geometries using different simulation tools.
papers.authors: Keto L, Seppälä S, Ndubuaku D, Mäki A, Mäki-Marttunen T, Linne ML, Manninen T.
papers.abstract: Computational modeling of spatial biochemical processes in neuroscience is increasingly important as advances in experimental and imaging techniques provide detailed insights into cellular organization. Reaction-diffusion models are commonly used to study the diffusion and interactions of ions and molecules within neuronal cells, and multiple open-access simulation platforms have been developed to support such analysis. However, a comprehensive analysis of commonly used simulation tools, including MCell, STEPS, NeuroRD, and NEURON, remains lacking, particularly for realistic glial cell geometries, as these tools were originally developed for neurons. Here, we present a systematic analysis of these four simulation environments by implementing equivalent calcium diffusion and calcium-calmodulin reaction-diffusion models across a range of spatial domains. These include simplified geometries (cylinders and rectangular cuboids) as well as biologically realistic astroglial morphologies derived from electron microscopy data, including mouse Bergmann glia and mouse and human cortical astrocytes. Using matched kinetic parameters and diffusion constants, we examine simulation outputs and morphological variations across platforms under comparable conditions. We find that all tools produce overall consistent results for the systems considered, indicating that each can reliably capture diffusion and reaction-diffusion dynamics in simplified and complex geometries. At the same time, we show that the structural heterogeneity of branchlets from human astrocytes and mouse Bergmann glia gives rise to distinct calcium signaling, demonstrating that fine-scale morphology critically shapes astroglial dynamics and must be accurately captured by simulation frameworks. In addition, notable differences emerge in geometry representation, implementation strategies, computational aspects, and usability of the tools. By highlighting key trade-offs between geometric fidelity, flexibility, and computational cost in modeling intracellular biochemical processes, these findings provide practical guidance for selecting appropriate simulation tools. More broadly, our results support the use of reaction-diffusion modeling in morphologically realistic astrocytic environments and contribute to enabling mechanistic studies of localized signaling events at synaptic and perisynaptic sites.

papers.title: Early vs late fusion of qMIDS with machine learning based classifiers for oral cancer diagnosis from gene expression data.
papers.authors: Ben Ali F, Mporas I, Balaji V, Ibaranyanakaye D, Carey B, Teh MT, Adeleke S.
papers.abstract: Different fusion architectures of the quantitative Malignancy Index Diagnostic System (qMIDS) method with machine learning classifiers for oral cancer diagnosis from gene expression data are investigated. The proposed fusion architectures are tested on geographically and ethnically diverse datasets and the evaluation results showed performance improvements with late fusion, which significantly outperformed early fusion in more matched model configurations than the reverse in every cohort, although at the best-performing configuration the two architectures were statistically indistinguishable in most cohorts. Inter-dataset analysis showed robustness of the proposed architectures when the training/test samples are from different populations.

papers.title: Adma and Ackr3a regulate cardiac lymphatic vessel formation and function during heart development and regeneration.
papers.authors: Feng X, Chen HY, Sun Y, Sun F, Yan S, Kapuria S, Rodriguez R, Gamba L, Crump JG, Hong YK, Poss KD, Lien CL.
papers.abstract: Cardiac lymphatics regulate fluid homeostasis and immune cell clearance. The mechanisms underlying cardiac lymphatic vessel formation remain unclear. We perform spatial transcriptomics on the zebrafish heart at the single-cell level and investigate gene expression patterns in cardiac lymphatic endothelial cells (LECs). adrenomedullin a (adma) is mainly expressed in the epicardium adjacent to cardiac lymphatics. adma mutants develop edema and dilated outflow tracts with mis-patterned and reduced lymphatics, while their ventricular lymphatics are dilated with fewer sprouts, increased lyve1b expression, and altered lymphatic subpopulation composition. Loss of ackr3a, which encodes an Adm decoy receptor, increases lymphatic sprouts. During heart regeneration, adma and ackr3a are expressed in epicardium-derived cells within the wound. Neutrophil clearance is reduced in adma mutants but increased in ackr3a mutants. Our findings uncover the heterogeneity of cardiac LECs and show that Adm and Ackr3 regulate cardiac lymphatic vessel formation in the zebrafish heart.

papers.title: Inflammatory memory primes the intestine for enhanced regenerative potential.
papers.authors: Arozamena B, Moraitis I, Mularoni L, Wienskowska O, Taelman J, Stefanovic M, Modolell Farré I, Guedea F, Díaz M, Guiu J.
papers.abstract: How do inflammation and activation of the regenerative genetic program affect intestinal epithelial cell behavior and shape responses to future injuries? Following injury, which typically induces intestinal stem cell (ISC) death, regeneration occurs via the proliferation of surviving ISCs and via cellular plasticity through dedifferentiation of progenitors and committed cells. While inflammation and cellular plasticity are hallmarks of regeneration, its long-term effects on epithelial cell behavior are not well understood. Using single cell multiomics, we demonstrate that inflammatory exposure and cellular plasticity imprint a lasting transcriptional and epigenetic memory on ISCs and their progeny, priming them for enhanced repair after subsequent injuries. Mechanistically, we identify IFN-γ as a critical driver of this primed regenerative state. These findings uncover how prior inflammation reprograms regenerative capacity, with implications for tissue resilience and disease susceptibility.

papers.title: An extensible deep learning framework for multi-type chromatin interaction prediction through hierarchical adaptation strategies.
papers.authors: Wang S, Chen T, Liu W, Zheng X, Yang Z, Liang Z, Shen Y.
papers.abstract: Three-dimensional chromatin interactions play essential roles in gene regulation, yet computational prediction of diverse interaction types remains largely dependent on specialized, single-task models. Here, we present UniLoopNet, a multi-task deep learning framework that predicts multiple types of chromatin interactions including enhancer-promoter interactions, enhancer-enhancer interactions, CTCF-mediated loops, and stripe-associated interactions from DNA sequences. UniLoopNet employs a shared encoder-decoder architecture with hierarchical adaptation strategies, integrating multi-task, transfer, and continual learning based on task semantic similarity. Comprehensive benchmarking across multiple cell lines demonstrates that UniLoopNet outperforms existing specialized and multi-task approaches, with AUROCs exceeding 0.90 in most tasks. Under stringent evaluation settings, including chromosome-matched, distance-matched, realistic imbalanced, and locus-disjoint tests, AUROCs range from 0.8934 to 0.9366. In the realistic 1:5 class-imbalance setting, the AUPRCs for enhancer-promoter and enhancer-enhancer interaction prediction are 0.7956 and 0.6935, respectively. Cross-cell-line transfer experiments further show that applying UniLoopNet to another cell line requires adaptation by supervised fine-tuning on target-cell-line data, after which performance is comparable to that of within-cell-line training. Notably, the framework exhibits data efficiency in experiments with substantially reduced training data. Interpretability analyses reveal that the learned sequence features are associated with known transcription factor binding sites and uncover differential regulatory effects of disease-associated variants. UniLoopNet provides a versatile and data-efficient framework for sequence-based prediction and interpretation of diverse 3D genome interactions, complementing existing sequence-to-map approaches while improving the understanding of sequence-encoded regulatory potential.

papers.title: In silico prediction of metabolic trait robustness in microbial cells.
papers.authors: Gu C, Mustonen V, Jouhten P.
papers.abstract: Microbial strains undergo notable biomass expansion in industrial applications subjecting populations to Darwinian selection. The consequent adaptive evolution may threaten the often tediously developed desired metabolic traits of the strains, such as flavor or platform chemical production. Yet, it remains unresolved how to predict the evolutionary trait robustness. Here, we propose TRAEV (Trait Robustness Against EVolution), a computational framework for in silico prediction of evolutionary robustness of metabolic traits and trajectories of desired traits in application environments. TRAEV uses constraint-based metabolic models for predicting environment-dependent trait-fitness dependencies and accounts for the stochasticity of adaptive evolution by using Monte Carlo-based perturbation analysis. First, TRAEV predicts the immediate metabolic phenotype in the new environment, and then, the subsequent evolutionary trajectories of fitness and desired trait. Metabolic trait robustness is quantified from the evolutionary trajectories as two scores: Robustness Score (RS) and Trade-off Score (TS). RS represents trait robustness and the overall trait level during evolutionary adaptation, whereas TS captures trait-fitness trade-offs. We validated TRAEV by predicting relative evolutionary robustness of heterologous pigmentation of two engineered Saccharomyces cerevisiae strains and two desired aroma generation traits by multiple wine strains of S. cerevisiae if they were developed via a laboratory selection process. Thus, we showed how TRAEV predictions could guide strain development. TRAEV can be integrated into computational strain design workflows across microbial strains, desired metabolic traits, and application environments. Ultimately, model-predicted evolutionary robustness of desired metabolic traits can guide both strain and process development and help enhancing the economic attractiveness of industrial applications using microbial cells.

papers.title: KmerSignificance score: A discriminative and biologically informed framework for viral k-mer prioritization.
papers.authors: Lebatteux D, Corso F, Soudeyns H, Boucoiran I, Gantt S, Baniré Diallo A.
papers.abstract: Distinguishing closely related viral strains requires identifying genomic regions where subtle sequence differences carry biological significance. While k-mer-based approaches offer computational efficiency for genome analysis, existing methods lack standardized frameworks for evaluating which k-mers are most informative. Current selection strategies focus primarily on statistical discriminative power without integrating biological context. We introduce KmerSignificance Score (KSS), a k-mer prioritization framework combining three components: an information-theoretic method measuring strain-distinguishing capacity, an optimized amino acid substitution matrix (MIYATA_EVO) for mutation impact assessment, and a protein characterization score derived from annotations and database cross-references retrieved through UniProt. All three component scores and the integrated KSS are bounded in [0,1] by construction, providing a common numerical scale for ranking positions within a dataset. The discriminative component achieved a mean F1 of 0.881, not significantly different from chi-squared (0.876), the strongest of eight baselines. Top-ranked selections from the discriminative component nonetheless differed from those produced by chi-squared, especially for SARS-CoV-2 and HIV-1. The MIYATA_EVO matrix, optimized using a genetic algorithm, increased the composite agreement score across eight amino acid characteristics by 28.4% over the original MIYATA matrix. Across 17,471 viral proteins, the protein characterization score tracked UniProt's five-level annotation score closely (Kendall's τ=0.775), as expected for measures drawing on overlapping annotation content. Within each level, the continuous score provided finer numerical resolution among proteins. Literature cross-referencing on SARS-CoV-2 (278,738 sequences, 19 Pango-derived lineage labels), HIV-1 (12,223 sequences, 15 subtype labels), and human cytomegalovirus (HCMV; 399-646 sequences, 4-8 locus-specific genotypes) found that the top-ranked k-mers reported here map to established variant-defining mutations, subtype-specific polymorphisms, and genotype markers. KSS provides a standardized framework for viral k-mer prioritization with potential applications in variant surveillance, molecular epidemiology, and functional annotation. The tool is available at https://github.com/bioinfoUQAM/KmerSignificanceScore.

papers.title: Evolutionary and dynamic constraints converge on a conserved coupling sector in thermally adapted GH1 β-glucosidases.
papers.authors: Zheng LT, Li Y, He X, Yang LT, Zhao DR, Liu MT, Sang P, Yang LQ.
papers.abstract: How protein sequences evolve to maintain functional conformational dynamics under thermal stress remains an important question in molecular evolution. Thermophilic enzymes are often considered to achieve stability primarily through enhanced structural rigidity, yet thermal adaptation may also involve the preservation or reorganization of correlated motions across the protein scaffold. Here, we compared three glycoside hydrolase family 1 β-glucosidases-BsBgl1A, 9UPT, and LQBG8-that share a conserved (β/α)8 TIM-barrel fold but display distinct optimal temperatures of approximately 45, 65, and 70 °C, respectively. By integrating comparative structural analysis, three independent 1 μs molecular dynamics simulations at 300, 325, and 350 K, neural relational inference of residue-level dynamic coupling, and family-level coevolutionary analysis, we identified distinct dynamic strategies associated with their thermal phenotypes. All three enzymes retained their global compactness and principal secondary-structure framework across the simulated temperatures, indicating that differences in RMSD and residue flexibility did not reflect large-scale unfolding. BsBgl1A showed the strongest temperature sensitivity, with increased structural deviation and residue mobility at 350 K. Its inferred interaction network exhibited a non-monotonic response, characterized by pronounced overcoupling at 325 K followed by reduced connectivity at 350 K. In contrast, 9UPT maintained relatively restrained residue dynamics and a highly reproducible coupling topology across temperatures. LQBG8 combined substantial local conformational flexibility with persistent long-range coupling and retained the highest directed network density at 350 K. Across the three enzymes, the βα5-βα7 region repeatedly emerged as a shared structural and dynamic center. Coevolutionary couplings were also enriched in TIM-barrel-associated regions that spatially converged on this sector. These findings indicate that thermal adaptation in GH1 β-glucosidases is not adequately explained by uniform structural rigidification. Instead, enzymes with the same conserved fold may adopt distinct organizations of correlated motion, while greater thermal adaptation is associated with the persistence or reorganization of a βα5-βα7-centered dynamic coupling pattern under elevated temperature. The correspondence between dynamic coupling and coevolutionary enrichment is consistent with long-term evolutionary constraint on this structural sector, although it does not establish direct selection on the network as an independent functional unit. Our results therefore provide a testable framework in which thermostability reflects a balance among local stabilization, regional flexibility, and the resilience of higher-order dynamic organization.

papers.title: Microsatellite expansion redirects chromatin modifiers to confer insect resistance to Bt bioinsecticides.
papers.authors: Ouyang C, Sun K, Wang F, Ye F, Zhu L, Dong L, Bai Y, Cheng Z, Wu M, Crickmore N, Zhou X, Zhang Y, Guo Z.
papers.abstract: Microsatellites are highly mutable genomic elements, yet their role in adaptive gene regulation in insects remains poorly understood. Here, we show that a tetranucleotide (ATGT) microsatellite expansion in the promoter of ABCC2, a key Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) toxin receptor gene, epigenetically silences its expression and confers resistance to Bt Cry1Ac toxin in Plutella xylostella (L.). Mechanistically, long repeats (≥27 units) in Cry1Ac-resistant strains preferentially recruit the histone methyltransferase E(z), promoting H3K27me2/3 deposition, chromatin compaction, and transcriptional silencing, whereas short repeats in susceptible strains maintain open chromatin through Tip60-mediated H4K5 acetylation. This repeat expansion alone is sufficient to repress ABCC2, thereby conferring Bt resistance, while repeat length, chromatin state, and associated phenotypes partially revert under relaxed selection. These findings define a previously uncharacterized cis-acting element dynamically orchestrating insecticide resistance-associated gene expression and identify microsatellite-driven chromatin remodeling as a general and plastic regulatory strategy underlying rapid xenobiotic-resistance evolution in insects.

papers.title: Uracil overload triggers global genome instability and dUTPdysgenesis.
papers.authors: Yin QL, He M, Zhang K, Li K, Wang Y, Ding WJ, Zhu Y, Ye C, Zheng DQ.
papers.abstract: Uracil accumulation in DNA is a pervasive threat to genomic integrity, yet the global dynamics of how uracil overload drives genome instability remain elusive. Using Saccharomyces cerevisiae strains with attenuated dUTPase (DUT1) expression, we mapped the landscapes of genomic alterations including point mutations, recombination, and aneuploidy. Deletion of the UNG1 suppressed most induced mutations and loss-of-heterozygosity (LOH), identifying base excision repair as the primary driver of genomic alterations, whereas aneuploidy directly depends on the persistence of intact genomic uracil. Mechanistically, beyond localized bypass of static AP sites by translesion synthesis polymerases, the massive influx of uracil lesions induces a repair bottleneck by depleting Ung1 and Apn1. This resource titration, coupled with downstream processing intermediates, primarily drives mutagenesis at heterologous nonthymine positions. Furthermore, persistent static AP sites preferentially stimulate homologous recombination sub-pathway that yield interstitial LOH, whereas Apn1-mediated processing channels recombination toward terminal LOH. Crucially, we define a novel post-zygotic isolation mechanism, dUTPdysgenesis, where parental wild-type Ung1 unleashes an immediate enzymatic shock against a uracil-preloaded genome upon mating, triggering G1-phase chromosomal shattering and mutations. Collectively, this study transitions the paradigm of uracil mutagenesis from localized errors to a global engine of genome instability, bridging nucleotide metabolism, DNA repair kinetics, and speciation barriers.

papers.title: Rice Expression Database (RED) 2.0: an updated rice database integrating diverse RNA expression profiles based on the telomere-to-telomere reference genome.
papers.authors: Wang Z, Li M, Chen M, Li Z, Yang D, Zou D, Zhang Z, Xu T.
papers.abstract: Rice Expression Database (RED) is a rice gene expression database derived from large-scale RNA-seq data across different tissues and experimental conditions. Here, we present RED 2.0 (https://ngdc.cncb.ac.cn/red) with significant updates and enhancements. Specifically, RED 2.0 contains 357 projects covering 6471 bulk RNA-seq experiments across 18 tissues and 78 single-cell RNA-seq experiments comprising 984 495 cells. All projects are further manually curated and grouped into diverse biological contexts, including abiotic stress, biotic stress, hormone, development, genotype, and anatomy. Notably, based on the telomere-to-telomere assembly of the Nipponbare genome, RED 2.0 incorporates comprehensive expression profiles for 57 359 protein-coding genes (67 818 transcripts), 16 522 long non-coding RNA genes (47 396 transcripts), and 79 007 circular RNAs. In addition, it is equipped with online tools for differential expression analysis, functional enrichment analysis, co-expression network construction, and genome browser. Collectively, RED 2.0 provides a comprehensive expression landscape for both coding and non-coding genes across diverse conditions, serving as an important resource for rice functional genomics and molecular breeding.

papers.title: HGVD: Human Genetic Variation Database update 2026 with sequencing of 4344 genetically diverse Japanese individuals.
papers.authors: Murakami Y, Higasa K.
papers.abstract: Population-scale genome resources remain biased toward European ancestry, limiting variant interpretation in underrepresented populations. Here, we expanded the Human Genetic Variation Database (HGVD), a free Japanese allele-frequency resource launched in 2013. HGVD v3.1 integrates 1209 exomes with whole-genome sequencing (WGS) data from 3135 Japanese individuals selected by principal component analysis (PCA) to span genetic diversity, providing aggregate variant statistics for 4344 individuals, 3248 genotyped individuals, and expression quantitative trait loci (eQTL) from 300 individuals. For research and clinical use, HGVD provides coordinated JBrowse-based browsers for GRCh37/hg19, GRCh38/hg38, and T2T-CHM13. The non-GRCh37 variant tracks were generated by liftOver from the GRCh37 call set. Variant frequencies, sample counts, and coverage are available across assemblies, whereas eQTL annotations are currently available only on hg19. A downloadable, graph-genome-ready structural-variant release is provided, and the new pathSTR portal reports population-level distributions for 68 medically relevant tandem-repeat loci, derived by applying STRdust to long-read Oxford Nanopore data from 1019 individuals of the 1000 Genomes Project remapped to T2T-CHM13. HGVD v3.1 supports population-matched interpretation of rare pathogenic and pharmacogenomic variants, comparison of repeat-expansion alleles with long-read reference distributions, and structural-variant-aware reference construction, supporting precision medicine for Japan and East Asian populations. HGVD is available at https://www.hgvd.genome.med.kyoto-u.ac.jp/.

papers.title: OSCAR: an omics atlas of paired single-cell ATAC-seq and RNA-seq for decoding cell-specific gene regulation.
papers.authors: Song C, Zhou Y, Feng C, Dai X, Xiao J, Fan X, Wang K, Xiao P, Zheng Y, Luo W, Li C, Wang Q.
papers.abstract: Paired single-cell chromatin accessibility and transcriptome profiles provide a powerful framework for dissecting cell-specific regulatory programs underlying diverse biological processes and human diseases. The rapid accumulation of paired single-cell assay for transposase-accessible chromatin sequencing (scATAC-seq) and single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data has led to an urgent need to comprehensively integrate these data to illustrate the regulatory landscape at single-cell resolution. To address this need, we developed OSCAR (an Omics atlas of paired Single-Cell ATAC and RNA-seq, https://bio.liclab.net/OSCAR/) to curate large-scale paired scATAC-seq and scRNA-seq data and to provide comprehensive regulatory annotations and analyses. The current version of OSCAR catalogs 7749 898 human cells from 1136 samples across 30 tissue types. Importantly, OSCAR integrates paired scATAC-seq and scRNA-seq profiles for joint cell clustering and peak-to-gene linkage identification, and provides detailed (epi)genetic annotations for marker peaks and regulatory elements of marker genes, including super-enhancers, enhancers, enhancer RNAs (eRNAs), common and risk single nucleotide polymorphisms, expression quantitative trait loci, transcription factor binding sites, transcription factor/transcription co-factor binding peaks, Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats (CRISPR)/Cas9 target sites, DNase I hypersensitivity sites, chromatin accessibility regions, DNA methylation sites, chromatin interaction regions, and topologically associating domains. Furthermore, OSCAR provides three online analysis tools, including cell type enrichment analysis, sequence-based peak regulatory analysis, and peak-to-gene linkage analysis. Hence, OSCAR is a useful platform to query, browse, analyze, and visualize cell-specific regulatory programs across diverse human tissues and diseases.

papers.title: CellMarker 3.0: an updated resource of manually curated and computationally predicted cell markers in human/mouse and interactive web tools for single-cell and spatial transcriptomics analysis.
papers.authors: Hu C, Li T, Zhu M, Li L, Ren B, Yang K, Wang Z, Li M, Qi B, Long Y, Lv N, Yang X, Fu R, Bai J, Li X, Zhang Y.
papers.abstract: The updated CellMarker 3.0 resource (http://bio-bigdata.hrbmu.edu.cn/CellMarker) offers a comprehensive resource, integrating experimentally validated and robustly algorithm-predicted marker genes for diverse cell types across human and mouse tissues. In addition, web tools for analyzing single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) and spatial transcriptomics (ST) data are described. CellMarker 3.0 was updated with more data and new features, including (i) appending 274 tissues, 1877 cell types, 64 040 markers, and 1 245 923 tissue-cell type-marker entries over the previous version. The current release contains 930 tissues, 4455 cell types, and 90 955 cell markers, resulting in a total of 1 329 284 tissue-cell type-marker entries. (ii) Expanding the resource to include computationally predicted cell-type markers derived from six algorithms, namely Spapros, Seurat::FindAllMarkers, SEMITONES, Cepo, CelliD, and COSG. (iii) New marker information was incorporated from 168 sequencing technologies, such as CEL-Seq2 and SNARE-seq. (iv) Covering 35 types of cell markers, including protein-coding genes, rRNAs, and pseudogenes. (v) The cell tool module was comprehensively restructured and upgraded, with the original six scRNA-seq analysis modules systematically optimized and two new spatial transcriptomics modules, Spatial Expression, and Spatial Chat, added. CellMarker 3.0 is a valuable resource that integrates cell identity identification, single-cell transcriptomics, and spatial transcriptomics analysis.

papers.title: Urbanisation drives parallel genomic divergence across cities and bumble bee species.
papers.authors: Theodorou P, Paxton RJ.
papers.abstract: Background Urbanisation imposes pervasive environmental change, yet it remains unclear whether evolutionary responses to cities are largely idiosyncratic or whether similar selective pressures across cities repeatedly generate predictable genomic outcomes. Results Here, we analyse whole-genome data from 524 individuals of three widespread bumble bee species sampled across nine independent urban-rural pairs in Central Europe to test whether urban environments drive parallel evolutionary responses across cities and species. Genetic diversity responded idiosyncratically to urbanisation, with two species showing no detectable urban-rural differences and one species exhibiting reduced diversity in cities, consistent with species-specific ecological traits and habitat requirements. Despite weak population structure and high gene flow in all species, we detected consistent and replicated genomic divergence associated with urban environments. Genome-environment association analyses revealed parallel allele-frequency shifts at the same loci across independent cities for each species, while selective sweep scans identified repeated signals of positive selection in urban populations. Across species, urban-associated divergence was highly polygenic and occurred predominantly in non-coding regions with potential regulatory roles. Although the specific genes involved were largely species-specific, functional enrichment analyses revealed strong convergence across species, particularly in pathways related to physiological stress responses, neurocognitive and behavioural processes, metabolism and immunity. Conclusions Together, these results suggest that urban environments can impose recurrent selective pressures, generating predictable and parallel genomic responses across cities and species despite ongoing gene flow. More broadly, our findings highlight polygenic, potentially regulatory adaptation as an important component of evolutionary responses to urban environments.

papers.title: Extracting candidate motif patterns for multiple RNA modifications using direct RNA sequencing.
papers.authors: Alagna N, Miedema J, Basiony Y, Gerber S.
papers.abstract: RNA modifications have emerged as key regulators of virtually all aspects of RNA biology, driving growing interest in computational approaches for their transcriptome-wide detection. For some RNA modifications, the search space can be reduced by exploiting characteristic sequence motifs, as exemplified by the canonical DRACH motif associated with m⁶A. However, comparable sequence preferences remain largely unknown for most other RNA modifications, making systematic motif discovery considerably more challenging. Here, we applied exponential population analysis to direct RNA sequencing data from HEK293T cells and peripheral human blood to identify candidate motif patterns for pseudouridine (Ψ), inosine (I), and 5-methylcytosine (m⁵C). Our results demonstrate that exponential population analysis provides a systematic framework for identifying candidate motif patterns from nanopore-derived RNA modification predictions, thereby prioritizing sequence contexts for future biological validation.

papers.authors: Zhu X, Lu J, Lu Y, Zhang Y, Feng F.
