papers.title: Multiproperty optimization of therapeutic antibodies through sequence editing via large language model and reinforcement learning.
papers.authors: Qiu M, Wang Z, Liu X, Wang H, Hua Q, Shu Q, Luo S, Niu M, Ma F, Huang F, Wang Y, Xiong Z, Zhang W.
papers.abstract: Discovering antibodies with multiple beneficial properties is essential for therapeutic drug development, but experimentally identified antibodies require further optimization. Joint optimization remains challenging because sequence space is vast, annotations are sparse and property tradeoffs are common. Herein, we propose AbOptimizer, a reinforcement learning framework for multiproperty antibody optimization through parallel multisite sequence editing. AbOptimizer identifies promising editing sites and edit actions, including 'reservation', 'substitution' and optional 'insertion' or 'deletion', before recommending mutations from protein language models, while surrogate evaluation and Pareto rewards shape policy training. We evaluate AbOptimizer on three therapeutic antibodies across multiproperty, data-limited and indel-inclusive optimization. In silico, AbOptimizer improves optimized properties and outperforms baseline methods. In vitro, selected variants show affinity-specificity co-optimization for emibetuzumab, improved affinity and specificity with largely maintained thermal stability for siltuximab, and indel-inclusive affinity optimization for trastuzumab. These results validate AbOptimizer as a practical framework for therapeutic antibody optimization.

papers.title: Emergence of chiral multi-armed spirals in an open system of migrating cells under continuous cell supply.
papers.authors: Hayakawa M, Bhattacherjee B, Kuwayama H, Shibata T.
papers.abstract: From molecular assemblies to multicellular tissues, chirality organizes living and active-matter systems into striking collective states. Across cellular collectives and active materials, weak microscopic chiral cues in motion and interaction can systematically skew how constituents coordinate, flow, and break spatial symmetries. Yet the principles that govern chiral ordering in open systems, where elements are continuously supplied and removed, remain poorly understood. Here, we show that chemotaxis-deficient Dictyostelium discoideum mutants (KI cells) form centimeter-scale, clockwise, multi-armed spirals. Each arm is a traveling band produced by short-range alignment interactions and guided by a polar-ordered rotating core that encircles the cell source. A subtle clockwise bias in single-cell migration is amplified by collective ordering into tissue-scale chirality. To uncover the minimal ingredients, we developed an open chiral Vicsek model and found that intrinsic chirality, polar alignment, and continuous cell supply are the key factors. Our study establishes a general route by which weak microscopic chirality and sustained material flux generate macroscopic chiral order, offering new insight into chiral patterning in multicellular systems.

papers.title: Single-cell landscape of human adipose tissue reveals THBS1 as a potential driver of fibro-inflammation in metabolic disease.
papers.authors: Jung J, Park ES, Lee NK, Lee JJ, Juang U, Huang Q, Park YS, Kim HJ, Kim JK, Oh TJ, Suh JM, Kim JB, Moon JH, Kim JK, Choi SH.
papers.abstract: The cellular complexity of adipose tissue plays a critical role in the pathogenesis of metabolic disease; however, mechanisms underlying adipose dysfunction remain poorly understood. Here, we constructed a single-nucleus and bulk transcriptomic atlas of human visceral adipose tissues from an ethnically homogeneous cohort with defined metabolic states: lean with normal glucose tolerance, obesity, and obesity with type 2 diabetes. Single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) revealed a fibro-inflammatory subpopulation of adipose stem cells and adipocytes characterized by high THBS1 expression, which were enriched in individuals with obesity and obesity with type 2 diabetes compared to lean controls. Through complementary in vitro (human primary ASCs, THP-1 macrophages, and Matrigel-captured mature adipocytes), ex vivo (mouse and human visceral adipose tissue explants), and in vivo (gain-of-function and antibody-mediated neutralization) experiments, we demonstrated that THBS1 promoted adipose fibrosis and inflammation via macrophage-mediated TGFβ activation, impairing adipogenesis and adipocyte function. Inhibition of THBS1 attenuated fibro-inflammatory features in metabolically dysfunctional adipose tissues. Moreover, THBS1 levels in plasma and adipocytes correlated with metabolic traits, including BMI and HbA1c. Collectively, our study provides a cellular atlas of human visceral adipose tissues across metabolic disease states and identifies THBS1 as a key pathogenic driver and potential therapeutic target.

papers.title: SureChEMBL in 2026: an open database of chemical and biomedical annotations from the patent literature.
papers.authors: Bosc N, Kizilören T, Félix E, Arsalan M, Moreno-Vélez CA, Webster J, Arcila R, Adasme MF, Ismail I, Nowotka M, Zavarin Y, Magariños MP, Falaguera MJ, Gaulton A, Hersey A, Leach AR, Zdrazil B, O'Boyle NM.
papers.abstract: The patent literature is a major source of scientific and technical information for drug discovery, often disclosing chemical structures, biological targets, therapeutic indications, and structure-activity relationships before they appear in the scientific literature. However, patent documents are difficult to analyse at scale because of their volume, legal and technical language, heterogeneous formats, and frequent use of nonmachine-readable representations for chemical structures. Since 2015, SureChEMBL has provided open access to chemical information automatically extracted from patent documents. Here, we present a major redesign of the SureChEMBL resource. The updated platform is built on a modern architecture and includes redesigned extraction, chemistry registration, search and data-delivery workflows, together with large-scale reprocessing of the historical corpus through a unified standardization pipeline. SureChEMBL also introduces automatically generated biomedical annotations for genes, proteins, diseases, and mechanisms, linking patent chemistry to biological context. The resource currently contains 122 million patents, 44 million chemically annotated documents, 31 million chemical structures, and 1 million biomedical entity annotations, accessible through https://www.surechembl.org/, an API and the downloadable Bulk Data.

papers.title: KEGG for characterizing genomes and pathways in the biosphere.
papers.authors: Kanehisa M, Furumichi M, Sato Y, Matsuura Y, Ishiguro-Watanabe M.
papers.abstract: The KEGG database (https://www.kegg.jp) has been developed as a model of the biological systems. By organizing knowledge of cellular and organism-level functions in the form of molecular wiring diagrams, the model enables generating new knowledge and finding practical applications. The KO (KEGG Orthology) dataset plays the basic role of organizing knowledge. KO is an ortholog with functional relevance, generalizing experimental evidence in specific organisms to other organisms. KEGG molecular networks, including pathway maps and modules, are generic networks with KOs as network nodes, and thus KEGG mapping from genomes to pathways can be applied to any organism. As the number of KOs increases and the KO annotation rate improves, KEGG mapping is further expanded. A set of KOs in the genome and a set of modules in the metabolic pathways are now used to characterize various data objects in the biosphere, including organisms, organism groups, microbiomes, viruses, and their combinations, such as endosymbiont-host, microbiome-host, and virus-host relationships. Furthermore, a simple measure of similarity either by KO compositions or module compositions is introduced to compare organism groups. The resulting similarity dendrograms possibly reflect similarity of cellular functions or, more specifically, metabolic functions, which can be compared with phylogenetic trees.

papers.title: SynBioFooDB: a comprehensive resource for synthetic biology-driven food biomanufacturing.
papers.authors: Wei F, Deng X, Li H, Wang R, Mao Z, Mao Y, Liu Y, Niu Q, Qin Y, Du J, Liao X, Bai Y, Yuan Q, Ma H.
papers.abstract: Enabled by synthetic biology and metabolic engineering, microbial biomanufacturing is reshaping the production of food-related compounds by offering sustainable alternatives to resource-intensive extraction and conventional chemical synthesis. However, information linking food-related compounds to biosynthetic pathways and microbial biomanufacturing evidence remains fragmented across the literature and poorly represented in existing food-oriented resources, hindering cross-study comparison, evidence synthesis, and rational design of microbial production systems. Here, we present SynBioFooDB (https://synbiofoodb.biodesign.ac.cn/), a knowledgebase dedicated to synthetic biology-driven food biomanufacturing. SynBioFooDB integrates 74 237 food-related compounds with standardized chemical identities and annotations covering food occurrence, bioactivity, toxicity, and regulatory information. It further provides expert-curated biomanufacturing evidence for 1054 compounds from 5592 publications, linking microbial hosts, substrates, genetic modifications, and quantitative production metrics through structured and traceable records. The database also contains 2002 literature-reported biosynthetic pathways for 971 compounds, enabling comparison of alternative precursors, enzyme combinations, and pathway architectures. For compounds without literature-reported pathways, SynBioFooDB provides computationally predicted candidate pathways to facilitate pathway prioritization and experimental evaluation. By integrating compound-level context, biomanufacturing evidence, and biosynthetic pathway information, SynBioFooDB supports systematic exploration, comparison, and rational design of microbial production strategies for food-related compounds.

papers.title: PED in 2027: integrating experimental and predicted protein conformational ensembles at scale.
papers.authors: Monzon AM, Ghafouri H, Castro XA, Khezrian S, Aspromonte MC, Singla K, Barethiya S, Bernadó P, Bonomi M, Chen J, Cordeiro T, Cortés J, De Castro S, Emenecker R, Feig M, Forman-Kay JD, Head-Gordon T, Holehouse A, Janson G, Lindorff-Larsen K, Liu ZH, Longhi S, Pajkos M, Robustelli P, Rodriguez S, Schnapka V, Sibille N, Vendruscolo M, Tosatto SCE.
papers.abstract: The Protein Ensemble Database (PED; https://proteinensemble.org) is the primary deposition resource for structural ensembles of intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) and intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs). PED 2027 (released in September 2026) substantially expands its scope by integrating ensembles determined or refined using experimental data with clearly identified collections of computational predictions. The release introduces a multi-method collection targeting 3319 DisProt proteins and 2452 manually curated disordered regions, together with AlphaFlex ensembles for 10 022 human proteins containing IDRs. Alternative predictions for the same sequence are retained as independent records with method-specific provenance, enabling comparison across ensemble-generation approaches. A scalable deposition workflow accommodates individual experimental studies and proteome-scale collections while preserving quality control and curator oversight. The PED controlled vocabulary standardizes experimental data acquisition, computational generation, selection, and refinement. Precomputed IDPEnsembleTools and CIDER analyses provide structural and sequence-derived descriptors directly on ensemble pages. A redesigned interface and extended REST API support discovery, visualization, download and programmatic access. Interoperability with UniProt, DisProt, MobiDB, and experimental-data repositories connects ensembles with sequences, annotations, and supporting measurements. PED 2027 therefore provides an interoperable, analysis-ready platform for studying IDP/IDR conformational behaviour.

papers.title: VarNexus: an integrative database for interpreting disease-associated regulatory variants through multimodal predictions and functional evidence.
papers.authors: Gong L, Tan C, Zhang J, Shu R, Guo S, Xiao T, Shi J, Wang J, Ni T, Ding R.
papers.abstract: Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified numerous loci associated with complex diseases and traits, yet the functional interpretation of non-coding risk variants remains challenging. Sequence-to-function models like AlphaGenome provide large-scale multi-modal predictions of variant effects, but their predictions lack direct experimental support. In contrast, empirical resources such as molecular quantitative trait loci (QTLs) and massively parallel reporter assays (MPRAs) offer population-based or experimental support for variant function, but suffer from limited genomic coverage. Here, we present VarNexus (https://biomed.imu.edu.cn/varnexus), an integrative resource for connecting disease-associated variants with predicted, population-based, and experimental evidence. VarNexus currently contains 230 404 fine-mapped candidate variants across 1891 disease-related phenotypes from UK Biobank and FinnGen. It integrates precomputed AlphaGenome predictions across 11 regulatory output types with bulk and single-cell xQTLs, MPRA measurements, and GWAS-eQTL colocalization results. VarNexus enables cross-linked searches by variant, phenotype, and gene, together with on-demand AlphaGenome prediction, multi-omics genome-browser visualization, and regulatory network exploration. By combining sequence-based predictions with population-based and experimental evidence, VarNexus provides a framework for prioritizing candidate regulatory mechanisms supported by multiple evidence layers.

papers.title: OmniVira: a knowledgebase of source-linked evidence on viral spillover and cross-species transmission.
papers.authors: Zhao P, Han Y, Jin Q, Yang F, Wu Z.
papers.abstract: Zoonotic viral emergence poses persistent challenges to global health, yet evidence relevant to spillover and cross-species transmission is dispersed across surveillance, epidemiological, experimental, mechanistic, and genomic studies. Here, we present OmniVira (https://omnivira.org/), a curated knowledgebase that transforms literature-derived findings into structured, traceable, and reusable OmniVira Evidence (OVE) records. OmniVira implements an auditable article-evidence framework linking individual findings and supporting text to normalized virus, host, and geographic entities, and relevant biological context. A domain-specific ontology organizes 14 evidence types into five categories: Zoonotic Surveillance, Transmission Evidence, Experimental Infection, Functional Mechanism, and Genomic Evolution. The platform integrates ontology-guided curation, large language model-assisted literature screening and candidate extraction, automated consistency checks, and curator review of flagged or ambiguous records, enabling daily updates. As of 4 August 2026, OmniVira contained 8072 publicly retrievable OVE records derived from 2623 source articles, spanning 60 ICTV virus families, 55 host orders, and 121 countries. Its responsive interface supports evidence-centred retrieval, source-text verification, and exploration of linked virus-host-literature relationships across desktop and mobile browsers. OmniVira provides a transparent, context-preserving resource for systematic comparison and synthesis of evidence related to zoonotic viral emergence and cross-species transmission.

papers.title: ArthroVerse: mapping protein family diversity across arthropod-associated microbiomes.
papers.authors: Chasapi IN, Aplakidou E, Chasapi MN, Lamari E, Galaras A, Diplari S, Iliopoulos I, Emiris IZ, Georgakopoulos-Soares I, Patalano S, Stravopodis DJ, Karatzas E, Baltoumas FA, Kyrpides NC, Pavlopoulos GA.
papers.abstract: Metagenomic studies of arthropod-associated microbiomes have generated vast amounts of sequence data, yet the functional and structural organization of these proteins remains largely unexplored. Here, we present ArthroVerse, the first comprehensive database of protein families derived from arthropod-associated metagenomes. Non-redundant protein families were generated after rigorous filtering, deduplication, and clustering. The protein families were further annotated with microbial taxonomy, host associations, protein structural information, and carbohydrate-active enzymes predictions. The resulting dataset integrates both metagenomic and reference genome-derived proteins, enabling systematic exploration of functional diversity, evolutionary relationships, and host-microbe interactions in insect microbiomes. ArthroVerse provides a valuable resource for the study of microbial ecology and arthropod physiology, offering unprecedented insight into the protein landscape of insect-associated microbial communities. ArthroVerse is publicly accessible at https://envofams.org/arthroverse/.

papers.title: Omni-ARMD: an integrated genomic and clinical knowledgebase bridging clinical phenotypes and molecular determinants of antimicrobial resistance.
papers.authors: Tang H, Xie X, Zheng S, Wang L, Yao R, Ding X, Tian GB, Li W.
papers.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a major global health threat, yet its molecular determinants remain difficult to characterize in real-world settings, as genomic and clinical data are fragmented across resources. Existing databases typically separate gene-level mechanisms, curated genotype-phenotype associations, and large-scale clinical antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) data, limiting cross-scale interpretation. Here, we present Omni-ARMD, an open-access knowledgebase that integrates multi-source genomic and clinical data to systematically infer genotype-phenotype relationships in AMR. Omni-ARMD bridges large-scale clinical AST records and gene-level resistance evidence through a confidence-weighted log-odds enrichment framework, which quantifies genotype-phenotype associations at the organism-antimicrobial level and integrates these associations into aggregated cross-domain evidence representations. The current release includes over 12 million de-identified microbiology records from more than 1 million patients, harmonized to generate over 7.83 million standardized AST records. It also integrates over 0.36 million gene-phenotype associations, spanning 38 organisms, 52 antimicrobials, and 375 resistance genes. Omni-ARMD links over 5.16 million clinical records to genomic evidence, achieving a 65.86% match rate and a 2.61% coverage of organism-antimicrobial pairs. Omni-ARMD provides interactive modules for clinical investigation, genomic evidence analysis, mechanistic interpretation, and artificial intelligence-assisted exploration, enabling integrative and data-driven discovery in AMR. Omni-ARMD is freely available at www.omniarmd.cn.

papers.title: Cell3D: a comprehensive database for interactive 3D visualization and crosstalk analysis of single-cell and spatial omics.
papers.authors: Liu Q, He Y, Sun R, Wang B, Cui R, Shan X, Xu B, Xu Z, Zhang X, Gao Y, Ning S, Wang L, Wang P, Guo Q.
papers.abstract: Single-cell and spatial transcriptomics yield large-scale, high-dimensional datasets. However, cross-feature integrative exploration is constrained, since most current platforms support a single data type and lack interactive visualization for multi-feature analysis. To address this unmet need, we developed Cell3D, an accessible and versatile interactive platform designed to advance integrative multi-level feature analysis. Cell3D curates 898 publicly available datasets, comprising 397 single-cell and 501 spatial transcriptomic datasets, encompassing 2 924 646 single cells and spatial spots across 105 diseases, 756 cell types, and 83 organs/tissues from 11 species. The database integrates twelve mainstream functional annotation systems, providing a comprehensive landscape for dissecting molecular features across spatial and cellular dimensions. Users can explore data at multiple levels, from gene expression and cell clusters to pathway activities and clinical phenotypes. Cell3D offers a suite of user-friendly functionalities, including customizable 2D/3D interactive visualization for dynamic multi-level feature projection, flexible data integration with automatic recognition, quantitative crosstalk analysis, and microenvironment-focused integrative analysis supporting disease research and biomarker discovery. Collectively, Cell3D enables exploration of tissue microenvironments at both cellular and spatial resolutions, bridging molecular perturbations and tissue architecture in health and disease. The database is freely accessible at https://bio-bigdata.hrbmu.edu.cn/Cell3D.

papers.title: Chromosome-scale genome assembly and annotation of Octodon degus.
papers.authors: Chiu JH, Zemke NR, Gao X, Garduño M, Yang B, Oakes ML, Bartosik WM, Wong K, Pezo-Valderrama P, Xie Y, Urra C, Macias-Velasco JF, Tomlinson C, Cogram P, Xu X, Ren B.

papers.title: Integration-free and cluster-free detection of localized differential gene coexpression in single-cell data with DiCoLo.
papers.authors: Li R, Yang J, Su PC, Jaffe A, Lindenbaum O, Kluger Y.

papers.title: Calsequestrin localization at RyR2 clusters enables calcium wave propagation in ventricular myocytes.
papers.authors: Conesa D, Echebarria B, Hove-Madsen L, Shiferaw Y, Alvarez-Lacalle E.
papers.abstract: Intracellular calcium waves in cardiac myocytes propagate through a fire-diffuse-fire mechanism in which calcium released from one RyR2 cluster diffuses to neighboring clusters and triggers their activation. Yet propagation faces a fundamental physical difficulty: the calcium signal must cross distances of 1-2 μm between Z-planes while being attenuated by cytosolic buffering and diffusion, and at the same time the release site depletes its local sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium store. How waves propagate efficiently despite these constraints has remained unclear. We developed a three-dimensional computational model of mouse ventricular myocytes at submicrometer resolution to address this question. Our central finding is that co-localization of calsequestrin2 (CASQ2) with RyR2 clusters is required for robust wave propagation. In a physiological model, where CASQ2 is concentrated at release sites as observed experimentally, calcium waves propagate reliably across the cell with velocities that match the experimental range. In contrast, when CASQ2 is distributed uniformly throughout the sarcoplasmic reticulum, keeping total CASQ2 unchanged, the wavefront stalls. These results identify CASQ2-RyR2 co-localization as a key structural requirement for effective calcium wave propagation in ventricular myocytes.

papers.title: An integrative computational approach for obstacle avoidance during action selection.
papers.authors: Zhong S, Pouratian N, Schrater P, Christopoulos V.
papers.abstract: Action selection in cluttered environments, where individuals must simultaneously pursue goals and avoid obstacles, presents a significant challenge for the brain. To understand the underlying mechanisms of action selection in such contexts, we propose a computational model that extends stochastic optimal control theory through a novel framework for obstacle avoidance. The model decomposes action selection into a weighted combination of individual control policies, each generated for either target approach or obstacle avoidance. By integrating value information from goals, obstacles, and actions into a unified measure of "relative desirability", the model dynamically determines the contribution of each policy to the overall action selection process. We evaluated the framework using simulated target-reaching tasks in cluttered environments based on previous human studies. The results showed that the model qualitatively captures key features of human motor behavior, including the influence of obstacle properties on movement trajectories and the transient tendency to initiate movements toward obstacles before avoidance. This work offers new insights into the dynamic interaction between approach and avoidance behaviors, providing a basis for future studies of action selection in more complex and naturalistic settings.

papers.title: Thirteen quick tips for bacteriophage genome annotation.
papers.authors: Zaki BM, Bouras G, Kropinski AM, Wattam AR, Edwards RA, Aziz RK.

papers.title: Genomic in vitro transcription and Nanopore direct RNA sequencing of a human B-Lymphocyte cell line.
papers.authors: Tzadikario T, Akeson S, Dorer S, Esfahani NG, Stein AJ, Kakhaki PD, Choudhary U, Amar K, Jain M.

papers.title: SSAlign: fast and sensitive protein structure search at scale.
papers.authors: Wang L, Zhang X, Wang Y, Xue Z.
papers.abstract: Motivation Predicted protein structure resources now contain hundreds of millions of models, turning structural comparison from a pairwise alignment task into a database-scale retrieval problem. Exhaustive structural aligners are computationally impractical at this scale, whereas fast structural-alphabet searches may discard remote or low-complexity homologs during prefiltering. Database-scale search therefore requires methods that combine rapid retrieval with sensitivity to global structural similarity. Results We present SSAlign, a protein structure search method that integrates SaProt sequence-structure embeddings, entropy-reduced dense retrieval, an SS-score predictor, and two-stage alignment refinement. In benchmarks on the Swiss-Prot, SCOPe40, and AFDB50 datasets, SSAlign showed competitive alignment quality and returned more TM-align-supported hits than Foldseek in recall-oriented evaluations. On AFDB50, 1000 queries against 53.7 million structures completed in 3150 s on CPUs and 2290 s with GPU prefiltering, corresponding to 103-fold and 142-fold speedups over Foldseek, respectively. On SCOPe40, SSAlign increased the area under the curve (AUC) by 20.2% at family level and 33.3% at superfamily level. In simple-fold antimicrobial peptide case studies, SSAlign retrieved candidates that were not returned by Foldseek under the tested settings, indicating its utility as a fast candidate-generation tool for proteome-scale structural search. Availability and implementation The source code for SSAlign is publicly available at https://github.com/ISYSLAB-HUST/SSAlign. The software version and test data used in this study are archived on Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23432919. Datasets and prebuilt indices can be downloaded from http://bioinfo.isyslab.info/ssalign/download/section/ssalign/.

papers.title: Neuronal DNA repair mediates systemic mitochondrial maintenance through acetylcholine signaling.
papers.authors: da Silva PFL, Ropert B, Mares D, Rieckher M, Rive C, Schumacher B.
papers.abstract: DNA repair defects such as nucleotide excision repair (NER) mutations can lead to progeroid syndromes characterized by growth retardation and accelerated aging with distinct tissue type specific pathologies. DNA-damage-induced dysfunction of specific cell types can impair the organism's overall function. It is unknown whether, in reverse, DNA repair in specific tissues can have non-cell-autonomous consequences on other tissues carrying DNA damage. To explore the organismal consequences of cell-type-specific DNA repair, we restricted NER activity to specific tissues and monitored consequences on organismal health in Caenorhabditis elegans. Unexpectedly, we observed that tissue-specific DNA repair is sufficient to improve overall DNA damage resistance. Strikingly, NER activity restricted to neurons only is sufficient to provide similar overall DNA damage resistance as whole-body NER in almost all tissues tested. We show that this systemic DNA damage resilience is mediated by neuronal acetylcholine signaling that promotes the maintenance of mitochondrial activity throughout the organism.

papers.title: Structural basis for coupled DNA replication and uracil repair by a family of DNA polymerases from phages with T-modified genomes.
papers.authors: Missoury S, Lucas-Staat S, Sieskind R, Delarue M.
papers.abstract: Replicative DNA polymerases (DNAPs) play a critical role in genome duplication, ensuring the accurate transmission of genetic information in all domains of life. DNAPs are also essential for DNA viruses, as well as bacteriophages, where a uracil-DNA glycosylase (UDG) is often encoded in trans or is present in the DNAP gene. Here, we identify a new group of A-family DNAPs in phages that are fused to an active UDG domain and contain other large insertions. Several members of this subfamily, including phages SP-15 and YerA41, are known to be hypermodified on their thymidine base through glycosylation of a linker attached to the C5 position of thymine. We determined the atomic cryo-EM structures for two of its members in various active functional and conformational states, from YerA41 and phiLo phages. The structures reveal how these large DNAPs function as replicative DNAPs, and how they can recognize dU bases ahead of the replication fork through their UDG domain, generating abasic sites that are preferentially bypassed through dA incorporation. Such dU errors would need to be eliminated to preserve phage genome integrity. Additionally, we report the co-occurrence of both an X-family DNAP and a DNA ligase in the corresponding phage genomes and show that both enzymes can execute the final steps of base excision repair most probably on-the-fly during replication, revealing a DNA-replication-coupled repair process. The structures of these large polymerases can serve as a model of other large platform DNAPs that can recruit additional enzymatic activities necessary for phage or virus survival.

papers.title: SMARTFlexDB: a paired apo-holo RNA structure database and analysis platform for RNA conformational flexibility and small-molecule recognition.
papers.authors: Jiang S, Wei J, Taghavi A, Seabra G, Childs-Disney JL, Li C, Disney MD, Li Y.
papers.abstract: RNA structures can undergo substantial conformational changes upon small-molecule binding, yet existing structural resources provide only static RNA-ligand snapshots without connecting ligand-bound (holo) RNA structures to corresponding ligand-free (apo) conformations. SMARTFlexDB is a curated database and analysis platform that uses paired apo-holo RNA structures to characterize conformational differences and RNA-small molecule recognition. Candidate pairs were identified from the Protein Data Bank by matching RNA chains with at least 90% sequence identity and coverage, and fully conserved binding pocket nucleotides. The current release contains 434 binding pockets from 266 holo structures, linked to 186 apo structures to yield 1187 pocket-level apo-holo pairs organized into 734 database entries, spanning 150 small molecules and 23 RNA functional classes. Each entry integrates RNA sequence and secondary-structure annotations, apo and holo three-dimensional structures, RNA-ligand atomic interactions, and quantitative descriptors of global and local conformational changes. An interactive web interface enables users to explore sequence alignments and structural overlays, compare secondary structures and RNA motifs, and upload paired apo-holo structures for customized analysis. By linking ligand-bound and ligand-free RNA structures, SMARTFlexDB provides a robust foundation for investigating RNA structural flexibility and supporting RNA-targeted small-molecule drug discovery. The database and analysis platform are available at https://aidd.rc.ufl.edu/app/smartflexdb/.

papers.title: SpatialRegNet: spatially resolved mapping of active regulatory network of human and mouse.
papers.authors: Li F, Fan W, Kang A, Liu W, Qi Q, Zha Z, Pei L, Tian F, Zhang Y, Xu Y.
papers.abstract: The spatial microenvironment and cellular functional states are governed by spatiotemporally dynamic gene regulatory networks (GRNs), making their dissection essential for understanding disease pathogenesis and normal tissue programs. Despite the rapid development of multiple spatial transcriptomics databases, most lack systematic integration of intracellular GRNs and their spatial coupling patterns. Here, we present SpatialRegNet (https://bio-bigdata.hrbmu.edu.cn/SpatialRegNet/), a comprehensive database curating 1322 tissue slices derived from 152 human and mouse spatial transcriptomic datasets that span 68 tissue types and 93 distinct diseases or disease subtypes, encompassing 3 744 216 spatial spots. The database quantifies spot-level activity for 6733 transcription factor (TF)-mediated regulon networks, which collectively contain over 12.7 million TF-target gene pairs, and archives 802 935 regulon networks that are highly active in distinct spatial niches/cell types. SpatialRegNet embeds a suite of interactive online tools for analyzing regulon networks in spatial contexts, enabling users to interrogate the correlations between regulon network activity and cellular identities, map spatial regulatory heterogeneity and specificity, track dynamic regulon network activity across cell differentiation trajectories, reconstruct intercellular communication signaling cascades, and generate three-dimensional visualizations of regulon network activity. Collectively, SpatialRegNet constitutes a valuable public resource to advance mechanistic investigations of physiological tissue function, disease etiology, and biomarker discovery in spatially resolved GRNs.

papers.title: LncACTdb 4.0: an updated resource of experimentally supported ceRNA interactions and multi-level regulatory networks for precision oncology.
papers.authors: Guo Q, Liu Q, He Y, Zhang X, Xu Z, Sun R, Wang B, Shan X, Xu B, Gao Y, Ning S, Zhi H, Wang P.
papers.abstract: Non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs) can function as competing endogenous RNAs (ceRNAs) to sequester microRNAs, assembling complex regulatory networks that exert critical roles in diverse diseases. Although experimentally validated ceRNA interactions have rapidly accumulated, few resources systematically curate disease-associated ceRNA networks across multi-scale biological contexts. Here, we present LncACTdb 4.0 (https://bio-bigdata.hrbmu.edu.cn/LncACTdb), an updated repository housing manually curated, experimentally supported ceRNA interactions and multi-level regulatory networks for precision oncology. This release includes major data expansions: 15 008 high-confidence ceRNA-disease associations, 18 974 cancer-related biomarkers, as well as transcriptomic profiles from >60 000 individuals and ∼600 000 single cells covering 69 tissues. It implements a four-tier data architecture spanning tissue, cell line, organoid, and single-cell levels and provides a panel of 12 web-based tools to perform bulk-cohort, single-sample, and single-cell ceRNA analyses, with specialized single-cell modules supporting quantification, clustering, trajectory reconstruction, and cell-state annotation. Featuring a user-friendly interface and integrative analytical utilities, LncACTdb 4.0 enables investigation of ceRNA regulatory mechanisms ranging from tissue architecture to cellular resolution and facilitates biomarker mining for precision oncology research.

papers.title: Sequence-specific targeting of GC-rich gene loci by parallel triplex-forming oligonucleotides containing a modified nucleobase.
papers.authors: Ma R, Brazzill M, Justice D, Buckham N, Chen C, Hoshika S, Benner SA, Rusling DA.
papers.abstract: Targeting GC-rich gene loci is a major challenge owing to their high duplex stability, repetitive sequence composition, and propensity to adopt alternative DNA structures. Triplex-forming oligonucleotides (TFOs) provide a programmable strategy toward the recognition of GC-rich DNA, but their application is restricted by the limited recognition capabilities of natural nucleobases in a cellular setting. Here, we overcome this barrier using parallel-binding TFOs containing the synthetic nucleobase 6-amino-5-nitropyridin-2-one (Z), which enables pH-independent recognition of G-C base pairs. Using two structurally distinct regulatory elements within the MYC promoter, we show that Z-modified TFOs form stable, sequence-selective triplexes that repress promoter activity by 50%-80% in both episomal reporter assays and at endogenous gene loci. Notably, the greatest repression was observed at a GC-rich quadruplex-forming element that functions as a structural hub for transcription factor recruitment. To our knowledge, this represents the first demonstration that a simple nucleobase modification alone is sufficient to enable parallel-binding TFOs to repress expression of an endogenous gene, establishing a general strategy for targeting GC-rich regulatory elements through programmable DNA recognition.

papers.title: Structural basis of DnaB ring opening by the ancestral helicase loader DciA.
papers.authors: Araújo-Bazán L, Arias-Palomo E.
papers.abstract: Ring-shaped helicases must be opened and loaded onto DNA to initiate genome replication. In bacteria, most species lack canonical AAA+ helicase loaders and instead rely on DciA, an evolutionarily conserved, ATP-independent factor whose mechanism has remained unclear. Here we define how DciA remodels the bacterial replicative helicase DnaB. A 3.5 Å cryo-EM structure reveals a DnaB6·DciA3 complex in which DciA binds the periphery of the helicase and stabilizes a right-handed open-helical conformation with a single cracked interface. Three DciA molecules dock onto alternate linker-helix/docking-helix modules, while one N-terminal domain (NTD) engages the cracked interface, occupying the pocket vacated by the displaced linker helix and acting as a wedge to promote ring opening. Functional analyses reveal how DciA couples ATPase suppression with efficient helicase loading through coordinated actions of its NTDs and C-terminal domains. Together, these findings define a minimal, ATP-independent mechanism for helicase loading and show how an ancestral loader remodels DnaB to overcome a fundamental topological barrier.

papers.title: Reversible autoinhibition of the bacterial replication-licensing Hda-β clamp complex.
papers.authors: Jiang X, Danev R, Luan Y, Nakakido M, Tsumoto K, Kikkawa M.
papers.abstract: Bacterial DNA replication must be tightly controlled to ensure once-per-cell-cycle initiation, requiring precise regulation of the initiator DnaA. The conserved RIDA pathway inactivates DnaA through the Hda-β sliding clamp (DnaN) complex, yet how this system is dynamically regulated has remained unclear. Here, we show that the Hda-DnaN complex exists as a concentration-dependent oligomeric ensemble rather than a static assembly. Using cryo-electron microscopy and mass photometry, we resolve multiple structural states, including an autoinhibited hetero-octamer, a hetero-hexamer intermediate, and a RIDA-compatible hetero-trimer. Structural comparison of these states suggests a plausible route of oligomeric interconversion involving progressive destabilization of Hda self-association, accompanied by exposure of the catalytic arginine finger required for DnaA inactivation. We further propose that this equilibrium operates as a titration-like mechanism that converts local protein concentration into functional states. Together, our findings establish reversible oligomerization as a potential regulatory principle for bacterial replication licensing.

papers.title: CPSF6 maintains genomic stability by stabilizing RAD52 and promoting CHK1 activation.
papers.authors: Wu H, Fu H, Fan Z, Qin J, Gong Y, Zheng H, An R, Miao X, Tang TS, Guo C.
keywords: Rad52 DNA Repair and Recombination Protein
papers.abstract: RAD52 and CHK1 are critical factors that play pleiotropic roles in the DNA damage response (DDR), including the resolution of transcription-replication conflicts (TRCs). However, how their functions are modulated remains incomplete. Here, we reveal that the cleavage and polyadenylation specificity factor subunit 6 (CPSF6) is an unexpected DDR factor that enhances RAD52 stability and CHK1 activation. Specifically, CPSF6 competitively interacts with RAD52, thereby preventing RAD52 from interacting with the E3 ubiquitin ligase UHRF1 and subsequent proteasomal degradation. In addition, CPSF6 enhances the ATR-CHK1 interaction to promote CHK1 activation, thereby facilitating the activation of downstream CHK1-PLK1-RAD51 pathway. The dual functions of CPSF6 in RAD52 stabilization and CHK1 activation contribute to its role in TRC resolution. CPSF6 depletion causes R-loop accumulation and transcription-associated DNA damage. Notably, these roles of CPSF6 in the DDR are independent of its canonical role in pre-mRNA 3'-end processing. Collectively, our findings establish that CPSF6 is a novel factor critical for maintaining genomic stability, with the resolution of TRCs as an important mechanism.

papers.title: NEAT1 remodeling rewires the MYC degradation pathway.
papers.authors: Jang H, Suh BK, Zhang F, Lin A, Tan M, Liu Y, Chua MS, So S, Kay MA.
papers.abstract: MYC is among the most frequently amplified oncogenes in human cancer, yet its intrinsically disordered nature has rendered it refractory to direct pharmacological targeting. Here, we demonstrate that the long noncoding RNA NEAT1_1 functions as a molecular gatekeeper that controls MYC protein stability by regulating its access to the E3 ubiquitin ligase UBR5. We show that NEAT1_1 forms a ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complex with both MYC and UBR5, and that NEAT1_1 suppression disrupts this interaction, leading to decreased MYC polyubiquitination and enhanced protein stability. To systematically map the regulatory architecture of NEAT1_1 without altering its abundance, we screened 88 antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) mixmers tiling across the transcript. Strikingly, this phenotypic screen identified region-specific mixmers that elicit bidirectional control over MYC, either driving robust MYC destabilization or promoting its stabilization in a strictly expression-independent manner. Mechanistically, MYC-destabilizing mixmers selectively enhance the interaction between MYC and UBR5 to accelerate proteasomal degradation. A focused CRISPR screen targeting the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway independently validated UBR5 as the essential E3 ligase mediating this mixmer-induced turnover. In vivo, our lead mixmer ASO_#24 significantly suppressed tumor growth in MYC-high xenografts, whereas MYC-low tumors remained unaffected. Our findings reveal that the functional output of a scaffold lncRNA is encoded in its sub-domain architecture rather than bulk transcript levels, establishing domain-specific RNA targeting as a tractable strategy to rewire protein turnover pathways for otherwise undruggable oncogenes.

papers.title: Emerging roles of RIF1 in mitosis.
papers.authors: Roy S, Brisebois B, Masson JY, Elowe S.
papers.abstract: Faithful chromosome segregation during cell division requires precise coordination of kinase- and phosphatase-driven signaling pathways. Defects in this balance can cause chromosome missegregation and cytokinesis failure, resulting in genomic instability. Rap1-interacting factor 1 (RIF1) is known for its interphase functions in DNA damage repair, DNA replication timing, and chromatin organization. However, recent work has established RIF1 as a critical mitotic regulator that functions primarily through its role as a protein phosphatase 1 (PP1) adaptor. During early mitosis, the localization of RIF1 to the mitotic apparatus is thought to be actively suppressed by mitotic kinases, including cyclin-dependent kinase 1 (CDK1), aurora kinase B (AURKB), and polo-like kinase 1 (PLK1), preventing premature PP1 engagement and dephosphorylation. Following anaphase onset, relief of this inhibition allows PLK1-interacting checkpoint helicase (PICH)-dependent recruitment of RIF1 to ultrafine anaphase DNA bridges (UFBs), where RIF1-associated PP1 activity determines pathway choice for UFB resolution. In cytokinesis, PLK1 promotes RIF1 recruitment to the midbody, where PP1 antagonizes AURKB activity to enable timely cytokinetic abscission. Herein, we review recent advances defining the spatial and temporal regulation of RIF1 during mitosis, highlight unresolved mechanistic questions in UFB resolution and PP1 regulation, and discuss emerging links between the mitotic functions of RIF1 and genomic instability.

Condensins-mediated mitotic folding persists as a structural echo in interphase chromatin.
papers.authors: Yunusova A, Tsoi E, Smirnov A, Shnaider T, Pristyazhnuk I, Gridina M, Kazakov E, Kireev I, Myakinkov I, Nuriddinov M, Fishman V, Battulin N.
papers.abstract: The structural maintenance of chromosomes (SMC) protein complexes, cohesin and condensins, orchestrate cell cycle-dependent transitions in chromosome folding: from the relatively decondensed interphase chromatin, organized into dynamic DNA loops by cohesin, to the highly condensed arrays of DNA loops in mitotic chromosomes formed by condensins. Here, using Hi-C data from mouse embryonic stem cell lines with auxin-inducible degron-tagged subunits of SMC complexes, we clarify the role of condensins in shaping chromatin contacts within the interphase nucleus. We found that depletion of condensin I leads to weakened segregation of chromatin into A and B compartments. We also show that the contact patterns established by condensins during mitosis are preserved in interphase, suggesting a structural memory of mitotic chromosome folding. Condensins influence chromocenter organization: in the absence of condensin II during mitosis, centromeres tend to cluster, forming hyperclusters of pericentric heterochromatin. In contrast, depletion of condensin I reduces the number of heterochromatin clusters, consistent with enhanced chromosome territoriality. By combining a cohesin-degron system with Mcph1 knockout, we established an artificial model in which condensin II becomes the major driver of chromatin folding in interphase nuclei following cohesin depletion. Unlike extrusive cohesin, condensin II does not stall at sequence-specific sites and forms large, randomly positioned loops on interphase chromatin. Moreover, condensin II activity during interphase does not interfere with cohesin-dependent structures such as TADs and chromatin loops.

papers.title: E. coli RsmF activity depends on prior modification of 16S rRNA helix 44.
papers.authors: Barmada MI, Hanna A, Bair CR, McGinity EN, Zelinskaya N, Dey D, Conn GL.
papers.abstract: Bacterial ribosomal RNA (rRNA) methylations are important for accurate translation. Four distinct methylations incorporated by RsmE, RsmF, and RsmH/ RsmI form a cluster of three modified 16S rRNA nucleotides (m3U1498, m5C1407, and m4Cm1402) surrounding the decoding center of the 30S subunit. Given their common substrate requirement of a late-stage intermediate 30S subunit, these enzymes likely act contemporaneously during subunit biogenesis, but whether there exists a required modification order is unknown. Here, using hypomethylated 30S subunits obtained from a collection of rsmH/I/E/F-deleted Escherichia coli strains, we identify RsmF activity to be highly dependent on prior modification of h44 both in vitro and in E. coli. RsmF activity on hypomethylated 30S subunits could be partially rescued by prior in vitro methylation using RsmE and RsmH, indicating that incorporation of these methyl groups directly shapes h44 for recognition by RsmF. RNA structure probing using selective 2'-hydroxyl acylation analyzed by primer extension and mutational profiling and molecular dynamics simulations reveal specific alterations in 16S rRNA structure and dynamics in the absence of the m4C1402 (RsmH) and m3U1498 (RsmE) modifications that likely restrict RsmF action. These studies thus uncover a previously unappreciated "order of operations" for 16S rRNA modification during ribosome biogenesis with important implications for studies on the collective functions of these modifications.

papers.title: Ultrafast single-qubit gates through multi-photon transition removal.
papers.authors: Gao Y, Galicia A, Da Costa Jesus JD, Liu Y, Haddad Y, Volkov DA, Guimarães JR, Bhardwaj H, Jerger M, Neis M, Li B, Cárdenas-López FA, Motzoi F, Bushev PA, Barends R.
papers.abstract: Fast qubit control is essential for scalable quantum computing. However, the strong driving that is required can induce significant leakage from the computational subspace, particularly in weakly anharmonic qubits. We demonstrate single qubit gates with a total leakage error consistently below 2.0 × 10 -5 on a transmon qubit, and obtain fidelities above 99.98% at 6.8 ns pulse duration in both X and X/2 gates. This is achieved by removing direct transitions beyond nearest-neighbor levels using double recursive applications of Derivative Removal by Adiabatic Gate pulse shape. We also introduce the amplified leakage error sequence which can directly measure the leakage error down to 10 -6 . We test single qubit gates across a range of pulse durations using multiple benchmarking methods to reveal the error channels. The presented approach can be straightforwardly adapted by other platforms.

A computational framework for modeling fluid and solid stresses in porous tissues with application to the trabeculated embryonic heart.
papers.authors: Buffinton CM, Baish JW.
papers.abstract: This study provides a framework for efficient solutions of computational fluid-solid interaction models of porous tissue, with a focus on blood flow through the developing heart wall in the critical chamber and valve formation stages, when trabeculation fills much of the ventricles. This porous, trabeculated tissue is the site of complex mechanotransduction processes, but accurately estimating solid and fluid stresses within such intricate geometries is difficult. We addressed this with three levels of modeling and verification. Images of E12.5 mouse ventricles were first obtained through confocal microscopy and 3D reconstruction. These guided creation of explicit pore-scale finite element simulations with fluid-solid interaction. Idealized and image-derived unit cells were analyzed to determine hydraulic permeability. Next, a multi-pore representation of the ventricular wall was solved with full fluid and solid equations. A continuum model based on Brinkman equations then replaced the explicit pore structure, and sensitivity to permeability was evaluated in terms of fluid flow in the open channel and porous region. Permeabilities obtained from unit-cell simulations followed trends from Kozeny-Carman solid-pore and fiber theory for the rigid case, while simulations for hyperelastic unit-cell material quantified the effects of tissue elasticity. Comparison of continuum and explicit model results showed the Brinkman equation, which incorporates the diffusion of shear stress from flow in the free fluid into the porous media, but not explicitly inertial effects, could significantly improve the accuracy of continuum models compared to Darcy's law. A 3D model of blood flow through the ventricles of the developing mouse heart demonstrated the application of the technique to more realistic geometry, showed locations of peak solid and shear stress, and produced physiologically reasonable flow. Furthermore, we developed methodologies to estimate local wall shear and solid stress from continuum-based calculations. This approach can enable efficient, whole-organ parametric analyses of fluid flow, circumventing the need for computationally expensive explicit pore modeling.

papers.title: Visuomotor coordination on the road: Low-dimensional representations reveal adaptive, context-dependent reductions in the dimensionality of natural driving behavior.
papers.authors: Madrid-Carvajal J, Derakhshan S, König P.
papers.abstract: The brain's ability to transform complex, high-dimensional sensory and motor inputs into coordinated, goal-directed behavior remains a central challenge in neuroscience research. Current research suggests that behavior is generated through patterns within a low-dimensional structure. What visuomotor patterns underlie complex, unconstrained behaviors such as driving, and how stereotypical they are, remain poorly understood. Driving involves complex perception-action interactions, which we hypothesize are specific to the driver's role and adapt to task demands. Here, we unfold these dynamics using an immersive virtual drive that recreates ten hazardous on-road events. We collected eye, head, and vehicle movements from participants assigned to either a manual or an automated driving condition. From the behavioral movements of 284 drivers, we constructed a common time-resolved behavioral state space based on collective variance, computed via principal component analysis across participants. The obtained low-dimensional representation thus captures generalized visuomotor coordination strategies. We then characterized the evolving low-dimensional structure with cosine similarity and various measures of effective dimensionality. We tested whether leading components contained condition-specific information using discriminant analysis. Throughout the entire drive, few components accounted for most of the variance in behavior, and effective dimensionality decreased reliably around critical events, indicating tighter coordination between perceptual and motor variables. During periods of low effective dimensionality, the contributions of eye, head, steering, and vehicle heading reorganized toward leading dimensions in a task-dependent manner. Across events, between-subject similarity was partially stable and stronger among manual drivers. This reorganization also made behaviors more distinct across driving conditions, enabling better classification of driving modes using only the first two components. These results show that naturalistic driving is supported by shared low-dimensional visuomotor coordination strategies that are flexibly reshaped by contextual demands, and provide a principled behavioral framework for linking neural manifolds, human driver models, and the design of adaptive automated vehicles.

papers.title: Intron retention regulates STAT2 function and associates with immunotherapy response in lung cancer.
papers.authors: Englander RP, Brugiolo M, Devoucoux M, Wu TC, Kostich M, Leclair NK, Walawalkar I, Kang HG, Park S, Marches F, Peeples ME, Chen P, Banchereau J, Yu P, Salner A, Banchereau R, Palucka K, Anczuków O.

papers.title: The evolutionary accessibility of cultural fitness landscapes.
papers.authors: Fogarty L, Hoyle RB.
papers.abstract: Many human cultural and technological traits have a complex and peculiar structure. They are often characterized by multiple closely interacting parts that can form modules, and change as a result of innovation, collaboration, and social learning. A full understanding of the ways in which such cultural traits evolve requires a model that accounts for the close epistatic interaction of the constituent parts, and for the uniquely cultural processes that act on them. Here, we generalize the concept of 'adaptive landscapes', where populations search a landscape for optimal combinations of components. This generalization accounts for epistatic interactions, and includes processes such as modularization, communication, and collaboration, that are not features of genetic systems but may be quite common features of cultural systems. We show that modularization in combination with collaborative communication of search results is more successful, but sometimes more costly, than searching a full adaptive landscape. However, in many of the circumstances under which technology evolves, a full search of many thousands of possible modules may not be feasible since time, financial, energetic, and environmental constraints are likely to be strong. Under these conditions, our models suggest that there is a critical value for the number of modules to search below which the global optimum is more likely to be reached by searching the full landscape. The value of this threshold depends on the complexity of the technology. Overall, we suggest that analysis of cultural fitness landscapes is likely to be a fruitful avenue for research into technological change especially when combined with elements of human learning and interaction known to be important features of cultural evolution.

papers.title: Cell-type dependence of effects from transcranial electric brain stimulation.
papers.authors: Dahle S, Einevoll GT, Ness TV.
papers.abstract: There is an urgent need for better treatment options for many neurological conditions, including Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, depression, and epilepsy. Transcranial electrical stimulation (tES) is a non-invasive, safe, inexpensive, and promising method that could address some of this unmet need. The therapeutic value of tES has been well demonstrated, but the effect is highly variable. To enable tES to reach its full potential requires a better understanding of how tES modulates neural activity so that tES treatments can be tailored to specific neurological conditions and individual patients. The neural response to tES is, however, highly complex, and the parameter space involved in optimizing tES treatments is daunting. This has made it difficult to obtain general insights into how tES modulates neural activity, and a central challenge lies in the cell-type-specific and frequency-dependent nature of these responses. In this study, we investigated cell-type-specific neuronal responses to tES over a broad frequency range, using a large database of biophysically detailed neuron models. We found that pyramidal cells respond strongly to low-frequency tES, but their responses drop sharply with frequency. In contrast, inhibitory neurons show a smaller reduction and, on average, become more responsive than pyramidal cells above ~60 Hz. By leveraging a reciprocity theorem we demonstrated that the effect of tES on a given cell-type is proportional to the frequency-dependent current-dipole moment that determines the EEG-signal contribution of this cell-type. We further identified the dendritic asymmetry as key in determining tES responses across the frequency spectrum. Counterintuitively, we also found that while total cell length increases tES sensitivity at low frequencies, it can have the opposite effect at high frequencies. Furthermore, we derived an analytical formula for idealized neuron models which can approximately predict the tES sensitivity of different cell types at any given frequency. By characterizing the role of morphology and stimulation frequency in determining tES responses of single cells, this is an important step towards a better understanding of tES at the fundamental level. These results also provide an efficient and accurate method for characterizing and comparing the tES responses of different neural populations across the frequency spectrum, which facilitates optimizing tES for cell-type specific targeting.

papers.title: Correction to 'A specific N-terminal extension of the 8 kDa domain is required for DNA end-bridging by human Polµ and Polλ'.
Fast and accurate taxonomic domain assignment of short metagenomic reads using BBERT.
papers.authors: Alekhin D, Alon M, Sidi T, Mazeh SP, Carmi G, Finkel OM, Erez A.
papers.abstract: Shotgun metagenomes from complex environments such as soil uncover vast biodiversity. Yet most short reads produced by shotgun sequencing cannot be taxonomically or functionally annotated, as they lack a sufficiently comprehensive reference, obscuring the true structure and function of microbial communities. We introduce BBERT, a nucleotide large language model optimized for short reads. Testing on a large cohort of soil metagenomes, we found that BBERT identifies bacterial sequence syntax without relying on reference databases, enabling accurate assignment of taxonomic domain, coding potential, and reading frame directly from reads as short as 100 bp. BBERT is small and fast enough to analyze metagenomes using a modest GPU and can be used to convert short metagenomic reads directly to bacterial amino acid sequences for downstream applications. BBERT also improves de novo metagenomic assembly, reducing mismatches and gaps while accelerating runtime. Using metagenomes from wild legume nodules, we demonstrate that BBERT filtering improves bin quality while significantly accelerating de novo assembly. By providing fast, reference-free classification of short reads, BBERT unlocks large metagenomic archives for more accurate ecological and evolutionary analyses.

papers.title: Disentangling polymer confinement from specific-folding interactions reveals the drivers of Escherichia coli chromosome organization.
papers.authors: Delafrouz P, Nesterova T, Harris FE, Farooq H, Du L, Liu J, Ma A, Xiao J, Liang J.
papers.abstract: The three-dimensional organization of the bacterial chromosome is critical for gene regulation. Chromosome conformation capture (Hi-C) has enabled genome-wide mapping of chromosomal folding, yet ensemble-averaged contact maps entangle biologically specific-folding interactions (SFIs) with nonspecific polymer compaction and mask single-cell heterogeneity. Here, we developed a polymer-based simulation framework in Escherichia coli to address these limitations. We found that a null model of 300 000 random polymer configurations recapitulated the global chromosomal organization observed in Hi-C data, establishing that most Hi-C signals reflect generic polymer behavior in a confined volume. Contrasting null-model predictions with experimental Hi-C data isolated a small subset of SFIs (<7%) and generated a specific-fold ensemble of 20 000 single-cell conformations that reproduced chromosomal interaction domains and single-cell heterogeneity. SFIs were enriched in the ter region, reduced nucleoid accessibility, colocalized with cryptic prophages, and depleted in positively supercoiled regions. H-NS and MatP emerged as major chromosome-wide and local determinants of SFIs, respectively. Furthermore, high-SFI regions correlated with stress-adaptive genes, whereas low-SFI regions harbored housekeeping genes. Together, our results established that a small number of biologically encoded SFIs superimposed on a polymer background shape the E. coli chromosome and gene expression, providing a quantitative framework for dissecting chromosome architecture and function.

papers.title: Genome replication and cell division control by the methylation-sensitive GcrA regulator in Agrobacterium tumefaciens.
papers.authors: Fournes F, Martin S, Pellaton N, Taschner M, Bojkowska K, Marquis J, Gruber S, Collier J.
papers.abstract: Bacteria with complex genomes including secondary chromosomes and/or megaplasmids face unique challenges when controlling their cell cycle: they not only need to coordinate genome replication with other cell cycle events such as cell growth and cell division, but also to synchronize the replication of different replicons. In Alphaproteobacteria, replication and maintenance of large extrachromosomal replicons are usually dependent on RepABC modules, as seen for the plant pathogen Agrobacterium tumefaciens. In this study, we demonstrate that the conserved GcrA protein is an essential methylation-dependent transcriptional regulator playing at least two critical roles during the A. tumefaciens cell cycle. First, GcrA is required for the on-time and synchronized firing of the three RepABC-dependent origins of replication of A. tumefaciens that are needed for chromosomal and megaplasmid replication. Second, GcrA triggers the expression of several essential cell division genes for the timely assembly of a functional divisome. These findings highlight how this conserved global regulator can control and then synchronize a variety of essential cell cycle events in Alphaproteobacteria with complex genomes, notably coordinating the maintenance of several RepABC-dependent replicons with cell division.

papers.title: TargetMITO: a rule-based model for generating functional synthetic mitochondrial targeting sequences in yeast.
papers.authors: Gombeau K, Wan R, James JS, Tribouillard-Tanvier D, Cai Y.
papers.abstract: Mitochondria are essential organelles containing their own genomes, encoding a few proteins essential for energy production. Most of the mitochondrial proteins are nucleus-encoded, translated as precursors in the cytosol, with a large fraction of these precursors properly addressed by an N-terminal mitochondrial targeting sequence (MTS). These MTS share common features but no consensus sequence can explain their functionality nor the precursors-specific determinants of mitochondrial import. To help understand this mechanism, we created a simple computational model to generate functional synthetic MTS while maintaining a tight control on the design parameters. Using the budding yeast, we demonstrated the presence of precursors-specific import capabilities in addressing artificially nucleus-relocated OXPHOS proteins. Our research confirms the existence of cargo-dependent functional compatibilities and takes us one step closer towards improving gene therapy-based treatment of mitochondrial diseases.

papers.title: scTraitReg: a single-cell multi-omic database of trait-relevant transcription factor eRegulons.
papers.authors: Chen H, Liu Y, Rui X, Li S, Sun L, Xiao G, Tang H, Sun Y, Guan X, Cao C.
papers.abstract: Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) identify loci associated with human diseases and disease-related traits, but the regulators and cellular contexts linked to these signals remain difficult to resolve. We present scTraitReg, a database of trait-relevant transcription factor (TF) eRegulons-TFs with their target genes and linked cis-regulatory regions-at single-cell resolution. scTraitReg integrates 655 sets of curated GWAS summary statistics covering 122 Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) disease terms with 111 human single-cell multi-omic datasets profiling RNA and chromatin accessibility in the same cells. The resource spans 34 tissues, 252 cell types, 2 081 538 cells, and 2208 curated GWAS-single-cell analysis pairs. Across these analyses, it contains 2 840 939 TF-cell-type records for 886 regulators; 67 666 records met all three criteria-cell-type specificity, genetic relevance, and the trait-associated regulon score-and were included as candidate trait-relevant eRegulon records. Each record links to the TF-target regulatory network with its cis-regulatory regions, cell-type-resolved evidence, per-cell regulon module scores, and target-gene enrichment, all available as downloadable tables. Users can search by disease, tissue, cell type, or regulator and examine these associations through interactive visualizations. scTraitReg thus provides a searchable and reusable resource linking genetic associations to cell-type-specific regulatory programs, and is freely available at https://www.sctraitreg.bio/.

papers.title: ENflorA: a flexible tool for the bulk submission of next generation sequencing data to the European Nucleotide Archive.
papers.authors: Alfaro de Prado Martín A, Fajardo-Gutiérrez F, de Mestier A, Reichel K.
papers.abstract: Background With the advancement of sequencing technologies and increasing quality of assembly and annotation tools, the amount of biological sequence data produced by research grows rapidly. To keep this data accessible for potential re-analysis, it is typically stored in public online databases, such as the European Nucleotide Archive (ENA). However, the increase in data entails an increase in time needed for metadata curation and upload. We propose a tool to simplify and automatize the upload of experimental and metadata to public repositories. Results We developed ENflorA, a set of scripts by which sample, sequence read and (annotated) assembly data can be uploaded to ENA in a simple and standardized manner. Our software allows easy metadata entry via spreadsheets, is suitable for batch upload of data from different sources, and can be fully integrated in bioinformatic workflows. It is platform independent and can be run natively on High Performance Computers, integrates an lftp upload option for big files and a test upload option. Conclusions By easing the ENA submission process, ENflorA contributes to making high-throughput sequencing data findable, accessible, interoperable and reusable.

papers.title: The average individual genome: a survey of nearly 1 million whole-genome sequences.
papers.authors: Wright HIW, Beaumont RN, Fasham J, Leslie JS, Chundru VK, Hall TS, Cannon SJ, Pagnamenta AT, Baple EL, Wood AR, Murray A, Jackson L, Weedon MN, Patel K, Hawkes G, Wright CF.
papers.abstract: Background As whole-genome sequencing (WGS) is increasingly used in clinical and public health contexts, clearer expectations regarding the amount of variation present in the "average" human genome are required to contextualise findings. Methods We analysed WGS data from two large population cohorts: 490,541 individuals in UK Biobank (UKB) and 414,830 individuals in All of Us. Following variant and genotype QC, we aimed to assess the range of neutral and disease-associated variation across six genetically-inferred ancestry groups. Results The "average" genome contains ~4.3-5.3 million variants, of which ~1.5% are rare (within-cohort allele frequency 10,000 basepairs per genome, and rare autosomal copy number variants > 1 Mb present in ~ 1 in 41 (2.5%) individuals. On average, ~32-42% of variants per person are homozygous and individuals have ~4 unique runs of homozygosity > 1.5 Mb, with marked variation observed across ancestry groups. Of the ~21- 26,000 SNVs/indels per person in coding exons of MANE Select transcripts, ~48% are predicted to alter the protein, of which ~0.8% are high-confidence loss-of-function and ~0.1% have REVEL score > 0.7 suggestive of pathogenicity. Depending upon parental age, the average genome contains ~63 de novo variants, of which ~75-80% are paternal in origin. Considering only rare variants in GenCC-curated monogenic disease-associated genes, the average genome contains ~1-3 ClinVar pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants, ~2-5 high-confidence loss-of-function variants, and ~50 ClinVar variants of uncertain significance. Most ClinVar pathogenic variants are heterozygous in recessive disease genes, consistent with carrier status, and have multiple ClinVar submitters. Finally, applying polygenic scores (PGS) for 28 common diseases within UKB, we estimate that the average person is in the top 10% for ~3 conditions, and around 1 in 5 people are in the top 1% for at least one PGS. Conclusions The ubiquity of genetic variation in individuals has important implications for policy-makers considering genomic screening and clinicians counselling families. The continued underrepresentation of many global populations reflects a broader limitation of contemporary genomic research, underscoring the need for more inclusive datasets worldwide in order to enable equitable precision medicine.

papers.title: Recordanelles for transcriptome-wide single-cell RNA recording in human cells.
papers.authors: Reinkemeier CD, Manero-Carranza M, Farouni R, Filice F, Klotz A, Schneider-Heieck K, Andermann TL, Platt RJ.
papers.abstract: Transcriptomic measurement technologies provide powerful approaches to understand biology but are limited to providing either a high-resolution snapshot at a moment in time or a low-resolution history of transcription constrained to a few genes over a narrow time range. Here, we introduce the 'recordanelle', a single-component synthetic organelle capable of recording the transcriptome in human cells. Recordanelles are composed of a mitochondrial membrane anchor, a condensate assembler and a poly(A)-binding protein. We demonstrate that the recordanelle can be engineered to recruit engineered RNAs or a sampling of up to 90% of all endogenous mRNAs and protect them over several days. We further show that transient and dynamic transcriptional responses resulting from inducible promoters or interferon signaling are preserved throughout time within the recordanelle at the single-cell level. This work provides a nondisruptive and unbiased transcriptome-wide single-cell RNA recording technology to enable a deeper understanding of biology.

papers.title: Deep dynamical models of single-cell multiomic velocities predict loss-of-function and rescue perturbations in B cells.
papers.authors: Karbalayghareh A, Pelzer B, Chin CR, Melnick A, Barisic D, Leslie CS.

papers.title: Programmable design of functional proteins from natural language.
papers.authors: Dai F, You S, Zhu Y, Gao Y, Fu L, Zhou X, Su J, Wang C, Fan Y, Tan Q, Ma X, Deng X, Yu L, Qian H, He Y, Ke Y, Zhang Z, Han C, Chang X, Zheng L, Wang S, Ji Y, Hao K, Cao L, Wang Y, Zeng A, Wang S, Zhan C, Zhao J, Si T, Liu J, Lu H, Yuan F.

papers.title: An environmentally regulated dichotomy in cell lineages of the root.
papers.authors: Oliva M, Stuart T, Tang D, Khan A, Clement O, Makosa D, Poppe D, Pflueger J, Jabbari JS, Gigante S, Dragwidge JM, Petterson M, Whelan J, Lewsey MG, Lister R.
papers.abstract: Plant development is highly plastic, with growth and architecture continuously shaped by environmental conditions. Roots, for instance, adjust their development to local water, nutrient and soil conditions. Despite this plasticity, individual root cell types are generally viewed as largely homogeneous populations that progress along a single developmental trajectory 1 . Here we show that rather than progressing along a single developmental trajectory, most Arabidopsis root cell lineage trajectories exhibit a stereotyped bifid topology, as revealed by single-cell RNA sequencing and spatial transcript mapping. One branch is characterized by a transcriptional program that is shared across multiple cell types and enriched for genes associated with environmental responses, including abscisic acid (ABA) signalling. This state occurs reproducibly in a subset of cells across multiple cell types, independent of developmental lineage, thereby revealing an additional layer of root cell identity. It is conserved across Arabidopsis ecotypes and persists despite major perturbations in developmental identity. Moreover, it is reduced in ABA-deficient and ABA-insensitive mutants and becomes more prevalent under water-deficit conditions. Together, these findings reveal an additional layer of root cell identity that is superimposed on developmental lineage and its prevalence is modulated by environmental conditions. These results uncover a previously unrecognized source of environment-associated transcriptional heterogeneity shared across root cell types.

papers.title: HRDPath: an explainable multi-model deep learning architecture for predicting homologous recombination deficiency from histopathology images.
papers.authors: Wu CI, Banda K, Arora R, Soong TR, Radke M, Dillon M, Nik-Zainal S, Swisher EM, Sailem HZ.
papers.abstract: Homologous recombination deficiency (HRD) is a critical biomarker for guiding treatment decisions in high-grade serous tubo-ovarian carcinoma (HGSOC), a cancer with few reliable biomarkers. However, existing genomics-based tests for HRD are variable, expensive, and time-consuming. We develop HRDPath, a patient-level deep learning architecture that predicts HRD status from whole slide images, requiring no additional molecular testing. HRDPath is validated across three cohorts of female patients and achieves an AUC of 0.846, significantly outperforming previously reported results in HGSOC. By incorporating multiple slides per patient and targeted optimization strategies, we strengthen the model clinical utility, with both specificity and sensitivity reaching 0.90. Our interpretability pipeline enhances model trustworthiness and reveals important clinical and biological insights into HRD-positive cancers, highlighting the associated morphological and pathological changes at the cellular and tissue levels. HRDPath provides a foundation for an accessible and scalable digital biomarker to improve treatment stratification in ovarian cancer globally.

papers.title: High-content morphological profiling by Cell Painting in 3D spheroids.
papers.authors: Ringers C, Holmberg D, Larsson A, Jung B, Jarvius M, Luchniak A, Rosén D, Johansson M, Georgiev P, Seashore-Ludlow B, Visnes T, Flobak Å, Carreras-Puigvert J, Spjuth O.
papers.abstract: Cell Painting is a popular high-content imaging assay that captures the shape and internal organization of 2D cell cultures at scale. While 3D cell cultures are more physiologically relevant models - especially for studying drug perturbations - they remain challenging to image because light scatters before it reaches the cultures' interior. Here, we introduce a scalable method to adapt Cell Painting for 3D spheroids. We show that tissue-clearing, a technique that makes spheroids transparent, combined with a focusing routine that locates spheroids on the fly, enables Cell Painting at single-cell level inside intact spheroids. By profiling 52 clinically relevant drugs, we show that single-cell fingerprints clustered by biological pathway and resolved drug effects more robustly than those of flattened spheroid-wide views. Notably, the effect of two drugs, 5-fluorouracil and olaparib, nearly indistinguishable in 2D monolayers, diverged in spheroids. This finding was then corroborated by DNA-damage, cell-cycle, and gene-expression assays. The workflow runs on a spinning-disk confocal microscope in a standard 384-well plate format, making single-cell 3D profiling accessible to laboratories already performing Cell Painting.
