papers.title: Proton transport drives allosteric conformational changes in the MmpL3 transporter.
papers.authors: Yang L, North EJ, Zgurskaya HI, Jackson M, Gumbart JC.
papers.abstract: Tuberculosis (TB), caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), remains a global health crisis, further complicated by increasing drug resistance. The mycobacterial membrane protein MmpL3, which is essential for transporting cell wall precursors such as trehalose monomycolate (TMM), is a promising therapeutic target. However, the mechanistic link between proton-driven dynamics and substrate transport in MmpL3 is not fully understood. In this study, we use molecular dynamics simulations to investigate how protonation of conserved Asp-Tyr dyads (Asp256-Tyr646 and Asp645-Tyr257) in Mycobacterium smegmatis (Msmg) MmpL3 regulates conformational changes and TMM binding. Protonation at Asp256 induces an open dyad conformation, increases local water accessibility, and is associated with a tendency toward more open configurations of the periplasmic binding pocket. In contrast, protonation at Asp645 stabilizes a closed dyad conformation, reduces water accessibility, and narrows the transmembrane binding pocket. These findings support a proposed sequential protonation model in which protonation-dependent conformational changes are allosterically coupled to substrate translocation.

papers.title: Multiscale modeling reveals non-linear dynamics of AKT-mediated NO-ROS crosstalk in shear stress-induced endothelial phenotype.
papers.authors: Zhang YY, Wang YT, Qiu Y, Li YJ, Chen D, Qin KR.
papers.abstract: Endothelial dysfunction is a critical initiating event in atherosclerosis. The regulatory role of the AKT signaling pathway in the transition between injury and repair remains unclear. This study developed a multiscale model to elucidate how AKT signaling modulates endothelial repair under shear stress. The framework integrates hemodynamic stimuli, cellular behaviors, and nonlinear AKT/NO/ROS biochemical kinetics coupled with endothelial phenotypic transitions. Results demonstrate that endothelial dysfunction is driven by a spatial mismatch between NO production and ROS consumption rather than global deficiency. Phenotypic restoration is governed by the nonlinear interactions within the NO-ROS network. Systematic simulations identified a golden window, where Day 1 intervention and moderate AKT activation effectively restored endothelial cells and normalized redox status. Conversely, excessive activation caused supra-physiological over-suppression. These findings suggest that repair is determined by the tight coupling of redox homeostasis and immune dynamics, highlighting intervention timing and dosage as critical factors for precision vascular therapy.

papers.title: Environmental volatility is associated with adaptive caution in visual search.
papers.authors: Qiu N, Allenmark F, Chen S, Müller HJ, Shi Z.
papers.abstract: Real-world distractors occur in environments whose states change at different rates. We asked whether such volatility alters initial overt oculomotor allocation, later target verification and response commitment, or both. Observers performed an additional-singleton search task with concurrent eye tracking while distractor presence followed high- or low-volatility sequences, with overall distractor prevalence held constant. Trial-pooled oculomotor capture was higher under high volatility, a pattern that appears to indicate altered filtering. Matching the same-location run position removed that difference, with no detectable difference in capture across volatility regimes at matched run position. The pooled capture effect was therefore consistent with a structural consequence of the volatility manipulation, which enriched high-volatility blocks with early-run positions where capture is intrinsically high. The volatility effect itself appeared on distractor-absent trials. Under high volatility, response times were longer, fixations more frequent, final-target dwell longer, and errors fewer, while target-acquisition latency itself was unchanged. Same-location repetition learning showed no detectable difference in slope across regimes. A hierarchical drift-diffusion model (DDM) and a complementary volatility Kalman-filter (VKF) comparison converged in showing that manual responses carried both boundary-related and drift-related structure. With distractor frequency held constant, the per-trial effect of volatility therefore emerged after the first saccade as an increase in response caution rather than in oculomotor capture. This pattern is consistent with precision-weighted adjustment to environmental uncertainty.

papers.title: The successor representation in high-risk drinking and alcohol-related contexts.
papers.authors: Musial MPM, Hall-McMaster S, Shimomura K, Kato A, Bode EL, Grundmann CC, Ebrahimi C, Morita K, Gershman SJ, Endrass T, Schlagenhauf F.
papers.abstract: The successor representation (SR) is a reinforcement learning strategy which has been suggested to underlie nuanced forms of habitual behavior, rendering it a candidate mechanism for mental health conditions thought to involve habitual control, such as addiction. However, paradigms used to assess habits in humans cannot detect SR use. Together with the fact that they are usually conducted in disorder-irrelevant contexts, this may explain why the evidence for a hypothesized shift from goal-directed to habitual behavior in addiction is inconsistent. Here, we tested whether individuals with high-risk (n = 260) compared to low-risk drinking behavior (n = 260) rely more on SR or a rigid goal-based dimension-reduced SR variant (redSR), particularly in alcohol-related contexts. An online multi-stage decision-making task performed in either a virtual bar or apartment context allowed us to dissociate (red)SR from model-based and model-free learning strategies by testing how well participants adapted their choices to different types of distal changes in the environment. Findings suggest that a particular type of SR, namely a (reduced) random-policy SR-like strategy, contributes to human behavior, but that high-risk drinkers do not differ from low-risk drinkers in their use of this strategy. Instead, both groups seem to rely less on what is likely a (reduced) random-policy SR strategy in alcohol-related contexts - and instead more on model-free control. Results suggest that the use of an adaptive, resource-efficient decision-making strategy is selectively downregulated in substance-related contexts. This study highlights the importance of considering contextual modulation and nuanced decision strategies in understanding habitual and goal-directed behavior in mental health conditions such as addiction.

papers.title: Spatio-temporal machine learning for multi-horizon prediction of bluetongue outbreaks.
papers.authors: Devlin LM, Nguyen PH, Cuthbert RN, Doan PN, Tran VH, Zhang Z, Murchie AK, Bamford CGG, Dick JTA, Morgan ER, Mai TS.
papers.abstract: Reliable early warning of infectious disease outbreaks remains a major challenge for surveillance systems, particularly for vector-borne pathogens whose transmission depends on interactions among hosts, vectors, and climate-sensitive environmental conditions. Data-driven forecasting offers a promising approach for predicting outbreak risk using surveillance and environmental data. This study develops a logit-weighted ensemble (LWE), a machine-learning framework that predicts outbreak occurrence 1-6 months ahead at the administrative unit-month scale using routinely available outbreak notifications and gridded climate data. Bluetongue virus (BTV), an arbovirus of ruminants transmitted by Culicoides biting midges, provides a well-characterised system in which transmission is strongly shaped by climate, making it a useful system for applying and testing this approach. The framework is evaluated using surveillance data collected between 2005 and 2024 from France, Greece, and Italy, selected for their long-running and high-quality outbreak surveillance records. Across all three countries, the LWE achieved the strongest and most stable predictive performance under a recall-focused evaluation that prioritises correctly identifying outbreak months. It outperformed or matched 14 benchmark models, with differences becoming more pronounced at longer lead times (month +3 onward), when predictions are more uncertain and outbreaks are relatively rare. Predictability varied across countries, with the highest performance in Greece, strong performance in France, and lower, more variable performance in Italy, reflecting differences in how consistently outbreaks occur and spread across regions. Overall, the results demonstrate that horizon-aware, climate-informed forecasting can reliably identify months and locations at elevated risk of outbreak occurrence up to six months in advance, supporting surveillance planning and preparedness across heterogeneous European settings. The ensemble framework provides a robust and portable strategy for outbreak prediction using routinely collected surveillance and environmental data.

papers.title: SADRP: A structurally aware multi-modal framework for drug response prediction.
papers.authors: Qi R, Liu S, Quan T, Wu T, Shaytan AK, Liu B.
papers.abstract: Motivation Predicting drug sensitivity across diverse cancer samples is a fundamental challenge in personalized therapy and drug discovery. This task requires comprehensive characterization of both drug and cancer cell line features. Current approaches often fail to fully capture the complex structural characteristics and interactions of drug compounds and struggle to integrate multi-omics features derived from the same sample, limiting their feature representation capacity. Consequently, there is a need for modeling frameworks that can jointly model molecular structural features and multi-modal cellular contexts in a unified manner. Results We present SADRP, a structurally aware multi-modal framework for drug response prediction, designed to model complex molecular structures and multi-omics data. For drug representation, SADRP incorporates Shortest Distance Path (SDP) encoding and edge encoding to capture both topological relationships and bond-type chemical semantics. For cell line profiling, a multi-view interactive encoder integrates gene expression and DNA methylation, capturing cross-omics synergistic complementarity. SADRP consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, while also identifying potential therapeutic candidates and biomarkers, providing mechanistic insights and supporting applications in drug discovery and personalized medicine.

papers.title: pxGPT: a schema-constrained multimodal large language model framework for plant phenotyping.
papers.authors: Zheng PX, Ou JY, Wu YL, Wang RS, Wu TL, Hsu TC, Lin YC.
papers.abstract: Summary Deep learning can scale image-based plant phenotyping but typically targets predefined traits, whereas manual phenotypic description is more flexible but difficult to scale. We present Phenotype eXplorer Generative Plant Traits (pxGPT), a Python framework that converts multi-view plant images into structured phenotype records. The workflow combines free-text description, dataset-specific schema generation with human review, and schema-constrained information extraction. We evaluated the extraction stage on three Brassica datasets using 78 973 annotations from 10 annotators who had no access to pxGPT predictions. For 38-45 qualitative traits per dataset, pxGPT-human agreement ranged from 0.572 to 0.712, compared with 0.620 to 0.739 agreement among human annotators. All 32 736 required trait fields were present; 93 values were empty, and no qualitative descriptor violations were recorded. For selected morphological structures, pooled false-positive rates were 0.5%-8.0%, while sensitivity varied across structure types in one mature-plant dataset (37.5%-100%). The curated schemas were applied unchanged with two commercial models and one locally hosted open-weight model, with differences in mean accuracy of 0.03 or less. In the evaluated Brassica datasets, these results support schema-guided extraction of visible plant traits without separate model training for each trait. Human-guided schema development offers a path to extend pxGPT to other crops and imaging conditions, with accuracy requiring validation in each new setting. Availability and implementation The software is available at https://github.com/YaoChengLab/pxgpt and an archival version of the source code is available on Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22931745). Curated schemas used in this study, annotation guides, phenotype records, and human annotations are available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22907554.

papers.title: Engineered human Argonaute 2 for targeted C-to-U RNA base editing.
papers.authors: Lusi RF, Moncayo von Hase S, Model C, Banik SM.
papers.abstract: Tools for manipulating RNA that rely on nonhuman proteins, such as ISC-based and Cas-based scaffolds, can lead to unintended and little-understood effects on human cells and present challenges in therapeutic translation. Replacing them with human proteins engineered for expanded, programmable functions could bypass the limitations of these foreign proteins. Here we demonstrate that human Argonaute 2 (AGO2) can be repurposed as a modular RNA targeting domain. AGO2 fused to a C-to-U deaminase enables AGO-led targeted editing of RNA (ALTER). Using guide RNAs that remodel target RNA structure for selective editing and reduced nuclease activity, we show that ALTER achieves, on average, 1.9-fold higher C-to-U editing on mRNA targets in HEK293T cells compared with Cas13 editors CURE and RESCUE. Transcriptome-wide RNA-seq revealed similar or lower levels of off-target editing compared to the same Cas13-based editors. Machine learning models predict that far fewer immunogenic peptides will result from ALTER and we show that ALTER is amenable to a validated workflow for artificial intelligence-directed deimmunization.

papers.title: High-risk antimicrobial resistance genomic traits in multidrug-resistant Salmonella across China's food chain: projections to 2050.
papers.authors: Baker M, Lu X, Luo C, Wu G, Maciel-Guerra A, Pinpimai K, Luo M, Wang M, Zhang Y, Meng W, Zhu B, Kan B, Dottorini T.
papers.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is rising globally, yet factors shaping its genomic evolution remain poorly understood. We investigated how socioeconomic, climate, and health factors are associated with AMR spread in multi-drug resistant (MDR) Salmonella enterica across China's food chain, mapped hotspots and forecasted genomic trait prevalence to 2050. We analysed 2,536 MDR genomes from 15 provinces over 16 years, covering patients, food and non-food workers, meat, livestock, and environmental sources. A machine learning framework integrated genomic surveillance with risk assessment to identify high-risk AMR traits (clinically relevant, MDR, mobile). Regression models linked trait prevalence to socioeconomic, climate, health, and antimicrobial consumption data, informing projections to 2050. Eighty-four high-risk traits, including carbapenem, colistin, and β-lactam resistance, are projected to rise, with antibiotic use, population growth, healthcare spending, and urbanisation. Projections were trait-specific: bla CTX-M-64 and bla TEM-1 may increase up to 20%, while bla CTX-M-65 and bla CTX-M-14 remain below 5%. A mechanistic shift in fluoroquinolone resistance is projected: mutation-based resistance (gyrA 87) declines while plasmid-mediated genes (qnrB17, qnrS1) rise. Food workers emerged as a potential reservoir, showing higher trait prevalence than food sources, uniquely carrying last-resort antibiotic-resistance genes (bla TEM-30 , bla NDM-5 , bla CTX-M-64 ). Integrating genomic with socioeconomic surveillance could shift AMR interventions from reactive to preventive.

papers.title: Epithelial NF-κB shapes protective Treg cell responses to restrain intestinal inflammation.
papers.authors: Barleben L, Schneegans AJ, Uyar B, Bruneau A, Vasileva G, Flohr F, Kabrani E, Vasilakis T, Hammann L, Gebert P, Dietrich C, Bochow-Fitzner B, Arnold A, Sai S, Gröne F, Sander M, Conrad T, Gérard A, Piseddu I, Anz D, Jochum C, Akalin A, Hammerich L, Klose CSN, Tacke F, Di Virgilio M, Kolesnichenko M.
papers.abstract: Inflammation resolution depends on coordinated communication between tissue compartments, yet how the intestinal epithelium shapes its immune microenvironment remains poorly understood. Here, using colonic biopsies from patients with ulcerative colitis (UC) and mouse models enabling tissue-wide visualization of NF-κB activity, we combine single-cell RNA sequencing and secretome analysis to define epithelial communication during colitis. We show that, paradoxically, the NF-κB-driven pro-inflammatory secretome of intestinal epithelial cells (IECs) is essential for recovery and prevents unrestrained inflammation. Mechanistically, epithelial NF-κB promotes CCL22-dependent regulatory T cell (Treg cell) recruitment and promotes a tolerogenic, pro-repair cell state, accompanied by induction of the lipid-metabolism-associated GDPD3 and CCR4. In UC, epithelial NF-κB is not uniformly activated but instead induces a selective pro-inflammatory transcriptional program while repressing targets regulating T cell recruitment. Thus, we identify dynamic epithelial-immune communication and demonstrate a protective IEC NF-κB-Treg cell axis important for resolution of intestinal inflammation.

papers.title: Type I IFN promotes ILC2-to-ILC1 plasticity in pre-clinical radiation-induced lung injury.
papers.authors: Kim J, Li H, Mannan R, Doherty TA, McGee HM.
papers.abstract: Radiation-induced lung injury (RILI) is a common dose-limiting toxicity after radiotherapy for lung cancer, but the immunological mechanisms contributing to RILI pathogenesis remain poorly understood. Here we analyze a RILI mouse model using high-dose, restricted-field irradiation to the left lung. Flow cytometry and cytokine profiling analysis of innate lymphoid cells (ILC) reveals a radiation-induced shift from lung-resident type 2 ILCs (ILC2) toward pro-inflammatory type 1 ILCs (ILC1). Single-cell RNA-sequencing analysis of mouse lung ILC populations after radiation suggests that type I interferon (IFN) promotes radiation-induced ILC2-to-ILC1 plasticity. In vitro, IFN-β stimulation of mouse ILC2s leads to increased expression of the ILC1 markers T-bet and IFN-γ, while IFN-β stimulation of human peripheral blood mononuclear cells increases the ILC1-to-ILC2 ratio. In vivo, inhibition of type I IFN signaling attenuates lung damage after irradiation in our RILI model. Thus, our findings indicate that radiation-induced type I IFN induces ILC2-to-ILC1 plasticity to contribute to RILI pathogenesis, and suggest that targeting type I IFN signaling may be a therapeutic strategy to mitigate radiation-induced lung injury.

papers.title: Asymmetric crosstalk between the BMP and TGF-β pathways resolves signaling ambiguity.
papers.authors: Auth JM, Eizenberg-Magar I, Erez Dekel O, Zachar O, Shmueli MD, Zigdon I, Shoham A, Mindel V, Olender T, Asulin Berrebi M, Tennenhouse A, Bar-Hai N, Ben-Yishay R, Ishay-Ronen D, Antebi YE.

papers.title: ct-validation: an open framework for benchmarking target-indication evidence against clinical trial outcomes.
papers.authors: Kostiuk K, Igumnov D, Fedichev P, Feizi A.
papers.abstract: Summary Human genetic evidence provides a strong foundation for selecting drug targets. However, consistent benchmarking of target-indication evidence against clinical trial outcomes has been hindered by proprietary data and customized pipelines. To address this, we present the Python package ct-validation, which evaluates whether target-indication pairs supported by specific evidence sources are enriched for clinical progression. This package computes relative success (RS) and odds ratios with confidence intervals across clinical phase transitions. It also supports ontology-based semantic disease matching and offers interfaces in Python, on the command line, and via the Model Context Protocol. By remapping the benchmark from Minikel et al. (2024) to the Experimental Factor Ontology, we reproduced their per-transition enrichment, with a maximum difference of only 1.4% across any transition. In a systematic 3 × 3 benchmark that independently varies the genetic evidence and clinical trial sources, we found that a single curated open clinical trial source reproduces the signal of the proprietary comparator (RS = 2.92 versus 2.65; 2.34 versus 2.55 without oncology). However, aggregating open clinical trial registries compresses this signal (RS = 1.52); this loss is primarily driven by the breadth of the indication data rather than the genetic evidence. Availability and implementation ct-validation is implemented in Python (version 3.11 or higher), distributed via pip, and freely available at https://github.com/gero-science/ct-validation, with support for Python, command-line, and Model Context Protocol interfaces. Archived code: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22901497. Benchmark data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22901451.

papers.title: Integration of polygenic risk with single cell methylation data using met-scDRS.
papers.authors: Li X, Shi Z, Hou K, Eyring KW, Liu C, Heffel MG, Luo C, Geschwind DH, Pasaniuc B.
papers.abstract: Motivation Although large scale genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified many risk variants for psychiatric traits their functional implication remain largely unknown. One potential mechanism for their risk is through cellular context-dependent epigenetics such as methylation. Previous methodologies have focused on integrating GWAS with single cell transcriptomics, which allowed identification of within-cell-type heterogeneity in disease risk association. We extended this framework to provide a method called met-scDRS that integrates GWAS with single cell epigenomics and investigates how psychiatric disease risk can manifest through methylomics at single cell resolution. Results We propose an approach that integrates single cell methylomes with disease associated genes identified from GWAS at single-cell resolution. We found our method to be well calibrated and powered in different scenarios. We then analysed a publicly available single cell methylome dataset of the human brain for 75 different traits and generated disease relevance scores for each cell for each trait. We find high brain specificity with major cell type enrichments congruent with known findings. We identify within-cell-type heterogeneity for psychiatric disease risk along the brain spatial axis as well as subpopulations that are differentially associated with diseases. Finally, we showed that genes with high correlation between methylation levels and disease relevance scores to be highly enriched in specific functional pathways such as synaptic formation and transmission. Availability met-scDRS is freely available in GitHub as a python package under MIT license: https://github.com/bogdanlab/met-scDRS. Source code is also available from Zenodo with DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.21841506. All dataset used in this work are publicly available.

papers.title: DNA-BFN: Bayesian flow networks for generative modeling of regulatory DNA sequences.
papers.authors: Yu H, Du Q, Wei L, Wang X.
papers.abstract: Motivation Designing regulatory DNA sequences is challenging due to their discrete nucleotide alphabet and complex higher-order dependencies underlying regulatory function. Many existing generative models, particularly diffusion-based approaches, learn by injecting stochastic noise into sequences and training denoising processes, which can distort discrete sequence structure and weaken biological constraints. Results Here, we introduce DNA Bayesian Flow Networks (DNA-BFN), a generative framework that models regulatory DNA sequences through iterative Bayesian updates of per-position nucleotide distributions. By directly modeling per-position categorical beliefs, DNA-BFN realizes a diffusion-like generative process without explicitly perturbing discrete nucleotide sequences, enabling fully differentiable training while preserving discrete sequence structure. Across eight regulatory sequence datasets spanning diverse species, scales, and sequence lengths, DNA-BFN consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, faithfully preserves sequence feature statistics and regulatory patterns, enables few-shot sequence design, and achieves faster sampling efficiency. These results show that framing sequence generation as progressive uncertainty reduction in probability space provides an effective and generalizable approach for nucleotide sequence design. Availability and implementation The software and its source code are publicly available at https://github.com/WangLabTHU/DNA-BFN. The dataset, source code and model weights are available in the Zenodo repository: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20177972.

papers.title: MARDy 2.0: a platform for exploring and analysing antifungal resistance mutations.
papers.authors: Webber J, Gifford H, Rhodes J, Farrer RA.
papers.abstract: Motivation The rising incidence of antifungal drug resistance represents a major and growing threat to global public health and food security. Therefore, understanding the genetic and molecular mechanisms that underpin antifungal resistance is essential for both clinical management and agricultural disease control. Results We present MARDy 2.0, an updated platform replacing the original Mycology Antifungal Resistance Database. MARDy 2.0 provides an interactive platform for exploring antifungal resistance data from the community resource FungAMR, and protein structures from UniProtKB or predicted structures using AlphaFold. The platform provides enhanced tools for data exploration and analysis and is freely accessible via an interactive web interface that supports search filtering and downloads, BLAST-based sequence similarity searches, an experimental natural-language query interface for exploratory analysis, a mutation plot for visualizing mutations in a protein context, and structural predictions showing mutation locations. MARDy 2.0 provides a platform to facilitate research into antifungal resistance evolution, surveillance, and mitigation strategies. MARDy should be used and cited alongside the underlying resources it integrates, FungAMR. Availability and implementation Accessible at https://mardy.net.

papers.title: FMCerNet: frequency-aware multi-label learning for fine-grained cervical cytology screening.
papers.authors: Zhou L, Cai Q, Wang X, Li W, Yang J, Song M, Zhang J, Zhou F, You Q, Wang Y, Feng Z, Zhang X.
papers.abstract: Motivation Automated cytology screening is essential for early cervical cancer prevention, where gigapixel whole-slide images (WSIs) are typically partitioned into tiles for tile-level feature extraction and subsequent WSI-level diagnosis aggregation. However, existing tile-level methods remain constrained by limited input sizes, which frequently obscures sparse and morphologically subtle abnormal cells. Furthermore, these methods commonly formulate tile-level representation learning as a coarse single-label classification task, thereby failing to capture the complex co-occurrence patterns and morphological heterogeneity of cervical cytological abnormalities. Results We propose the Frequency-Aware Multi-Label Learning Network (FMCerNet), a tile-level feature extractor equipped with a Large-Field Frequency-Enhanced ViT backbone and a Coarse-to-Fine multi-label classification head. The former incorporates a Dual-Tree Complex Wavelet Transform module to efficiently extract frequency-domain features from large-scale tiles, whereas the latter enhances fine-grained tile representation decoding through hierarchical supervision. Experiments on both public and private datasets demonstrate that FMCerNet improves the accuracy of positive screening and fine-grained subtype classification while maintaining high inference speed. Availability and implementation Code at https://github.com/imAzhou/FMCerNet and archived on Zenodo (doi: 10.5281/zenodo.22886105).

papers.title: MR-MAS: an end-to-end multi-agent system for autonomous Mendelian randomization analysis.
papers.authors: Wei W, Fan Y, Li L, Le TD, Li X, Cheng D, Feng Z.
papers.abstract: Motivation Understanding disease-related causal mechanisms is essential for biomedical research, yet the practical use of Mendelian Randomization (MR) remains constrained by fragmented analytical workflows and a strong dependence on specialized expertise. These challenges limit the efficient, standardized, and reproducible execution of end-to-end MR analyses. Results We propose MR-MAS, an end-to-end automated MR analysis system built on a multi-agent architecture. MR-MAS leverages the reasoning and coordination capabilities of large language models (LLMs) and integrates external tools to unify data acquisition, causal effect estimation, results interpretation, and manuscript preparation into a single workflow, thereby reducing manual effort. MR-MAS further incorporates a structured Mendelian Randomization Knowledge Base (MRKB) to support MR method implementation and targeted repair of MR analysis code. Across diverse test scenarios, MR-MAS demonstrated stable workflow execution, reproduced several literature-supported causal signals, and maintained consistent causal estimates across repeated runs and different model backends. Additional evaluations showed robust trait retrieval and improved code-repair performance with MRKB guidance. These results suggest that MR-MAS may provide practical support for scalable, standardized, and reproducible MR analyses in biomedical research. Availability and implementation The source code, MRKB, and benchmark data are freely available at https://github.com/Zaiwen/MR-MAS, with the version used in this study archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20342636.

papers.title: Highly effective viral RdRP translocation hindrance by the remdesivir nucleotide.
papers.authors: Li R, Shao Q, Wang M, Feng C, Xu Q, Wang Q, Shang L, Xu Y, Gong P.
papers.abstract: Nucleoside/nucleotide analogs (NAs) typically interfere with substrate selection and catalysis steps of polymerase nucleotide addition cycle (NAC), thereby affecting polymerase catalytic efficiency. In contrast, their interference with post-chemistry translocation is rarely considered in rational design, partly due to a lack of direct and quantitative evidence for such interference. Remdesivir (RDV) is an adenosine analog with broad-spectrum antiviral activity against diverse RNA virus families and has been approved for COVID-19 treatment. RDV is capable of inducing a characteristic "delayed" intervention, wherein the interference occurs several NACs after its incorporation. By combining X-ray crystallography, quench-flow kinetics, and molecular dynamics simulations, we show that the composite rate of RDV translocation from product strand position -3 to -4 and subsequent catalysis is at least 100-fold slower than that of adenosine in an enterovirus RdRP. However, mutating the corresponding roadblock residue serine417 to glycine largely abolishes this difference. Nonetheless, the incorporated RDV nucleotide can still alter the free-energy landscape even in the S417G mutant complex, enabling the capture of an over-translocated state. Our work demonstrates translocation-related intervention as an effective and broadly applicable polymerase intervention strategy in NA rational design.

papers.title: Integrative analysis reveals extensive interactions among C2H2 zinc finger proteins at chromatin loop anchors.
papers.authors: Radovani E, Nabeel-Shah S, Marcon E, Pu S, Zhong G, Tang H, Guo H, Kaplow IM, Emili A, Hughes TR, Greenblatt JF.
papers.abstract: Cys2-His2-zinc-finger proteins (C2H2-ZFPs) form the largest class of human transcription factors, yet their potential roles in higher-order genome organization remain poorly defined. To date, only a few C2H2-ZFPs, e.g. CTCF, have been implicated in chromatin organization. Here, we systematically examined the global relationship between C2H2-ZFPs and long-range chromatin interactions (LRIs). By integrating ChIP-seq datasets for 216 C2H2-ZFPs with genome-wide chromatin interaction maps, we find that >40% of human C2H2-ZFPs are significantly enriched at LRI anchors. Depletion of a subset of such C2H2-ZFPs is associated with altered expression of genes linked by the LRIs they occupy. To investigate whether protein-protein interactions (PPIs) contribute to this pattern, we generated a large-scale interactome using affinity purification-mass spectrometry, encompassing 345 C2H2-ZFPs, and LUMIER binary interaction assays for 204 C2H2-ZFPs, revealing extensive connectivity among the family members. Integrative analysis of PPIs, ChIP-seq, and chromatin interaction datasets revealed that interacting C2H2-ZFP pairs are significantly co-enriched at LRIs and frequently localize to the same or opposing loop anchors. Finally, we show that ∼35% of LRI-associated C2H2-ZFP binding sites overlap somatic mutations in cancer genomes. Together, our results reveal a widespread network of C2H2-ZFP interactions at chromatin loop anchors, providing an important resource for understanding chromatin organization.

papers.title: Exploring the bistable equilibrium of methylated CpG DNA recognition by the MBD2 protein.
papers.authors: Volkenandt S, Belyaeva J, Li T, Elgeti M, Metzler R, Imhof P, Williams DC, Bagherpoor Helabad M.
papers.abstract: Methyl-CpG binding domain 2 (MBD2) is a critical epigenetic regulator that selectively binds methylated CpG dinucleotides, key marks controlling gene regulation and chromatin organization. Understanding the interactions and conformational dynamics underlying this high selectivity is essential to elucidate MBD2's regulatory role. Here, using extensive classical MD simulations, we explored the formation of the MBD2-mCpG recognition complex. By initially positioning MBD2 one base pair downstream of its target, we observed its transition to the target site within microseconds. Notably, upon binding, MBD2 adopts two distinct stable conformations: a primary state closely resembling the X-ray crystal structure, and a secondary state of reduced affinity that nevertheless retains comparable selectivity for mCpG. Our results establish S189 as a key macro-switch; loss of its interaction with the methylcytosine backbone shifts the equilibrium toward the secondary state. This is corroborated by MD simulations of the S189A mutant, which preferentially adopts the secondary state-like conformation. Complementary NMR experiments confirm that S189A mutation does not alter mCpG selectivity, while fluorescence polarization measurements reveal a reduced binding affinity, consistent with our MD simulations results. Together, these findings indicate that MBD2 binding to methylated CpG involves a bistable equilibrium, providing new insights into how high affinity and adaptability are balanced in epigenetic recognition. In a broader context, our findings suggest that such alternative bound-state equilibria may represent an inherent feature of specific protein-DNA complexes.

papers.title: Decoding coupled epigenetic-fragmentomic signals in circulating cell-free DNA for interpretable cancer diagnosis.
papers.authors: Wang Y, Hou Y, Liu X, Li Q, Zhang W, Zhou X.
papers.abstract: Background Plasma cell-free DNA (cfDNA) whole-genome methylation sequencing enables simultaneous characterization of DNA methylation and fragmentomic features for cancer detection. However, it remains unclear whether methylation library preparation faithfully preserves fragmentomic signals, how methylation and fragmentation are biologically coupled, and how these two modalities can be systematically integrated. Methods We systematically evaluated the preservation of cfDNA fragmentomic features in whole-genome bisulfite sequencing (WGBS) and enzymatic methyl sequencing (EM-seq) relative to conventional whole-genome sequencing (WGS). We next investigated the biological relationship between methylation and fragmentation and delineated methylation haplotype blocks (MHBs) directly from plasma cfDNA as biologically interpretable units for organizing multimodal cfDNA signals. Guided by these findings, we developed multimodal diagnostic models integrating complementary methylation and fragmentomic features. Results Canonical cfDNA fragmentomic patterns were partially preserved across methylation sequencing protocols, although the degree of preservation varied among individual features. DNA methylation levels were associated with characteristic fragment length and end-motif patterns. Plasma-derived MHBs exhibited tissue-associated regulatory features and distinct patterns of chromatin accessibility, repeat enrichment, and methylation heterogeneity, providing biologically interpretable units for integrated cfDNA analysis. Within these regions, methylation and fragmentomic signals exhibited coordinated yet complementary patterns. Leveraging this framework, we developed Fragmentomics And Methylation Ensemble (FAME), an interpretable multimodal model integrating MHB-centered methylation and fragmentomic features for cancer detection and tissue-of-origin prediction, and further extended it with complementary genome-wide methylation and fragmentomic features to generate a genome-wide-augmented FAME model (FAME-GW). Across cross-validation, independent validation, and comparisons with THEMIS (THorough Epigenetic Marker Integration Solution), SPOT-MAS (screening for the presence of tumor by methylation and size), and DELFI (DNA evaluation of fragments for early interception), FAME-based models achieved robust diagnostic performance, with FAME providing a compact and interpretable representation and FAME-GW delivering the strongest overall predictive performance. Conclusions Our study demonstrates that cfDNA whole-genome methylation sequencing partially preserves informative fragmentomic signals and establishes plasma-derived MHBs as biologically interpretable units for organizing and integrating complementary methylation and fragmentomic information. This framework provides insight into the coupling of epigenetic and fragmentomic information and an effective strategy for interpretable cfDNA-based cancer diagnosis.

papers.title: The molecular heterogeneity and clinical impact of genomic driver alterations in prostate cancer.
papers.authors: Pellegrina D, Kiriy D, C L Cheng K, Favero F, Miletti E, Klein ZP, Hernando B, Olsen AV, Sahli A, Fu Y, Lutsik P, Jaratlerdsiri W, Hutchison WJ, Bova GS, Brewer DS, Brook M, Brors B, Butler A, Cancel-Tassin G, Corcoran NM, Cussenot O, Gihawi A, Girma EG, Gnanapragasam VJ, Hamid AA, He HH, Imada ELL, Jakobsdottir GM, Jung CH, Khani F, Kote-Jarai Z, Lamy P, Leeman G, Loda M, Molania R, Queiroz LR, Rausch T, Robinson B, Sørensen KD, Uhrig S, Xu Y, Yamaguchi TN, Zanettini C, Pan Prostate Cancer Group, Mangiola S, Voith von Voithenberg L, Marchionni L, Papenfuss AT, Pope B, Hayes VM, Schlomm T, Bristow RG, Hovens CM, Eeles RA, Cooper CS, Gerhauser C, Macintyre G, Gruber AJ, Wedge DC, Weischenfeldt J, Reimand J.
papers.abstract: Prostate cancer is a common malignancy with a heterogeneous disease course. Prior studies have identified a paucity of point mutations in protein-coding genes and only a few clinically relevant driver alterations. Here, using the Pan Prostate Cancer Group whole genome sequencing dataset from 1001 men, we perform an integrative analysis of cancer driver genes by quantifying recurrent genomic alterations among small mutations, structural variants, and copy number alterations in 961 primary prostate tumour samples. We identify at least one recurrent somatic or germline alteration in 97% of tumours and identify putative driver genes and mechanisms of dysregulation including frequently altered regulatory elements. A prominent example is the activation of oncogenes by structural variation-mediated hijacking of onco-enhancers of the solute carrier gene family including SLC30A4. Other recurrent alterations including FOXA1, MDM4, COL5A1, TP53, and BRCA1 stratify with metastatic disease, with additional drivers enriched in African-ancestry tumours. One quarter of tumours have acquired genome-informed therapeutic targets. Unsupervised analysis of alterations reveals four oncotypes with distinct genetic and clinical characteristics, including two clinically unfavourable oncotypes with shorter metastasis-free survival. Our study uncovers the full spectrum and recurrence patterns of genomic driver alterations in primary prostate cancers and delivers targets for biomarker development, mechanistic studies, and potential therapeutic interventions.

papers.title: Weak dispersal and landscape size inevitably promote local biodiversity in heterogeneous metacommunities of competing species.
papers.authors: De Laender F, Gonzalez A, Bleeckx O, Ebert D, Barabás G.
papers.abstract: We provide a general theoretical explanation for a longstanding result in spatial ecology: weak dispersal among habitat patches promotes local species richness. Using analytical approximations of spatial Lotka-Volterra competition models, we show that local species persistence in heterogeneous landscapes can be expressed as the balance between the total density across patches and the local exclusion rate. We further demonstrate that local multispecies coexistence is governed by the feasibility domain, linking spatial coexistence to a structural property of nonspatial competitive systems. Together, these results explain why weak dispersal increases local species richness and why this effect strengthens with the number of available patches, i.e., landscape size. We test these predictions using numerical simulations and find that the theory breaks down only when both dispersal and competitive interactions are very strong, in which case dispersal has a unimodal effect on coexistence. In contrast, landscape size retains a positive effect on coexistence whenever an effect is detectable. We then apply the theory to long-term data from a natural metacommunity of microcrustaceans. We detect strong competition among species and find no detectable effect of dispersal rate on local coexistence, whereas species co-occurrence increases with local landscape size, as predicted by theory. Together, our results identify how dispersal, interaction strength, and landscape size jointly regulate local species richness in competitive systems.

papers.title: Computational deconvolution of drug sensitivity via single-cell-to-bulk transcriptome mapping.
papers.authors: Coudray A, Forey R, Bejar Haro B, Martins F, Carlevaro-Fita J, Sheppard S, Offner SE, La Manno G, Obozinski G, Trono D.
papers.abstract: Analyses routinely conducted in both fundamental research and biomedical studies often report aggregate signals derived from heterogeneous mixtures of cells. These mixtures reflect the intrinsic anatomical and functional complexity of the tissues and organs from which they are derived. Such bulk measurements obscure cell-specific signals, thereby hindering accurate interpretation of the underlying biological processes. Here, we introduce CLIMB and CLIFF, a two-step machine-learning framework that deconvolves bulk RNA-seq into cell-type composition and expression, and then resolves bulk drug sensitivity measurements into cell subtype- and single-cell-specific profiles. We first validate CLIMB using in-vitro mixtures of leukemic cell lines with experimentally known cell-type proportions, then extend this validation to large-scale, cross-dataset pseudo-bulk analyses built from independent scRNA-seq references across two disease contexts and five cancer types - mimicking the reference-to-target mismatches encountered in real applications - and show that CLIMB accurately infers the cellular composition of bulk samples, outperforming state-of-the-art bulk deconvolution methods. We emphasize CLIMB's effectiveness in acute myeloid leukemia, where it offers highly accurate estimation of leukemic stem cell fractions across three test datasets and three patient cohorts. We then validate CLIFF, our algorithm for estimating cell subtype- and single-cell-specific drug sensitivity, first on the same in-vitro cell line mixtures using experimentally measured drug responses, and then through in-depth, realistic-scale pseudo-bulk simulations. We applied our deconvolution strategy to the beatAML cohort dataset, currently the most extensive database of ex-vivo drug screening data. This analysis generated a cell subtype-resolved drug sensitivity landscape for 121 compounds, revealing multiple compounds putatively active against leukemic stem cells, including midostaurin, A-674563, SNS-032, and foretinib. Collectively, our work introduces a general computational framework for resolving bulk functional measurements at cell-type and single-cell resolution, providing an attractive new computational tool for drug development and precision medicine.

papers.title: DNAharvester: a nextflow pipeline for analysing highly degraded DNA from ancient and historical specimens.
papers.authors: Sharif B, Kutschera VE, Oskolkov N, Guinet B, Lord E, Chacón-Duque JC, Oppenheimer J, van der Valk T, Díez-Del-Molino D, Heintzman PD, Dalén L.
papers.abstract: Motivation Ancient DNA (aDNA) research has advanced rapidly with the development of high-throughput sequencing, enabling genome-wide analyses of large collections of prehistoric specimens. However, analysing palaeontological and archaeological material with highly degraded DNA constitutes a major bioinformatic challenge. DNA from such samples is characterized by short fragment lengths, low endogenous content, post-mortem damage, and cross-species contamination, which can increase spurious mapping and reference bias, affecting downstream population genetic inferences. Results We present DNAharvester, a modular and reproducible pipeline designed specifically for processing highly degraded DNA from ancient and historical specimens. DNAharvester integrates metagenomic filtering, competitive mapping, adaptive aligner selection (incorporating BWA-aln, BWA-mem, and Bowtie2), and systematic evaluation of reference bias and spurious mapping. By incorporating flexible mapping and filtering strategies, the pipeline can be adapted to varying sample preservation, focusing on maximizing authentic data recovery. DNAharvester features subworkflows for iterative assembly of mitogenomes, identification of genomic repeats and CpG sites, taxonomic classification, microbial/pathogen screening, genetic sex determination, and variant calling. To accommodate varying sequencing depths, the pipeline supports diploid variant calling, genotype likelihood estimation, and pseudo-haploid random allele calling. We validated the pipeline using simulated and empirical datasets, demonstrating its ability to systematically mitigate complex background contamination while preserving authentic genomic signals. By streamlining complex bioinformatic tasks through simple configuration files, DNAharvester establishes a standardized approach for analysing aDNA datasets and makes genomic analyses of ancient remains accessible to the broader research community. Availability and implementation Implemented in Nextflow, DNAharvester provides a highly scalable, containerized framework that enhances reproducibility, portability, and robustness in aDNA analyses. DNAharvester is open source under the GNU General Public License v3.0 and freely available at https://github.com/NBISweden/DNAharvester.

papers.title: Deepweed: automated individual segmentation and tracking for duckweed lineage analysis.
papers.authors: Oyeniran T, Akindipe B, Islam T, Scheel JD, Josephs EA, Oliveira SMD.
papers.abstract: Motivation Aquatic duckweeds, including Wolffia australiana, are the smallest and fastest growing flowering plants on the planet, with numerous emerging biotechnological applications. Duckweed populations grow through rapid clonal budding, but existing phenotypic characterization and image analysis tools typically operate only at the population level, tracking neither individual plants nor their lineage structure. Deepweed addresses this gap, combining automated individual segmentation, temporal tracking, and clonal lineage reconstruction from time-lapse imaging of duckweed. Results Deepweed processes time-lapse duckweed imaging datasets using deep-learning-based instance segmentation and multi-object tracking to assign persistent identities to individual fronds and infer mother-daughter relationships. The workflow outputs lineage graphs, individual-level morphological metrics, and population-level growth summaries, supported by lineage-annotated time-lapse visualizations. Applied to dense Wolffia populations, in both freely growing or controlled microfluidic environments, our framework can track hundreds of Wolffia plants simultaneously, resolves overlapping individuals, and reconstructs multi-generation lineage structure, enabling analyses that are inaccessible with population-level phenotyping methods. Availability Deepweed is implemented in Python using PyTorch, scikit-image, OpenCV, and btrack. Source code, trained models, example datasets, and documentation are freely available at https://github.com/SamOliveiraLab/Deepweed. The Deepweed code is archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18844282 and the datasets are archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18843917.

papers.title: Seq2Pocket: augmenting protein language models for spatially consistent binding site prediction.
papers.authors: Škrhák V, Polák L, Novotný M, Hoksza D.
papers.abstract: Motivation Protein-ligand binding site prediction (LBS) is important for many areas of structural biology and molecular modeling, where, as in other tasks, protein language models (pLMs) have shown great promise. In their application to LBS, the pLM classifies each amino acid as binding or not, but translating these predictions into three-dimensional binding pockets remains challenging; in particular, residue-centric predictions tend to produce spatially fragmented pockets. Results We present Seq2Pocket, a methodology for pocket-level LBS prediction that combines pLM finetuning, data enhancement, and structure-aware post-processing. First, we introduce sc-PDBenhanced, an extended training dataset that augments an existing sc-PDB dataset with additional small-molecule and ion-binding sites, improving coverage of non-obvious and small pockets. Second, we employ an embedding-supported smoothing classifier to refine residue-level predictions. Third, we define the Pocket Fragmentation Index and use it to select a clustering approach that preserves a consistent mapping between predictions and ground-truth pockets. We evaluate Seq2Pocket on two tasks: general binding site prediction using the LIGYSIS benchmark and cryptic binding site prediction using CryptoBench benchmark. Across both benchmarks, Seq2Pocket achieves state-of-the-art DCCtop-N and DCCtop-(N + 2) performance. In particular, for general binding site prediction on the LIGYSIS benchmark, it improves distance-center-to-center recall by up to 13%, outperforming existing predictors. This improvement originates from training data quality rather than model architecture, as demonstrated by an ablation study. We believe that these findings contribute to more reliable evaluation practices in ligand binding site prediction, highlight the importance of training data curation, and provide pocket-level prediction tools that are better suited for downstream applications such as drug discovery. Availability The Seq2Pocket web interface is available at https://seq2pocket.projekty.ms.mff.cuni.cz, running the ESM-2 650M variant. The sc-PDBenhanced is published using Zenodo platform at https://zenodo.org/records/18271517. The models are published at HuggingFace: https://huggingface.co/skrhakv/seq2pocket.

Motion-corrected Noise2Noise denoising for structural analysis of cells and tissues with (cryo-)FIB/SEM.
papers.authors: González-Ruiz V, Fernández JJ.
papers.abstract: Motivation (Cryo-)FIB/SEM enables 3D ultrastructural analysis of cells and tissues at nanoscale resolution. However, its characteristically low signal-to-noise ratio severely hinders interpretation of the volume data. Noise2Noise (N2N) has emerged as a state-of-the-art denoising paradigm with outstanding performance in 3D electron microscopy-particularly cryo-ET-but its direct application to (cryo-)FIB/SEM remains unfeasible due to the inherent acquisition workflows. Results A method to enable N2N denoising in (cryo-)FIB/SEM is introduced. The input volume is split into even and odd slices, followed by the application of motion correction methods to estimate and compensate for the structural differences between the two subvolumes. The resulting motion-corrected subvolumes are then used to train the N2N model, which is ultimately applied to denoise the original volume. Representative (cryo-)FIB/SEM volumes have been used to validate the method and to demonstrate the critical importance of the motion correction stage for volumes with a slice thickness >10 nm. Availability and implementation Code is available at https://github.com/microscopy-processing/N2N-REO and https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22303478.

papers.title: A new phased assembly of the Antarctic spiny plunderfish provides novel insights into the evolution of the notothenioid radiation.
papers.authors: Martelossi J, Krasheninnikova K, Denton A, Wood JMD, Mathers TC, Durbin R, Fong N, Bentley DL, Clark MS, Bista I.
papers.abstract: Background Notothenioids are a well characterised species flock endemic to the Antarctic and an important model group for studying genome adaptation to extreme cold. A new reference assembly and clade-wide comparative genomic analysis allow for investigation of cryonotothenioid evolution and the appearance of novel functionalities linked to cold adaptation. Results A new phased assembly of a model notothenioid, Harpagifer antarcticus, demonstrated low levels of haplotypic variability across the genome. Nevertheless, numerous insertions from multiple LINE-L2 clades were found, suggesting ongoing transposition with potential contribution to speciation. Contrary to expectations the afgp locus was highly similar between haplotypes, except for large length allelic variants of afgp genes. Analysis suggests a model for the afgp locus expansion in H. antarcticus through segmental tandem duplications involving two pairs of afgp genes at time. Syntenic reconstruction of genomes from across the clade demonstrates conserved macrosyntenic relationships and group specific chromosomal fusions of notothenioids. Quantification of genome gain and transposition rates during cryonotothenioid diversification showed a first ancestral slow genome expansion concurrent with historic temperature drops. This was followed by lineage-specific massive peaks of genomic gain and transposition activity. Finally, we identified a set of genes that underwent ancestral diversifying selection and acquired novel conserved non-coding elements during the cryonotothenioid emergence. These were related to antioxidants and proteostasis, which may have facilitated the notothenioid Antarctic radiation. Conclusions Diversifying selection and genomic gain linked to transposon activity are primary contributors to lineage-specific evolutionary dynamics through the clade which facilitated adaptation to life in the cold.

papers.authors: Maier G, Hariharan M, Ramasamy RK, Glina A, van Rosmalen L, Pathak SJ, Deota S, Patel S, Lin T, Lam MTY, Le HD, Powale K, Shimomura T, Otobe Y, Rothenberg V, Sun M, Sakurai T, Chin T, Wu Y, Castanon R, Bartlett A, Chen H, Nery JR, Barragan C, Devulapalli S, Patel HH, Saghatelian A, Yoshitane H, Sahoo D, Keach SM, Ecker JR, Panda S.
papers.abstract: Exercise reduces all-cause mortality, yet its molecular effects across organs, sexes, and circadian phases remain incompletely understood. We subjected mice to 8 weeks of voluntary wheel running and collected 22 tissues and plasma during active and inactive phases for bulk RNA sequencing, metabolomics, proteomics, and single-nucleus RNA and methylation sequencing. Exercise induced canonical fiber-type switching and widespread, tissue-specific remodeling, with the largest transcriptomic changes in skeletal muscle. Except for the hypothalamus, kidney, and lung, most tissues changed more during the active phase. Females showed broader transcriptional responses, with distinct downregulation. Pairing single-nucleus methylomes with transcriptomes resolved the cell types driving exercise-induced epigenetic remodeling-changes undetectable by bulk studies. These included coordinated gene-body demethylation and transcription that tracked with fiber-type switching in specific myonuclei. Cell-type-resolved methylation, including partially methylated domains characterized in muscle, revealed a strong, sex-biased epigenetic response to training. Machine learning identified conserved exercise signatures across mammalian species.

papers.title: Comprehensive benchmarking of somatic mutation detection by the SMaHT Network.
papers.authors: Somatic Mosaicism across Human Tissues Network. Electronic address: abyzov.alexej@mayo.edu, Somatic Mosaicism across Human Tissues Network.
papers.abstract: Somatic mosaicism is increasingly recognized as a fundamental feature of human biology, yet the detection of somatic mutations remains challenging. The Somatic Mosaicism across Human Tissues (SMaHT) Network conducted large-scale benchmarking experiments involving cell lines and donor tissues to evaluate sequencing technologies, experimental approaches, and computational methods for detecting different types of somatic mutations, generating community resources with >1,000× short-read and 100-400× long-read data for nine analyzed samples. We determined effective strategies for utilizing short- and long-read sequencing for mutation detection and demonstrated that using donor-specific and pangenome-inferred diploid assemblies improved calling, extending mutation catalogs to challenging genomic regions. We benchmarked six duplex technologies and showed that single-cell sequencing resolves cell-type-specific mutational patterns and heterogeneity. Our results indicate that bulk, single-cell, and duplex analyses are complementary and that leveraging all three provides comprehensive characterization of mosaicism within tissues. Together, these findings provide the scientific and clinical communities with a roadmap for accurate genome-wide somatic mutation analysis.

papers.title: A telomere-to-telomere map of somatic mutation burden and functional impact in a cancer.
papers.authors: Sohn MH, Dubocanin D, Vollger MR, Kwon Y, Minkina A, Munson KM, Hart SFM, Ranchalis JE, Parmalee NL, Sedeño-Cortés AE, Ou J, Neph SJ, Au NYT, Bohaczuk S, Carroll B, Frazar CD, Harvey WT, Hoekzema K, Huang MF, Jacques CN, Jensen DM, Kolar JT, Lee R, Lin J, Loy K, Mack T, Mao Y, Mitchell MW, Pham MM, Scheinfeldt LB, Smith G, Ryke E, Smith JD, Sutherlin L, Swanson EG, Weiss JM, SMaHT Assembly WG, Carvalho CMB, Coorens THH, Harris K, Wei CL, Eichler EE, Altemose N, Bennett JT, Stergachis AB.
papers.abstract: Cancer genomes harbor extensive somatic genetic and epigenetic variation, yet large portions of the genome remain inaccessible to conventional reference-based analyses. Here, we demonstrate that pairing a near-telomere-to-telomere (near-T2T) diploid assembly of a donor with deep short- and long-read sequencing of their melanoma reveals that 16% of somatic variants localize to sequences absent from GRCh38, with satellite repeats acting as hotspots for UV-associated mutagenesis. Centromere kinetochore binding domains emerge as focal sites of chromosome arm aneuploidy breakpoints and somatic genetic variation, features we further demonstrate are also present in non-cancerous tissues. By contrast, extensive epigenetic remodeling of kinetochore binding domains appears specific to oncogenesis. Single-molecule telomere analyses reconstruct the cycle of telomere erosion and telomerase-mediated extension during tumor evolution, while haplotype-resolved chromatin maps reveal widespread somatic epimutations impacting regulatory elements. Together, these findings define previously inaccessible dimensions of somatic variation and establish a framework for telomere-to-telomere studies of human mosaicism.

papers.title: ScopeNovo: a de novo peptide sequencing method using spectrum-spectrum similarity to refine the prediction accuracy.
papers.authors: Song Z, Ding Z, Wang L.
papers.abstract: Motivation De novo peptide sequencing from tandem mass spectra is essential for characterizing unknown proteins, identifying novel post-translational modifications, and analysing samples without reference databases. While recent deep learning models have improved the predicted peptide accuracy, they typically select the predicted peptide sequence based solely on sequence-level decoding scores. Very often, high scores are assigned to peptides without the direct support from the observed mass spectrum. Results We present "ScopeNovo", a de novo peptide sequencing method that improves predicted peptide accuracy by using spectrum-spectrum similarity between the input spectrum and the "representative" spectrum corresponding to the predicted peptide sequence. ScopeNovo generates multiple candidate peptides using an existing peptide de novo sequencing learning model and reranks candidates based on spectrum-spectrum similarity. To test our method, we use π-PrimeNovo as the base learning model. Experimental results on the standard nine-species benchmark datasets V1 and V2 show that ScopeNovo can substantially improve the prediction accuracy. We designed two settings, where Setting 1 is for well-annotated species, and Setting 2 is for species that are not well annotated. For Setting 1, ScopeNovo improves the average peptide accuracies of π-PrimeNovo over the nine species by 6.1% and 4.0% on V1 and V2, respectively. For Setting 2, ScopeNovo can still improve the peptide accuracy of π-PrimeNovo over the nine species by 3.4% and 1.9% on the V1 and V2 benchmark datasets, respectively. Compared to the best-known method, RankNovo, the peptide accuracies over the nine species on V1 and V2 of our method for Setting 1 are 0.711 and 0.737, where the peptide accuracies for RankNovo are 0.687 and 0.682. Even for Setting 2, the peptide accuracies of our method are comparable to those of RankNovo. Availability and implementation ScopeNovo is implemented in Python under an MIT license. The source code is freely available at https://github.com/SoSongzhi/ScopeNovo.git. The test data are available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23181841.

papers.title: Leveraging spatial structure to design spatially-targeted malaria interventions at the community-scale.
papers.authors: Evans MV, Roche B, Herbreteau V, Révillion C, Catry T, Bonds MH, Finnegan KE, Mitsinjoniala E, Ihantamalala FA, Randriamihaja M, Raobela O, Garchitorena A.
papers.abstract: Progress in malaria control has stagnated since the early 21st century in many countries, requiring new approaches such as the use of spatially-targeted interventions. However, evidence on the effectiveness of spatially-targeted interventions is mixed, depending on both the setting and intervention. In addition, the potential role of community health programs in implementing spatial targeting is underexplored, with models focusing on coarser spatial scales than those needed to guide programmatic activities. We developed a two-age-class, spatially-explicit model of malaria at the community-scale for a district in southeastern Madagascar, accounting for environmental heterogeneity and spatial structure, to explore spatially-targeted community health interventions. The model was fit to field-based case notifications and malaria prevalence data and then used to simulate three interventions: indoor residual spraying (IRS), supplemental coverage of long-lasting insecticide-treated nets (LLIN), and active case detection (ACD). We compared five scenarios, one with no spatial targeting and others targeting communities (i) nearest to clinics, (ii) furthest from clinics, (iii) with highest incidence, and (iv) that are spatially central. The non-targeted intervention was generally the most effective, but the least resource efficient. The second most effective intervention was based on spatial centrality, which reached a larger population while using fewer transportation resources than the non-targeted intervention. No combination of interventions was able to eliminate malaria in the district, although detecting symptomatic cases through ACD could avert 100% of severe malaria cases at high detection rates. These results highlight the potential for targeted malaria interventions, especially in low-income settings, that take into account spatial structure in the human population and transport networks to reduce malaria burdens using fewer resources than conventional district-wide interventions. [A French language abstract is available as Text A in S1 Appendix].

papers.title: Computation-through-Dynamics Toolkit: Simulated datasets and quality metrics for dynamical models of neural activity.
papers.authors: Versteeg C, McCart JD, Ostrow M, Zoltowski DM, Washington CB, Driscoll L, Codol O, Michaels JA, Linderman SW, Sussillo D, Pandarinath C.
papers.abstract: A primary goal of systems neuroscience is to discover how ensembles of neurons transform inputs into goal-directed behavior, a process known as neural computation. A powerful framework for understanding neural computation uses neural dynamics - the rules that govern how neural activity evolves over time - to explain how goal-directed input-output transformations occur. As dynamical rules are not directly observable, we need computational models that can infer neural dynamics from recorded neural activity. We typically validate such models using synthetic datasets with known ground-truth dynamics, but unfortunately existing synthetic datasets don't reflect fundamental features of neural computation and may therefore be poor proxies for neural systems. Further, the field lacks validated metrics for quantifying the accuracy of the dynamics inferred by models. The Computation-through-Dynamics Toolkit (CtDToolkit) addresses these critical gaps by providing: 1) synthetic datasets that reflect computational properties of biological neural circuits, 2) interpretable metrics for quantifying model performance, and 3) a standardized pipeline for training and evaluating models with or without known external inputs. In this manuscript, we demonstrate how CtDToolkit can help guide the development, tuning, and troubleshooting of neural dynamics models. In summary, CtDToolkit provides a necessary framework for model developers to better understand and characterize neural computation through the lens of dynamics.

papers.title: From prompts to genomes: A constraint-first framework for AI-driven sequence design across life and viruses.
papers.authors: Wicaksono A, Parikesit AA.
papers.abstract: A constraint-first framework for future 'prompt-to-genome' AI across Bacteria, Archaea, Eukaryota, and viruses is proposed. Genome-scale models can now generate long DNA sequences, and experimentally viable genome-scale designs have begun to appear, but sequence generation alone does not establish biological feasibility. Constraints should not require designs to remain within natural sequence space; rather, they should define testable boundaries for function, inheritance, lifecycle coherence and safe use, including new-to-nature designs. We propose a two-part system. First, a Constraint Compiler translates natural-language prompts into machine-checkable specifications defining scope, context, objectives, assumptions and governance requirements. Second, a modular Validator Stack (C1-C6) evaluates candidate designs for sequence integrity, gene and regulatory plausibility, genome completeness, comparative coherence, systems-level feasibility, and safety and governance. Extreme prompts serve as stress tests to expose hidden assumptions, conflicting objectives, and refusal points, complemented by adversarial testing and risk assessment. A phased roadmap and community benchmarks are proposed to measure specification accuracy, biological feasibility, robustness, and governance performance. The goal is to move prompt-to-genome systems from impressive generation toward reliable, auditable, and accountable biological design.

papers.title: Ten simple rules to build genomics capacity for routine laboratory practice in the Global South.
papers.authors: Conceição EC, Sharma A, Marcon DJ, Ribeiro LR, Dos Santos DKC, Freitas LEO, Souza AB, de Jesus HNR, Lourenço MCDS, Andrade VDGD, de Oliveira MAA, Ramos TCA, Mesquita Cavalcante ÍJ, de Melo ALES, Ismail N, de Oliveira T, Warren RM, Ferreira AA, Bessa TCB, Frota CC, Suffys PN, Lima KVB, REVIGET Consortium.
papers.abstract: Developing sustainable genomics capacity in the Global South requires more than technology transfer; it depends on human-centered approaches based on the workflows and existing expertise of laboratory personnel, institutional collaboration, and long-term integration into health systems. Drawing on lessons learned from regional capacity-building initiatives, this article proposes ten simple rules for implementing and sustaining genomics capacity within public health and clinical laboratory settings. These rules emphasize local context, strategic planning, continuous learning, and equitable collaboration. Together, they provide a roadmap for laboratories aiming to transform genomic technologies from research tools for diagnosis, surveillance and decision-making, into routine instruments for public health in low- and middle-income countries.

papers.title: PanRes: a database of latent and acquired antimicrobial resistance allowing 3D-based protein homology search.
papers.authors: Vojtková M, Baltušis M, Martiny HM, Baral A, Pyrounakis N, Beleon A, Freitag R, Pico-Tomàs A, Kaas RS, Petersen TN, Munk P.
papers.abstract: Motivation Antimicrobial resistance databases are central to genomic surveillance, but resistance determinants remain distributed across resources with different scopes, structures, and annotations. Results We developed PanRes, a curated resistance database of 11 717 genes integrating acquired and latent determinants of antibiotic, biocide, and metal resistance within a unified ontology. We predicted representative protein structures and clustered them by structural similarity, grouping proteins into 505 high-confidence structurally conserved clusters coherent despite sequence divergence. Their structure-guided alignments were used to build Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) for remote homology search. In seven wastewater metagenomes from five European cities, PanRes 3D-based HMMs expanded detection beyond what was possible with BLAST, with 35.3% of retained hits identified only by the HMMs and generally showing greater divergence from known proteins. For beta-lactamases, several proteins retained beta-lactamase-like folds and catalytic geometry despite weak sequence similarity. Availability and implementation PanRes is available through an interactive web platform (https://panres.rambio.dk/), a structure-informed resource for exploring the whole resistome. The database, HMM profiles, and ontology are available at Zenodo (10.5281/zenodo.22876216).

papers.title: Correction to 'Transcriptome-wide analysis of Arabidopsis DICER-LIKE1 RNA substrates'.
The MODNAP benchmark set for modeling ribose-based modified nucleic acid and nucleic acid-protein complexes: a case study with AlphaFold 3.
papers.authors: Fu J, Milam VT, McShan AC.
papers.abstract: Modified nucleic acids play important roles in biology and biotechnology. However, their chemical and structural diversity as well as effects on nucleic acid structure and intermolecular interactions remain incompletely characterized. The performance of structure prediction and co-folding algorithms for modeling modified nucleic acids and nucleic acid-protein complexes has also not been evaluated. Here, we systematically analyze ribose-based modified nucleotides present in structures deposited in the Protein Data Bank. Modified nucleotides are primarily localized to the nucleobase, where they exhibit chemical and structural diversity shaped by molecular size, topological shape descriptors, and polarity-related properties. We develop MODNAP, the first curated dataset of experimentally determined structures containing modified nucleotides. Using MODNAP, we benchmark AlphaFold 3 on 1039 nucleic acid and nucleic acid-protein complex structures spanning a range of nucleotide modifications, tertiary folds, and biological functions. AlphaFold 3 achieves success rates exceeding 80% at an RMSD threshold of 2.5 Å. However, its accuracy in positioning modified nucleotides is variable and decreases for structures not explicitly represented in training. PoseBusters analysis reveals frequent intramolecular validity failures, primarily due to non-ideal ribose ring geometries. Together, these results establish MODNAP as a resource for evaluating and improving structure prediction methods for modified nucleic acids.

papers.title: Chemically stabilized long antisense oligonucleotides perturb RNA exosome function.
papers.authors: Hofacker DT, Gackstatter S, Deisling V, Stafforst T.
papers.abstract: The interaction with intracellular proteins shapes the pharmacology and toxicity of RNA drugs like gapmers and siRNAs. Here, we identify the RNA exosome as a modification-sensitive interaction partner of long, chemically stabilized, single-stranded RNA drugs. Using proximity biotinylation proteomics, we observe preferential binding of the catalytic exosome subunits DIS3 and EXOSC10 to oligonucleotides stabilized by 2'-ribose modifications and phosphorothioate linkages. RNA drug binding correlates with exosome impairment as measured by dose-dependent stabilization of promoter upstream transcripts and accumulation of ribosomal RNA processing intermediates leading to reduced cell viability. Consistent with structural requirements for substrate threading through the exosome channel, oligonucleotides longer than 24 nucleotides can impair exosome function. Systematic variation of ribose and backbone chemistry reveals that exosome inhibition is highly sensitive to the spatial arrangement of chemical modifications and can be mitigated by incorporation of bulky 2'-MOE residues or alternative internucleoside linkages like mesyl phosphoramidate. In contrast to the clinically established RNA drug modalities, class-specific liabilities of emerging ADAR-recruiting oligonucleotides remain poorly understood. Importantly, we demonstrate that ADAR-recruiting oligonucleotides can be designed that preserve editing activity while minimizing exosome interference. These findings illuminate critical variables that must be considered in the safer design of next-generation RNA base editing therapeutics.

OAS-nano: the Observed VHH Space Database.
papers.authors: Gillis CMC, Kropivšek Brumat K, de Marco A, Obrezanova O, De Genst E, Croasdale-Wood R, Deane CM, Raybould MIJ.
papers.abstract: VHHs, the variable regions of camelid heavy-chain antibodies, are increasingly used as therapeutic, diagnostic, and research tools because of their small size and stability. Despite the growing number of publicly available VHH repertoire sequencing studies, there is no large-scale, web-accessible database of VHH sequences. Here, we present OAS-nano, a database containing over 73 million unique VHH sequences collected from 16 public repertoire sequencing datasets and 1 previously unpublished dataset, spanning alpaca, llama, and Bactrian camel repertoires. Sequence reads were processed using a standardized pipeline to extract high-quality VHH sequences. Experimental metadata and sequence annotations enable users to identify sequences appropriate for their use case. OAS-nano is freely available at https://oas-nano.opig.stats.ox.ac.uk/.
