papers.title: Evidence for multi-Li+ clustering in lithium-ion battery electrolytes.
papers.authors: Stevenson JM, Agarwal G, Debnath S, Goldsmith ZK, Mondal M, Svirinovsky-Arbeli A, Yeu IW, Metlay AS, Kwon Y, Bhai L, Guha RD, Keeler EG, Weber JL, Steingart DA, Marbella LE, Urban A, Jacobson LD, Halls MD, Friesner RA.
papers.abstract: In lithium-ion batteries, the bulk solvation structure of the electrolyte is a major determinant of the physical and electrochemical properties of the cell, for example, conductivity, viscosity, salt dissociation and subsequent reactivity, the electrochemical stability window (and thus solid electrolyte interphase formation), and the composition of the electrochemical double layer 1-3 . However, elucidation of this structure at an atomic level of detail has been challenging to accomplish via a purely experimental approach. Here we combine machine-learning-enabled atomistic simulations 4-16 , nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy, electrochemical data 3,17-20 and quantum-chemical calculations to reveal previously unstudied multi-Li + complexes without bound anions that are uniquely facile for reduction. This insight explains the success of empirically chosen ethylene-carbonate-containing solvent mixtures and provides a foundation for the rational design of improved electrolytes. Furthermore, our machine-learning force-field-based lithium-ion-battery electrolyte simulations accurately reproduce a wide range of condensed-phase experiments 3,21-24 , despite being parameterized to only quantum-chemical gas-phase cluster calculations, and hence provide a compelling demonstration that machine-learning force-field-based models developed from first principles can robustly represent a complex chemical system to atomic resolution.

papers.title: A microexon regulatory code reveals autism-linked genetic variation.
papers.authors: Parada GE, Bretschneider H, Li JD, Fine JL, Dupas SJ, Ellis JD, Braunschweig U, Bonnal S, Dalal T, Engchuan W, Zarrei M, Wei W, Zafar N, Hemberg M, Attisano L, Ellis J, Irimia M, Wainberg M, Trost B, Scherer SW, Morris QD, Blencowe BJ.
papers.abstract: Neuronal microexons are a highly conserved class of alternative splicing events enriched in genes with critical functions in nervous system biology 1,2 . Microexon splicing is often disrupted in the brains of autistic individuals, and mice with microexon deficiencies display autism-like phenotypes 1,3,4 . However, the full landscape of microexons is not known, and the impact of genetic variation on these exons has not been systematically investigated. Here, through extensive transcriptome profiling, we detect hundreds of new microexons, including many with neuronal subtype-specific splicing patterns, and others that activate nonsense-mediated mRNA decay. Using machine learning, we define a sequence code predictive of neuronally spliced microexons and use this to identify critical regulatory elements surrounding the expanded microexon repertoire. This code further reveals genomic variants predicted to alter microexon splicing in individuals affected by autism, with rare variants having the strongest estimated impact. These variants are mostly detected in idiopathic individuals and are associated with autism status. They also converge on synaptic and other autism-linked genes, as well as genes not previously linked to autism. Our results collectively define an expanded repertoire of microexons, delineate their regulatory code, and pinpoint variants predicted to affect their splicing, with implications for the disruption of functions central to neuronal biology and brain disorders.

papers.title: Advancing subseasonal forecasting with machine learning.
papers.authors: Guan H, Mouatadid S, Orenstein P, Cohen J, Dong H, Ni Z, Berman J, Flaspohler G, Lu A, Schloer J, Talib J, Weyn JA, Mackey L.
papers.abstract: Decision-makers rely on weather forecasts to plant crops, manage wildfires, allocate water and energy and prepare for weather extremes 1-3 . Today, such forecasts enjoy unprecedented accuracy as far as 2 weeks thanks to steady advances in physics-based dynamical models and data-driven artificial intelligence models 4-10 . However, model skill drops precipitously at subseasonal timescales (2-6 weeks ahead) due to compounding errors, systemic model biases and the chaotic nature of the atmosphere 11-15 . To counter this degradation, we introduce probabilistic bias correction, a machine learning framework that substantially reduces systematic error by learning to correct historical probabilistic forecasts. When applied to the leading dynamical and artificial intelligence models from the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF), probabilistic bias correction doubles the modest subseasonal skill of the AI Forecasting System 16 and improves the skill of the operationally debiased dynamical model 17 for 91% of pressure, 92% of temperature and 98% of precipitation targets. We designed probabilistic bias correction for operational deployment, and, in the 2025 real-time forecasting competition of ECMWF 18 , its global forecasts were the best for all weather variables and lead times, outperforming the dynamical models from six operational forecasting centres, an international dynamical multimodel ensemble, the AI Forecasting System of ECMWF and the forecasting systems of 34 teams worldwide. These probabilistic skill gains translate into more accurate prediction of extreme events and have the potential to improve agricultural planning, energy management and disaster preparedness in vulnerable communities 19 .

papers.title: Sexual dimorphism in epidermal stem cell dynamics.
papers.authors: Engelman D, Hochstetter J, Bauduin A, Patil S, Valenti M, Song Y, Lian Q, Toniolo A, Ghiasloo M, Bansaccal N, Delaunois AL, Liagre M, De Luca M, Hoste E, De Rosa L, Shwartz Y, Simons BD, Blanpain C.
papers.abstract: The epidermis is a stratified epithelium comprising proliferative basal cells and differentiated suprabasal cells that are continuously renewed throughout life. Conflicting theories have been proposed regarding the heterogeneity of the basal cell layer, with some studies proposing that all proliferative cells have self-renewal potential during homeostasis 1-5 . Meanwhile, others posit a model in which stem cell differentiation occurs through an intermediate transit-amplifying-like progenitor state with strictly limited proliferative potential 6-10 . Here, to determine the heterogeneity and pattern of cell fate, we performed intravital time-lapse imaging to track the fate of lineage-labelled cells in the skin interfollicular epidermis. Results from quantitative analyses of clonal dynamics support a two-compartment model of epidermal homeostasis, whereby basal cells are organized in a stem cell-transit-amplifying cell hierarchy. Critical to these conclusions was the discovery of sexual dimorphism in epidermal fate, with female mice showing a highly synchronized pattern of cell division, differentiation and delamination that contributes to accelerated wound healing. Single-cell RNA sequencing, transcriptional profiling and clonal analyses of castrated mice revealed that male sex hormones promote stem cell differentiation and delamination. In summary, our study provides insight into the functional identity of the stem cell population and identifies sex-specific differences in the regulation of epidermal stem cells and transit-amplifying cell fate.

papers.title: Divergent genomic evolution in astrocytomas and oligodendrogliomas.
papers.authors: Chowdhury T, Tesileanu CMS, Kocakavuk E, Johnson KC, Lee JH, Erson-Omay Z, Heo C, Aldape K, Amin SB, Anderson KJ, Ashley DM, Barthel FP, Barnholtz-Sloan JS, Brat DJ, Brodbelt AR, Castro AV, Claus EB, Connelly JM, Costello JF, Datta I, Elliott C, Finocchiaro G, French PJ, Gan HK, Garofano L, Ghospurkar PL, Golebiewska A, Gundla PS, Hermes B, Hong C, Hoogstrate Y, Horbinski C, Huse JT, Iavarone A, Karadag C, Khasraw M, Kouwenhoven MCM, LaViolette PS, Li K, Lowman A, McCortney K, Moon HE, Sanai N, Nasrallah MP, Ng HK, Ormond DR, Kwan B, Padovan M, Paek SH, Poisson LM, Puri S, Shen E, Mehta S, Sloan AE, Vallentgoed WR, Van Meir EG, Vaubel R, Wade TE, Walenkamp AME, Watts C, Weiss T, Weller M, Wesseling P, Westcott K, Westerman BA, Ye GY, Alfred Yung WK, GLASS Consortium, Varn FS, Verhaak RGW.
papers.abstract: Astrocytomas and oligodendrogliomas are isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH)-mutant gliomas that most commonly arise in adults under the age of 50 and exhibit variable responses to treatment 1-3 . To understand the genetic drivers of disease progression, here we used whole-genome and whole-exome sequencing to characterize longitudinally collected tumour specimens from 183 patients with IDH-mutant glioma. Samples were collected through the Glioma Longitudinal Analysis (GLASS) Consortium 4 . Most primary surgery samples were classified as grade 2 on the basis of histology (73% for astrocytomas and 93% for oligodendrogliomas). We validated known genomic markers of tumour progression, including hypermutation and homozygous deletion of CDKN2A or CDKN2B (hereafter, CDKN2A/B) 5 , and discovered genetic alterations that distinguish between the evolutionary trajectories of astrocytomas and those of oligodendrogliomas. Mutations in phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K) and NOTCH1 were newly acquired in recurrent oligodendrogliomas, regardless of treatment, and were associated with an increased tumour mutational burden. In recurrent astrocytomas, however, again irrespective of treatment, acquired focal oncogene amplifications and CDKN2A/B homozygous deletions were associated with an increase in chromosomal imbalances, which converged with markers of chromosomal instability such as chromothripsis and whole-genome doubling. In both types of IDH-mutant glioma, we observed a convergence of acquired alterations, genome-wide changes and worse patient outcomes, suggesting that treatment-refractory clones were being selected. Treatment with temozolomide was associated with the mutational signatures SBS11 and SBS119 in both tumour types, whereas the radiotherapy-associated ID8 signature increased in astrocytomas specifically. We show that the genomes of oligodendrogliomas and astrocytomas adapt to the selective pressures of tumour progression and treatment in distinct ways, suggesting that oligodendrogliomas and astrocytomas differ in their responses to treatment-induced DNA damage.

papers.title: De novo design of cysteine proteases.
papers.authors: Choi H, Bauer MS, Coventry B, Venkatesh P, Chen A, Kim D, Bera AK, Kang A, Nguyen H, Sadre S, Decarreau J, Joyce E, Shankaran B, Thompson TR, Greenstein G, Didi K, Schaaf LL, Gershon JM, Shida AF, Lee GR, Hilvert D, Pellock SJ, Baker D.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence-enabled clinical phenotyping of human brown fat.
papers.authors: Gómez-Banoy N, Barrero JA, Pinheiro de Carvalho LR, Jiang CS, Lama TD, Karandikar N, Koenen M, Lam T, Plucińska K, Morozova K, Chahwan S, Barraza G, Agridag Ucpinar B, Liu JE, Sharma R, Lafontaine D, Schöder H, Cohen P.
papers.abstract: Adipose tissue has a central role in systemic energy balance and the pathogenesis of obesity and its sequelae 1,2 . In contrast to white adipose tissue, brown adipose tissue (BAT) uses energy to produce heat 3 . Detectable BAT in humans is associated with decreased prevalence of cardiometabolic diseases 4 . However, the complete spectrum of health conditions associated with BAT remains unknown, and high-throughput methods to quantify BAT activity in humans are lacking 5,6 . Here we leveraged big data and artificial intelligence to systematically define the clinical impact of BAT in a cohort of 101,243 patients from a large cancer centre. Our unbiased analyses revealed that, across all diagnoses, cardiovascular and psychiatric diseases were less prevalent in people with BAT. Using a machine learning approach, we semi-automatically quantified BAT activity in approximately 8,700 patients and demonstrated that higher BAT activity, especially in the axillary depot, is associated with lower odds of cardiometabolic diseases and healthier white fat distribution. People with BAT also exhibited more favourable glycaemic parameters, lipid profiles, inflammatory markers and echocardiographic indices. Analysis of medication usage demonstrated that angiotensin receptor blocker use was positively associated with BAT presence. As proof of concept, we showed that the angiotensin receptor blocker losartan increased brown adipocyte activity and whole-body energy expenditure. Altogether, our studies harnessing artificial intelligence and big data identify new clinical phenotypes linked to BAT and serve as a platform for drug repurposing to activate this tissue in humans.

papers.title: Mitotic and meiotic midbody remnants: Divergent architectures with distinct clinical applications.
papers.authors: Schindler K, Skop AR.
papers.abstract: Midbody remnants (MBRs), once considered inert cytokinetic debris, are now recognized as architecturally specialized, translationally active organelles whose functions reflect the mode of cell division. This review compares MBR biology in symmetric somatic mitosis and asymmetric oocyte meiosis. In somatic cells, MBRs can be retained or secreted as large extracellular vesicles that carry midbody proteins, RNAs, and translation machinery; their enrichment in stem and cancer cells implicates them in cell-state regulation and identifies them as promising, though unvalidated, substrates for liquid-biopsy biomarkers and therapeutic targeting. In oocytes, meiotic midbodies form a distinctive ring-cap architecture that concentrates local translation and restricts maternal products to the egg, thereby supporting developmental competence. Together, these studies establish division mode as a key determinant of midbody architecture, cargo, fate, and translational potential, linking cytokinesis to cancer biology and reproductive medicine.

papers.title: How compartmentalization and proliferation shape the splenic T cell repertoire during an immune response to a complex antigen in mice.
papers.authors: Buytenhuijs F, Tune C, Smits TC, Schampel A, Schierloh LK, Pagel R, Westermann J, Textor J.
papers.abstract: The adaptive immune system recognizes billions of unique antigens using highly variable T cell receptors (TCRs). To what extent TCR features shape the spatial distribution of the TCR repertoire (TCR-R) within lymphoid organs remains unclear. Here, we compared the TCR-R composition in T cell zones (TCZ), B cell zones (BCZ), and germinal centers (GC) of the spleen by analyzing the complementarity-determining region 3 of the beta chain (CDR3β) in microdissected splenic compartments from naïve and immunized mice. While we found substantial differences in TCR-R composition between these compartments, these differences largely disappeared once the effects of compartment size and proliferation were accounted for: During steady state, the few T cells found in BCZs strongly resemble random subsets of those found in TCZs. After immunization, expanded clones started appearing in the TCZ at day 3 and later shifted to the BCZ. GCs harbored even further expanded clones that were grouped into clusters with high sequence similarity. TCR-R differences during the immune response were well explained by a Galton-Watson model of T cell proliferation, suggesting that this could be the central factor shaping the observed TCR-R differences. Similarly, while TCR length and closeness to germline initially showed more pronounced differences between the compartments, our models of random distribution and proliferation explained these differences almost entirely. Hence, our findings suggest that splenic TCR-Rs are shaped predominantly by compartment size and proliferation rates rather than TCR sequence features. This would imply that quantitative assessment of TCR-R dynamics across heterogeneous spatial compartments during an immune response is only possible when these effects are explicitly accounted for.

papers.title: MEGH-DDI: MolT5-driven edge-aware graph learning with Hop2Token representation for drug-drug interaction prediction.
papers.authors: Zhou L, Zuo Y, He W, Deng Z.
papers.abstract: Drug-drug interactions (DDIs) are critical in pharmacology, as synergistic or antagonistic effects between co-administered drugs can enhance therapeutic outcomes or cause toxicity, posing major challenges for drug safety assessment and new drug development. Current molecular representation methods often fail to capture dynamic substructure relationships or semantic interactions among functional groups. To overcome these limitations, this study proposes MEGH-DDI, a multimodal framework that integrates complementary molecular representation learning with graph-structure dynamic perception. The framework employs a dual-channel semantic module that combines Mol2vec-based substructure representations with MolT5 chemical language embeddings, while SHAP-based dynamic feature selection reduces redundancy. For fine-grained structural modeling, we introduce an edge-aware GCNII equipped with bond-level attention to distinguish different types of chemical bonds. Furthermore, the Hop2Token module converts multi-hop neighborhoods into token sequences, enabling Transformer-based modeling of high-order substructure dependencies. Experimental results demonstrate that MEGH-DDI achieves competitive performance across both transductive and inductive settings. On the DrugBank dataset, MEGH-DDI attains an accuracy of 98.36% in the transductive task, outperforming earlier baselines and surpassing recent state-of-the-art methods, with both AUC and AP exceeding 99.7%. On the ChChMiner dataset, MEGH-DDI achieves an F1 score of 99.05%, improving over the best existing method by 2.74 percentage points. In the inductive settings, MEGH-DDI achieves competitive performance across most evaluation metrics on both datasets, showing advantages over competing methods on several key metrics. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of MEGH-DDI in predicting DDI involving previously unseen drugs and its potential to generalize to complex DDI prediction scenarios. To enhance interpretability, MEGH-DDI incorporates a three-level mechanism spanning atoms, chemical bonds, and topological paths, highlighting key atoms and bond contributions. Overall, MEGH-DDI provides an efficient, accurate, and interpretable solution for drug safety assessment and new drug discovery. Code and datasets are available at https://github.com/Lilyjoys/MEGH-DDI, and a free web platform is provided at http://www.edgh-ddi.com.

papers.title: CRISPR-HAWK: haplotype- and variant-aware guide design toolkit for CRISPR-Cas.
papers.authors: Kumbara A, Tognon M, Carone G, Fontanesi A, Bombieri N, Giugno R, Pinello L.
papers.abstract: Motivation Current CRISPR guide RNA design tools rely on reference genomes, overlooking how genetic variation impacts editing outcomes. As genome editing advances toward clinical applications, incorporating population diversity becomes essential for ensuring therapeutic efficacy across diverse populations. Results We present CRISPR-HAWK, a framework integrating individual- and population-scale variants and haplotypes into gRNA design. Analyzing therapeutic targets across 79 648 genomes reveals that genetic variants substantially alter guide performance. For the clinically approved sickle cell disease therapeutic guide targeting BCL11A, we identify haplotypes that completely abolish predicted cutting activity. Across seven therapeutic loci, 82.5% of guides contain variants modifying on-target activity. Variants also create novel protospacer adjacent motif sites generating individual-specific guides invisible to reference-based design. These findings demonstrate that variant-aware selection is critical for equitable genome editing. Availability CRISPR-HAWK is available at https://github.com/pinellolab/CRISPR-HAWK and https://github.com/InfOmics/CRISPR-HAWK.

papers.title: scChronos: hierarchical temporal context learning for missing snapshot prediction in single-cell time series.
papers.authors: Yao J, Zhang Y, Xu Y, Ma J, Wu S.
papers.abstract: Motivation Single-cell time-series atlases provide discrete cross-sectional snapshots of continuous developmental processes, making missing-snapshot prediction essential for reconstructing trajectories and dynamic programs. However, destructive scRNA-seq profiling prevents tracking the same cells across time, yielding unpaired population snapshots and making missing-snapshot prediction challenging. Existing methods typically rely on explicit dynamical propagation or transport-based coupling between snapshots, which may ignore the statistical constraints of the overall population distribution and be sensitive to sampling noise and cell-to-cell variability. Results We introduce scChronos, a hierarchical temporal context learning framework that formulates missing-snapshot prediction as target-conditioned population distribution prediction rather than individual-cell propagation. Unlike cell-centric propagation approaches, scChronos explicitly captures dual-level dynamics: (i) within each observed snapshot, scChronos compresses cell populations into cluster-representative cell representations with a transcriptomic encoder, preserving population information while reducing noise and (ii) across reference snapshots, the dual-branch temporal context integration module fuses information from all available and nearby time points into a temporal representation, which is then decoded with learnable cell-generation seeds to predict the target distribution. Extensive experiments demonstrate that scChronos improves both interpolation-style recovery and extrapolation-style forecasting compared with state-of-the-art methods. Beyond reducing distributional discrepancy, scChronos better preserves developmental topology and maintains cell-type-specific marker and pathway programs. Availability The code and data are available at https://github.com/yjs193/scChronos and https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20933283.

papers.title: HURDLER: a cloning method to overcome length limits in designed repeat proteins.
papers.authors: Dai W, Schuster M, Zerbe O.
papers.abstract: The number of internal repeat modules remains a major limiting factor in the construction and functional exploration of long repeat proteins. As a solution, we present High-Utility Recursive Directional Ligation for Extended Repeat proteins (HURDLER)-a modular cloning strategy combining codon optimization, seamless insertion of restriction sites, and modified recursive directional ligation. It presents a very robust technique to clone DNA for large repeat proteins, which may also contain non-repetitive parts, with high fidelity requiring a minimal number of individual cloning steps. Using HURDLER, we cloned designed armadillo repeat proteins with up to 85 internal modules, corresponding to >3700 residues. The method also generates intermediate variants with defined numbers of internal repeats, enabling systematic investigation of how the number of modules influences protein structure and function. HURDLER thereby provides a reliable solution to overcome restrictions in the overall number of internal modules used in the construction of very long repeat proteins. Such proteins are increasingly utilized as building blocks in macromolecular protein assemblies with defined structures.

papers.title: Attribute Network-based Ranking (ANeR) identifies conserved translational fingerprints of M-phase.
papers.authors: Eivers SB, Baumgartner A, Dorn M, Jessus C, Silva-Bernardes J, Daldello EM.
papers.abstract: Entry into M-phase requires mRNA translation, but whether mitotic and meiotic divisions share a conserved translational programme and which newly synthesized proteins promote Cdk1 activation remain unclear. We developed Attribute Network-based Ranking (ANeR), a multi-objective network-based method that ranks mRNAs according to their proximity to a training group across heterogeneous two-condition omics datasets. Applied to 30 datasets covering mitotic and meiotic divisions, ANeR identified a conserved M-phase translational fingerprint. Benchmarking ANeR predictions against independent mitotic datasets, together with experimental validation in Xenopus oocytes, confirmed that ANeR prioritizes proteins whose accumulation increases during both mitotic and meiotic M-phases. Application of ANeR to the meiotic translational programme identified Fam76b and Cdca3 as previously unrecognized translationally activated regulators required for timely Cdk1 activation, demonstrating that ANeR can uncover new regulators of meiotic M-phase. Analysis of the oocyte translational programme established how broadly CPE/PAS regulatory rules apply, identified transcripts that do not conform to these rules, and experimentally validated their translational activation. Together, these findings establish that vertebrate mitotic and meiotic transitions share a conserved programme of translationally regulated transcripts and demonstrate that ANeR can identify new regulators of cell division. Broadly, ANeR provides a flexible framework for investigating diverse biological questions using a collection of two-condition datasets.

papers.title: Structural basis of assembly-dependent activation of the MAD3-MAD4 nuclease in the Pseudomonas aeruginosa MADS defense system.
papers.authors: Zhang J, Li Z, Ye L, Hou Y, Liu K, Min J.
papers.abstract: The methylation-associated defense system (MADS) is a bacterial antiphage immune system that cooperates with CRISPR-Cas systems to restrict phage infection. Within MADS, the MAD3-MAD4 module has been proposed to function as an ATPase-nuclease module related to the OLD nuclease family, but the molecular basis of its assembly and function remains unknown. Here, we combined cryo-electron microscopy, X-ray crystallography, biochemical assays, and mutagenesis to elucidate the architecture and assembly mechanism of the MAD3-MAD4 complex. We found that MAD3 and MAD4 assemble into a stable 2:2 heterotetramer. Structural and biochemical analyses revealed that MAD3 alone lacks detectable ATPase activity, whereas MAD4 is insoluble when expressed alone. Assembly of the MAD3-MAD4 complex induces a conformational rearrangement in which MAD3 adopts an ATPase-competent dimeric conformation, while MAD4 is stabilized through intersubunit interactions. This heterotetrameric assembly exhibits both ATPase and DNA cleavage activities. Overall, our findings reveal the molecular basis of MAD3-MAD4 heterotetramer assembly and provide the first structural and biochemical insights into the function of the MAD3-MAD4 module within the MADS defense system.

papers.title: The MODNAP benchmark set for modeling ribose-based modified nucleic acid and nucleic acid–protein complexes: a case study with AlphaFold 3
A tripartite RpoS-CRP-cAMP-Cra circuit orchestrates metabolic reprogramming during stress adaptation.
papers.authors: Chen W, Feng Y, Liu L, Ma R, Danchin A, You C.
papers.abstract: The alternative sigma factor RpoS (σS) governs stress adaptation in many bacterial clades, yet how it coordinates stress responses with metabolic demands remains poorly understood. Thus, by integrating RNA-seq, ChIP-seq, and physiological and molecular assays, we redefined the RpoS regulon in Escherichia coli, expanding it to 667 genes and demonstrating that metabolic genes unexpectedly predominate over stress-response targets. RpoS directly drives a massive metabolic reprogramming event: it activates glycolytic and sugar transport genes while simultaneously repressing the trichloroacetic acid cycle and oxidative phosphorylation. This metabolic pivot is finely tuned by a novel RpoS-CRP-cAMP-Cra tripartite circuit to balance energy efficiency with survival during stationary phase. Furthermore, we provide a mechanistic framework for RpoS-mediated bidirectional regulation rooted in σS-factor competition, where transcriptional efficiency in the absence of RpoS dictates the regulatory mode: highly efficient promoters are repressed by RpoS displacement, whereas weak promoters are activated. This study advances our understanding of transcriptional precision during bacterial adaptation and offers an architectural blueprint for synthetic metabolic engineering.

papers.title: RiboBA: a bias-aware probabilistic framework for robust ORF identification across diverse ribosome profiling protocols.
papers.authors: Bai J, Yang R.
papers.abstract: By mapping ribosome-protected fragments genome-wide, ribosome profiling (Ribo-seq) has uncovered extensive translation beyond conventional coding sequences, revealing non-canonical ORFs (ncORFs) with roles in diverse biological processes. However, robust ncORF identification remains challenging when Ribo-seq datasets exhibit attenuated periodicity. Protocol-induced biases during library construction is an important contributor to this loss, yet most ORF callers do not explicitly model these distortions. Here, we present RiboBA, a bias-aware probabilistic framework for robust ORF identification from Ribo-seq data. RiboBA combines a generative module that jointly infers protocol-induced biases and codon-level ribosome occupancy with a supervised module that identifies translated ORFs and initiation sites from the bias-adjusted profiles. In simulations with known P-site positions, RiboBA improved exact nucleotide- and codon-level P-site assignment relative to a conventional fixed-offset approach. Across simulations and diverse empirical Ribo-seq datasets, together with orthogonal immunopeptidomics evidence, RiboBA accurately recovers protocol-induced parameters and improves ncORF identification, with pronounced advantages for RNase I libraries with attenuated periodicity, and for MNase and nuclease P1 datasets, while maintaining competitive runtimes. In a Drosophila case study, RiboBA identified candidate ncORFs with coding potential, including recurrent upstream translation in ThrRS and Mettl2, linking ncORF translation to threonine-related translational regulation.

papers.title: Substrate energetics in non-templated DNA synthesis by terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase.
papers.authors: Mogannam K, Lupták A.
papers.abstract: DNA polymerases typically use deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates (dNTPs) for DNA synthesis, yet the contribution of the γ-phosphate to catalysis remains unclear. Here, we examine the role of substrate energetics in enzyme-catalyzed polymerization using a fidelity-independent model polymerase, terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT). Relative to dNTPs, we find that TdT utilizes the canonical deoxyribonucleoside diphosphates (dNDPs) with reduced rates and catalytic efficiencies, but diminished substrate bias. This lower specificity indicates that the γ-phosphate contributes primarily to nucleotide discrimination, rather than phosphodiester bond formation. Furthermore, our work shows that dNDPs and dNTPs with the same nucleobase exhibit comparable activation energies for the rate-limiting step during DNA synthesis, supporting a model in which the γ-phosphate is not required for lowering the energetic barrier for TdT-catalyzed polymerization. These findings define a mechanistic framework for understanding non-templated DNA synthesis and its application in enzymatic DNA synthesis technologies.

papers.title: Representation-aware conformal prediction for reliable uncertainty quantification in drug-target affinity.
papers.authors: Li X, Zhang Y, Zeng X, Zhou D, Cheng Y, Shi S.
papers.abstract: Motivation Quantifying predictive uncertainty is essential for computational drug discovery to reduce experimental costs and false positives. However, most drug-target affinity (DTA) models focus on improving prediction accuracy without reliable uncertainty estimates. Results We propose representation-aware conformal prediction (RCP)-DTA, a representation-aware conformal prediction framework that constructs adaptive prediction intervals based on feature similarity. By constructing local calibration sets, our approach generates sample-specific prediction intervals that achieve empirical coverage close to the nominal confidence level. To improve representation quality, RCP-DTA employs a cross-modal architecture that integrates pretrained sequence representations and structural information. Binding site context is incorporated via virtual pocket feedback to enhance residue representations, followed by gated fusion for adaptive integration of sequence and structural modalities. Evaluations across multiple DTA benchmark datasets demonstrate that RCP-DTA achieves competitive affinity prediction performance while providing reliable uncertainty quantification. Availability and implementation Code and data are available at: https://github.com/Lee515628/RCP-DTA.

papers.title: CryoTriplane: triplane-based neural radiance field representation for high-resolution cryo-EM 3D homogeneous reconstruction.
papers.authors: Cheng Y, He B, Zeng Q, Zhang F, Han R.
papers.abstract: Motivation Determining the three-dimensional (3D) structure of proteins is a cornerstone of structural biology, providing essential insights into their underlying biological mechanisms and functional roles. Cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) single-particle analysis allows researchers to investigate biomolecules at near-atomic resolutions, unraveling the structure of biomolecular complexes. However, reconstructing high-fidelity 3D volumes from extremely noisy projections, particularly under the interference of structural heterogeneity, remains a challenging task. Traditional Fourier-domain methods often suffer from frequency-dependent signal attenuation and uneven information distribution. While recent deep-learning-based frameworks attempt to predict high-frequency components directly in frequency space, they are highly susceptible to noise and often introduce artifacts. State-of-the-art (SOTA) real-space method circumvents Fourier-domain defects, yet remains constrained by the inherent spectral bias of multi-layer perceptrons, as fixed positional encoding fails to sufficiently capture intricate high-frequency details. Results We propose cryoTriplane, a real-space 3D homogeneous reconstruction network that utilizes a hybrid spatial representation to adaptively capture fine structural details. By combining fixed positional encoding for noise-robust structural initialization with structure-aware positional encoding for high-frequency refinement, our method achieves 3D reconstructions that are simultaneously globally consistent and locally fine-grained. Comprehensive qualitative and quantitative evaluations across five simulated and four real-world datasets demonstrate that cryoTriplane significantly outperforms existing methods in resolving fine structural features. Furthermore, validation through downstream atomic modeling underscores cryoTriplane's ability to recover high-quality density maps. Specifically, our method achieves sequence coverage improvements of 4.6% and 5.5% on the EMPIAR-10005 and EMPIAR-10492 datasets over the SOTA approach, respectively. Availability and implementation Our code is available at https://github.com/chengyr1999/CryoTriplane. The real datasets used in this study are publicly available from EMPIAR.

papers.title: In vivo engineering of CAR natural killer cells for immunotherapy using ligand-directed lipid nanoparticles.
papers.authors: Chen Y, Monkovic J, Mughal H, Chen B, Thadhani E, McMullen P, Self A, Chen Y, Hu Y, Detmer S, Chen M, Lapteva A, Kamat R, Vernon A, Langer R, Anderson DG.

papers.authors: Robertson NA, Chandra T.

papers.title: HIP: Hessian Interatomic Potentials without derivatives.

papers.title: LLMs predict material properties based on atom types and not atom positions.
CD200+ fibroblasts prime the immunoregulatory function of granulocytic myeloid-derived suppressor cells in inflammatory arthritis.
papers.authors: Angeli MR, Schütz C, Schmidt H, Demmler R, Chang J, Labinsky H, Raimondo MG, Lalazi B, Stergioula K, Huang K, Fedorchenko V, Li M, Winter Z, Tsiami S, Lienert A, Rütten S, Weber S, Luber M, Bäuerle T, Bahrami R, Boehm H, Schett G, Rauber S, Baraliakos X, Ramming A.
papers.abstract: Granulocytic myeloid-derived suppressor cells (G-MDSCs) are immunoregulatory cells of the neutrophil lineage. Here, we show that immunoregulation by G-MDSCs is imprinted by the joint tissue microenvironment in patients with axial spondyloarthritis and in animal models of inflammatory arthritis. We demonstrate that the suppressive function of G-MDSCs is significantly enhanced in the joint tissue, but not in the circulation. Analysis of public single-cell RNA sequencing datasets was consistent with Cd200r1 high Hmgb2 + precursors differentiating into G-MDSCs following interaction with Cd200 + fibroblasts. In hTNFtg/Il23mc mice, treatment with a CD200R1 agonist promoted an immunoregulatory signature associated with PD-L1 expression, whereas CD200 blockade reversed the phenotype. Following adoptive transfer of G-MDSC precursor cells into arthritic mice, administration of a CD200-blocking antibody impaired the differentiation of PD-L1 + G-MDSCs and exacerbated disease severity. These findings reveal a tissue-intrinsic program that facilitates resolution of inflammation through fibroblast-myeloid crosstalk that enhances G-MDSC function.

papers.title: Rare k-mers reveal centromere haplogroups underlying human diversity and cancer translocations.
papers.authors: Shiraishi Y, Ochi Y, Sugawa M, Sakamoto Y, Kimura K, Tsujimura T, Okada A, Okuda R, Namba S, Hori T, Kobayashi Y, Miyauchi T, Mateos RN, Suzuki H, Chiba K, Ito Y, Nakamura W, Ohka F, Motomura K, Yamamoto T, Kawai Y, Okada Y, Suzuki H, Fukagawa T, Kato M, Saito R, Garrison E, Logsdon GA, Ogawa S.
papers.abstract: Human centromeres are highly variable but remain among the least characterized regions of the genome because their repetitive structure has hindered conventional analysis of population diversity and disease relevance. Here, we show that rare k-mers in centromeric regions capture lineage-specific variation, defining discrete haplogroups with distinct structural features. We developed ascairn to infer these haplogroups from short-read whole-genome sequencing (WGS) data. Applying this framework to >3,300 genomes reveals extensive global diversity in centromere haplogroups and signatures of population history. Analyzing short-read WGS data from 142 oligodendroglioma cases with 1p/19q co-deletion, we mapped breakpoints to the centromere regions of chromosomes 1 and 19, revealing a clear positional relationship to kinetochore attachment sites and a link between centromere haplotype structure and rearrangement susceptibility. Rare k-mers thus open centromeres to population-scale analysis, linking centromere structural diversity to human evolutionary history and disease-associated genomic instability.

papers.title: Interpretable neural networks prioritize cancer driver genes from genome-wide dependency landscapes.
papers.authors: Yin Q, Chen L.
papers.abstract: Identifying cancer driver genes and their therapeutic impact remains a core challenge in computational cancer biology. We introduce xNNDriver and xAEDriver, two interpretable neural network frameworks that connect cancer mutations with genome-wide DepMap gene dependencies, pathway activity, and drug-response patterns. xNNDriver is a supervised pathway-guided model that evaluates whether a gene's mutation status is encoded in the genome-wide dependency landscape; we interpret model fitness as a driver potential score, which quantifies the strength of this mutation-dependency signal and prioritizes genes with broad functional footprints. Across 3,008 candidate genes, xNNDriver recovers major established drivers and highlights literature-supported candidates, while pathway analyses reveal biologically coherent programs related to metabolism, growth factor signaling, and immune regulation. To capture combinatorial functional states, xAEDriver uses an unsupervised autoencoder to learn Driver Variant Representations (DVRs), latent binary features guided by the frequency distribution of known driver mutations. DVRs capture cell-line-specific dependency patterns and expression patterns and are associated with drug sensitivity and pathway activity. Together, these interpretable deep learning models demonstrate that gene dependency landscapes encode rich, interpretable signals of oncogenic function and provide a hypothesis-generating framework for prioritizing drivers, pathways, and therapeutic vulnerabilities for further experimental validation.

papers.title: Forecasting of infectious disease epidemics in sexual networks using attenuated renewal processes.
papers.authors: Green WD, Overton CE, Ward T, McCarthy CV, Funk S.
papers.abstract: Forecasting emerging infectious disease outbreaks is particularly challenging for sexual networks of men who have sex with men (MSM), where transmission can be shaped by heterogeneous and overdispersed contact structures, mixing assortativity, and both one-time and recurrent partnerships. Using stochastic epidemic simulations on synthetic MSM networks and empirical mpox case data from major cities, we systematically evaluated five classes of short-term forecasting models, from random walk approaches to semi-mechanistic attenuated renewal processes. Model performance was assessed using the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS). Across both simulated and empirical epidemics in heterogeneous networks, renewal models attenuated by a reverse-sigmoid curve, to account for early depletion of highly-connected nodes, consistently outperformed alternatives, achieving more balanced and reliable forecasts. Our findings suggest a practical approach for robust forecasting in highly overdispersed networks, where distinguishing network effects from other factors remains challenging and usually requires additional data.

papers.title: Going around phase defects: Addressing a fundamental flaw of phase singularity detection.
papers.authors: Verstraeten B, Lootens S, Van Den Abeele R, Van Nieuwenhuize V, Okenov A, Hendrickx S, Santos Bezerra A, Nezlobinskii T, Kappadan V, Handa BS, Ng FS, Duytschaever M, Vandersickel N.
papers.abstract: Phase mapping is a widespread method for identifying rotational electrical activity sustaining cardiac arrhythmias. However, conventional implementations assume that the cardiac phase map is continuous, leading to ill-defined phase indices in regions affected by functional conduction block, fibrosis, or anatomical boundaries. These regions of discontinuous or undefined phase, termed phase defects, lead to both false positive and false negative detections of rotational drivers. This work introduces an improved phase mapping implementation termed extended phase mapping that explicitly detects and accounts for phase defects, enabling robust calculation of the phase index around them. Extended phase mapping is applied to (1) simulated excitation patterns using the Fenton-Karma model, (2) experimental optical mapping data of rat ventricular fibrillation, and (3) a clinical CARTO activation map of atrial tachycardia. Across all datasets, the extended approach eliminates erroneous detections and resolves previously missed rotations. Our results demonstrate that proper treatment of phase defects yields a unified and physiologically consistent characterization of all rotational drivers including near-complete and anatomical reentries. Therefore, we propose that explicitly accounting for phase defects, rather than tracking singular points alone, gives a more complete and consistent characterization of rotational dynamics in cardiac tissue.

papers.title: Distinct extracellular architectures shape mechanical persistence in GPVI and CLEC-2 receptor assemblies.
papers.authors: Zhang Y, Cheng Y, Soe HN, Xu Z.
papers.abstract: Glycoprotein VI (GPVI) and C-type lectin-like receptor 2 (CLEC-2) are platelet-activating receptors whose extracellular organization contributes to receptor association and signaling during thrombus formation, yet how alternative receptor architectures influence mechanical persistence remains unclear. We used molecular dynamics to compare a GPVI dimer based on 2GI7, a domain-swapped GPVI assembly derived from 7NMU, and a crystallographic CLEC-2 contact using the same pulling protocol and constant-force conditions. During the first 5 nm of imposed separation, reconstructed GPVI required less force and mechanical work than CLEC-2 and domain-swapped GPVI. Under constant-force loading from 400 to 600 pN, reconstructed GPVI also reached the same extension endpoint markedly earlier than the domain-swapped assembly, with passage times differing by more than an order of magnitude under several conditions. Extended pulling to approximately 10 nm produced complete loss of interreceptor heavy-atom contacts in reconstructed GPVI while local peptide and disulfide connectivity remained intact. In contrast, the domain-swapped preparation retained resistance over a larger part of the separation pathway and showed substantially greater mechanical persistence. These results show that alternative extracellular arrangements of the same receptor are not mechanically equivalent and that uncertainty in GPVI architecture can translate into large differences in force transmission and persistence under load. Such architecture-dependent persistence may influence the stability of extracellular receptor associations during thrombus formation and thereby affect the mechanical lifetime of receptor clusters under load.

papers.title: Natural killer cell receptor signaling and activation depend on cell cycle stages.
papers.authors: Wethington D, Nayak I, Jensen H, Stewart WC, Aguilar OA, Chen SY, Nolan GP, Behbehani GK, Lanier LL, Das J.
papers.abstract: Natural Killer (NK) cells are lymphocytes of the innate immunity and provide key protection against infection and cancer. NK cells express a wide array of inhibitory and activating receptors on the cell surface including the activating receptor NKG2D. Receptor signaling in NK cells leads to rapid post-translational modification (e.g., phosphorylation) of sub-cellular signaling proteins within minutes of receptor stimulation that ultimately give rise to diverse effector functions including cell proliferation. Recent single-cell mass cytometry (i.e., CyTOF) experiments in macrophages showed variations of abundances of phosphorylated signaling proteins across cell cycle stages indicating a dependence of cell signaling kinetics on an order of magnitude slower kinetics (~ several hours) of cell cycle transitions. We investigated cell cycle dependence of NKG2D signaling kinetics in NK cells using longitudinal CyTOF measurements up to 256 minutes post stimulation performed on IL-2-treated NKG2D-stimulated primary human CD56dim NK cells. The CyTOF experiments revealed cell stage specific kinetics of signaling proteins such as pVav1, pErk, and pS6, with the degranulation marker CD107a showing its largest upregulation specifically in the combined G2 and M (G2 - M) stage. We developed stochastic minimal computational models coupling signaling and cell cycle processes to investigate the effect of cell cycle transitions on NK cell receptor induced signaling kinetics. These models suggest that the observed cell stage specific NK cell receptor signaling kinetics arise due to active modulation of the receptor signaling kinetics by cell cycle progression. The framework can be extended to study the interplay between receptor signaling and cell cycle progression in other cell types.

papers.title: The influence of cell morphology on the dynamics and stability of model bacterial communities.
papers.authors: Lim IX, Halabeya F, Milstein JN.
papers.abstract: Understanding how structures arise in microbial communities remains an outstanding challenge in bacterial ecology. When replicating within dense and confined environments, bacterial populations may collectively self-organize as a result of mechanical interactions. We previously observed that model dual-populations of bacteria, colonizing open-ended microchannels, either quickly fixate to a single population or segregate into long-lived, coexisting populations. This latter quasi-stability results from the alignment of bacteria into lanes, forcing cells to grow toward the open ends of the channel, with inter-lane invasion events driving the boundary dynamics between populations. Here we apply agent-based (AB) simulations to explore the boundary dynamics between dual-bacterial populations of varying morphology and division rate. We find that the simulated boundary dynamics are well-described by a simple drift-diffusion model, which enables us to estimate the mean time to fixation within competitive scenarios where the fixation time is difficult to access by AB simulations. Coccus-like cells display a competitive advantage over bacillus cells as they can more effectively invade and ultimately fixate, while coexisting populations of bacillus cells are "effectively" stable. And while faster-dividing cells should have a selective advantage, their morphology determines if this advantage drives fixation or acts as a defensive strategy to maintain their population. These findings highlight the critical role that cell morphology and mechanics play in shaping bacterial communities.

papers.title: DipSkmer: Reference-free population genomics with diploid genome skims.
papers.authors: Charvel E, Alves Monteiro HJ, Mirarab S, Bafna V.
papers.abstract: Ecologists and conservation biologists rely on genetic diversity as an essential biodiversity variable (EBV) used to track population health and dynamics, and utilize the population-scaled mutation parameter θ as a key metric of diversity. While whole-genome sequencing (WGS) is increasingly affordable, it will be considerable time before the full diversity of life is represented by high-quality assembled genomes; even then, constant monitoring will still require repeated sampling across time and space. In contrast, genome skimming (low-coverage, short-read wgs) is highly cost-effective but challenging to analyze because the coverage is too low for assembly and reliable error correction. Mature methods, such as Mash, exist for estimating pairwise genomic distances based on the Jaccard similarity of k-mer sets computed using sketching techniques. Some, such as Skmer, additionally model the impacts of low coverage. These methods have been successfully applied to assembly-free species identification and phylogenetics; however, their use in population genetics has been limited. Among other limitations, these methods implicitly treat genomes as haploid, and heterozygosity confounds estimates of genomic distance for diploid organisms. In this paper, we address this problem through several technical advances. First, we use coalescent theory to mathematically derive how the Jaccard index between the k-mer sets of two diploid samples changes with θ under a neutral Kingman's coalescent model. Next, we model the impact of coverage and sequencing error to derive an estimate of θ from the Jaccard index, in addition to several auxiliary variables, which we also estimate from the genome skims. The resulting method, DipSkmer, enables more accurate estimates of coverage, sequencing error, and θ for diploid samples. Analyses of both simulated and empirical datasets show that for diploids and low distances (e.g., < 2%), DipSkmer's estimate outperforms existing alignment-free methods such as Mash and Skmer, and closely approximates ANGSD, a reference and alignment-based tool.

papers.title: Letters and biological process: linguistic structure encodes hierarchical depth in the gene ontology.
papers.authors: Ahmad S.
papers.abstract: Motivation We asked whether the natural language used to name Gene Ontology (GO) Biological Process terms encodes hierarchical position in the GO directed acyclic graph. Results Semantic representations of term names, combined with Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection visualization and k-means clustering (k=20) recovered biologically coherent semantic groups whose depth distributions differed strongly (Kruskal-Wallis H=5244; p Availability and implementation The go_lingdepth Python package, regenerated result tables, and figure-generation scripts are available at https://github.com/Sadiya-ISU/Letters-and-Biological-Process and archived on Zenodo (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.21501473).

papers.title: Efficient and scalable Python implementation of ANCOM-BC and ANCOM-BC2 for omics differential abundance testing.
papers.authors: Wu Z, Lin H, Morton JT, Zhu Q.
papers.abstract: Summary Analysis of Compositions of Microbiomes with Bias Correction (ANCOM-BC) and its successor ANCOM-BC2 are critical algorithms for differential abundance analysis. Designed for handling compositional data, they feature the ability to estimate the unknown sampling fractions and correct the bias induced by their differences. While the original R package implementing the two methods is robust for standard dataset sizes, the increasing magnitude of modern multiomics studies presents computational challenges, often resulting in a runtime bottleneck for high-dimensional data. Here, we present native Python implementations of both ANCOM-BC and ANCOM-BC2 in the scikit-bio package, significantly accelerating the workflow and enabling their application to large-scale datasets. By leveraging vectorization with NumPy and numerical optimization in SciPy, we enhanced the efficiency of both methods without compromising their statistical accuracy. The benchmarking results revealed a dramatic increase in performance in both simulated and real datasets. We demonstrated that our Python implementations generated test results matching the original R code, while achieving 380- and 147-fold faster runtimes and 97.4% and 96.2% lower memory consumption on the largest tested dataset, respectively. The Python implementations allow for the analysis of datasets that are significantly larger than previously possible, and enable applications to alternative omics data types and complex statistical models that vary greatly by the number of samples, features, and covariates. Availability and implementation https://github.com/scikit-bio/scikit-bio.

papers.title: Inverse probability weighting-based mediation analysis for microbiome data.
papers.authors: Zhang Y, Wang J, Shen J, Galloway-Peña J, Shelburne S, Wang L, Hu J.
papers.abstract: Motivation Mediation analysis is an important tool for elucidating causal mechanisms in biomedical research and has recently gained increasing attention in microbiome studies. Motivated by a microbiome study of acute myeloid leukemia (AML) patients, we investigate whether the effect of induction chemotherapy (IC) intensity on infection status is mediated through gut microbial taxa. This problem poses substantial methodological challenges due to the high dimensionality, zero inflation, and dependence of microbial mediators, as well as the presence of an exposure-induced mediator-outcome confounder, antibiotic use. Results To address these challenges, we propose a novel nonparametric identification formula for the interventional indirect effect, a causal mediation estimand that remains identifiable in the presence of exposure-induced mediator-outcome confounding. Building on this identification result, we develop an inverse probability-weighting estimator and construct standard normal bootstrap confidence intervals for inference. Simulation studies demonstrate that the proposed method achieves accurate effect estimation and maintains appropriate type I error rates and power in finite samples. Application to the AML microbiome study provides evidence of a statistically significant interventional indirect effect of IC intensity on infection risk through alterations in the gut microbiome. Availability and implementation The R code for the simulation studies is available at https://github.com/YX-ZHANG-1/CausalMediationMicrobiome and archived on Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21960802.

papers.title: Seumetry: a versatile and comprehensive R toolkit to accelerate high-dimensional flow and mass cytometry data analysis.
papers.authors: Borggrewe M, Flosbach M, Testa L, Ly C, Baumdick M, Prinz I, Hamburg Intestinal Tissue Study Group, Billeb E, Bonn S, Bunders MJ.
papers.abstract: Motivation Recent progress in flow and mass cytometry technologies enables the simultaneous measurement of over 50 parameters for an individual cell. The resulting increase in data volume and complexity present challenges for conventional analysis methods, which are based on manual gating, are time-consuming and fail to capture unknown or minor cell populations. Advances in single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNAseq) technologies have prompted the development of computational analysis tools designed to process and analyze high-dimensional biological data. Building on these advances, we here present Seumetry, a framework that combines flow and mass cytometry data-specific analysis methods with the capabilities of Seurat, a powerful tool for the analysis of scRNAseq data. Results Seumetry offers methods for advanced quality control, data visualizations, and differential population abundance and protein expression analysis. We tested Seumetry on an in-house generated complex dataset of immune cells from different layers of human intestines, demonstrating that Seumetry accurately identifies distinct immune cell populations. Furthermore, benchmarking against public datasets showed that Seumetry aligns with manual-gated results, further validating its use for high-dimensional flow and mass cytometry data. In summary, Seumetry provides a new scalable framework for the comprehensive analysis of high-dimensional cytometry data with seamless integration into commonly used scRNAseq analysis tools, enabling in-depth analysis methods to facilitate biological interpretations. Availability Seumetry code is available open source under an MIT license and the current version can be viewed and used via Github: https://github.com/imsb-uke/Seumetry; and archived on Zenodo: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21216681. Flow cytometry data generated for this manuscript is available via Zenodo: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.11935872.

papers.title: PXL: a nucleic acid-binding module of the promyelocytic leukemia protein.
papers.authors: Fairchild D, Semenova IV, Geddes-Buehre D, Li Y, Szczepaniak R, Weller SK, Hao B, Bezsonova I.
papers.abstract: The promyelocytic leukemia protein (PML) is a stress-response factor that assembles into PML nuclear bodies, dynamic subnuclear compartments involved in tumor suppression and antiviral defense. The most abundant isoform, PML-1, has been linked to transcriptional regulation, genome stability, and antiviral responses, yet the molecular basis of these functions remains unclear and is generally attributed to proteins associated with PML nuclear bodies. Here, we report that PML-1 itself harbors a previously structurally uncharacterized nucleic acid-binding domain. The domain, termed PXL, is encoded by exon 9 of the PML gene and is unique to isoform 1. Its structure reveals an exonuclease III fold, but lacks the catalytic residues required for activity, defining PXL as a pseudo-exonuclease. Biochemical, structural, mutational, and cellular analyses demonstrate that PXL specifically binds G-rich oligonucleotides implicated in G-quadruplex formation and displays a strong in vitro preference for polyUG RNA. Furthermore, deletion of the PXL domain significantly decreases PML colocalization with G-quadruplexes in cells, downregulates genomic maintenance pathways, and modulates the expression of E2F target and interferon-α response genes. These findings provide a molecular basis for previous observations implicating PML in nucleic acid-associated functions and establish a mechanistic framework for future studies of PML-mediated stress responses, nuclear organization, and gene regulation.

papers.title: Genomic sequence context differentially impacts stepwise oxidation by TET enzymes to shape DNA hydroxymethylation landscapes.
papers.authors: Erlitzki N, Loo CE, Fowler JM, Zhou W, Kohli RM.
papers.abstract: Ten-eleven translocation (TET) enzymes reverse gene silencing imposed by 5-methylcytosine (5mC) in mammalian genomes by catalyzing the stepwise oxidation of 5mC to 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC), 5-formylcytosine (5fC), and 5-carboxycytosine (5caC). 5hmC both acts as an independent epigenetic mark and promotes replication-dependent DNA demethylation by antagonizing maintenance DNA methylation. Oxidation of 5hmC to 5fC/5caC instead marks the committed step in replication-independent DNA demethylation, whereby 5fC/5caC are actively excised and reverted to unmodified cytosine. Although prior work indicates that TET-mediated oxidation is influenced by bases neighboring 5mC, these studies have been unable to resolve more than two of the relevant species-5mC, 5hmC, and 5fC/5caC-at the same time. As 5hmC is the key fulcrum in DNA demethylation, we established a high-throughput enzymology approach to probe these three cytosine states at base resolution simultaneously across hundreds of sites. We reveal distinct context dependencies for 5hmC generation versus decay, with flanking bases differentially impacting 5hmC persistence. Notably, we demonstrate these predictable preferences in duplexed DNA are lost in single-stranded DNA, mechanistically linking these features to TET-mediated base-flipping. Furthermore, analysis of genomic 5hmC patterns uncovers evidence of sequence context bias in cellular 5hmC accumulation, suggesting a role for TET-intrinsic preferences in shaping cellular epigenetic landscapes.

papers.title: Double-base deletions and signatures associated with platinum adducts in metastatic cancer.
papers.authors: Smid M, van Leeuwen L, Wilting SM, Martens JWM.
papers.abstract: Platinum compounds preferably create intrastrand G-G adducts to halt replication in cancer cells. When successfully bypassed, resulting somatic variants end up in the genome. Unexpectedly, current double-base substitution signatures associated with platinum lack a GG component, and we hypothesized that deletion was missing from the possible solutions to circumvent a double-base lesion. We investigated a large pan-cancer metastatic cohort and generated platinum specific de novo double-base substitution and deletion (DBSD) signatures. One of the oxaliplatin associated DBSD signatures had GG deletion as dominant characteristic and also included new and known substitutions associated with platinum. Unforeseen among the additional results, DBSD signatures with deletion of TT as singular characteristic were strongly associated with microsatellite instability in multiple cohorts and provisionally in liquid biopsies. This study showed that DBSD signatures increase our understanding and cataloging of the effects caused by platinum and, in general, may aid in the discovery of new biological insights.

papers.title: Fast, flexible gene cluster family delineation with IGUA.
papers.authors: Larralde M, Blom J, Gourlé H, Radoykova HS, Paoli L, Zeller G, Carroll LM.
papers.abstract: Prokaryotic genomes harbor a variety of functional elements encoded as contiguous multi-gene clusters. To identify homologous gene clusters, computational tools that account for multi-gene architectures are needed to group gene clusters into Gene Cluster Families (GCFs). However, existing GCF delineation methods do not scale well to large datasets and are often limited to certain subclasses of gene clusters. Here, we present IGUA (Iterative Gene clUster Analysis; https://github.com/zellerlab/IGUA), a scalable, flexible GCF delineation method for genomic segments with multi-gene architectures. On a biosynthetic gene cluster (BGC) clustering task, IGUA is 29× and 10× faster than the state-of-the-art (BiG-SCAPE v2 and BiG-SLiCE v2, respectively; 28 CPUs), without sacrificing accuracy. To highlight its scalability, we use IGUA to cluster >2.8 million BGCs from ≈1 million prokaryotic genomes in <18 h (n = 2 829 071 BGCs to 56 960 GCFs). To showcase its utility beyond BGC clustering, we use IGUA to cluster five additional prokaryotic gene cluster types (secretion systems, prophages, genomic islands, phage-plasmids, and carbohydrate active enzyme [CAZyme] gene clusters). Overall, IGUA represents a versatile GCF delineation tool with unmatched computational efficiency and flexibility, enabling (meta)genomic mining applications at unprecedented scales.

papers.title: CRISPR-mediated gap-based replacement enables site-specific DNA lesion insertion into long DNA and nucleosomes.
papers.authors: Kim Y, An S, Choi J, Choi M, Lee G, Takata KI, Anand R, Myung K, Lee JY.
papers.abstract: Defined DNA lesions are essential substrates for dissecting DNA repair mechanisms, yet existing approaches remain limited in positional flexibility, lesion diversity, efficiency, or compatibility with long and chromatinized DNA. Here, we present CGRID (CRISPR-mediated Gap-based Replacement for Insertion of DNA damage), a programmable strategy for site-specific installation of DNA lesions into long DNA and nucleosomes. CGRID uses paired Cas9 nickases to generate two adjacent nicks, followed by gap formation and replacement with a synthetic lesion-containing oligonucleotide. This design enables easy and efficient insertion of diverse DNA lesions at user-defined positions without pre-engineered nicking sites or substrate redesign. Applied to long λ-DNA, CGRID supports efficient installation of single lesions and internal double-strand breaks at predefined positions, which are challenging to obtain using existing methods. These molecules enable high-throughput single-molecule analysis of diverse repair pathways including base excision repair (BER), nonhomologous end joining, and microhomology-mediated end joining without hydrodynamic force. CGRID further allows efficient site-specific lesion incorporation into nucleosomal DNA, enabling systematic repositioning of damage within a nucleosome. This shows that nucleosome context and lesion orientation strongly influence APE1 incision efficiency. Together, CGRID establishes a broadly applicable platform for programmable DNA damage engineering, bridging biochemical and single-molecule methodologies, and facilitates mechanistic studies of chromatin-dependent genome maintenance.

papers.title: Distinct ways by which Srs2 helicase and Rrp1 translocase shape Rad51-DNA interactions in fission yeast.
papers.authors: Misiorna D, Dziadkowiec D, Kramarz K.
papers.abstract: Precise regulation of homologous recombination is essential for genome stability. Multiple helicases and translocases prevent toxic, unscheduled association of the Rad51 recombinase with chromatin, and their levels are frequently dysregulated in cancer. It remains unclear how anti-recombinogenic enzymes act on distinct pools of Rad51. Using Schizosaccharomyces pombe, we show that the Srs2 helicase and Rrp1 translocase may target distinct Rad51 species through recombinase substrate specificity and activity control. Genetic analyses support a model in which Srs2 may preferentially regulate Rad52-dependent Rad51 nucleofilaments associated with single-stranded DNA (ssDNA), whereas Rrp1 may preferentially regulate a distinct Rad51 population associated with double-stranded DNA. Accordingly, Rrp1 can alleviate the toxicity caused by Rad51 overproduction, a function not shared by Srs2. Unexpectedly, both loss and overproduction of Srs2 promote Rad51 accumulation, suggesting that excessive helicase levels may generate ssDNA substrates that promote Rad51 nucleation. Both Srs2 and Rrp1 fail to remove strand-exchange-deficient Rad51 from DNA. Both enzymes restrict Rad51 occupancy at centromeric regions, whereas only Srs2 acts within ribosomal DNA (rDNA) repeats, revealing locus-specific regulation. Our findings support a model in which anti-recombinogenic enzymes differentially regulate Rad51 according to its DNA substrate, thereby contributing to a regulatory system that balances Rad51 functions during DNA repair across different genomic regions.

papers.title: CircACVR2A(2-4) regulates stem cell pluripotency by uncoupling CDK-activating kinase functions.
papers.authors: Webb S, Conn VM, van Battum EY, Kirk K, Geiger AB, Singh S, Gabryelska M, Roach MJ, Marri S, Lin H, Liu R, Binelli J, Toubia J, Tran J, Colella AD, Colunga T, Kulik M, Bardy C, Jolly L, Pasterkamp RJ, McKinnon RA, Dalton S, Kristensen LS, Sullivan AE, Conn SJ.
papers.abstract: Differentiation of stem cells is driven by tightly coordinated transcriptional programs, yet the contribution of circular RNAs (circRNAs) to lineage specification remains poorly defined. Here, we profiled circRNA and messenger RNA expression during differentiation of human embryonic stem cells into five germ layer-derived lineages. Targeted silencing of dynamically regulated circRNAs revealed that depletion of circACVR2A(2-4), but not its linear counterpart, induced rapid loss of pluripotency accompanied by neuroectoderm-biased differentiation, phenotypically and transcriptionally. Mechanistically, circACVR2A(2-4) interacts with cyclin H within the cyclin-dependent kinase (CDK)-activating kinase (CAK) complex to modulate RNA polymerase II (RNAPII) phosphorylation independently of CDK activation, with lineage commitment consistent with destabilization of RNAPII pausing at poised neuroectodermal loci. In vivo, circACVR2A(2-4) silencing impaired neuronal migration in the embryonic mouse brain and attenuated glioblastoma progression in mouse orthotopic xenografts. Together, these findings identify a circRNA-mediated mechanism that uncouples CAK complex activity to modulate stem cell fate.

papers.title: ZBP1 specifically binds pre-formed Z-RNA, limiting its potential pool of nucleic acid ligands compared to ADAR1.
papers.authors: Krall JB, Beck LG, Nichols PJ, Welty R, Vicens Q, Henen MA, Vögeli B.
papers.abstract: ZBP1 senses foreign nucleic acids in the unusual, left-handed Z-conformation via binding through its Zα1 and Zα2 domains and initiates cell death pathways that enable viral clearance. dsDNA and dsRNA can adopt Z-conformations; however, both typically require chemical modifications or protein binding to induce Z-form conversion and stabilization. ZBP1 has been previously shown to bind and convert B-DNA to the Z-conformation and was assumed to be able to convert A-RNA as well, despite the lack of experimental validation. Here, we use NMR and other biophysical and biochemical experiments to characterize the Z-DNA and Z-RNA binding properties of ZBP1's Zα1 and Zα2 domains. While ZBP1's Zα domains are able to convert and stabilize unmodified dsDNA in the Z-conformation, they are incapable of flipping unmodified (CpG)n repeat dsRNA. ZBP1's Zα domains require dsRNAs with Z-promoting chemical modifications to be able to bind and stabilize the Z-conformation. These results contrast with ADAR1's Zα domain, which can bind and flip both dsDNA and dsRNA into the Z-conformation, potentially indicating finely tuned competition between ADAR1 and ZBP1 for pro-survival and pro-death outcomes, respectively. This work highlights the functional variability of Zα domains and narrows down potential physiological substrates of ZBP1 in infection and disease.
