papers.title: TorchGWAS 1.0: GPU-accelerated GWAS at scale.
papers.authors: Zhao X, Xie Z, Islam SMS, Xia T, Chen C, Zhi D.
papers.abstract: Motivation Imaging, molecular and machine-learning workflows can generate thousands of quantitative phenotypes in one cohort. Repeating genome-wide scans trait by trait creates a computational and output bottleneck. Results TorchGWAS is a GPU-accelerated framework that uses batched operations for high-throughput, covariate-adjusted linear association testing across large panels of quantitative phenotypes. Across 500 036 allele-harmonized tests, its test statistics agreed with PLINK 2.0, with a Pearson correlation difference from one of 1.3 × 10 - 1 2 . On an NVIDIA H100 with 80 gigabytes of memory and a 48-core Intel Xeon Gold 6442Y host, median end-to-end runtimes for 4.57 billion associations spanning 8 931 083 variants, 512 phenotypes and 35 365 samples ranged from 28.46 to 58.95 seconds across four genotype formats. These measurements included writing 36.7 gigabytes of binary summary statistics. TorchGWAS supports efficient fixed-effect association screening at scale. Availability and implementation TorchGWAS is implemented in Python and distributed as a documented source repository at https://github.com/ZhiGroup/TorchGWAS.

papers.title: Decoding channel pore dynamics mechanism in Anopheles gambiae Orco homotetramer.
papers.authors: Chidambara Thanu V, Jabeen A, Kythreoti G, Iatrou K, Zographos SE, Taylor PW, Ranganathan S.
papers.abstract: Motivation Insect odorant receptors (iORs) essential for olfaction function as 7-transmembrane-domain (7TM) ion channels. iORs form tetrameric complexes that include a highly conserved odorant receptor co-receptor (Orco). Functional Orco homotetramers have also known to form ex vivo . Blocking Orco ex vivo and in vivo disrupts olfactory signalling, making it a promising target for functional intervention. Understanding its gating behaviour is critical for developing strategies to disrupt odour-guided behaviours in disease-vector insects. Thus, insights into the dynamic gating of the Anopheles gambiae Orco have implications on the rational design of vector-control strategies against malaria. We studied molecular dynamics (MD) simulations on homotetrameric Agam Orco models generated using template-based modelling (TBM) and AlphaFold3 (AF3), to investigate ligand-dependent pore dynamics. Agonist and antagonist bound systems were analysed to understand the ligand-dependent gating. Results Our results show that apo and antagonistic IPC-bound Agam Orco homotetramer models remain in a stable, closed, and non-conductive state across both models. TBM, but not AF3, successfully captures agonistic VUAA1-induced activation, consistent with experimental observations, exhibiting asymmetric pore widening and conformational changes. Antagonist displacement simulations confirm IPC-mediated pore closure. Overall, the TBM Agam Orco model provides a reliable framework for structure-guided discovery of novel agents for control of insect pests and vector diseases.

papers.title: dbcan-nf: a Nextflow pipeline for accurate CAZyme annotation in metagenomes.
papers.authors: Zhang X, Yi H, Zheng J, Yin Y.
papers.abstract: Motivation Carbohydrate-active enzymes (CAZymes) are crucial for carbohydrate degradation in any ecological environment. However, CAZyme annotation is not easy in whole-genome shotgun (WGS) metagenomes, due to the lack of accurate, scalable, robust, and reproducible workflows. We previously published dbCAN as a web server and associated standalone tool run_dbcan that performs CAZyme annotation with assembled genomes as the input but not with raw WGS reads. Results Here, we present dbcan-nf, an accurate and scalable Nextflow pipeline integrating run_dbcan as a component step, for automated CAZyme annotation in metagenomes. dbcan-nf supports multiple analytical routes, including individual sample assembly (IA), multisample coassembly (CA), assembly-free (AF), and subsampling (SS), and accepts both short and long reads. Using five benchmark datasets, we showed that dbcan-nf (IA and AF routes) had a much higher accuracy (recall and F1 score) and detected more CAZyme families than the competing tool Cayman. Among the different routes, dbcan-nf-IA produced the most accurate CAZyme annotation, especially when the sequencing depth is sufficient (e.g., >1.0 Gb). However, as a read assembly-based method, dbcan-nf-IA had a higher computational cost than Cayman. Finally, dbcan-nf leverages Nextflow-supported high-performance computing execution for workflow-level scalability through concurrent processing of multiple samples. Availability and implementation https://github.com/bcb-unl/dbcan-nf.

papers.title: PerSeqPIPE: Nextflow workflow for per-sequence analysis of small RNA-sequencing data.
papers.authors: Trachtová K, Al Tukmachi D, Bystrý V, Slabý O.
papers.abstract: Summary Small RNA sequencing enables high-throughput profiling of diverse small non-coding RNAs, but their complex biology creates substantial bioinformatic challenges. Conventional gene-centric pipelines often discard multi-mapping reads or impose arbitrary feature assignments, leading to biased quantification results. We present PerSeqPIPE, a modular, fully containerized Nextflow pipeline implementing a sequence-centric approach that quantifies each unique read sequence and annotates it with all compatible genomic and transcriptomic features. This preserves biologically relevant signals and enables broad small non-coding RNA profiling. PerSeqPIPE integrates harmonized reference resources for multiple small non-coding RNA classes and supports reproducible execution using Docker and Apptainer. The accompanying Streamlit-based PerSeqPIPE VIZ application enables interactive exploration, filtering, visualization, and differential expression analysis. Application to a published extracellular vesicle dataset revealed isomiR diversity and multi-mapped sncRNAs that were obscured by conventional approaches. Together, PerSeqPIPE and PerSeqPIPE VIZ provide an open, scalable, and transparent framework for small RNA-seq analysis. Availability and implementation PerSeqPIPE is freely available at https://github.com/ktrachtova/perseqpipe and PerSeqPIPE VIZ at https://github.com/ktrachtova/perseqpipe_viz. PerSeqPIPE is implemented in Nextflow, Python, Bash, and R; PerSeqPIPE VIZ is a Streamlit app. Both are compatible with macOS and Linux operating systems.

papers.title: Critical assessment in the age of AI: challenges and opportunities for computational biology.
papers.authors: Schwartz R, Zhang X, Ma J, Bromberg Y, Murphy RF, Hunter LE, Parida L, Saez-Rodriguez J, Stolovitzky G, Pop M, Ranganathan S, Slonim DK, Gaasterland T.
papers.abstract: Motivation Effective computational tool development depends on our ability to measure progress with rigorous benchmarking, allowing developers to showcase advances and users to select the best of the available options. Computational biology has developed a robust infrastructure of benchmarking standards, tools/resources, and best practices to allow for rigorous and unbiased assessment. This infrastructure, however, faces growing challenges as modern artificial intelligence (AI) methods move to the forefront of computational analysis. The field has imperfectly adapted to issues problematic for benchmarking AI methods, including data entanglement, data leakage, problem-specific performance, limited theoretical guarantees, elusive ground-truth, opaque and often closed models that make reproducibility of results difficult, and dependence on impermanent data sources. Results In this paper, we consider how the field should tackle benchmarking in the AI era. We revisit why benchmarking matters and its history in computational biology, examine emerging AI-specific challenges, and outline practical paths forward. We argue that benchmarks should be treated as long-lived community infrastructure rather than one-off artifacts bundled with individual papers. We envision a future of critical assessment i.e. dynamic and responsive to evolving use cases, sustaining progress for advancing science in the age of AI. Availability and implementation N/A.

papers.title: User-driven development and evaluation of an agentic framework for analysis of large pathway diagrams.
papers.authors: Corradi M, Djidrovski I, Ladeira L, Staumont B, Verhoeven A, Sanz Serrano J, Rougny A, Vaez A, Hemedan A, Mazein A, Niarakis A, de Carvalho E Silva A, Auffray C, Willighagen E, Kuchovska E, Schreiber F, Balaur I, Calzone L, Matthews L, Veschini L, Gillespie ME, Kutmon M, König M, van Welzen M, Hiroi N, Lopata O, Klemmer P, Overall R, Hofer T, Satagopam V, Schneider R, Teunis M, Geris L, Ostaszewski M.
papers.abstract: As biomedical knowledge keeps growing, resources storing available information multiply and grow in size and complexity. Such resources can be in the format of molecular interaction maps, which represent cellular and molecular processes under normal or pathological conditions. However, these maps can be complex and hard to navigate, especially to novice users. Large language models (LLMs), particularly in the form of agentic frameworks, have emerged as a promising technology to support this exploration. In this article, we describe a user-driven process of prototyping, development, and user testing of Llemy, an LLM-based system for exploring these molecular interaction maps. By involving domain experts from the very first prototyping in the form of a hackathon and collecting both fine-grained and general feedback on more refined versions, we were able to evaluate the perceived utility and quality of the developed system, in particular for summarizing maps and pathways, as well as prioritize the development of future features. We recommend continued user-driven development and benchmarking to keep the community engaged. This will also facilitate the transition towards open-weight LLMs to support the needs of the open research environment in an ever-changing technology landscape.

papers.title: TSLC: differential abundance analysis method for identifying biologically relevant known microbes.
papers.authors: Beblavy R, Monaco CL, Newkirk CE, Xiao J, Sohn MB.
papers.abstract: Motivation Identifying biologically relevant microbes is a crucial task in human microbiome studies. Numerous computational and statistical methods have been proposed for this task. However, most existing methods are based solely on taxonomic information, even when whole-metagenome sequencing data are available, and thus cannot account for the fact that different microbes can perform the same or similar functions (known as functional redundancy ) and for the contribution of unknown microbes to functional abundance. Hence, the identified differentially abundant microbes might not be biologically relevant to manifested phenotypes. Results To address the issues with existing methods, we propose a two-stage procedure: (i) determining differentially abundant functions between groups; and then (ii) determining microbes significantly associated with each identified differentially abundant function. This procedure involves ℓ1 -penalized log-contrast models and debiasing procedures to account for the compositional nature of microbiome data and the bias induced by the ℓ1 penalty. We performed extensive simulation studies to illustrate the consequences of ignoring functional redundancy and the contribution of unknown microbes, and to assess the performance of the proposed method. We applied the proposed method to two whole-metagenome sequencing datasets and showcased substantial differences between the typical taxonomic-based analysis and the proposed method. Availability and implementation An R package for the proposed method is available at https://github.com/rgbeblavy/TSLC.

papers.title: OOPSIE (OOPS informatics extension).
papers.authors: Telerman SB, Kalmar L, Patel SK, Willis AE, Lilley KS.
papers.abstract: Motivation The RNA-bound proteome represents a dynamic and pleiotropic network of RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) that integrate diverse cellular pathways. RNA-binding dynamics profiling using cross-linking-based enrichment strategies including Orthogonal Organic Phase Separation (OOPS), generates complex peptide-level quantitative mass spectrometry datasets, yet dedicated computational workflows for standardized normalization and differential analysis remain limited. Results OOPS relies on phase partitioning of RNA binding proteomes, upon UV cross-linking. As glycoproteins have been shown to co-partition independently of cross-linking due to their physicochemical properties, they provide a cross-link-independent reference population that can be leveraged for normalization of RNA-binding-dependent changes. We introduce OOPSIE (Orthogonal Organic Phase Separation Informatics Extension), an R-based script that provides a reproducible framework of peptide-level OOPS-derived data using protein-level normalization and differential analysis of RNA-binding capacity. We demonstrate its utility using OOPS-derived datasets generated from A549 lung adenocarcinoma cells. Availability and implementation OOPSIE is implemented in R as a standalone workflow and is freely available at https://github.com/CambridgeCentreForProteomics/oopsie, together with documentation and example datasets.

papers.title: DNA breathing and shape encode distinct mechanisms of transcription factor binding.
papers.authors: Chiu TP, Tang WY, Butt W, Lai B, Qian S, Alexandrov BS, Duan J, He X, Rohs R.
papers.abstract: Motivation Interactions between transcription factors (TFs) and DNA play a key role in regulating gene expression. While these interactions are often viewed primarily as recognition of DNA sequence motifs, several studies have shown the limitation of this approach and highlighted the impact of physical properties of DNA. Prior studies have supported the importance of DNA shape features as determinant of TF-DNA recognition. Another physical property is DNA breathing, the spontaneous and transient opening of double-stranded DNA through thermal motions, which has not been systematically examined. Results We analyzed in vitro TF-DNA binding data and found that DNA breathing features in motif regions are correlated with binding affinity, highlighting a role of locally and temporally melted DNA. Here, we compared contributions of DNA breathing and shape to TF binding. These analyses suggest that DNA breathing provides sequence-dependent information related to DNA structure not fully captured by DNA shape. Extending the analysis to ChIP-seq data, we found that breathing features are associated with TF binding in vivo , although the direction and magnitude of these associations vary across TFs. Our results support DNA breathing as an additional physical feature contributing to TF-DNA interactions alongside DNA sequence motifs and DNA shape. Availability and implementation Data and analysis code are available at https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/UAHBJ and https://github.com/TsuPeiChiu/DNAbreathing.

papers.title: Advancements in forecasting liver cytosol metabolic stability: a comprehensive update on machine learning predictive models.
papers.authors: Lim G, Jain S, Xu X, Shah P.

papers.title: BandQuant: a web application for western blot quantification.
papers.authors: He M, Jin S, Wan H, Zhang C.
papers.abstract: Motivation Western blot quantification typically requires multiple tools and manual data handling, which is time-consuming and difficult to audit. Existing software is either tied to proprietary hardware or requires local installation, and none provides an integrated path from raw image to fold-change. Results We present BandQuant, a free, browser-based web application that integrates the entire western blot quantification workflow into a single session. It combines automated band detection, rolling-ball background subtraction, housekeeping normalization, fold-change computation, and interactive bar-chart visualization in a single interface. A relational database binds experimental metadata to the image at upload, enabling automated normalization and cross-experiment queries without manual relabeling. BandQuant measurements showed high agreement with Fiji (Pearson r = 0.994), and analysis time was reduced by 65%. Availability and implementation BandQuant is freely available at https://www.tiaodaibao.com/? locale=en-US. Source code: https://github.com/wanhj-git/BandQuant. Archived release: https://zenodo.org/records/19453998.

papers.title: BLITSFR: scalable comparative genomics with self-contained interactive single file report.
papers.authors: Permana B, Cuddihy T, Forde BM.
papers.abstract: Motivation Comparative genomics routinely requires the alignment of query genomes against a reference to delineate conserved and variable regions, yet existing tools often produce static visualisations or necessitate centralised web services and data uploads. Results To address this, we present BLITSFR (BLAST Interactive Tracks in Single-File Report), a command-line tool that compares query genomes against a reference and returns a single interactive HTML file. The report opens in any modern browser, requiring no server or data upload, and lets users explore conserved and variable regions across the genomes. BLITSFR handles both assembled genomes and raw reads, and processes hundreds of genomes in minutes on a standard laptop with genome tracks sorting, filtering, and colouring by metadata are performed within the report, without requirement for re-running the analysis. We demonstrate its utility by analysing vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium ST78 genomes to confirm the conservation of Tn1549-like transposons and a case of β-lactam-resistant Corynebacterium diphtheriae , where coverage depth resolved resistance transposon copy number. Availability and implementation BLITSFR and SCIFR are freely available at the provided GitHub repositories (https://github.com/nalarbp/blitsfr, https://github.com/nalarbp/scifr).

papers.title: FerroEnrich: an interactive web platform for liver-focused ferroptosis index scoring, enrichment, and ferroptosis-senescence cross-talk analysis.
papers.authors: Tirumalasetty MB, Choubey M, Mohiuddin MS, Barua R, Md W, Miao QR.
papers.abstract: Motivation Ferroptosis is an iron-dependent regulated cell death process involving lipid peroxidation, redox imbalance, and impaired antioxidant defense. It is increasingly relevant to metabolic liver disease and non-alcoholic steatohepatitis. Existing ferroptosis resources mainly provide gene annotations and disease associations, but they do not offer an integrated workflow for user-uploaded transcriptome data, liver-focused enrichment, dataset-level scoring, and ferroptosis-senescence cross-talk analysis. Results We developed FerroEnrich, an open-source web platform for analyzing ferroptosis and senescence programs in human and mouse liver transcriptome datasets. FerroEnrich supports count matrix upload, metadata-guided differential expression analysis, identification of ferroptosis-prone and ferroptosis-resistant genes, dataset-level ferroptosis index scoring, sample-level susceptibility estimation, curated liver module enrichment, interaction network visualization, and ferroptosis-senescence cross-talk analysis. Application to human advanced non-alcoholic steatohepatitis and mouse diet-induced liver disease datasets demonstrated cross-species utility and identified conserved remodeling, including reduced ferroptosis-protective signatures and increased senescence- and fibrosis-associated modules. Availability and implementation FerroEnrich is freely available at https://ferroenrich.shinyapps.io/ferroenrich/. Source code, documentation, and demo datasets are available at the FerroEnrich GitHub repository.

papers.title: Employing AlphaFold and TED to explore the structural impacts of stress-associated mutations in rice.
papers.authors: Shahid F, Sen N, Orengo C, Lam SD.
papers.abstract: Motivation Plants have evolved adaptive mechanisms to handle environmental stress. However, genome-wide association studies (GWASs) have identified genetic variations associated with stress resistance, yet their structural and functional impacts remain poorly understood. This limits our ability to develop more resilient crops. Results Using predicted three-dimensional protein structures from the AlphaFold Database, chopped into domains by The Encyclopedia of Domains, we analysed how mutations identified in rice GWASs affect protein structure and function. The analysis revealed 102 mutations in 76 high-quality protein domains likely to impact structure and function. Thirty-nine mutations were positioned within 5 Å of predicted functional sites, including those near post-translational modification sites (3), allosteric sites (5), protein-protein interaction sites (25), ligand-binding sites (15), and conserved regions (9). We identified potential interaction partners for 18 proteins with mutations at predicted interfaces and modelled their complex structures. Six mutations were predicted to enhance binding affinity with their protein partners. Availability and implementation This study utilized only open-access tools and and provides a framework that could strengthen plant defence mechanisms. However, experimental validation is essential to confirm the applicability of these findings for plant breeding programs.

papers.title: RCSB PDB AI Help Desk: retrieval-augmented generation for protein structure deposition support.
papers.authors: Chithari VR, Young JY, Persikova I, Liang Y, Crichlow GV, Flatt JW, Ghosh S, Hudson BP, Peisach E, Sekharan M, Shao C, Burley SK.
papers.abstract: Motivation Structural biologists have contributed more than 260 000 experimentally determined three-dimensional structures of biological macromolecules to the Protein Data Bank. Incoming depositions are validated and biocurated by approximately 20 expert biocurators at the collaborating data centers worldwide. Biocurators at the Research Collaboratory for Structural Bioinformatics Protein Data Bank, who process more than 40% of global depositions, face growing difficulty sustaining efficient Help Desk operations, having received roughly 19 000 depositor messages across some 8000 entries in 2025. Results We developed an artificial intelligence Help Desk assistant built on retrieval-augmented generation. Source documents are converted to Markdown with layout preserved, divided by a two-stage chunking procedure, embedded, and stored in a relational vector database. At query time, maximal marginal relevance retrieval selects diverse supporting passages, a topical guardrail filters out-of-scope questions, and a purpose-built system prompt prevents disclosure of internal curation terminology. Separate language model configurations handle question condensing and answer generation. The service runs in production on a container orchestration platform, providing around-the-clock depositor assistance with streaming, citation-backed responses. Availability and implementation Freely available at https://rcsb-deposit-help.rcsb.org. Source code: https://github.com/rcsb/rcsb-pdb-helpdesk (archived at Zenodo: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19560785).

papers.title: Transcriptomic buffering detection: a computational approach to identifying essential gene dependencies in pancreatic cancer.
papers.authors: Boman M, Afentaki E, Greely JM, Ezaz-Nikpay N, Zain R, Smith CIE.

papers.title: pycmplot: fast, low-memory multi-track circular and linear Manhattan plotting in Python.
papers.authors: Esoh K, Osman F, Fortes-Lima C, Awandare GA, Wonkam A.
papers.abstract: Motivation Manhattan plots remain the standard visual summary for genome-wide association studies and other per-variant scans (iHS, FST, XP-EHH). Existing Manhattan visualization tools either lack multi-track support (gwaslab, qmplot, and qqman) or do not provide a Circos-style multi-track circular Manhattan view. CMplot (R) does, but its memory and runtime costs on multi-million-variant inputs are substantial. Results We present pycmplot, a Python package for generating multi-track linear and Circos-style circular Manhattan plots from one or more GWAS summary statistics. On a 10-million-variant scan, pycmplot is 5.5× faster and uses ∼5× less memory than CMplot for linear Manhattan plotting, 1.6× faster (and 3× faster with optional pre-filtering) for circular Manhattan, and 7.7× faster for qq rendering. Multi-track comparisons of two summary statistics are 4.5× faster (linear) and 3.5× faster (circular) than CMplot's equivalent mode. Transparent hg18/hg19 → hg38 liftover lets users mix coordinate systems within a single plot, and a lightweight bundle of Ensembl GFF3 gene information files (hg19 and hg38) enables nearest gene annotation. Availability and implementation pycmplot is freely available under the MIT license at https://github.com/esohkevin/pycmplot; and from PyPI (pip install pycmplot). Documentation is at https://pycmplot.readthedocs.io.

papers.title: NeighborFinder: an R package inferring local microbial network around a species of interest.
papers.authors: Sola M, Paravel A, Auger S, Chatel JM, Plaza Oñate F, Le Chatelier E, Leclerc M, Veiga P, Frioux C, Mariadassou M, Berland M.
papers.abstract: Motivation Understanding interactions from microbiome data is a central aspect in microbial ecology, as it provides insights into ecosystem stability, disease mechanisms, and can be used to design synthetic communities. Current network inference tools reconstruct global networks from co-abundance data, which means they capture the overall correlation structure for the entire set of taxa considered. These approaches are computationally intensive and suboptimal when the focus is on the local neighborhood of one or a few taxa of interest. Results We introduce NeighborFinder, a local network inference method that enables the targeted discovery of direct neighbors around a species of interest. Using cross-validated multiple linear regression with ℓ1 penalty and microbiome-specific filters, our approach infers interpretable species-centered interactions, with F1 score ≥ 0.95 on simulated cohorts ranging from 250 to 1000 samples. This method is well-suited for large metagenomic datasets and is particularly valuable for exploratory studies where the targeted hypotheses outweigh the need for global community structure. The approach complements existing methods by being biologically intuitive and computationally efficient. Availability and implementation The R package is available on CRAN https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=NeighborFinder. The data and source code used to calculate performances and produce the use case example can be found respectively at: https://doi.org/10.57745/UPITJ0 and https://doi.org/10.57745/HJLWW4. Supplementary information Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics Advances online.

papers.title: Correction: Bioinformatics in Español: expanding open, diverse, and collaborative science through SEH2Bioinfo.
papers.abstract: [This corrects the article DOI: 10.1093/bioadv/vbag182.].
